The Germans he dislikes as unchivalrous;\rbut though his life lay inthe period of the Hundred Years\' War\rbetween England andFrance, and though he describes many of the events\rof that war, he is asfriendly to England as to France.\r \rBy birth Froissartbelonged to the bourgeoisie, but his tastes and\rassociations made him an aristocrat.Glimpses of the sufferings which\rthe lower classesunderwent in the wars of his time appear in his\rpages, but they are givenincidentally and without sympathy. His\rinterests are all in thesomewhat degenerate chivalry of his age, in\rthe splendor of courts,the pomp and circumstance of war, in tourneys,\rand in pageantry. Full ofthe love of adventure, he would travel\racross half of Europe tosee a gallant feat of arms, a coronation, a\rroyal marriage. Whenthe soldiers within saw that, they went into\rthe castle: the Englishmenwent into the town, and two days together\rthey made sore assaults,so that when they within saw no succour, they\ryielded up, their livesand goods saved, and so departed. The\rEnglishmen had theirpleasure of that good town and castle, and when\rthey saw they might notmaintain to keep it, they set fire therein and\rbrent it, and made theburgesses of the town to enter into their\rships, as they had donewith them of Barfleur, Cherbourg and\rMontebourg, and of othertowns that they had won on the sea-side. All\rthis was done by thebattle that went by the sea-side, and by them on\rthe sea together.[1]\r \r      [1] Froissart is mistaken in supposingthat a division of the\r      land army went to these towns. Edward arrived atPoissy on 12th August.\r      Philip of Valois left Paris on the 14th,the English crossed the\r      Seine at Poissy on the 16th, and theSomme at Blanche-taque on\r      the 24th.\r \r      [2] \'Set themselves for safety in a gateat the entry of the\r      bridge.\'\r \rThen the constable and theearl of Tancarville, being in the little\rtower at the bridge foot,looked along the street and saw their men\rslain without mercy: theydoubted to fall in their hands. There were someof the Frenchmen of Artois and Picardy that\rwere as glad to joust inthe water as on the dry land.\r \rThe Frenchmen defended sowell the passage at the issuing out of the\rwater, that they had muchto do. The Genoways did them great trouble\rwith their cross-bows: onthe other side the archers of England shot\rso wholly together, thatthe Frenchmen were fain to give place to the\rEnglishmen. There was asore battle, and many a noble feat of arms\rdone on both sides.Finally the Englishmen passed over and assembled\rtogether in the field. Theking and the prince passed, and all the\rlords; then the Frenchmenkept none array, but departed, he that might\rbest. When sir Godemar sawthat discomfiture, he fled and saved\rhimself: some fled toAbbeville and some to Saint-Riquiers. They that\rwere there afoot could notflee, so that there were slain a great\rnumber of them ofAbbeville, Montreuil, Rue and of Saint-Riquiers: the\rchase endured more than agreat league. And as yet all the Englishmen\rwere not passed the river,and certain currours of the king of Bohemia\rand of sir John ofHainault came on them that were behind and took\rcertain horses andcarriages and slew divers, or they could take the\rpassage.\r \rThe French king the samemorning was departed from Airaines, trusting\rto have found theEnglishmen between him and the river of Somme: but\rwhen he heard how that sirGodemar du Fay and his company were\rdiscomfited, he tarried inthe field and demanded of his marshals what\rwas best to do. They said,\'Sir, ye cannot pass the river but at the\rbridge of Abbeville, forthe flood is come in at Blanche-taque\': then\rhe returned and lodged atAbbeville.\r \rThe king of England whenhe was past the river, he thanked God and so\rrode forth in like manneras he did before. Then he called Gobin Agace\rand did quit him hisransom and all his company, and gave him a\rhundred nobles and a goodhorse. And so the king rode forth fair and\reasily, and thought tohave lodged in a great town called Noyelles;\rbut when he knew that thetown pertained to the countess d\'Aumale,\rsister to the lord Robertof Artois,[1] the king assured the town and\rcountry as much aspertained to her, and so went forth; and his\rmarshals rode to Crotoy onthe sea-side and brent the town, and found\rin the haven many shipsand barks charged with wines of Poitou,\rpertaining to themerchants of Saintonge and of Rochelle: they brought\rthe best thereof to theking\'s host. Then one of the marshals rode to\rthe gates of Abbeville andfrom thence to Saint-Riquiers, and after to\rthe town ofRue-Saint-Esprit. This was on a Friday, and both battles\rof the marshals returnedto the king\'s host about noon and so lodged\rall together near toCressy in Ponthieu.\r \r      [1] She was in fact his daughter.\r \rThe king of England waswell informed how the French king followed\rafter him to fight. Thenhe said to his company: \'Let us take here\rsome plot of ground, forwe will go no farther till we have seen our\renemies. I have good causehere to abide them, for I am on the right\rheritage of the queen mymother, the which land was given at her\rmarriage: I will challengeit of mine adversary Philip of Valois.\' And\rbecause that he had notthe eighth part in number of men as the French\rking had, therefore hecommanded his marshals to chose a plot of\rground somewhat for hisadvantage: and so they did, and thither the\rking and his host went.Then he sent his currours to Abbeville, to see\rif the French king drewthat day into the field or not. They went\rforth and returned again,and said how they could see none appearance\rof his coming: then everyman took their lodging for that day, and to\rbe ready in the morning atthe sound of the trumpet in the same place.\rThis Friday the Frenchking tarried still in Abbeville abiding for his\rcompany, and sent his twomarshals to ride out to see the dealing of\rthe Englishmen, and atnight they returned, and said how the\rEnglishmen were lodged inthe fields. That night the French king made\ra supper to all the chieflords that were there with him, and after\rsupper the king desiredthem to be friends each to other. The king\rlooked for the earl ofSavoy, who should come to him with a thousand\rspears, for he hadreceived wages for a three months of them at Troyes\rin Champagne.\r \r \r \r \rOF THE ORDER OF THEENGLISHMEN AT CRESSY, HOW THEY MADE THREE BATTLES\rAFOOT\r \r \rOn the Friday, as I saidbefore, the king of England lay in the\rfields, for the countrywas plentiful of wines and other victual, and\rif need had been, they hadprovision following in carts and other\rcarriages. That night theking made a supper to all his chief lords of\rhis host and made themgood cheer; and when they were all departed to\rtake their rest, then theking entered into his oratory and kneeled\rdown before the altar,praying God devoutly, that if he fought the\rnext day, that he mightachieve the journey to his honour: then about\rmidnight he laid him downto rest, and in the morning he rose betimes\rand heard mass, and theprince his son with him, and the most part of\rhis company were confessedand houselled; and after the mass said, he\rcommanded every man to bearmed and to draw to the field to the same\rplace before appointed.Then the king caused a park to be made by the\rwood side behind his host,and there was set all carts and carriages,\rand within the park wereall their horses, for every man was afoot;\rand into this park therewas but one entry. Then he ordained three\rbattles: in the first wasthe young prince of Wales, with him the earl\rof Warwick and Oxford, thelord Godfrey of Harcourt, sir Raynold\rCobham, sir ThomasHolland, the lord Stafford, the lord of Mohun, the\rlord Delaware, sir JohnChandos, sir Bartholomew de Burghersh, sir\rRobert Nevill, the lordThomas Clifford, the lord Bourchier, the lord\rde Latimer, and diversother knights and squires that I cannot name:\rthey were an eight hundredmen of arms and two thousand archers, and a\rthousand of other with theWelshmen: every lord drew to the field\rappointed under his ownbanner and pennon. In the second battle was\rthe earl of Northampton,the earl of Arundel, the lord Ros, the lord\rLucy, the lord Willoughby,the lord Basset, the lord of Saint-Aubin,\rsir Louis Tufton, the lordof Multon, the lord Lascelles and divers\rother, about an eighthundred men of arms and twelve hundred archers.\rThe third battle had theking: he had seven hundred men of arms and\rtwo thousand archers. Thenthe king leapt on a hobby,[1] with a white\rrod in his hand, one ofhis marshals on the one hand and the other on\rthe other hand: he rodefrom rank to rank desiring every man to take\rheed that day to his rightand honour. He spake it so sweetly and with\rso good countenance andmerry cheer, that all such as were discomfited\rtook courage in the seeingand hearing of him. And when he had thus\rvisited all his battles,it was then nine of the day: then he caused\revery man to eat and drinka little, and so they did at their leisure.\rAnd afterward they orderedagain their battles: then every man lay\rdown on the earth and byhim his salet and bow, to be the more fresher\rwhen their enemies shouldcome.\r \r      [1] \'Un petit palefroi.\'\r \r \r \r \rTHE ORDER OF THE FRENCHMENAT CRESSY, AND HOW THEY BEHELD THE\rDEMEANOUR OF THEENGLISHMEN\r \r \rThis Saturday the Frenchking rose betimes and heard mass in Abbeville\rin his lodging in theabbey of Saint Peter, and he departed after the\rsun-rising. When he wasout of the town two leagues, approaching\rtoward his enemies, someof his lords said to him: \'Sir, it were good\rthat ye ordered yourbattles, and let all your footmen pass somewhat\ron before, that they benot troubled with the horsemen.\' Then the king\rsent four knights, theMoine (of) Bazeilles, the lord of Noyers, the\rlord of Beaujeu and thelord d\'Aubigny to ride to aview the English\rhost; and so they rode sonear that they might well see part of their\rdealing. The Englishmensaw them well and knew well how they were come\rthither to aview them:they let them alone and made no countenance\rtoward them, and let themreturn as they came. And when the French\rking saw these fourknights return again, he tarried till they came to\rhim and said: \'Sirs, whattidings?\' These four knights each of them\rlooked on other, for therewas none would speak before his companion;\rfinally the king said to(the) Moine, who pertained to the king of\rBohemia and had done inhis days so much, that he was reputed for one\rof the valiantest knightsof the world: \'Sir, speak you,\' Then he\rsaid: \'Sir, I shall speak,sith it pleaseth you, under the correction\rof my fellows. Sir, wehave ridden and seen the behaving of your\renemies: know ye for truththey are rested in three battles abiding\rfor you. Sir, I willcounsel you as for my part, saving your\rdispleasure, that you andall your company rest here and lodge for\rthis night: for or theythat be behind of your company be come hither,\rand or your battles be setin good order, it will be very late, and\ryour people be weary andout of array, and ye shall find your enemies\rfresh and ready to receiveyou. Early in the morning ye may order your\rbattles at more leisureand advise your enemies at more deliberation,\rand to regard well whatway ye will assail them; for, sir, surely they\rwill abide you.\'\r \rThen the king commandedthat it should be so done. Then his two\rmarshals one rode before,another behind, saying to every banner:\r\'Tarry and abide here inthe name of God and Saint Denis.\' They that\rwere foremost tarried, butthey that were behind would not tarry, but\rrode forth, and said howthey would in no wise abide till they were as\rfar forward as theforemost: and when they before saw them come on\rbehind, then they rodeforward again, so that the king nor his\rmarshals could not rulethem. So they rode without order or good\rarray, till they came insight of their enemies: and as soon as the\rforemost saw them, theyreculed then aback without good array, whereof\rthey behind had marvel andwere abashed, and thought that the foremost\rcompany had been fighting.Then they might have had leisure and room\rto have gone forward, ifthey had list: some went forth and some abode\rstill. The commons, ofwhom all the ways between Abbeville and Cressy\rwere full, when they sawthat they were near to their enemies, they\rtook their swords andcried: \'Down with them! let us slay them all.\'\rThere is no man, though hewere present at the journey, that could\rimagine or shew the truthof the evil order that was among the French\rparty, and yet they were amarvellous great number. That I write in\rthis book I learned itspecially of the Englishmen, who well beheld\rtheir dealing; and also certainknights of sir John of Hainault\'s, who\rwas always about kingPhilip, shewed me as they knew.\r \r \r \r \rOF THE BATTLE OF CRESSYBETWEEN THE KING OF ENGLAND AND THE FRENCH\rKING\r \r \rThe Englishmen, who werein three battles lying on the ground to rest\rthem, as soon as they sawthe Frenchmen approach, they rose upon their\rfeet fair and easilywithout any haste and arranged their battles. The\rfirst, which was theprince\'s battle, the archers there stood in\rmanner of a herse and themen of arms in the bottom of the battle. The\rearl of Northampton andthe earl of Arundel with the second battle\rwere on a wing in goodorder, ready to comfort the prince\'s battle, if\rneed were.\r \rThe lords and knights ofFrance came not to the assembly together in\rgood order, for some camebefore and some came after in such haste and\revil order, that one ofthem did trouble another. When the French king\rsaw the Englishmen, hisblood changed, and said to his marshals: \'Make\rthe Genoways go on beforeand begin the battle in the name of God and\rSaint Denis.\' There wereof the Genoways cross-bows about a fifteen\rthousand,[1] but they wereso weary of going afoot that day a six\rleagues armed with theircross-bows, that they said to their\rconstables: \'We be notwell ordered to fight this day, for we be not\rin the case to do anygreat deed of arms: we have more need of rest.\'\rThese words came to theearl of Alengon, who said: \'A man is well at\rease to be charged withsuch a sort of rascals, to be faint and fail\rnow at most need.\' Alsothe same season there fell a great rain and a\rclipse[2] with a terriblethunder, and before the rain there came\rflying over both battles agreat number of crows for fear of the\rtempest coming. Then anonthe air began to wax clear, and the sun to\rshine fair and bright, thewhich was right in the Frenchmen\'s eyen and\ron the Englishmen\'s backs.When the Genoways were assembled together\rand began to approach,they made a great leap[3] and cry to abash the\rEnglishmen, but they stoodstill and stirred not for all that: then\rthe Genoways again thesecond time made another leap and a fell cry,\rand stept forward alittle, and the Englishmen removed not one foot:\rthirdly, again they leaptand cried, and went forth till they came\rwithin shot; then theyshot fiercely with their cross-bows. Then the\rEnglish archers steptforth one pace and let fly their arrows so\rwholly (together) and sothick, that it seemed snow. When the Genoways\rfelt the arrows piercingthrough heads, arms and breasts, many of them\rcast down their cross-bowsand did cut their strings and returned\rdiscomfited. When theFrench king saw them fly away, he said: \'Slay\rthese rascals, for theyshall let and trouble us without reason.\' Then\rye should have seen themen of arms dash in among them and killed a\rgreat number of them: andever still the Englishmen shot whereas they\rsaw thickest press; thesharp arrows ran into the men of arms and into\rtheir horses, and manyfell, horse and men, among the Genoways, and\rwhen they were down, theycould not relieve[4] again, the press was so\rthick that one overthrewanother. And also among the Englishmen there\rwere certain rascals thatwent afoot with great knives, and they went\rin among the men of arms,and slew and murdered many as they lay on\rthe ground, both earls,barons, knights and squires, whereof the king\rof England was afterdispleased, for he had rather they had been taken\rprisoners.\r \r      [1] Villani, a very good authority on thesubject, says 6000,\r      brought from the ships at Harfleur.\r \r      [2] A mistranslation of \'une esclistre,\'\'a flash of lightning.\'\r \r      [3] These \'leaps\' of the Genoese areinvented by the translator,\r      and have passed from him into severalrespectable English\r      text-books, sometimes in company with theeclipse above\r      mentioned. Froissart says \'Ilcommencièrent à juper moult\r      epouvantablement\'; that is, \'to uttercries.\' Another text makes\r      mention of the English cannons at thispoint: \'The English\r      remained still and let off some cannonsthat they had, to\r      frighten the Genoese.\'\r \r      [4] The translator\'s word \'relieve\'(relyuue) represents\r      \'relever,\' for \'se relever.\'\r \rThe valiant king ofBohemia called Charles of Luxembourg, son to the\rnoble emperor Henry ofLuxembourg, for all that he was nigh blind,\rwhen he understood theorder of the battle, he said to them about him:\r\'Where is the lord Charlesmy son?\' His men said: \'Sir, we cannot\rtell; we think he befighting.\' Then he said: \'Sirs, ye are my men, my\rcompanions and friends inthis journey: I require you bring me so far\rforward, that I may strikeone stroke with my sword.\' They said they\rwould do his commandment,and to the intent that they should not lose\rhim in the press, theytied all their reins of their bridles each to\rother and set the kingbefore to accomplish his desire, and so they\rwent on their enemies. Thelord Charles of Bohemia his son, who wrote\rhimself king of Almaineand bare the arms, he came in good order to\rthe battle; but when hesaw that the matter went awry on their party,\rhe departed, I cannot tellyou which way. The king his father was so\rfar forward that he strakea stroke with his sword, yea and more than\rfour, and fought valiantlyand so did his company; and they adventured\rthemselves so forward,that they were there all slain, and the next\rday they were found in theplace about the king, and all their horses\rtied each to other.\r \rThe earl of Alençon cameto the battle right ordinately and fought\rwith the Englishmen, andthe earl of Flanders also on his part. These\rtwo lords with theircompanies coasted the English archers and came to\rthe prince\'s battle, andthere fought valiantly long. The French king\rwould fain have comethither, when he saw their banners, but there was\ra great hedge of archersbefore him. The same day the French king had\rgiven a great blackcourser to sir John of Hainault, and he made the\rlord Tierry of Senzeilleto ride on him and to bear his banner. The\rsame horse took the bridlein the teeth and brought him through all\rthe currours of theEnglishmen, and as he would have returned again,\rhe fell in a great dikeand was sore hurt, and had been there dead, an\rhis page had not been, whofollowed him through all the battles and\rsaw where his master layin the dike, and had none other let but for\rhis horse, for theEnglishmen would not issue out of their battle for\rtaking of any prisoner.Then the page alighted and relieved his\rmaster: then he went notback again the same way that they came, there\rwas too many in his way.\r \rThis battle between Broyeand Cressy this Saturday was right cruel and\rfell, and many a feat ofarms done that came not to my knowledge. In\rthe night[5] diversknights and squires lost their masters, and\rsometime came on theEnglishmen, who received them in such wise that\rthey were ever nigh slain;for there was none taken to mercy nor to\rransom, for so theEnglishmen were determined.\r \r      [5] \'Sus le nuit,\' \'towards nightfall.\'\r \rIn the morning[6] the dayof the battle certain Frenchmen and Almains\rperforce opened the archersof the prince\'s battle and came and fought\rwith the men of arms handto hand. Then the second battle of the\rEnglishmen came to succourthe prince\'s battle, the which was time,\rfor they had as then muchado; and they with the prince sent a\rmessenger to the king, whowas on a little windmill hill. Then the\rknight said to the king:\'Sir, the earl of Warwick and the earl of\rOxford, sir Raynold Cobhamand other, such as be about the prince your\rson, are fiercely foughtwithal and are sore handled; wherefore they\rdesire you that you andyour battle will come and aid them; for if the\rFrenchmen increase, asthey doubt they will, your son and they shall\rhave much ado.\' Then theking said: \'Is my son dead or hurt or on the\rearth felled?\' \'No, sir,\'quoth the knight, \'but he is hardly matched;\rwherefore he hath need ofyour aid.\' \'Well,\' said the king, \'return to\rhim and to them that sentyou hither, and say to them that they send\rno more to me for anyadventure that falleth, as long as my son is\ralive: and also say tothem that they suffer him this day to win his\rspurs;[7] for if God bepleased, I will this journey be his and the\rhonour thereof, and tothem that be about him.\' Then the knight\rreturned again to them andshewed the king\'s words, the which greatly\rencouraged them, andrepoined[8] in that they had sent to the king as\rthey did.\r \r      [6] The text has suffered by omissions.What Froissart says is\r      that if the battle had begun in themorning, it might have gone\r      better for the French, and then heinstances the exploits of\r      those who broke through the archers. Thebattle did not begin\r      till four o\'clock in the afternoon.\r \r      [7] \'Que il laissent à l\'enfant gaegnierses esperons.\'\r \r      [8] i.e. \'they repoined\': Fr. \'sereprisent.\'\r \rSir Godfrey of Harcourtwould gladly that the earl of Harcourt his\rbrother might have beensaved; for he heard say by them that saw his\rbanner how that he wasthere in the field on the French party: but sir\rGodfrey could not come tohim betimes, for he was slain or he could\rcome at him, and so wasalso the earl of Aumale his nephew. In another\rplace the earl of Alençonand the earl of Flanders fought valiantly,\revery lord under his ownbanner; but finally they could not resist\ragainst the puissance ofthe Englishmen, and so there they were also\rslain, and divers otherknights and squires. Also the earl Louis of\rBlois, nephew to theFrench king, and the duke of Lorraine fought\runder their banners, butat last they were closed in among a company\rof Englishmen andWelshmen, and there were slain for all their\rprowess. Also there wasslain the earl of Auxerre, the earl of\rSaint-Pol and many other.\r \rIn the evening the Frenchking, who had left about him no more than a\rthree-score persons, oneand other, whereof sir John of Hainault was\rone, who had remountedonce the king, for his horse was slain with an\rarrow, then he said to theking: \'Sir, depart hence, for it is time;\rlose not yourselfwilfully: if ye have loss at this time, ye shall\rrecover it again anotherseason.\' And so he took the king\'s horse by\rthe bridle and led himaway in a manner perforce. Then the king rode\rtill he came to the castleof Broye. The gate was closed, because it\rwas by that time dark:then the king called the captain, who came to\rthe walls and said: \'Whois that calleth there this time of night?\'\rThen the king said: \'Openyour gate quickly, for this is the fortune\rof France.\'[9] The captainknew then it was the king, and opened the\rgate and let down thebridge. Then the king entered, and he had with\rhim but five barons, sirJohn of Hainault, sir Charles of Montmorency,\rthe lord of Beaujeu, thelord d\'Aubigny and the lord of Montsault. The\rking would not tarrythere, but drank and departed thence about\rmidnight, and so rode bysuch guides as knew the country till he came\rin the morning to Amiens,and there he rested.\r \r      [9] \'C\'est la fortune de France\': but thebetter MSS. have\r      \'c\'est li infortunés rois de France.\'\r \rThis Saturday theEnglishmen never departed from their battles for\rchasing of any man, butkept still their field, and ever defended\rthemselves against allsuch as came to assail them. This battle ended\rabout evensong time.\r \r \r \r \rHOW THE NEXT DAY AFTER THEBATTLE THE ENGLISHMEN DISCOMFITED DIVERS\rFRENCHMEN\r \r \rOn this Saturday, when thenight was come and that the Englishmen\rheard no more noise of theFrenchmen, then they reputed themselves to\rhave the victory, and theFrenchmen to be discomfited, slain and fled\raway. Then they made greatfires and lighted up torches and candles,\rbecause it was very dark.Then the king avaled down from the little\rhill whereas he stood; andof all that day till then his helm came\rnever on his head. Then hewent with all his battle to his son the\rprince and embraced him inhis arms and kissed him, and said: \'Fair\rson, God give you goodperseverance; ye are my good son, thus ye have\racquitted you nobly: yeare worthy to keep a realm.\' The prince\rinclined himself to theearth, honouring the king his father.\r \rThis night they thankedGod for their good adventure and made no boast\rthereof, for the kingwould that no man should be proud or make boast,\rbut every man humbly tothank God. On the Sunday in the morning there\rwas such a mist, that aman might not see the breadth of an acre of\rland from him. Then theredeparted from the host by the commandment of\rthe king and marshals fivehundred spears and two thousand archers, to\rsee if they might see anyFrenchmen gathered again together in any\rplace. The same morningout of Abbeville and Saint-Riquiers in\rPonthieu the commons ofRouen and of Beauvais issued out of their\rtowns, not knowing of thediscomfiture of the day before. They met\rwith the Englishmenweening they had been Frenchmen, and when the\rEnglishmen saw them, theyset on them freshly, and there was a sore\rbattle; but at last theFrenchmen fled and kept none array. There were\rslain in the ways and inhedges and bushes more than seven thousand,\rand if the day had beenclear there had never a one escaped. Anon\rafter, another company ofFrenchmen were met by the Englishmen, the\rarchbishop of Rouen andthe great prior of France, who also knew\rnothing of thediscomfiture the day before, for they heard that the\rFrench king should havefought the same Sunday, and they were going\rthitherward. When they metwith the Englishmen, there was a great\rbattle, for they were agreat number, but they could not endure\ragainst the Englishmen;for they were nigh all slain, few escaped; the\rtwo lords were slain. Thismorning the Englishmen met with divers\rFrenchmen that had losttheir way on the Saturday and had lain all\rnight in the fields, andwist not where the king was nor the captains.\rThey were all slain, asmany as were met with; and it was shewed me\rthat of the commons andmen afoot of the cities and good towns of\rFrance there was slainfour times as many as were slain the Saturday\rin the great battle.\r \r \r \r \rHOW THE NEXT DAY AFTER THEBATTLE OF CRESSY THEY THAT WERE DEAD WERE\rNUMBERED BY THE ENGLISHMEN\r \r \rThe same Sunday, as theking of England came from mass, such as had\rbeen sent forth returnedand shewed the king what they had seen and\rdone, and said: \'Sir, wethink surely there is now no more appearance\rof any of our enemies.\'Then the king sent to search how many were\rslain and what they were.Sir Raynold Cobham and Sir Richard Stafford\rwith three heralds went tosearch the field and country: they visited\rall them that were slainand rode all day in the fields, and returned\ragain to the host as theking was going to supper. They made just\rreport of that they hadseen, and said how there were eleven great\rprinces dead, fourscorebanners, twelve hundred knights, and more than\rthirty thousand other.[1]The Englishmen kept still their field all\rthat night: on the Mondayin the morning the king prepared to depart:\rthe king caused the deadbodies of the great lords to be taken up and\rconveyed to Montreuil, andthere buried in holy ground, and made a cry\rin the country to granttruce for three days, to the intent that they\rof the country mightsearch the field of Cressy to bury the dead\rbodies.\r \r      [1] Another text makes the loss ofpersons below the rank of\r      knight 15,000 or 16,000, including themen of the towns. Both\r      estimates must be greatly exaggerated.Michael of Northburgh says\r      that 1542 were killed in the battle andabout 2000 on the next\r      day. The great princes killed were theking of Bohemia, the duke\r      of Lorraine, the earls of Alençon,Flanders, Blois, Auxerre,\r      Harcourt, Saint-Pol, Aumale, the grandprior of France and the\r      archbishop of Rouen.\r \rThen the king went forthand came before the town of\rMontreuil-by-the-sea, andhis marshals ran toward Hesdin and Brent\rWaben and Serain, but theydid nothing to the castle, it was so strong\rand so well kept. Theylodged that night on the river of Hesdin\rtowards Blangy. The nextday they rode toward Boulogne and came to the\rtown of Wissant: there theking and the prince lodged, and tarried\rthere a day to refresh hismen, and on the Wednesday the king came\rbefore the strong town ofCalais.\r \r \r \r \rTHE BATTLE OF POITIERS\r \rOF THE GREAT HOST THAT THEFRENCH KING BROUGHT TO THE BATTLE OF\rPOITIERS\r \r \rAfter the taking of thecastle of Romorantin and of them that were\rtherein, the prince thenand his company rode as they did before,\rdestroying the country, approachingto Anjou and to Touraine. The\rFrench king, who was atChartres, departed and came to Blois and there\rtarried two days, and thento Amboise and the next day to Loches: and\rthen he heard how that theprince was at Touraine[1] and how that he\rwas returning by Poitou:ever the Englishmen were coasted by certain\rexpert knights of France,who alway made report to the king what the\rEnglishmen did. Then theking came to the Haye in Touraine and his men\rhad passed the river ofLoire, some at the bridge of Orleans and some\rat Meung, at Saumur, atBlois, and at Tours and whereas they might:\rthey were in number atwenty thousand men of arms beside other; there\rwere a twenty-six dukesand earls and more than sixscore banners, and\rthe four sons of the king,who were but young, the duke Charles of\rNormandy, the lord Louis,that was from thenceforth duke of Anjou, and\rthe lord John duke ofBerry, and the lord Philip, who was after duke\rof Burgoyne. The sameseason, pope Innocent the sixth sent the lord\rBertrand, cardinal ofPerigord, and the lord Nicholas, cardinal of\rUrgel, into France, totreat for a peace between the French king and\rall his enemies, firstbetween him and the king of Navarre, who was in\rprison: and thesecardinals oftentimes spake to the king for his\rdeliverance during thesiege at Bretuel, but they could do nothing in\rthat behalf. Then thecardinal of Perigord went to Tours, and there he\rheard how the French kinghasted sore to find the Englishmen: then he\rrode to Poitiers, for heheard how both the hosts drew thitherward.\r \r      [1] \'En Touraine.\'\r \rThe French king heard howthe prince hasted greatly to return, and the\rking feared that he shouldscape him and so departed from Haye in\rTouraine, and all hiscompany, and rode to Chauvigny, where he tarried\rthat Thursday in the townand without along by the river of Creuse,\rand the next day the kingpassed the river at the bridge there,\rweening that theEnglishmen had been before him, but they were not.\rHowbeit they pursued afterand passed the bridge that day more than\rthreescore thousandhorses, and divers other passed at Chatelleraut,\rand ever as they passedthey took the way to Poitiers.\r \rOn the other side theprince wist not truly where the Frenchmen were;\rbut they supposed thatthey were not far off, for they could not find\rno more forage, wherebythey had great fault in their host of victual,\rand some of them repentedthat they had destroyed so much as they had\rdone before when they werein Berry, Anjou and Touraine, and in that\rthey had made no betterprovision. The same Friday three great lords\rof France, the lord ofCraon, the lord Raoul of Coucy and the earl of\rJoigny, tarried all day inthe town of Chauvigny, and part of their\rcompanies. The Saturdaythey passed the bridge and followed the king,\rwho was then a threeleagues before, and took the way among bushes\rwithout a wood side to goto Poitiers.\r \rThe same Saturday theprince and his company dislodged from a little\rvillage thereby, and sentbefore him certain currours to see if they\rmight find any adventureand to hear where the Frenchmen were. They\rwere in number athreescore men of arms well horsed, and with them was\rthe lord Eustaced\'Aubrecicourt and the lord John of Ghistelles, and\rby adventure theEnglishmen and Frenchmen met together by the foresaid\rwood side. The Frenchmenknew anon how they were their enemies; then\rin haste they did on theirhelmets and displayed their banners and\rcame a great pace towardsthe Englishmen: they were in number a two\rhundred men of arms. Whenthe Englishmen saw them, and that they were\rso great a number, thenthey determined to fly and let the Frenchmen\rchase them, for they knewwell the prince with his host was not far\rbehind. Then they turnedtheir horses and took the corner of the wood,\rand the Frenchmen afterthem crying their cries and made great noise.\rAnd as they chased, theycame on the prince\'s battle or they were ware\rthereof themselves; theprince tarried there to have word again from\rthem that he sent forth.The lord Raoul de Coucy with his banner went\rso far forward that he wasunder the prince\'s banner: there was a sore\rbattle and the knightfought valiantly; howbeit he was there taken,\rand the earl of Joigny,the viscount of Brosse, the lord of Chauvigny\rand all the other taken orslain, but a few that scaped. And by the\rprisoners the prince knewhow the French king followed him in such\rwise that he could noteschew the battle:[2] then he assembled\rtogether all his men andcommanded that no man should go before the\rmarshals\' banners. Thusthe prince rode that Saturday from the morning\rtill it was against night,so that he came within two little leagues\rof Poitiers. Then thecaptal de Buch, sir Aymenion of Pommiers, the\rlord Bartholomew ofBurghersh and the lord Eustace d\'Aubrecicourt, all\rthese the prince sentforth to see if they might know what the\rFrenchmen did. Theseknights departed with two hundred men of arms\rwell horsed; they rode sofar that they saw the great battle of the\rking\'s, they saw all thefields covered with men of arms. These\rEnglishmen could notforbear, but set on the tail of the French host\rand cast down many to theearth and took divers prisoners, so that the\rhost began to stir, andtidings thereof came to the French king as he\rwas entering into the cityof Poitiers. Then he returned again and\rmade all his host do thesame, so that Saturday it was very late or he\rwas lodged in the field.The English currours returned again to the\rprince and shewed him allthat they saw and knew, and said how the\rFrench host was a greatnumber of people. \'Well,\' said the prince, \'in\rthe name of God let us nowstudy how we shall fight with them at our\radvantage.\' That night theEnglishmen lodged in a strong place among\rhedges, vines and bushes,and their host well watched, and so was the\rFrench host.\r \r      [2] Or rather, \'that the French king hadgone in front of them\r      (les avoit advancez) and that he could inno way depart without\r      being fought with.\'\r \r \r \r \rOF THE ORDER OF THEFRENCHMEN BEFORE THE BATTLE OF POITIERS\r \r \rOn the Sunday in themorning the French king, who had great desire to\rfight with the Englishmen,heard his mass in his pavilion and was\rhouselled, and his foursons with him. After mass there came to him\rthe duke of Orleans, theduke of Bourbon, the earl of Ponthieu, the\rlord Jaques of Bourbon,[1]the duke of Athens, constable of France,\rthe earl of Tancarville,the earl of Sarrebruck, the earl of\rDammartin, the earl ofVentadour, and divers other great barons of\rFrance and of otherneighbours holding of France, as the lord\rClermont, the lord Arnoldd\'Audrehem, marshal of France, the lord of\rSaint-Venant, the lordJohn of Landas, the lord Eustace Ribemont, the\rlord Fiennes, the lordGeoffrey of Charny, the lord Chatillon, the\rlord of Sully, the lord ofNesle, sir Robert Duras and divers other;\rall these with the kingwent to counsel. Then finally it was ordained\rthat all manner of menshould draw into the field, and every lord to\rdisplay his banner and toset forth in the name of God and Saint\rDenis: then trumpets blewup through the host and every man mounted on\rhorseback and went intothe field, where they saw the king\'s banner\rwave with the wind. Theremight a been seen great nobless of fair\rharness and rich armouryof banners and pennons; for there was all the\rflower of France, therewas none durst abide at home without he would\rbe shamed for ever. Thenit was ordained by the advice of the\rconstable and marshals tobe made three battles, and in each ward\rsixteen thousand men ofarms all mustered and passed for men of arms.\rThe first battle the dukeof Orleans to govern, with thirty-six\rbanners and twice as manypennons, the second the duke of Normandy and\rhis two brethren the lordLouis and the lord John, the third the king\rhimself: and while thatthese battles were setting in array, the king\rcalled to him the lordEustace Ribemont, the lord John of Landas and\rthe lord Richard ofBeaujeu, and said to them; \'Sirs, ride on before\rto see the dealing of theEnglishmen and advise well what number they\rbe and by what means wemay fight with them, other afoot or\ra-horseback.\' These threeknights rode forth and the king was on a\rwhite courser and saida-high to his men: \'Sirs, among you, when ye be\rat Paris, at Chartres, atRouen or at Orleans, then ye do threat the\rEnglishmen and desire tobe in arms out against them. Now ye be come\rthereto: I shall now shewyou them: now shew forth your evil will that\rye bear them and revengeyour displeasures and damages that they have\rdone you, for withoutdoubt we shall fight with them.\' Such as heard\rhim said: \'Sir, in God\'sname so be it; that would we see[2] gladly.\'\r \r      [1] That is, Jaques de Bourbon, earl ofla Marche and Ponthieu.\r \r      [2] \'Verrons\': but a better reading is\'ferons,\' \'that will we\r      do gladly.\'\r \r \rTherewith the threeknights returned again to the king, who demanded\rof them tidings. Then sirEustace of Ribemont answered for all and\rsaid: \'Sir, we have seenthe Englishmen: by estimation they be two\rthousand men of arms andfour thousand archers and a fifteen hundred\rof other. Howbeit they bein a strong place, and as far as we can\rimagine they are in onebattle; howbeit they be wisely ordered, and\ralong the way they havefortified strongly the hedges and bushes: one\rpart of their archers arealong by the hedge, so that none can go nor\rride that way, but mustpass by them, and that way must ye go an ye\rpurpose to fight withthem. In this hedge there is but one entry and\rone issue by likelihoodthat four horsemen may ride afront. At the end\rof this hedge, whereas noman can go nor ride, there be men of arms\rafoot and archers aforethem in manner of a herse, so that they will\rnot be lightlydiscomfited,\'[3] \'Well,\' said the king, \'what will ye\rthen counsel us to do?\'Sir Eustace said: \'Sir, let us all be afoot,\rexcept three hundred menof arms, well horsed, of the best in your\rhost and most hardiest, tothe intent they somewhat to break and to\ropen the archers, and thenyour battles to follow on quickly afoot and\rso to fight with their menof arms hand to hand. This is the best\radvice that I can giveyou: if any other think any other way better,\rlet him speak.\'\r \r      [3] The translation of this passage isunsatisfactory. It should\r      be: \'Howbeit they have ordered it wisely,and have taken post\r      along the road, which is fortifiedstrongly with hedges and\r      thickets, and they have beset this hedgeon one side (_or\r      according to another text_, on one sideand on the other) with\r      their archers, so that one cannot enternor ride along their road\r      except by them, and that way must he gowho purposes to fight\r      with them. In this hedge there is but oneentry and one issue,\r      where by likelihood four men of arms, ason the road, might ride\r      a-front. At the end of this hedge amongvines and thorn-bushes,\r      where no man can go nor ride, are theirmen of arms all afoot,\r      and they have set in front of them theirarchers in manner of a\r      harrow, whom it would not be easy todiscomfit.\r \rThe king said: \'Thus shallit be done\': then the two marshals rode\rfrom battle to battle andchose out a three hundred knights and\rsquires of the most expertmen of arms of all the host, every man well\rarmed and horsed. Also itwas ordained that the battles of Almains\rshould abide still onhorseback to comfort the marshals, if need were,\rwhereof the earl ofSarrebruck, the earl of Nidau and the earl of\rNassau were captains. KingJohn of France was there armed, and twenty\rother in his apparel; andhe did put the guiding of his eldest son to\rthe lord of Saint-Venant,the lord of Landas and the lord Thibault of\rVaudenay; and the lordArnold of Cervolles, called the archpriest,[4]\rwas armed in the armour ofthe young earl of Alençon.\r \r      [4] Arnaud de Cervolles, one of the mostcelebrated adventurers\r      of the 14th century, called thearchpriest because though a\r      layman he possessed the ecclesiasticalfief of Vélines.\r \r \r \r \rHOW THE CARDINAL OFPERIGORD TREATED TO MAKE AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE\rFRENCH KING AND THE PRINCEBEFORE THE BATTLE OF POITIERS\r \r \rWhen the French king\'sbattles was ordered and every lord under his\rbanner among their ownmen, then it was commanded that every man\rshould cut their spears toa five foot long and every man to put off\rtheir spurs. Thus as theywere ready to approach, the cardinal of\rPerigord[1] came in greathaste to the king. He came the same morning\rfrom Poitiers; he kneeleddown to the king and held up his hands and\rdesired him for God\'s sakea little to abstain setting forward till he\rhad spoken with him: thenhe said: \'Sir, ye have here all the flower\rof your realm against ahandful of Englishmen as to regard your\rcompany,[2] and, sir, ifye may have them accorded to you without\rbattle, it shall be moreprofitable and honourable to have them by\rthat manner rather than toadventure so noble chivalry as ye have here\rpresent. Sir, I requireyou in the name of God and humility that I may\rride to the prince andshew him what danger ye have him in,\' The king\rsaid: \'It pleaseth mewell, but return again shortly.\' The cardinal\rdeparted and diligently herode to the prince, who was among his men\rafoot: then the cardinalalighted and came to the prince, who received\rhim courteously. Then thecardinal after his salutation made he said:\r\'Certainly, fair son, ifyou and your council advise justly the\rpuissance of the Frenchking, ye will suffer me to treat to make a\rpeace between you, an Imay,\' The prince, who was young and lusty,\rsaid: \'Sir, the honour ofme and of my people saved, I would gladly\rfall to any reasonableway.\' Then the cardinal said: \'Sir, ye say\rwell, and I shall accordyou, an I can; for it should be great pity if\rso many noblemen and otheras be here on both parties should come\rtogether by battle,\' Thenthe cardinal rode again to the king and\rsaid: \'Sir, ye need not tomake any great haste to fight with your\renemies, for they cannotfly from you though they would, they be in\rsuch a ground: wherefore,sir, I require you forbear for this day till\rtomorrow the sun-rising.\'The king was loath to agree thereto, for\rsome of his council wouldnot consent to it; but finally the cardinal\rshewed such reasons, thatthe king accorded that respite: and in the\rsame place there was pightup a pavilion of red silk fresh and rich,\rand gave leave for thatday every man to draw to their lodgings except\rthe constable\'s andmarshals\' battles.\r \r      [1] Talleyrand de Périgord.\r \r      [2] The meaning is, \'Ye have here all theflower of your realm\r      against a handful of people, for so theEnglishmen are as\r      compared with your company.\'\r \rThat Sunday all the daythe cardinal travailed in riding from the one\rhost to the other gladlyto agree them: but the French king would\rnot agree without he mighthave four of the principallest of the\rEnglishmen at hispleasure, and the prince and all the other to yield\rthemselves simply: howbeitthere were many great offers made. The\rprince offered to renderinto the king\'s hands all that ever he had\rwon in that voyage, townsand castles, and to quit all prisoners that\rhe or any of his men hadtaken in that season, and also to swear not\rto be armed against theFrench king in seven year after; but the king\rand his council would nonethereof: the uttermost that he would do\rwas, that the prince and ahundred of his knights should yield\rthemselves into the king\'sprison; otherwise he would not: the which\rthe prince would in nowise agree unto.\r \rIn the mean season thatthe cardinal rode thus between the hosts in\rtrust to do some good,certain knights of France and of England both\rrode forth the sameSunday, because it was truce for that day, to\rcoast the hosts and tobehold the dealing of their enemies. So it\rfortuned that the lordJohn Chandos rode the same day coasting the\rFrench host, and in likemanner the lord of Clermont, one of the\rFrench marshals, hadridden forth and aviewed the state of the English\rhost; and as these twoknights returned towards their hosts, they met\rtogether: each of thembare one manner of device, a blue lady\rembroidered in a sunbeamabove on their apparel. Then the lord\rClermont said: \'Chandos,how long have ye taken on you to bear my\rdevice?\' \'Nay, ye bearmine,\' said Chandos, \'for it is as well mine as\ryours.\' \'I deny that,\'said Clermont, \'but an it were not for the\rtruce this day between us,I should make it good on you incontinent\rthat ye have no right tobear my device.\' \'Ah, sir,\' said Chandos, \'ye\rshall find me to-morrowready to defend you and to prove by feat of\rarms that it is as wellmine as yours,\' Then Clermont said: \'Chandos,\rthese be well the words ofyou Englishmen, for ye can devise nothing\rof new, but all that yesee is good and fair.\' So they departed\rwithout any more doing,and each of them returned to their host.\r \rThe cardinal of Perigordcould in no wise that Sunday make any\ragreement between theparties, and when it was near night he returned\rto Poitiers. That nightthe Frenchmen took their ease; they had\rprovision enough, and theEnglishmen had great default; they could get\rno forage, nor they couldnot depart thence without danger of their\renemies. That Sunday theEnglishmen made great dikes and hedges about\rtheir archers, to be themore stronger; and on the Monday in the\rmorning the prince and hiscompany were ready apparelled as they were\rbefore, and about thesun-rising in like manner were the Frenchmen.\rThe same morning betimesthe cardinal came again to the French host\rand thought by hispreaching to pacify the parties; but then the\rFrenchmen said to him:\'Return whither ye will: bring hither no more\rwords of treaty nor peace:and ye love yourself depart shortly.\' When\rthe cardinal saw that hetravailed in vain, he took leave of the king\rand then he went to theprince and said: \'Sir, do what ye can; there\ris no remedy but to abidethe battle, for I can find none accord in\rthe French king.\' Then theprince said: \'The same is our intent and\rall our people: God helpthe right!\' So the cardinal returned to\rPoitiers. In his companythere were certain knights and squires, men\rof arms, who were morefavourable to the French king than to the\rprince; and when they sawthat the parties should fight, they stale\rfrom their masters andwent to the French host; and they made their\rcaptain the chatelain ofAmposte,[3] who was as then there with the\rcardinal, who knew nothingthereof till he was come to Poitiers.\r \r      [3] Amposta, a fortress in Catalonia.\r \rThe certainty of the orderof the Englishmen was shewed to the French\rking, except they hadordained three hundred men a-horseback and as\rmany archers a-horsebackto coast under covert of the mountain and to\rstrike into the battle ofthe duke of Normandy, who was under the\rmountain afoot. Thisordinance they had made of new, that the\rFrenchmen knew not of. Theprince was with his battle down among the\rvines and had closed inthe weakest part with their carnages.\r \rNow will I name some ofthe principal lords and knights that were\rthere with the prince: theearl of Warwick, the earl of Suffolk, the\rearl of Salisbury, theearl of Oxford, the lord Raynold Cobham, the\rlord Spencer, the lordJames Audley, the lord Peter his brother, the\rlord Berkeley, the lordBassett, the lord Warin, the lord Delaware,\rthe lord Manne, the lordWilloughby, the lord Bartholomew de\rBurghersh, the lord ofFelton, the lord Richard of Pembroke, the lord\rStephen of Cosington, thelord Bradetane and other Englishmen; and of\rGascon there was the lordof Pommiers, the lord of Languiran, the\rcaptal of Buch, the lordJohn of Caumont, the lord de Lesparre, the\rlord of Rauzan, the lordof Condon, the lord of Montferrand, the lord\rof Landiras, the lordsoudic of Latrau and other that I cannot name;\rand of Hainowes the lordEustace d\'Aubrecicourt, the lord John of\rGhistelles, and two otherstrangers, the lord Daniel Pasele and the\rlord Denis of Morbeke: allthe prince\'s company passed not an eight\rthousand men one andother, and the Frenchmen were a sixty thousand\rfighting men, whereofthere were more than three thousand knights.\r \r \r \r \rOF THE BATTLE OF POITIERSBETWEEN THE PRINCE OF WALES AND THE FRENCH\rKING\r \r \rWhen the prince saw thathe should have battle and that the cardinal\rwas gone without any peaceor truce making, and saw that the French\rking did set but littlestore by him, he said then to his men: \'Now,\rsirs, though we be but asmall company as in regard to the puissance\rof our enemies, let us notbe abashed therefor; for the victory lieth\rnot in the multitude ofpeople, but whereas God will send it. If it\rfortune that the journeybe ours, we shall be the most honoured people\rof all the world; and ifwe die in our right quarrel, I have the king\rmy father and brethren,and also ye have good friends and kinsmen;\rthese shall revenge us.Therefore, sirs, for God\'s sake I require you\rdo your devoirs this day;for if God be pleased and Saint George, this\rday ye shall see me a goodknight.\' These words and such other that\rthe prince spake comfortedall his people. The lord sir John Chandos\rthat day never went fromthe prince, nor also the lord James Audley of\ra great season; but whenhe saw that they should needs fight, he said\rto the prince: \'Sir, Ihave served always truly my lord your father\rand you also, and shall doas long as I live. This lord James was a right\rsage and a valiant knight,and by him was much of the host ordained\rand governed the daybefore. Theyentered a-horseback into the way where the\rgreat hedges were on bothsides set full of archers. As soon as the\rmen of arms entered, thearchers began to shoot on both sides and did\rslay and hurt horses andknights, so that the horses when they felt\rthe sharp arrows theywould in no wise go forward, but drew aback and\rflang and took on sofiercely, that many of them fell on their\rmasters, so that for pressthey could not rise again; insomuch that\rthe marshals\' battle couldnever come at the prince. So within ashort space the marshals\' battles were\rdiscomfited, for they fellone upon another and could not go forth;[4]\rand the Frenchmen thatwere behind and could not get forward reculed\rback and came on thebattle of the duke of Normandy, the which was\rgreat and thick and wereafoot, but anon they began to open behind;[5]\rfor when they knew thatthe marshals\' battle was discomfited, they\rtook their horses anddeparted, he that might best. True\rto say, the archers didtheir company that day great advantage; for\rthey shot so thick thatthe Frenchmen wist not on what side to take\rheed, and little andlittle the Englishmen won ground on them.\r \r      [4] \'Ne posient aler avant.\'\r \r      [5] \'Which was great and thick in front(pardevant), but anon\r      it became open and thin behind.\'\r \rAnd when the men of armsof England saw that the marshals\' battle was\rdiscomfited and that theduke\'s battle began to disorder and open,\rthey leapt then on theirhorses, the which they had ready by them:\rthen they assembledtogether and cried, \'Saint George! Guyenne!\' and\rthe lord Chandos said tothe prince: \'Sir, take your horse and ride\rforth; this journey isyours: God is this day in your hands: get us to\rthe French king\'s battle,for their lieth all the sore of the matter.\rI think verily by hisvaliantness he will not fly: I trust we shall\rhave him by the grace ofGod and Saint George, so he be well fought\rwithal: and, sir, I heardyou say that this day I should see you a\rgood knight.\' The princesaid, \'Let us go forth; ye shall not see me\rthis day return back,\' andsaid, \'Advance, banner, in the name of God\rand of Saint George,\' Theknight that bare it did his commandment:\rthere was then a sorebattle and a perilous, and many a man\roverthrown, and he thatwas once down could not be relieved again\rwithout great succour andaid. As the prince rode and entered in among\rhis enemies, he saw on hisright hand in a little bush lying dead the\rlord Robert of Duras andhis banner by him,[6] and a ten or twelve of\rhis men about him. Thenthe prince said to two of his squires and to\rthree archers: \'Sirs, takethe body of this knight on a targe and bear\rhim to Poitiers, andpresent him from me to the cardinal of Perigord,\rand say how I salute himby that token.\' And this was done. The prince\rwas informed that thecardinal\'s men were on the field against him,\rthe which was notpertaining to the right order of arms, for men of\rthe church that cometh andgoeth for treaty of peace ought not by\rreason to bear harness norto fight for neither of the parties; they\rought to be indifferent:and because these men had done so, the prince\rwas displeased with thecardinal, and therefore he sent unto him his\rnephew the lord Robert ofDuras dead: and the chatelain of Amposte was\rtaken, and the princewould have had his head stricken off, because he\rwas pertaining to thecardinal, but then the lord Chandos said: \'Sir,\rsuffer for a season:intend to a greater matter: and peradventure the\rcardinal will make suchexcuse that ye shall be content.\'\r \r      [6] The original adds, \'qui estoit deFrance au sentoir (sautoir)\r      de gueulles.\'\r \rThen the prince and hiscompany dressed them on the battle of the duke\rof Athens, constable ofFrance. There was many a man slain and cast to\rthe earth. As theFrenchmen fought in companies, they cried,\r\'Mountjoy! Saint Denis!\'and the Englishmen, \'Saint George! Guyenne!\'\rAnon the prince with hiscompany met with the battle of Almains,\rwhereof the earl ofSarrebruck, the earl Nassau and the earl Nidau\rwere captains, but in ashort space they were put to flight: the\rarchers shot so whollytogether that none durst come in their dangers:\rthey slew many a man thatcould not come to no ransom: these three\rearls was there slain, anddivers other knights and squires of their\rcompany, and there was thelord d\'Aubrecieourt rescued, by his own men\rand set on horseback, andafter he did that day many feats of arms and\rtook good prisoners. Whenthe duke of Normandy\'s battle saw the prince\rapproach, they thought tosave themselves, and so the duke and the\rking\'s children, the earlof Poitiers and the earl of Touraine, who\rwere right young, believedtheir governours and so departed from the\rfield, and with them morethan eight hundred spears, that strake no\rstroke that day. Then sir\rOudart alighted and cameto him or he could rise, and said, \'Yield\ryou, rescue or no rescue,or else I shall slay you.\' The Englishman\ryielded and went with him,and afterward was ransomed. Also it\rfortuned that anothersquire of Picardy called John de Hellenes was\rfled from the battle andmet with his page, who delivered him a new\rfresh horse, whereon herode away alone. The same season there was in\rthe field the lordBerkeley of England, a young lusty knight, who the\rsame day reared hisbanner, and he all alone pursued the said John of\rHellenes. And when he hadfollowed the space of a league, the said\rJohn turned again and laidhis sword in the rest instead of a spear,\rand so came running towardthe lord Berkeley, who lift up his sword to\rhave stricken the squire;but when he saw the stroke come, he turned\rfrom it, so that theEnglishman lost his stroke and John strake him as\rhe passed on the arm, thatthe lord Berkeley\'s sword fell into the\rfield. And John alighted off his horse and\rtook the knight\'s swordthat lay on the ground, and came to him and\rdemanded if he would yieldhim or not. The knight then demanded his\rname. \'Sir,\' said he, \'Ihight John of Hellenes; but what is your\rname?\' \'Certainly,\' saidthe knight, \'my name is Thomas and am lord of\rBerkeley, a fair castle onthe river of Severn in the marches of\rWales.\' \'Well, sir,\' quoththe squire, \'then ye shall be my prisoner,\rand I shall bring you insafe-guard and I shall see that you shall be\rhealed of your hurt.\'\'Well,\' said the knight, \'I am content to be\ryour prisoner, for ye haveby law of arms won me.\' There he sware to\rbe his prisoner, rescue orno rescue. There he was more than a year\rtill he was perfectlywhole; and when he departed he paid for his\rransom six thousandnobles, and so this squire was made a knight by\rreason of the profit thathe had of the lord Berkeley.\r \r \r \r \rHOW KING JOHN WAS TAKENPRISONER AT THE BATTLE OF POITIERS\r \r \rOftentimes the adventuresof amours and of war are more fortunate and\rmarvellous than any mancan think or wish. It happenedso well for him, that he was next to the\rking when they were aboutto take him: he stept forth into the press,\rand by strength of hisbody and arms he came to the French king and\rsaid in good French, \'Sir,yield you,\' The king beheld the knight and\rsaid: \'To whom shall Iyield me? The prince made lowly reverence to\rthe king and caused wineand spices to be brought forth, and himself\rserved the king in sign ofgreat love.\r \r \r \r \rHOW THE ENGLISHMEN WONGREATLY AT THE BATTLE OF POITIERS\r \r \rThus this battle wasdiscomfited, as ye have heard, the which was in\rthe fields of Maupertuis atwo leagues from Poitiers the twenty-second\rday of September the yearof our Lord MCCCLVI. It begun in the\rmorning[1] and ended atnoon, but as then all the Englishmen were not\rreturned from the chase;therefore the prince\'s banner stood on a bush\rto draw all his mentogether, but it was well nigh night or all came\rfrom the chase. Sir, I say not this to mock you,\rfor all that be on ourparty, that saw every man\'s deeds, are plainly\raccorded by true sentenceto give you the prize and chaplet.\'\rTherewith the Frenchmenbegan to murmur and said among themselves how\rthe prince had spokennobly, and that by all estimation he should\rprove a noble man, if Godsend him life and to persevere in such good\rfortune.\r \r \r \r \rHOW THE PRINCE RETURNED TOBORDEAUX AFTER THE BATTLE OF POITIERS\r \r \rWhen supper was done,every man went to his lodging with their\rprisoners. The same nightthey put many to ransom and believed them on\rtheir faiths and troths,and ransomed them but easily, for they said\rthey would set no knight\'sransom so high, but that he might pay at\rhis ease and maintainstill his degree. The next day, when they had\rheard mass and taken somerepast and that everything was trussed and\rready, then they tooktheir horses and rode towards Poitiers. The same\rnight there was come toPoitiers the lord of Roye with a hundred\rspears: he was not at thebattle, but he met the duke of Normandy near\rto Chauvigny, and the dukesent him to Poitiers to keep the town till\rthey heard other tidings.When the lord of Roye knew that the\rEnglishmen were so nearcoming to the city, he caused every man to be\rarmed and every man to goto his defence to the walls, towers and\rgates; and the Englishmenpassed by without any approaching, for they\rwere so laded with gold,silver and prisoners, that in their returning\rthey assaulted nofortress; they thought it a great deed if they might\rbring the French king,with their other prisoners and riches that they\rhad won, in safeguard toBordeaux. They rode but small journeys\rbecause of their prisonersand great carriages that they had: they\rrode in a day no more butfour or five leagues and lodged ever\rbetimes, and rode closetogether in good array saving the marshals\'\rbattles, who rode everbefore with five hundred men of arms to open\rthe passages as the princeshould pass; but they found no encounters,\rfor all the country was sofrayed that every man drew to the\rfortresses.\r \rAs the prince rode, it wasshewed him how the lord Audley had given to\rhis four squires the giftof the five hundred marks that he had given\runto him: then the princesent for him and he was brought in his\rlitter to the prince, whoreceived him courteously and said: \'Sir\rJames, we have knowledgethat the revenues that we gave you, as soon\ras ye came to yourlodging, you gave the same to four squires: we\rwould know why ye did so,and whether the gift was agreeable to you or\rnot.\' \'Sir,\' said theknight, \'it is of truth I have given it to them,\rand I shall shew you why Idid so. These four squires that be here\rpresent have a long seasonserved me well and truly in many great\rbusinesses and, sir, inthis last battle they served me in such wise\rthat an they had neverdone nothing else I was bound to reward them,\rand before the same daythey had never nothing of me in reward. Sir, I\ram but a man alone: but bythe aid and comfort of them I took on me to\raccomplish my vow longbefore made. I had been dead in the battle an\rthey had not been:wherefore, sir, when I considered the love that\rthey bare unto me, I hadnot been courteous if I would not a rewarded\rthem. I thank God I havehad and shall have enough as long as I live:\rI will never be abashedfor lack of good. Sir, if I have done this\rwithout your pleasure, Irequire you to pardon me, for, sir, both I\rand my squires shall serveyou as well as ever we did.\' Then the\rprince said: \'Sir James,for anything that ye have done I cannot blame\ryou, but can you goodthank therefor; and for the valiantness of these\rsquires, whom ye praise somuch, I accord to them your gift, and I\rwill render again to yousix hundred marks in like manner as ye had\rthe other.\'\r \rThus the prince and hiscompany did so much that they passed through\rPoitou and Saintongewithout damage and came to Blaye, and there\rpassed the river ofGironde and arrived in the good city of Bordeaux.\rIt cannot be recorded thegreat feast and cheer that they of the city\rwith the clergy made tothe prince, and how honourably they were there\rreceived. The princebrought the French king into the abbey of Saint\rAndrew\'s, and there theylodged both, the king in one part and the\rprince in the other. Theprince bought of the lords, knights and\rsquires of Gascoyne themost part of the earls of the realm of France,\rsuch as were prisoners,and paid ready money for them. There was\rdivers questions andchallenges made between the knights and squires\rof Gascoyne for taking ofthe French king; howbeit Denis Morbeke by\rright of arms and by truetokens that he shewed challenged him for his\rprisoner. Another squireof Gascoyne called Bernard of Truttes said\rhow he had right to him:there was much ado and many words before the\rprince and other lordsthat were there, and because these two\rchallenged each other tofight in that quarrel, the prince caused the\rmatter to rest till theycame in England and that no declaration\rshould be made but aforethe king of England his father; but because\rthe French king himselfaided to sustain the challenge of Denis\rMorbeke, for he inclinedmore to him than to any other, the prince\rtherefore privily causedto be delivered to the said sir Denis two\rthousand nobles tomaintain withal his estate.\r \rAnon after the prince cameto Bordeaux, the cardinal of Perigord came\rthither, who was sent fromthe pope in legation, as it was said. He\rwas there more thanfifteen days or the prince would speak with him\rbecause of the chatelainof Amposte and his men, who were against him\rin the battle of Poitiers.The prince believed that the cardinal sent\rthem thither, but thecardinal did so much by the means of the lord of\rCaumont, the lord ofMontferrand and the captal of Buch, who were his\rcousins, they shewed sogood reasons to the prince, that he was\rcontent to hear him speak.And when he was before the prince, he\rexcused himself so sagelythat the prince and his council held him\rexcused, and so he fellagain into the prince\'s love and redeemed out\rhis men by reasonableransoms; and the chatelain was set to his ransom\rof ten thousand franks,the which he paid after. Then the cardinal\rbegan to treat on thedeliverance of the French king, but I pass it\rbriefly because nothingwas done. Thus the prince, the Gascons and\rEnglishmen tarried stillat Bordeaux till it was Lent in great mirth\rand revel, and spentfoolishly the gold and silver that they had won.\rIn England also there wasgreat joy when they heard tidings of the\rbattle of Poitiers, of thediscomfiting of the Frenchmen and taking of\rthe king: greatsolemnities were made in all churches and great fires\rand wakes throughout allEngland. The knights and squires, such as\rwere come home from thatjourney, were much made of and praised more\rthan other.\r \r \r \r \rWAT TYLER\'S REBELLION\r \rHOW THE COMMONS OF ENGLANDREBELLED AGAINST THE NOBLEMEN\r \r \rIn the mean season whilethis treaty was, there fell in England great\rmischief and rebellion ofmoving of the common people, by which deed\rEngland was at a point tohave been lost without recovery. There was\rnever realm nor country inso great adventure as it was in that time,\rand all because of theease and riches that the common people were of,\rwhich moved them to thisrebellion, as sometime they did in France,\rthe which did much hurt,for by such incidents the realm of France\rhath been greatly grieved.\r \rIt was a marvellous thingand of poor foundation that this mischief\rbegan in England, and togive ensample to all manner of people I will\rspeak hereof as it wasdone, as I was informed, and of the incidents\rthereof. There was anusage in England, and yet is in divers\rcountries, that thenoblemen hath great franchise over the commons and\rkeepeth them in servage,that is to say, their tenants ought by custom\rto labour the lords\'lands, to gather and bring home their corns, and\rsome to thresh and to fan,and by servage to make their hay and to hew\rtheir wood and bring ithome. All these things they ought to do by\rservage, and there be moreof these people in England than in any\rother realm. Thus thenoblemen and prelates are served by them, and\respecially in the countyof Kent, Essex, Sussex and Bedford. These\runhappy people of thesesaid countries began to stir, because they\rsaid they were kept ingreat servage, and in the beginning of the\rworld, they said, therewere no bondmen, wherefore they maintained\rthat none ought to bebond, without he did treason to his lord, as\rLucifer did to God; butthey said they could have no such battle,[1]\rfor they were neitherangels nor spirits, but men formed to the\rsimilitude of their lords,saying why should they then be kept so\runder like beasts; thewhich they said they would no longer suffer,\rfor they would be all one,and if they laboured or did anything for\rtheir lords, they wouldhave wages therefor as well as other. And of\rthis imagination was afoolish priest in the country of Kent called\rJohn Ball, for the whichfoolish words he had been three times in the\rbishop of Canterbury\'sprison: for this priest used oftentimes on the\rSundays after mass, whenthe people were going out of the minster, to\rgo into the cloister andpreach, and made the people to assemble about\rhim, and would say thus:\'Ah, ye good people, the matters goeth not\rwell to pass in England,nor shall not do till everything be common,\rand that there be novillains nor gentlemen, but that we may be all\runited together, and thatthe lords be no greater masters than we be.\rWhat have we deserved, orwhy should we be kept thus in servage? We be\rall come from one fatherand one mother, Adam and Eve: whereby can\rthey say or shew that theybe greater lords than we be, saving by that\rthey cause us to win andlabour for that they dispend? They are\rclothed in velvet andcamlet furred with grise, and we be vestured\rwith poor cloth: they havetheir wines, spices and good bread, and we\rhave the drawing out ofthe chaff[2] and drink water; they dwell in\rfair houses, and we havethe pain and travail, rain and wind in the\rfields; and by that thatcometh of our labours they keep and maintain\rtheir estates: we becalled their bondmen, and without we do readily\rthem service, we bebeaten; and we have no sovereign to whom we may\rcomplain, nor that willhear us nor do us right. Let us go to the\rking, he is young, andshew him what servage we be in, and shew him\rhow we will have itotherwise, or else we will provide us of some\rremedy; and if we gotogether, all manner of people that be now in any\rbondage will follow us tothe intent to be made free; and when the\rking seeth us, we shallhave some remedy, either by fairness or\rotherwise.\' Thus John Ballsaid on Sundays, when the people issued out\rof the churches in thevillages; wherefore many of the mean people\rloved him, and such asintended to no goodness said how he said truth;\rand so they would murmurone with another in the fields and in the\rways as they wenttogether, affirming how John Ball said truth.\r \r      [1] The true text is, \'Mais ils n\'avoientpas cette taille,\'\r      \'but they were not of that nature.\' Thetranslator found the\r      corruption \'bataille\' for \'taille.\'\r \r      [2] Froissart says \'le seigle, le retraitet la paille,\' \'the\r      rye, the bran and the straw.\' Thetranslator\'s French text had\r      \'le seigle, le retraict de la paille.\'\r \rThe archbishop ofCanterbury, who was informed of the saying of this\rJohn Ball, caused him tobe taken and put in prison a two or three\rmonths to chastise him:howbeit, it had been much better at the\rbeginning that he had beencondemned to perpetual prison or else to\rhave died, rather than tohave suffered him to have been again\rdelivered out of prison;but the bishop had conscience to let him die.\rAnd when this John Ballwas out of prison, he returned again to his\rerror, as he did before.\r \rOf his words and deedsthere were much people in London informed, such\ras had great envy at themthat were rich and such as were noble; and\rthen they began to speakamong them and said how the realm of England\rwas right evil governed,and how that gold and silver was taken from\rthem by them that werenamed noblemen: so thus these unhappy men of\rLondon began to rebel andassembled them together, and sent word to\rthe foresaid countriesthat they should come to London and bring their\rpeople with them,promising them how they should find London open to\rreceive them and thecommons of the city to be of the same accord,\rsaying how they would doso much to the king that there should not be\rone bondman in allEngland.\r \rThis promise moved so themof Kent, of Essex, of Sussex, of Bedford\rand of the countriesabout, that they rose and came towards London to\rthe number of sixtythousand. And they had a captain called Water\rTyler, and with him incompany was Jack Straw and John Ball: these\rthree were chief sovereigncaptains, but the head of all was Water\rTyler, and he was indeed atiler of houses, an ungracious patron. When\rthese unhappy men beganthus to stir, they of London, except such as\rwere of their band, weregreatly affrayed. Then the mayor of London\rand the rich men of thecity took counsel together, and when they saw\rthe people thus coming onevery side, they caused the gates of the\rcity to be closed andwould suffer no man to enter into the city. But\rwhen they had well imagined,they advised not so to do, for they\rthought they shouldthereby put their suburbs in great peril to be\rbrent; and so they openedagain the city, and there entered in at the\rgates in some place ahundred, two hundred, by twenty and by thirty,\rand so when they came toLondon, they entered and lodged: and yet of\rtruth the third part[3] ofthese people could not tell what to ask or\rdemand, but followed eachother like beasts, as the shepherds[4] did\rof old time, saying howthey would go conquer the Holy Land, and at\rlast all came to nothing.In like wise these villains and poor people\rcame to London, a hundredmile off, sixty mile, fifty mile, forty\rmile, and twenty mile off,and from all countries about London, but\rthe most part came fromthe countries before named, and as they came\rthey demanded ever for theking. The gentlemen of the countries,\rknights and squires, beganto doubt, when they saw the people began to\rrebel; and though theywere in doubt, it was good reason; for a less\roccasion they might havebeen affrayed. So the gentlemen drew together\ras well as they might.\r \r      [3] \'Bien les trois pars.\'  i.e. \'three-fourths.\'\r \r      [4] \'Les pastoureaulx.\' The reference nodoubt is to the\r      Pastoureaux of 1320, who were destroyedat Aigues-Mortes when\r      attempting to obtain a passage to theHoly Land.\r \rThe same day that theseunhappy people of Kent were coming to London,\rthere returned fromCanterbury the king\'s mother, princess of Wales,\rcoming from herpilgrimage. She was in great jeopardy to have been\rlost, for these peoplecame to her chare and dealt rudely with her,\rwhereof the good lady wasin great doubt lest they would have done\rsome villany to her or toher damosels. Howbeit, God kept her, and she\rcame in one day fromCanterbury to London, for she never durst tarry\rby the way. The same timeking Richard her son was at the Tower of\rLondon: there his motherfound him, and with him there was the earl of\rSalisbury, the archbishopof Canterbury, sir Robert of Namur, the lord\rof Gommegnies and diversother, who were in doubt of these people that\rthus gathered together,and wist not what they demanded. This\rrebellion was well knownin the king\'s court, or any of these people\rbegan to stir out of theirhouses; but the king nor his council did\rprovide no remedytherefor, which was great marvel. And to the intent\rthat all lords and goodpeople and such as would nothing but good\rshould take ensample tocorrect them that be evil and rebellious, I\rshall shew you plainly allthe matter, as it was.\r \r \r \r \rTHE EVIL DEEDS THAT THESECOMMONS OF ENGLAND DID TO THE KING\'S\rOFFICERS, AND HOW THEYSENT A KNIGHT TO SPEAK WITH THE KING\r \r \rThe Monday before thefeast of Corpus Christi the year of our Lord God\ra thousand three hundredand eighty-one these people issued out of\rtheir houses to come toLondon to speak with the king to be made free,\rfor they would have had nobondman in England. And so first they came\rto Saint Thomas ofCanterbury, and there John Ball had thought to have\rfound the bishop ofCanterbury, but he was at London with the king.\rWhen Wat Tyler and JackStraw entered into Canterbury, all the common\rpeople made great feast,for all the town was of their assent; and\rthere they took counsel togo to London to the king, and to send some\rof their company over theriver of Thames into Essex, into Sussex and\rinto the counties ofStafford and Bedford, to speak to the people that\rthey should all come tothe farther side of London and thereby to\rclose London round about,so that the king should not stop their\rpassages, and that theyshould all meet together on Corpus Christi\rday. They that were atCanterbury entered into Saint Thomas\' church\rand did there much hurt,and robbed and brake up the bishop\'s chamber,\rand in robbing and bearingout their pillage they said: \'Ah, this\rchancellor of England hathhad a good market to get together all this\rriches: he shall give usnow account of the revenues of England and of\rthe great profits that hehath gathered sith the king\'s coronation.\'\rWhen they had this Mondaythus broken the abbey of Saint Vincent, they\rdeparted in the morningand all the people of Canterbury with them,\rand so took the way toRochester and sent their people to the villages\rabout.
