Andwhen they were come to Rochester, they had\rthere good cheer; for thepeople of that town tarried for them, for\rthey were of the samesect, and then they went to the castle there and\rtook the knight that hadthe rule thereof, he was called sir John\rNewton, and they said tohim: \'Sir, it behoveth you to go with us and\ryou shall be our sovereigncaptain and to do that we will have you,\'\rThe knight excused himselfhonestly and shewed them divers\rconsiderations andexcuses, but all availed him nothing, for they said\runto him: \'Sir John, if yedo not as we will have you, ye are but\rdead,\' The knight, seeingthese people in that fury and ready to slay\rhim, he then doubted deathand agreed to them, and so they took him\rwith them against hisinward will; and in like wise did they of other\rcounties in England, asEssex, Sussex, Stafford, Bedford and Warwick,\reven to Lincoln; for theybrought the knights and gentlemen into such\robeisance, that theycaused them to go with them, whether they would\ror not, as the lordMoylays, a great baron, sir Stephen of Hales and\rsir Thomas of Cosingtonand other.\r \rNow behold the greatfortune. If they might have come to their\rintents, they would havedestroyed all the noblemen of England, and\rthereafter all othernations would have followed the same and have\rtaken foot and ensample bythem and by them of Gaunt and Flanders, who\rrebelled against theirlord. The same year the Parisians rebelled in\rlike wise and found outthe mallets of iron, of whom there were more\rthan twenty thousand, asye shall hear after in this history; but\rfirst we will speak ofthem of England.\r \rWhen these people thuslodged at Rochester departed, and passed the\rriver and came toBrentford, alway keeping still their opinions,\rbeating down before themand all about the places and houses of\radvocates and procurers,and striking off the heads of divers persons.\rAnd so long they wentforward till they came within a four mile of\rLondon, and there lodgedon a hill called Blackheath; and as they\rwent, they said ever theywere the king\'s men and the noble commons of\rEngland:[1] and when theyof London knew that they were come so near\rto them, the mayor, as yehave heard before, closed the gates and kept\rstraitly all the passages.This order caused the mayor, who was called\rNicholas Walworth,[2] anddivers other rich burgesses of the city, who\rwere not of their sect;but there were in London of their unhappy\ropinions more than thirtythousand.\r \r      [1] \'That they were for the king and thenoble commons (or\r      commonwealth) of England.\'\r \r      [2] Froissart calls him John: his namewas really William.\r \rThen these people thusbeing lodged on Blackheath determined to send\rtheir knight to speak withthe king and to shew him how all that they\rhave done or will do isfor him and his honour, and how the realm of\rEngland hath not been wellgoverned a great space for the honour of\rthe realm nor for thecommon profit by his uncles and by the clergy,\rand specially by thearchbishop of Canterbury his chancellor; whereof\rthey would have account.This knight durst do none otherwise, but so\rcame by the river ofThames to the Tower. The king and they that were\rwith him in the Tower,desiring to hear tidings, seeing this knight\rcoming made him way, andwas brought before the king into a chamber;\rand with the king was theprincess his mother and his two brethren,\rthe earl of Kent and thelord John Holland, the earl of Salisbury, the\rearl of Warwick, the earlof Oxford, the archbishop of Canterbury, the\rlord of Saint John\'s,[3]sir Robert of Namur, the lord of Vertaing,\rthe lord of Gommegnies,sir Henry of Senzeille, the mayor of London\rand divers other notableburgesses. BetweenDurham and Newcastle is but twelve leagues\rEnglish and a goodcountry: there was no town, without it were closed,\rbut it was brent, and theyrepassed the river of Tyne where they had\rpassed before, and thencame before Newcastle and there rested. The earl of Northumberland\'s\rtwo sons were two younglusty knights and were ever foremost at the\rbarriers to scrimmish.There were many proper feats of arms done and\rachieved: there wasfighting hand to hand: among other there fought\rhand to hand the earlDouglas and sir Henry Percy, and by force of\rarms the earl Douglas wonthe pennon of sir Henry Percy\'s, wherewith\rhe was sore displeased andso were all the Englishmen. And the earl\rDouglas said to sir HenryPercy: \'Sir, I shall bear this token of your\rprowess into Scotland andshall set it on high on my castle of\rDalkeith, that it may beseen far off,\' \'Sir,\' quoth sir Henry, \'ye\rmay be sure ye shall notpass the bounds of this country till ye be\rmet withal in such wisethat ye shall make none avaunt thereof,\'\r\'Well, sir,\' quoth theearl Douglas, \'come this night to my lodging\rand seek for your pennon:I shall set it before my lodging and see if\rye will come to take itaway.\' So then it was late, and the Scots\rwithdrew to their lodgingsand refreshed them with such as they had.\rThey had flesh enough:they made that night good watch, for they\rthought surely to beawaked for the words they had spoken, but they\rwere not, for sir HenryPercy was counselled not so to do.\r \rThe next day the Scotsdislodged and returned towards their own\rcountry, and so came to acastle and a town called Pontland, whereof\rsir Edmund of Alphel waslord, who was a right good knight. There the\rScots rested, for theycame thither betimes, and understood that the\rknight was in his castle.Then they ordained to assail the castle, and\rgave a great assault, sothat by force of arms they won it and the\rknight within it. Then thetown and castle was brent; and from thence\rthe Scots went to the townand castle of Otterburn, an eight English\rmile from Newcastle[2] andthere lodged. That day they made none\rassault, but the nextmorning they blew their horns and made ready to\rassail the castle, whichwas strong, for it stood in the marish. That\rday they assaulted tillthey were weary, and did nothing. Then they\rsowned the retreat andreturned to their lodgings. Then the lords drew\rto council to determinewhat they should do. The most part were of the\raccord that the next daythey should dislodge without giving of any\rassault and to draw fairand easily towards Carlisle. But the earl\rDouglas brake that counseland said: \'In despite of sir Henry Percy,\rwho said he would come andwin again his pennon, let us not depart\rhence for two or threedays. Let us assail this castle: it is\rpregnable: we shall havedouble honour. And then let us see if he will\rcome and fetch his pennon:he shall be well defended.\'[3] Every man\raccorded to his saying,what for their honour and for the love of him.\rAlso they lodged there attheir ease, for there was none that troubled\rthem: they made manylodgings of boughs and great herbs and fortified\rtheir camp sagely with themarish that was thereby, and their\rcarriages were set at theentry into the marishes and had all their\rbeasts within the marish.Then they apparelled for to assault the next\rday: this was theirintention.\r \r      [2] Froissart says \'eight Englishleagues.\' In the next chapter\r      the distance becomes \'seven littleleagues,\' and later on, \'a\r      six English miles,\' where the original is\'lieues.\' The actual\r      distance is about thirty miles. Thetranslator gives the form\r      \'Combur\' here, but \'Ottenburge\' in thenext chapter, as the\r      name of the place. The knights of the country, such\ras were well expert inarms, spake against sir Henry Percy\'s opinion\rand said to him: \'Sir,there fortuneth in war oftentimes many losses.\rIf the earl Douglas havewon your pennon, he bought it dear, for he\rcame to the gate to seekit and was well beaten:[4] another day ye\rshall win as much of himor more. Sir, we say this because we know\rwell all the power ofScotland is abroad in the fields, and if we\rissue out and be not menenow to fight with them, and peradventure\rthey have made thisscrimmish with us to the intent to draw us out of\rthe town, and the numberthat they be of, as it is said, above forty\rthousand men, they maysoon enclose us and do with us what they will.\rYet it were better to losea pennon than two or three hundred knights\rand squires and put allour country in adventure,\' These words\rrefrained sir Henry andhis brother, for they would do nothing against\rcounsel. They acquitted\rthemselves that dayvaliantly: the earl\'s banner had been won, an they\rhad not been: theydefended it so valiantly and in the rescuing\rthereof did such feats ofarms, that it was greatly to their\rrecommendation and totheir heirs\' for ever after.\r \r      [1] In French, \'ilz se arresterent,\'without \'and.\'\r \rIt was shewed me by suchas had been at the same battle, as well by\rknights and squires ofEngland as of Scotland, at the house of the\rearl of Foix,--for anonafter this battle was done I met at Orthez two\rsquires of England calledJohn of Chateauneuf and John of Cantiron;\ralso when I returned toAvignon I found also there a knight and a\rsquire of Scotland; I knewthem and they knew me by such tokens as I\rshewed them of theircountry, for I, author of this book, in my youth\rhad ridden nigh over allthe realm of Scotland, and I was as then a\rfifteen days in the houseof earl William Douglas, father to the same\rearl James, of whom Ispake of now, in a castle of five leagues from\rEdinburgh in the countryof Dalkeith;[2] the same time I saw there\rthis earl James, a fairyoung child, and a sister of his called the\rlady Blanche,--and I wasinformed by both these parties[3] how this\rbattle was as sore abattle fought as lightly hath been heard of\rbefore of such a number;and I believe it well, for Englishmen on the\rone party and Scots on theother party are good men of war, for when\rthey meet there is a hardfight without sparing, there is no ho\rbetween them as long asspears, swords, axes or daggers will endure,\rbut lay on each uponother, and when they be well beaten[4] and that\rthe one party hathobtained the victory, they then glorify so in their\rdeeds of arms and are sojoyful, that such as be taken they shall be\rransomed or they go out ofthe field, so that shortly each of them is\rso content with other thatat their departing-courteously they will\rsay, \'God thank you\'; butin fighting one with another there is no\rplay nor sparing, and thisis true, and that shall well appear by this\rsaid rencounter, for itwas as valiantly foughten as could be devised,\ras ye shall hear.\r \r      [2] \'Which is called in the countryDalkeith.\' The French has\r      \'que on nomme au pays Dacquest,\' of whichthe translator makes\r      \'in the countrey of Alquest.\'\r \r      [3] \'By both sides,\' i.e. Scotch andEnglish.\r \r      [4] \'When they have well fought.\'\r \r \r \r \rHOW THE EARL JAMES DOUGLASBY HIS VALIANTNESS ENCOURAGED HIS MEN, WHO\rWERE RECULED AND IN AMANNER DISCOMFITED, AND IN HIS SO DOING HE WAS\rWOUNDED TO DEATH\r \r \rKnights and squires wereof good courage on both parties to fight\rvaliantly: cowards therehad no place, but hardiness reigned with\rgoodly feats of arms, forknights and squires were so joined together\rat hand strokes, thatarchers had no place of nother party. Thus, as I have\rsaid, the banners ofDouglas and Percy and their men were met each\ragainst other, envious whoshould win the honour of that journey. At\rthe beginning theEnglishmen were so strong that they reculed back\rtheir enemies: then theearl Douglas, who was of great heart and high\rof enterprise, seeing hismen recule back, then to recover the place\rand to shew knightlyvalour he took his axe in both his hands, and\rentered so into the pressthat he made himself way in such wise, that\rnone durst approach nearhim, and he was so well armed that he bare\rwell off such strokes ashe received.[1] Thus he went ever forward\rlike a hardy Hector,willing alone to conquer the field and to\rdiscomfit his enemies: butat last he was encountered with three\rspears all at once, theone strake him on the shoulder, the other on\rthe breast and the strokeglinted down to his belly, and the third\rstrake him in the thigh,and sore hurt with all three strokes, so that\rhe was borne perforce tothe earth and after that he could not be\ragain relieved. On the other part the\rearl George de la Marchand of Dunbar fought right valiantly and gave\rthe Englishmen much ado,and cried, \'Follow Douglas,\' and set on the\rsons of Percy: also earlJohn of Moray with his banner and men fought\rvaliantly and set fiercelyon the Englishmen, and gave them so much to\rdo that they wist not towhom to attend.\r \r      [1] \'No man was so well armed that he didnot fear the great\r      strokes which he gave.\'\r \r \r \r \rHOW IN THIS BATTLE SIRRALPH PERCY WAS SORE HURT AND TAKEN PRISONER BY\rA SCOTTISH KNIGHT\r \r \rOf all the battles andencounterings that I have made mention of\rherebefore in all thishistory, great or small, this battle that I\rtreat of now was one ofthe sorest and best foughten without cowardice\ror faint hearts. Chrétien died leaving the poem unfinished,\rand it was continued bythree other authors till it reached the vast\rsize of 63,000 lines. Thereligious signification of the Grail is\rsupposed to have beenattached to it early in the thirteenth century\rby Robert de Boron; and,perhaps a little later, in the French prose\r"Quest of the HolyGrail," Galahad takes the place of Perceval as the\rhero of the story. Thelater history of the various versions of the\rlegend is highlyintricate, and in many points uncertain. It was from\ra form of it embodied inthe French prose "Lancelot" that Sir Thomas\rMalory drew the chaptersof his "Morte d\'Arthur" which are here\rreprinted, and which, morethan the earlier versions, are the source\rfrom which the legend haspassed into modern English poetry.\r \rUntil a few years agoMalory himself was little more than a name, our\rinformation about himbeing limited to the statement in Caxton\'s\redition of the "Morted\'Arthur" that he was the author. It now appears\rprobable, however, thatSir Thomas Malory was an English knight born\rabout 1400, of an oldWarwickshire family. He served in the French\rwars under RichardBeauchamp, Earl of Warwick, "whom all Europe\rrecognized as embodyingthe knightly ideal of the age" and may well\rhave owed his enthusiasmfor chivalry to his association with this\rdistinguished nobleman. Hedied in 1471.\r \rMalory\'s book is acompilation from French and English sources. These\rare chosen without muchdiscrimination, and put together without great\rskill in arrangement. Butthe author\'s whole-hearted enthusiasm for\rchivalrous ideals and thenoble simplicity and fine rhythm of his\rprose have combined togive his work a unique place in English\rliterature. In it the ageof chivalry is summed up and closed. It is\rnot without reason thatthe date of its publication by Caxton, 1485,\rshould be conventionallyaccepted as the end of the Middle Ages in\rEngland. Romance hadpassed under the printing press, and a new age\rhad begun._\r \r \r \r \rTHE HOLY GRAIL\r \rBEING BOOKS XIII, XIV, XV,XVI and XVII OF THE BOOK OF KING ARTHUR AND\rOF HIS NOBLE KNIGHTS OFTHE ROUND TABLE\r \r \r \r \rTHE THIRTEENTH BOOK.\r \r \r \rCHAPTER I\r \rHOW AT THE VIGIL OF THEFEAST OF PENTECOST ENTERED INTO THE HALL\rBEFORE KING ARTHUR ADAMOSEL, AND DESIRED SIR LAUNCELOT FOR TO COME\rAND DUB A KNIGHT, AND HOWHE WENT WITH HER\r \r \rAt the vigil of Pentecost,when all the fellowship of the Round Table\rwere come unto Camelot andthere heard their service, and the tables\rwere set ready to themeat, right so entered into the hall a full fair\rgentlewoman on horseback,that had ridden full fast, for her horse was\rall besweated. To him wasallotted the task of writing the "Descriptions of\rBritain and England"from which the following chapters are drawn. He\rgathered his facts frombooks, letters, maps, conversations, and, most\rimportant of all, his ownobservation and experience; and he put them\rloosely together into whathe calls "this foul frizzled treatise."\rYet, with all his modesty,he claims to "have had an especial eye to\rthe truth of things";and as a result we have in his pages the most\rvivid and detailed picturein existence of the England into which\rShakespeare was born.\r \rIn 1876 Dr. Furnivallcondensed Harrison\'s chapters for the New\rShakspere Society, andthese have since been reprinted by Mr. Lothrop\rWithington in the moderndress in which the most interesting of them\rappear here. No apology isneeded for thus selecting and rearranging,\rsince in their originalform they were without unity, and formed part\rof a vast compilation.\r \rHarrison\'s merit does notlie in the rich interest of his matter\ralone. He wrote a racystyle with a strong individual as well as\rElizabethan flavor; andhis personal comment upon the manners of his\rtime serves as a piquantsauce to the solid meat of his historical\rinformation._\r \r \r \r \rA DESCRIPTION OFELIZABETHAN ENGLAND\r \r \r \rCHAPTER I\r \rOF DEGREES OF PEOPLE INTHE COMMONWEALTH OF ELIZABETHAN ENGLAND\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapter4; 1587, Book II., Chapter 5.][1]\r \r \r      [1] These references are to the first twoeditions of\r      Holinshed\'s _Chronicles_. Themodernization of the spelling,\r      etc., follows that of Mr. L. Wilkington,whose notes are signed\r      W.\r \rWe in England, divide ourpeople commonly into four sorts, as\rgentlemen, citizens orburgesses, yeomen, and artificers or labourers.\rOf gentlemen the first andchief (next the king) be the prince, dukes,\rmarquesses, earls,viscounts, and barons; and these are called\rgentlemen of the greatersort, or (as our common usage of speech is)\rlords and noblemen: andnext unto them be knights, esquires, and, last\rof all, they that aresimply called gentlemen. So that in effect our\rgentlemen are divided intotheir conditions, whereof in this chapter\rI will make particularrehearsal.\r \rThe title of prince dothpeculiarly belong with us to the king\'s\reldest son, who is calledPrince of Wales, and is the heir-apparent\rto the crown; as in Francethe king\'s eldest son hath the title of\rDauphin, and is namedpeculiarly _Monsieur_. So that the prince is so\rtermed of the Latin word_Princeps_, since he is (as I may call him)\rthe chief or principalnext the king. The king\'s younger sons be but\rgentlemen by birth (tillthey have received creation or donation from\rtheir father of higherestate, as to be either viscounts, earls, or\rdukes) and called aftertheir names, as Lord Henry, or Lord Edward,\rwith the addition of theword Grace, properly assigned to the king and\rprince, and now also bycustom conveyed to dukes, archbishops, and (as\rsome say) to marquessesand their wives.[2]...\r \r      [2] Here follow etymologies of the terms"Duke," "Marquess,"\r      and "Baron."--W.\r \rUnto this place I alsorefer our bishops, who are accounted\rhonourable, called lords,and hold the same room in the Parliament\rhouse with the barons,albeit for honour sake the right hand of the\rprince is given unto them,and whose countenances in time past were\rmuch more glorious than atthis present it is, because those lusty\rprelates sought afterearthly estimation and authority with far more\rdiligence than after thelost sheep of Christ, of which they had small\rregard, as men beingotherwise occupied and void of leisure to attend\rupon the same. Howbeit inthese days their estate remaineth no less\rreverend than before, andthe more virtuous they are that be of this\rcalling the better arethey esteemed with high and low. They retain\ralso the ancient name("lord") still, although it be not a little\rimpugned by such as loveeither to hear of change of all things or can\rabide no superiors. Fornotwithstanding it be true that in respect of\rfunction the office of theeldership[3] is equally distributed between\rthe bishop and theminister, yet for civil government\'s sake the first\rhave more authority givenunto them by kings and princes, to the end\rthat the rest may therebybe with more ease retained within a limited\rcompass of uniformity thanotherwise they would be if each one were\rsuffered to walk in hisown course. This also is more to be marvelled\rat, that very many callfor an alteration of their estate, crying to\rhave the word"lord" abolished, their civil authority taken from them,\rand the present conditionof the church in other things reformed;\rwhereas, to say truly, fewof them do agree upon form of discipline\rand government of thechurch succeedent, wherein they resemble the\rCapuans (of whom Livy dothspeak) in the slaughter of their senate.\rNeither is it possible toframe a whole monarchy after the pattern of\rone town or city, or tostir up such an exquisite face of the church\ras we imagine or desire,sith our corruption is such that it will\rnever yield to so greatperfection; for that which is not able to be\rperformed in a privatehouse will be much less be brought to pass in a\rcommonwealth and kingdom,before such a prince be found as Xenophon\rdescribeth, or such anorator as Tully hath devised.[4]...\r \r      [3] 1 Sam. ii. 15; 1 Kings i. 7.--H.\r \r      [4] Here follows a long paragraph on thecharacter of the clergy\r      which is more appropriate to the chapteron "The Church."--W.\r \rDukes, marquesses, earls,viscounts, and barons either be created of\rthe prince or come to thathonour by being the eldest sons or highest\rin succession to theirparents. For the eldest son of a duke during\rhis father\'s life is anearl, the eldest son of an earl is a baron, or\rsometimes a viscount,according as the creation is. The creation I\rcall the original donationand condition of the honour given by the\rprince for good servicedone by the first ancestor, with some\radvancement, which, withthe title of that honour, is always given to\rhim and his heirs malesonly. The rest of the sons of the nobility by\rthe rigour of the law bebut esquires; yet in common speech all dukes\'\rand marquesses\' sons andearls\' eldest sons be called lords, the which\rname commonly doth agreeto none of lower degree than barons, yet by\rlaw and use these be notesteemed barons.\r \rThe barony or degree of lordsdoth answer to the degree of senators of\rRome (as I said) and thetitle of nobility (as we used to call it in\rEngland) to the Roman_Patricii_. Also in England no man is commonly\rcreated baron except hemay dispend of yearly revenues a thousand\rpounds, or so much as mayfully maintain and bear out his countenance\rand port. But viscounts,earls, marquesses, and dukes exceed them\raccording to theproportion of their degree and honour. But though by\rchance he or his son haveless, yet he keepeth this degree: but if the\rdecay be excessive, andnot able to maintain the honour (as _Senatores\rRomani_ were _amoti àsenatu_), so sometimes they are not admitted to\rthe upper house in theparliament, although they keep the name of\r"lord" still,which cannot be taken from them upon any such occasion.\r \rThe most of these nameshave descended from the French invention, in\rwhose histories we shallread of them eight hundred years past.[5]...\r \r      [5] Here follows a learned disquisitionupon "Valvasors."--W.\r \rKnights be not born,neither is any man a knight by succession, no,\rnot the king or prince:but they are made either before the battle, to\rencourage them the more toadventure and try their manhood; or after\rthe battle ended, as anadvancement for their courage and prowess\ralready shewed, and thenare they called _Milites_; or out of the wars\rfor some great servicedone, or for the singular virtues which do\rappear in them, and thenare they named _Equites Aurati_, as common\rcustom intendeth. They aremade either by the king himself, or by his\rcommission and royalauthority given for the same purpose, or by his\rlieutenant in thewars.[6]...\r \r      [6] Here follows a discourse upon_Equites Aurati_.--W.\r \rSometime diverse ancientgentlemen, burgesses, and lawyers are called\runto knighthood by theprince, and nevertheless refuse to take that\rstate upon them, for whichthey are of custom punished by a fine, that\rredoundeth unto hiscoffers, and (to say truth) is oftentimes more\rprofitable unto him thanotherwise their service should be, if they\rdid yield unto knighthood.And this also is a cause wherefore there be\rmany in England able todispend a knight\'s living, which never come\runto that countenance, andby their own consents. The number of the\rknights in Rome was alsouncertain: and so is it of knights likewise,\rwith us, as at thepleasure of the prince. And whereas the _Equites\rRomani_ had _EquumPublicum_ of custom bestowed upon them, the knights\rof England have not so,but bear their own charges in that also, as in\rother kind of furniture,as armour meet for their defence and service.\rThis nevertheless iscertain, that whoso may dispend forty pounds by\rthe year of free land,either at the coronation of the king, or\rmarriage of his daughter,or time of his dubbing, may be informed unto\rthe taking of that degree,or otherwise pay the revenues of his land\rfor one year, which isonly forty pounds by an old proportion, and so\rfor a time be acquitted ofthat title.[7]...\r \r      [7] Here is a description of dubbing aknight.--W.\r \rAt the coronation of aking or queen, there be other knights made with\rlonger and more curiousceremonies, called "knights of the bath." But\rhowsoever one be dubbed ormade knight, his wife is by-and-by called\r"Madam," or"Lady," so well as the baron\'s wife: he himself having\radded to his name incommon appellation this syllable "Sir," which is\rthe title whereby we callour knights in England. His wife also of\rcourtesy so long as sheliveth is called "my lady," although she\rhappen to marry with agentleman or man of mean calling, albeit that\rby the common law she hathno such prerogative. If her first husband\ralso be of better birththan her second, though this latter likewise\rbe a knight, yet in thatshe pretendeth a privilege to lose no honour\rthrough courtesy yieldedto her sex, she will be named after the most\rhonourable or worshipfulof both, which is not seen elsewhere.\r \rThe other order ofknighthood in England, and the most honourable, is\rthat of the garter,instituted by King Edward the Third, who, after he\rhad gained many notablevictories, taken King John of France, and King\rJames of Scotland (andkept them both prisoners in the Tower o£ London\rat one time), expelledKing Henry of Castille, the bastard, out of his\rrealm, and restored DonPedro unto it (by the help of the Prince of\rWales and Duke ofAquitaine, his eldest son, called the Black Prince),\rhe then invented thissociety of honour, and made a choice out of his\rown realm and dominions,and throughout all Christendom of the best,\rmost excellent, andrenowned persons in all virtues and honour, and\radorned them with thattitle to be knights of his order, giving them a\rgarter garnished with goldand precious stones, to wear daily on the\rleft leg only; also akirtle, gown, cloak, chaperon, collar, and other\rsolemn and magnificentapparel, both of stuff and fashion exquisite\rand heroical to wear athigh feasts, and as to so high and princely an\rorder appertaineth....\r \rThe order of the gartertherefore was devised in the time of King\rEdward the Third, and (assome write) upon this occasion. The queen\'s\rmajesty then living, beingdeparted from his presence the next way\rtoward her lodging, hefollowing soon after happened to find her\rgarter, which slacked bychance and so fell from her leg, unespied in\rthe throng by such asattended upon her. His grooms and gentlemen also\rpassed by it, asdisdaining to stoop and take up such a trifle: but\rhe, knowing the owner,commanded one of them to stay and reach it up\rto him. "Why, andlike your grace," saith a gentleman, "it is but some\rwoman\'s garter that hathfallen from her as she followed the queen\'s\rmajesty.""Whatsoever it be," quoth the king, "take it up and give it\rme." So when he hadreceived the garter, he said to such as stood\rabout him: "You, mymasters, do make small account of this bule garter\rhere," and therewithheld it out, "but, if God lend me life for a few\rmonths, I will make theproudest of you all to reverence the like."\rAnd even upon this slenderoccasion he gave himself to the devising of\rthis order. Certes, I havenot read of anything that having had so\rsimple a beginning hathgrown in the end to so great honour and\restimation.[8]...\r \r      [8] Long details are given of Garterhistory, very inaccurate,\r      both here and in the last omittedpassage.--W.\r \rThere is yet another orderof knights In England called knights\rbannerets, who are made inthe field with the ceremony of cutting away\rthe point of his pennantof arms, and making it as it were a banner,\rso that, being before buta bachelor knight, he is now of an higher\rdegree, and allowed todisplay his arms in a banner, as barons do.\rHowbeit these knights arenever made but in the wars, the king\'s\rstandard beingunfolded.[9]...\r \r      [9] Derivations of "Esquire"and "Gentleman" are given.--W.\r \rMoreover, as the king dothdub knights, and createth the barons and\rhigher degrees, sogentlemen whose ancestors are not known to come in\rwith William Duke ofNormandy (for of the Saxon races yet remaining we\rnow make none accounted,much less of the British issue) do take their\rbeginning in England,after this manner in our times.\r \rWhosoever studieth thelaws of the realm, whoso abideth in the\runiversity (giving hismind to his book), or professeth physic and the\rliberal sciences, orbeside his service in the room of a captain in the\rwars, or good counselgiven at home, whereby his commonwealth is\rbenefited, can livewithout manual labour, and thereto is able and will\rbear the port, charge, andcountenance of a gentleman, he shall for\rmoney have a coat and armsbestowed upon him by heralds (who in the\rcharter of the same do ofcustom pretend antiquity and service, and\rmany gay things), andthereunto, being made so good cheap, be called\rmaster (which is the titlethat men give to esquires and gentlemen),\rand reputed for agentleman ever after, which is so much less to be\rdisallowed of for that theprince doth lose nothing by it, the\rgentleman being so muchsubject to taxes and public payments as is the\ryeoman or husbandman,which he likewise doth bear the gladlier for the\rsaving of his reputation.Being called also to the wars (for with the\rgovernment of thecommonwealth he meddleth little), whatsoever it cost\rhim, he will both arrayand arm himself accordingly, and shew the more\rmanly courage, and all thetokens of the person which he represented.\rNo man hath hurt by it buthimself, who peradventure will go in wider\rbuskins than his legs willbear, or, as our proverb saith, "now and\rthen bear a bigger sailthan his boat is able to sustain."\r \rCertes the making of newgentlemen bred great strife sometimes amongst\rthe Romans, I mean whenthose which were _Novi homines_ were more\rallowed of for theirvirtues newly seen and shewed than the old smell\rof ancient race, latelydefaced by the cowardice and evil life of their\rnephews and descendants,could make the other to be. But as envy hath\rno affinity with justiceand equity, so it forceth not what language\rthe malicious do give out,against such as are exalted for their\rwisdoms. This neverthelessis generally to be reprehended in all\restates of gentility, andwhich in short time will turn to the great\rruin of our country, andthat is, the usual sending of noblemen\'s and\rmean gentlemen\'s sons intoItaly, from whence they bring home nothing\rbut mere atheism,infidelity, vicious conversation, and ambitious and\rproud behaviour, wherebyit cometh to pass that they return far worse\rmen than they went out. Agentleman at this present is newly come out\rof Italy, who went thitheran earnest Protestant; but coming home he\rcould say after thismanner; "Faith and truth is to be kept where no\rloss or hindrance of afuture purpose is sustained by holding of the\rsame; and forgiveness onlyto be shewed when full revenge is made."\rAnother no less forwardthan he, at his return from thence, could add\rthus much: "He is afool that maketh account of any religion, but more\rfool that will lose anypart of his wealth or will come in trouble for\rconstant leaning to any;but if he yield to lose his life for his\rpossession, he is starkmad, and worthy to be taken for most fool of\rall the rest." Thisgay booty got these gentlemen by going Into Italy;\rand hereby a man may seewhat fruit is afterward to be looked for where\rsuch blossoms do appear."I care not," saith a third, "what you talk to\rme of God, so as I mayhave the prince and the laws of the realm on my\rside." Such men asthis last are easily known; for they have learned in\rItaly to go up and downalso in England with pages at their heels\rfinely apparelled, whoseface and countenance shall be such as sheweth\rthe master not to be blindin his choice. But lest I should offend too\rmuch, I pass over to say anymore of these Italianates and their\rdemeanour, which, alas! istoo open and manifest to the world, and yet\rnot called into question.\r \rCitizens and burgesseshave next place to gentlemen, who be those that\rare free within thecities, and are of some likely substance to bear\roffice in the same. Butthese citizens or burgesses are to serve the\rcommonwealth in theircities and boroughs, or in corporate towns where\rthey dwell, and in thecommon assembly of the realm wherein our laws\rare made (for in thecounties they bear but little sway), which\rassembly is called theHigh Court of Parliament: the ancient cities\rappoint four and theborough two burgesses to have voices in it, and\rgive their consent ordissent unto such things as pass, to stay there\rin the name of the city orborough for which they are appointed.\r \rIn this place also are ourmerchants to be installed as amongst the\rcitizens (although theyoften change estate with gentlemen, as\rgentlemen do with them, bya mutual conversion of the one into the\rother), whose number is soincreased in these our days that their\ronly maintenance is thecause of the exceeding prices of foreign\rwares, which otherwise,when every nation was permitted to bring in\rher own commodities, werefar better, cheaper, and more plentifully\rto be had. Of the want ofour commodities here at home, by their\rgreat transportation ofthem into other countries, I speak not, sith\rthe matter will easilybetray itself. Certes among the Lacedæmonians\rit was found out thatgreat numbers of merchants were nothing to the\rfurtherance of the stateof the commonwealth: wherefore it is to be\rwished that the huge heapof them were somewhat restrained, as also\rof our lawyers, so shouldthe rest live more easily upon their own,\rand few honest chapmen bebrought to decay by breaking of the\rbankrupt. I do not denybut that the navy of the land is in part\rmaintained by theirtraffic, and so are the high prices of wares kept\rup, now they have gottenthe only sale of things upon pretence of\rbetter furtherance of thecommonwealth into their own hands: whereas\rin times past, when thestrange bottoms were suffered to come in, we\rhad sugar for fourpencethe pound, that now at the writing of this\rTreatise is well worthhalf-a-crown; raisins or currants for a penny\rthat now are holden atsixpence, and sometimes at eightpence and\rtenpence the pound;nutmegs at twopence halfpenny the ounce, ginger\rat a penny an ounce,prunes at halfpenny farthing, great raisins\rthree pounds for a penny,cinnamon at fourpence the ounce, cloves at\rtwopence, and pepper attwelve and sixteen pence the pound. Whereby\rwe may see the sequel ofthings not always, but very seldom, to be\rsuch as is pretended inthe beginning. The wares that they carry out\rof the realm are for themost part broad clothes and carsies[10] of\rall colours, likewisecottons, friezes, rugs, tin, wool, our best\rbeer, baize, bustian,mockadoes (tufted and plain), rash, lead,\rfells, etc.: which, beingshipped at sundry ports of our coasts, are\rborne from thence into allquarters of the world, and there either\rexchanged for other waresor ready money, to the great gain and\rcommodity of ourmerchants. And whereas in times past their chief\rtrade was into Spain,Portugal, France, Flanders, Danske (Denmark),\rNorway, Scotland, andIreland only, now in these days, as men not\rcontented with thesejourneys, they have sought out the East and West\rIndies, and made now andthen suspicious voyages, not only unto the\rCanaries and New Spain,but likewise into Cathay, Muscovy, and\rTartaria, and the regionsthereabout, from whence (as they say) they\rbring home greatcommodities. But alas! I see not by all their travel\rthat the prices of thingsare any whit abated. Certes this enormity\r(for so I do account ofit) was sufficiently provided for (Ann. 9\rEdward III.) by a noblestatute made in that behalf, but upon what\roccasion the generalexecution thereof is stayed or not called on, in\rgood sooth, I cannot tell.This only I know, that every function and\rseveral vocation strivethwith other, which of them should have all\rthe water of commodity runinto her own cistern.\r \r      [10] Kerseys.\r \rYeomen are those which byour law are called _Legales homines_, free\rmen born English, and maydispend of their own free land in yearly\rrevenue to the sum offorty shillings sterling, or six pounds as money\rgoeth in our times. Someare of the opinion, by Cap. 2 Rich. 2 Ann.\r20, that they are the samewhich the Frenchmen call varlets, but, as\rthat phrase is used in mytime, it is very unlikely to be so. The\rtruth is that the word isderived from the Saxon term, _Zeoman_, or\r_Geoman_, which signifieth(as I have read) a settled or staid man,\rsuch I mean as, beingmarried and of some years, betaketh himself to\rstay in the place of hisabode for the better maintenance of himself\rand his family, whereofthe single sort have no regard, but are likely\rto be still fleeting nowhither now thither, which argueth want of\rstability in determinationand resolution of judgment, for the\rexecution of things of anyimportance. This sort of people have a\rcertain pre-eminence, andmore estimation than labourers and the\rcommon sort of artificers,and these commonly live wealthily, keep\rgood houses, and travel toget riches. They are also for the most part\rfarmers to gentlemen (inold time called _Pagani, et opponuntur\rmilitibus_, and thereforePersius calleth himself _Semipaganus_), or\rat the leastwiseartificers, and with grazing, frequenting of markets,\rand keeping of servants(not idle servants, as the gentlemen do, but\rsuch as get both their ownand part of their masters\' living), do come\rto great wealth, insomuchthat many of them are able and do buy the\rlands of unthriftygentlemen, and often setting their sons to the\rschools, to theuniversities, and to the Inns of the Court, or,\rotherwise leaving themsufficient lands whereupon they may live\rwithout labour, do makethem by those means to become gentlemen. These\rwere they that in timespast made all France afraid. And albeit they\rbe not called"Master," as gentlemen are, or "Sir," as to knights\rappertaineth, but only"John" and "Thomas," etc., yet have they been\rfound to have done verygood service.\r \rThe kings of England infoughten battles were wont to remain among\rthem (who were theirfootmen) as the French kings did amongst their\rhorsemen, the princethereby shewing where his chief strength did\rconsist.\r \rThe fourth and last sortof people in England are day-labourers, poor\rhusbandmen, and someretailers (which have no free land) copyholders,\rand all artificers, astailors, shoemakers, carpenters, brickmakers,\rmasons, etc.[11]\r \r      [11] Capite censi, or Proletarii--H.\r \rAs for slaves and bondmen,we have none; nay, such is the privilege\rof our country by theespecial grace of God and bounty of our\rprinces, that if any comehither from other realms, so soon as they\rset foot on land theybecome so free of condition as their masters,\rwhereby all note ofservile bondage is utterly removed from them,\rwherein we resemble (notthe Germans, who had slaves also, though\rsuch as in respect of theslaves of other countries might well be\rreputed free, but) the oldIndians and the Taprobanes,[12] who\rsupposed it a great injuryto Nature to make or suffer them to be\rbond, whom she in herwonted course doth product and bring forth\rfree. This fourth and lastsort of people therefore have neither\rvoice nor authority in thecommonwealth, but are to be ruled and not\rto rule other: yet theyare not altogether neglected, for in cities\rand corporate towns, fordefault of yeomen, they are fain to make up\rtheir inquests of suchmanner of people. And in villages they are\rcommonly madechurchwardens, sidesmen, aleconners, now and then\rconstables, and many timesenjoy the name of head boroughs. Unto this\rsort also may our greatswarms of idle serving-men be referred, of\rwhom there runneth aproverb, "Young servingmen, old beggars,"\rbecause service is noneheritage. These men are profitable to none;\rfor, if their condition bewell perused, they are enemies to their\rmasters; to their friends,and to themselves: for by them oftentimes\rtheir masters areencouraged unto unlawful exactions of their\rtenants, their friendsbrought unto poverty by their rents enhanced,\rand they themselvesbrought to confusion by their own prodigality and\rerrors, as men that,having not wherewith of their own to maintain\rtheir excesses, do searchin highways, budgets, coffers, mails, and\rstables, which way tosupply their wants. How divers of them also,\rcoveting to bear an highsail, do insinuate themselves with young\rgentlemen and noblemennewly come to their lands, the case is too\rmuch apparent, whereby thegood natures of the parties are not only a\rlittle impaired, but alsotheir livelihoods and revenues so wasted\rand consumed that, if atall, yet not in many years, they shall be\rable to recoverthemselves. It were very good therefore that the\rsuperfluous heaps of themwere in part diminished. And since\rnecessity enforceth tohave some, yet let wisdom moderate their\rnumbers, so shall theirmasters be rid of unnecessary charge, and the\rcommonwealth of manythieves. No nation cherisheth such store of them\ras we do here in England,in hope of which maintenance many give\rthemselves to idlenessthat otherwise would be brought to labour, and\rlive in order likesubjects. Of their whoredoms I will not speak\ranything at all, more thanof their swearing; yet is it found that\rsome of them do make thefirst a chief pillar of their building,\rconsuming not only thegoods but also the health and welfare of many\rhonest gentlemen,citizens, wealthy yeomen, etc., by such unlawful\rdealings. But how far haveI waded in this point, or how far may I\rsail in such a large sea?I will therefore now stay to speak any more\rof those kind of men. Inreturning therefore to my matter, this\rfurthermore among otherthings I have to say of our husbandmen and\rartificers, that they werenever so excellent in their trades as at\rthis present. But as theworkmanship of the latter sort was newer,\rmore fine, and curious tothe eye, so was it never less strong and\rsubstantial forcontinuance and benefit of the buyers. Neither is\rthere anything thathurteth the common sort of our artificers more\rthan haste, and abarbarous or slavish desire to turn the penny, and,\rby ridding their work, tomake speedy utterance of their wares: which\renforceth them to bungleup and despatch many things they care not\rhow so they be out oftheir hands, whereby the buyer is often sore\rdefrauded, and findeth tohis cost that haste maketh waste, according\rto the proverb.\r \r      [12] The Ceylonese. The Greek name forthe island of Ceylon was\r      Taprobane, which Harrison used merely asa classical scholar.--W.\r \rOh, how many trades andhandicrafts are now in England whereof the\rcommonwealth hath no need!How many needful commodities have we which\rare perfected with greatcost, etc., and yet may with far more ease\rand less cost be providedfrom other countries if we could use the\rmeans! I will not speak ofiron, glass, and such like, which spoil\rmuch wood, and yet arebrought from other countries better cheap than\rwe can make them here athome; I could exemplify also in many other.\rBut to leave these thingsand proceed with our purpose, and herein (as\roccasion serveth)generally, by way of conclusion, to speak of the\rcommonwealth of England, Ifind that it is governed and maintained by\rthree sorts of persons--\r \r1. The prince, monarch,and head governor, which is called the king,\ror (if the crown fall to awoman) the queen: in whose name and by\rwhose authority all thingsare administered.\r \r2. The gentlemen which bedivided into two sorts, as the barony or\restate of lords (whichcontaineth barons and all above that degree),\rand also those that be nolords, as knights, esquires, and simple\rgentlemen, as I have notedalready. Out of these also are the great\rdeputies and highpresidents chosen, of which one serveth in Ireland,\ras another did some timein Calais, and the captain now at Berwick, as\rone lord president dothgovern in Wales, and the other the north parts\rof this island, whichlater, with certain counsellors and judges, were\rerected by King Henry theEighth. But, for so much as I have touched\rtheir conditionselsewhere, it shall be enough to have remembered them\rat this time.\r \r3. The third and last sortis named the yeomanry, of whom and their\rsequel, the labourers andartificers, I have said somewhat even now.\rWhereto I add that theymay not be called _masters_ and _gentlemen_,\rbut _goodmen_, as GoodmanSmith, Goodman Coot, Goodman Cornell,\rGoodman Mascall, GoodmanCockswet, etc., and in matters of law these\rand the like are calledthus, _Giles Jewd, yeoman; Edward Mountford,\ryeoman; James Cocke,yeoman; Harry Butcher, yeoman_, etc.; by which\raddition they are exemptfrom the vulgar and common sorts. Cato\rcalleth them"_Aratores et optimos cives rei publicæ_," of whom also\ryou may read more in thebook of commonwealth which Sir Thomas Smith\rsome time penned of thisland.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER II\r \rOF CITIES AND TOWNS INENGLAND\r \r[1577, Book II., Chapter7, 1587, Book II., Chapter 13.]\r \r \rAs in old time we readthat there were eight-and-twenty flamines and\rarchflamines in the southpart of this isle, and so many great cities\runder their jurisdiction,so in these our days there is but one or\rtwo fewer, and each ofthem also under the ecclesiastical regiment of\rsome one bishop orarchbishop, who in spiritual cases have the charge\rand oversight of the same.So many cities therefore are there in\rEngland and Wales as therebe bishoprics and archbishoprics.[1] For,\rnotwithstanding thatLichfield and Coventry and Bath and Wells do seem\rto extend the aforesaidnumber unto nine-and-twenty, yet neither of\rthese couples are to beaccounted but as one entire city and see of\rthe bishop, sith onebishopric can have relation but unto one see, and\rthe said see be situatebut in one place, after which the bishop doth\rtake his name.[2]...\r \r      [1] If Harrison means to give us theimpression that a city has\r      any direct connection with episcopalaffairs, he is quite in\r      error. Cities are distinctly royal andimperial institutions.\r      The accident of the number of cities andsees being the same\r      comes from the natural tendency of thetwo institutions to drift\r      together, though of distinct origin--W.\r \r      [2] Here follows a long and learneddisquisition upon the Roman\r      and other early towns, especially aboutSt. Albans, a portion of\r      which will be found in the Appendix.--W.\r \rCertes I would gladly setdown, with the names and number of the\rcities, all the towns andvillages in England and Wales with their\rtrue longitudes andlatitudes, but as yet I cannot come by them in\rsuch order as I would;howbeit the tale of our cities is soon found by\rthe bishoprics, sith everysee hath such prerogative given unto it as\rto bear the name of a cityand to use _Regaleius_ within her own\rlimits. Which privilegealso is granted to sundry ancient towns in\rEngland, especiallynorthward, where more plenty of them is to be\rfound by a great deal thanin the south, The names therefore of our\rcities are these: London,York, Canterbury, Winchester, Carlisle,\rDurham, Ely, Norwich,Lincoln, Worcester, Gloucester, Hereford,\rSalisbury, Exeter, Bath,Lichfield, Bristol, Rochester, Chester,\rChichester, Oxford,Peterborough, Llandaff, St. Davids, Bangor, St.\rAsaph, whose particularplots and models, with their descriptions,\rshall ensue, if it may bebrought to pass that the cutters can make\rdespatch of them beforethis history be published.\r \rOf towns and villageslikewise thus much will I say, that there were\rgreater store in old time(I mean within three or four hundred years\rpassed) than at thispresent. And this I note out of divers records,\rcharters, and donations(made in times past unto sundry religious\rhouses, as Glastonbury,Abingdon, Ramsey, Ely, and such like), and\rwhereof in these days Ifind not so much as the ruins. Leland, in\rsundry places, complainethlikewise of the decay of parishes in great\rcities and towns, missingin some six or eight or twelve churches and\rmore, of all which hegiveth particular notice. For albeit that the\rSaxons builded many townsand villages, and the Normans well more at\rtheir first coming, yetsince the first two hundred years after the\rlatter conquest, they havegone so fast again to decay that the\rancient number of them isvery much abated. Ranulph, the monk of\rChester, telleth ofgeneral survey made in the fourth, sixteenth, and\rnineteenth of the reign ofWilliam Conqueror, surnamed the Bastard,\rwherein it was found that(notwithstanding the Danes had overthrown a\rgreat many) there were tothe number of 52,000 towns, 45,002 parish\rchurches, and 75,000knights\' fees, whereof the clergy held 28,015. He\raddeth moreover that therewere divers other builded since that time,\rwithin the space of ahundred years after the coming of the Bastard,\ras it were in lieu orrecompense of those that William Rufus pulled\rdown for the erection ofhis New Forest. For by an old book which I\rhave, and some timewritten as it seemeth by an under-sheriff of\rNottingham, I find even inthe time of Edward IV. 45,120 parish\rchurches, and but 60,216knights\' fees, whereof the clergy held as\rbefore 28,015, or at theleast 28,000; for so small is the difference\rwhich he doth seem to use.Howbeit, if the assertions of such as write\rin our time concerningthis matter either are or ought to be of any\rcredit in this behalf, youshall not find above 17,000 towns and\rvillages, and 9210 in thewhole, which is little more than a fourth\rpart of the aforesaidnumber, if it be thoroughly scanned.[3]...\r \r      [3] Here follows an allusion to the decayof Eastern cities.--W.\r \rIn time past in Lincoln(as the same goeth) there have been\rtwo-and-fifty parishchurches, and good record appeareth for\reight-and-thirty, but now,if there be four-and-twenty, it is all.\rThis inconvenience hathgrown altogether to the church by\rappropriations made untomonasteries and religious houses--a terrible\rcanker and enemy toreligion.\r \rBut to leave thislamentable discourse of so notable and grievous an\rinconvenience, growing asI said by encroaching and joining of house\rto house and laying landto land, whereby the inhabitants of many\rplaces of our country aredevoured and eaten up, and their houses\reither altogether pulleddown or suffered to decay little by little,\ralthough some time a poorman per adventure doth dwell in one of them,\rwho, not being able torepair it, suffereth it to fall down--and\rthereto thinketh himselfvery friendly dealt withal, if he may have an\racre of ground assignedunto him, wherein to keep a cow, or wherein to\rset cabbages, radishes,parsnips, carrots, melons, pompons,[4] or such\rlike stuff, by which heand his poor household liveth as by their\rprincipal food, sith theycan do no better. And as for wheaten bread,\rthey eat it when they canreach unto the price of it, contenting\rthemselves in the meantimewith bread made of oats or barley: a poor\restate, God wot! Howbeit,what care our great encroachers? But in\rdivers places where richmen dwelled some time in good tenements,\rthere be now no houses atall, but hop-yards, and sheds for poles, or\rperadventure gardens, aswe may see in Castle Hedingham, and divers\rother places. But toproceed.\r \r      [4] The old and proper form of the modernpumpkin.--W.\r \rIt is so that, our soilbeing divided into champaign ground and\rwoodland, the houses ofthe first lie uniformly builded in every town\rtogether, with streets andlanes; whereas in the woodland countries\r(except here and there ingreat market towns) they stand scattered\rabroad, each one dwellingin the midst of his own occupying. And as in\rmany and most great markettowns, there are commonly three hundred or\rfour hundred families ormansions, and two thousand communicants (or\rperadventure more), so inthe other, whether they be woodland or\rchampaign, we find notoften above forty, fifty, or three score\rhouseholds, and two orthree hundred communicants, whereof the\rgreatest part neverthelessare very poor folks, oftentimes without all\rmanner of occupying, siththe ground of the parish is gotten up into a\rfew men\'s hands, yeasometimes into the tenure of one or two or three,\rwhereby the rest arecompelled either to be hired servants unto the\rother or else to beg theirbread in misery from door to door.\r \rThere are some (saithLeland) which are not so favourable, when they\rhave gotten such lands, asto let the houses remain upon them to the\ruse of the poor; but theywill compound with the lord of the soil to\rpull them down foraltogether, saying that "if they did let them\rstand, they should buttoll beggars to the town, thereby to surcharge\rthe rest of the parish,and lay more burden upon them." But alas!\rthese pitiful men see notthat they themselves hereby do lay the\rgreatest log upon theirneighbours\' necks. For, sith the prince doth\rcommonly loose nothing ofhis duties accustomable to be paid, the rest\rof the parishioners thatremain must answer and bear them out: for\rthey plead more chargeother ways, saying: "I am charged already with\ra light horse; I am toanswer in this sort, and after that matter."\rAnd it is not yetaltogether out of knowledge that, where the king had\rseven pounds thirteenshillings at a task gathered of fifty wealthy\rhouseholders of a parishin England, now, a gentleman having three\rparts of the town in hisown hands, four households do bear all the\raforesaid payment, or elseLeland is deceived in his _Commentaries_,\rlib. 13, lately come to myhands, which thing he especially noted in\rhis travel over this isle.A common plague and enormity, both in the\rheart of the land andlikewise upon the coasts. Certes a great number\rcomplain of the increaseof poverty, laying the cause upon God, as\rthough he were in faultfor sending such increase of people, or want\rof wars that shouldconsume them, affirming that the land was never so\rfull, etc.; but few men dosee the very root from whence it doth\rproceed. Yet the Romansfound it out, when they flourished, and\rtherefore prescribedlimits to every man\'s tenure and occupying. Homer\rcommendeth Achilles foroverthrowing of five-and-twenty cities: but in\rmine opinion Ganges ismuch better preferred by Suidas for building of\rthree score in India,where he did plant himself. I could (if need\rrequired) set down in thisplace the number of religious houses and\rmonasteries, with thenames of their founders, that have been in this\risland: but, sith it is athing of small importance, I pass it over as\rimpertinent to my purpose.Yet herein I will commend sundry of the\rmonastical votaries,especially monks, for that they were authors of\rmany goodly borowes andendwares,[5] near unto their dwellings\ralthough otherwise theypretended to be men separated from the world.\rBut alas! their covetousminds, one way in enlarging their revenues,\rand carnal intent another,appeared herein too, too much. For, being\rbold from time to time tovisit their tenants, they wrought oft great\rwickedness, and made thoseendwares little better than brothel-houses,\respecially where nunnerieswere far off, or else no safe access unto\rthem. But what do I spendmy time in the rehearsal of these\rfilthinesses? Would to Godthe memory of them might perish with the\rmalefactors! My purposewas also at the end of this chapter to have\rset down a table of theparish churches and market towns throughout\rall England and Wales;but, sith I cannot perform the same as I would,\rI am forced to give overmy purpose; yet by these few that ensue you\rshall easily see what Iwould have used according to the shires, if I\rmight have brought it topass.\r \r      [5] The first is a variant on a Keltic,the second on a Saxon\r      word, both relating to matterssufficiently indicated in the\r      text.--W.\r \rShires.                  Market Towns. the great\rbenefit of our nation andeverlasting fame of the aforesaid parties.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER III\r \rOF GARDENS AND ORCHARDS\r \r[1587, Book II., Chapter20.]\r \r \rAfter such time as Calaiswas won from the French, and that our\rcountrymen had learned totrade into divers countries (whereby they\rgrew rich), they began towax idle also, and thereupon not only left\roff their formerpainfulness and frugality, but in like sort gave\rthemselves to live inexcess and vanity, whereby many goodly\rcommodities failed, and inshort time were not to be had amongst us.\rSuch strangers also asdwelled here with us, perceiving our\rsluggishness, and espyingthat this idleness of ours might redound to\rtheir great profit,forthwith employed their endeavors to bring in the\rsupply of such things aswe lacked continually from foreign countries,\rwhich yet more augmentedour idleness. For, having all things at\rreasonable prices (as wesupposed) by such means from them, we thought\rit mere madness to spendeither time or cost about the same here at\rhome. And thus we becameenemies to our own welfare, as men that in\rthose days reposed ourfelicity in following the wars, wherewith we\rwere often exercised bothat home and other places. Besides this, the\rnatural desire thatmankind hath to esteem of things far sought,\rbecause they be rare andcostly, and the irksome contempt of things\rnear hand, for that theyare common and plentiful, hath borne no small\rsway also in this behalfamongst us. For hereby we have neglected our\rown good gifts of God,growing here at home, as vile and of no value,\rand had every trifle andtoy in admiration that is brought hither from\rfar countries, ascribing Iwot not what great forces and solemn\restimation unto them,until they also have waxen old, after which they\rhave been so littleregarded, if not more despised, amongst us than\rour own. Examples hereof Icould set down many and in many things;\rbut, sith my purpose is todeal at this time with gardens and\rorchards, it shall sufficethat I touch them only, and show our\rinconstancy in the same,so far as shall seem and be convenient for my\rturn. I comprehendtherefore under the word "garden" all such grounds\ras are wrought with thespade by man\'s hand, for so the case\rrequireth.\r \rOf wine I have writtenalready elsewhere sufficiently, which commodity\r(as I have learned furthersince the penning of that book) hath been\rvery plentiful in thisisland, not only in the time of the Romans, but\ralso since the Conquest,as I have seen by record; yet at this present\rhave we none at all (orelse very little to speak of) growing in this\risland, which I impute notunto the soil, but the negligence of my\rcountrymen. Such herbs,fruits, and roots also as grow yearly out of\rthe ground, of seed, havebeen very plentiful in this land, in the\rtime of the first Edward,and after his days; but in process of time\rthey grew also to beneglected, so that from Henry the Fourth till the\rlatter end of Henry theSeventh and beginning of Henry the Eighth,\rthere was little or no useof them in England, but they remained\reither unknown or supposedas food more meet for hogs and savage\rbeasts to feed upon thanmankind. Whereas in my time their use is not\ronly resumed among thepoor commons. I mean of melons, pompons,\rgourds, cucumbers,radishes, skirets,[1] parsnips, carrots, cabbages,\rnavews,[2] turnips, andall kinds of salad herbs--but also fed upon as\rdainty dishes at thetables of delicate merchants, gentlemen, and the\rnobility, who make theirprovision yearly for new seeds out of strange\rcountries, from whencethey have them abundantly. Neither do they now\rstay with such of thesefruits as are wholesome in their kinds, but\radventure further uponsuch as are very dangerous and hurtful, as the\rverangenes, mushrooms,etc., as if nature had ordained all for the\rbelly, or that all thingswere to be eaten for whose mischievous\roperation the Lord in somemeasure hath given and provided a remedy.\r \r      [1] A vegetable something like a carrot.\r \r      [2] A kind of turnip.\r \rHops in time past wereplentiful in this land. Afterwards also their\rmaintenance did cease. Andnow, being revived, where are any better\rto be found? Where anygreater commodity to be raised by them? Only\rpoles are accounted to betheir greatest charge. But, sith men have\rlearned of late to sowashen kexes in ashyards by themselves, that\rinconvenience in shorttime will be redressed.\r \rMadder hath grownabundantly in this island, but of long time\rneglected, and now alittle revived, and offereth itself to prove no\rsmall benefit unto ourcountry, as many other things else, which are\rnow fetched from us: as webefore time, when we gave ourselves to\ridleness, were glad tohave them other.\r \rIf you look into ourgardens annexed to our houses, how wonderfully is\rtheir beauty increased,not only with flowers, which Columella calleth\r_Terrena sydera_[3]saying,\r \r  "_Pingit et in varios terrestria syderaflores_,"[4]\r \rand variety of curious andcostly workmanship, but also with rare and\rmedicinable herbs soughtup in the land within these forty years: so\rthat, in comparison ofthis present, the ancient gardens were but\rdunghills andlaistowes,[5] to such as did possess them. How art also\rhelpeth nature in thedaily colouring, doubling, and enlarging the\rproportion of our flowers,it is incredible to report: for so curious\rand cunning are ourgardeners now in these days that they presume to\rdo in manner what theylist with nature, and moderate her course in\rthings as if they were hersuperiors. It is a world also to see how\rmany strange herbs,plants, and annual fruits are daily brought unto\rus from the Indies,Americans, Taprobane, Canary Isles, and all parts\rof the world: the which,albeit that in respect of the constitutions\rof our bodies they do notgrow for us (because that God hath bestowed\rsufficient commoditiesupon every country for her own necessity), yet,\rfor delectation sake untothe eye and their odoriferous savours unto\rthe nose, they are to becherished, and God to be glorified also in\rthem, because they are hisgood gifts, and created to do man help and\rservice. There is notalmost one nobleman, gentleman, or merchant that\rhath not great store ofthese flowers, which now also do begin to wax\rso well acquainted withour soils that we may almost account of them\ras parcel of our owncommodities. They have no less regard in like\rsort to cherishmedicinable herbs fetched out of other regions nearer\rhand, insomuch that I haveseen in some one garden to the number of\rthree hundred or fourhundred of them, if not more, of the half of\rwhose names within fortyyears past we had no manner of knowledge. But\rherein I find some causeof just complaint, for that we extol their\ruses so far that we fallinto contempt of our own, which are in truth\rmore beneficial and aptfor us than such as grow elsewhere, sith (as I\rsaid before) every regionhath abundantly within her own limits\rwhatsoever is needful andmost convenient for them that dwell therein.\rHow do men extol the useof tobacco in my time, whereas in truth\r(whether the cause be inthe repugnancy of our constitution unto the\roperation thereof, or thatthe ground doth alter her force, I cannot\rtell) it is not found ofso great efficacy as they write. And beside\rthis, our common germanderor thistle benet is found and known to be\rso wholesome and of sogreat power in medicine as any other herb, if\rthey be used accordingly.I could exemplify after the like manner in\rsundry other, as the_Salsa parilla, Mochoacan_, etc., but I forbear\rso to do, because I covetto be brief. And truly, the estimation and\rcredit that we yield andgive unto compound medicines made with\rforeign drugs is one greatcause wherefore the full knowledge and use\rof our own simples hathbeen so long raked up in the embers. And as\rthis may be verified so tobe one sound conclusion, for, the greater\rnumber of simples that gounto any compound medicine, the greater\rconfusion is foundtherein, because the qualities and operations of\rvery few of theparticulars are thoroughly known. And even so our\rcontinual desire ofstrange drugs, whereby the physician and\rapothecary only hath thebenefit, is no small cause that the use of\rour simples here at homedoth go to loss, and that we tread those\rherbs under our feet,whose forces if we knew, and could apply them to\rour necessities, we wouldhonour and have in reverence as to their\rcase behoveth. Alas! whathave we to do with such Arabian and Grecian\rstuff as is daily broughtfrom those parties which lie in another\rclime? And therefore thebodies of such as dwell there are of another\rconstitution than ours arehere at home. Certes they grow not for us,\rbut for the Arabians andGrecians. And albeit that they may by skill\rbe applied unto ourbenefit, yet to be more skilful in them than in\rour own is folly; and touse foreign wares, when our own may serve the\rturn, is more folly; butto despise our own, and magnify above measure\rthe use of them that aresought and brought from far, is most folly of\rall: for it savoureth ofignorance, or at the leastwise of negligence,\rand therefore worthy ofreproach.\r \r      [3] Earthly stars.\r \r      [4] "And paints terrestrialconstellations with varied flowers."\r \r      [5] Refuse-heaps.\r \rAmong the Indians, whohave the most present cures for every disease\rof their own nation, thereis small regard of compound medicines, and\rless of foreign drugs,because they neither know them nor can use\rthem, but work wonderseven with their own simples. With them also the\rdifference of the climedoth show her full effect. For, whereas they\rwill heal one another inshort time with application of one simple,\retc., if a Spaniard orEnglishman stand in need of their help, they\rare driven to have alonger space in their cures, and now and then\ralso to use some additionof two or three simples at the most, whose\rforces unto them arethoroughly known, because their exercise is only\rin their own, as men thatnever sought or heard what virtue was in\rthose that came from othercountries. And even so did Marcus Cato, the\rlearned Roman, endeavourto deal in his cures of sundry diseases,\rwherein he not only usedsuch simples as were to be had in his own\rcountry, but also examinedand learned the forces of each of them,\rwherewith he dealt sodiligently that in all his lifetime he could\rattain to the exactknowledge but of a few, and thereto wrote of those\rmost learnedly, as wouldeasily be seen if those his books were\rextant. For the space alsoof six hundred years the colewort only was\ra medicine in Rome for alldiseases, so that his virtues were\rthoroughly known in thoseparts. * * *\r \rFor my part, I doubt notif the use of outlandish drugs had not\rblinded our physicians ofEngland in times past, but that the virtues\rof our simples here athome would have been far better known, and so\rwell unto us as those ofIndia are to the practitioners of those\rparts, and thereunto befound more profitable for us than the foreign\reither are or may be. Thisalso will I add, that even those which are\rmost common by reason oftheir plenty, and most vile because of their\rabundance, are not withoutsome universal and special efficacy, if it\rwere known, for ourbenefit: sith God in nature hath so disposed his\rcreatures that the mostneedful are the most plentiful and serving for\rsuch general diseases asour constitution most commonly is affected\rwithal. Great thankstherefore be given unto the physicians of our age\rand country, who not onlyendeavour to search out the use of such\rsimples as our soil dothyield and bring forth, but also to procure\rsuch as grow elsewhere,upon purpose so to acquaint them with our\rclime that they in time,through some alteration received from the\rnature of the earth, maylikewise turn to our benefit and commodity\rand be used as our own.\r \rThe chief workman (or, asI may call him, the founder of this device)\ris Carolus Clusius, thenoble herbarist whose industry hath\rwonderfully stirred themup into this good act. Idoubt not but, if this man were in England but\rone seven years, he wouldreveal a number of herbs growing with us\rwhereof neither ourphysicians nor apothecaries as yet have any\rknowledge. And even likethanks be given unto our nobility, gentlemen,\rand others, for theircontinual nutriture and cherishing of such\rhomeborne and foreignsimples in their gardens: for hereby they shall\rnot only be had at handand preserved, but also their forms made more\rfamiliar to be discernedand their forces better known than hitherto\rthey have been.\r \rAnd even as it fareth withour gardens, so doth it with our orchards,\rwhich were never furnishedwith so good fruit nor with such variety as\rat this present. For,beside that we have most delicate apples, plums,\rpears, walnuts, filberts,etc., and those of sundry sorts, planted\rwithin forty years past,in comparison of which most of the old trees\rare nothing worth, so havewe no less store of strange fruit, as\rapricots, almonds,peaches, figs, corn-trees[6] in noblemen\'s\rorchards. Sothat England for these commodities was\rnever better furnished,neither any nation under their clime more\rplentifully endued withthese and other blessings from the most high\rGod, who grant us gracewithal to use the same to his honour and\rglory! And not asinstruments and provocations into further excess and\rvanity, wherewith hisdispleasure may be kindled, lest these his\rbenefits do turn untothorns and briers unto us for our annoyance and\rpunishment, which he hathbestowed upon us for our consolation and\rcomfort.\r \r      [6] Probably _cornels_.\r \rWe have in like sort suchworkmen as are not only excellent in\rgrafting the naturalfruits, but their artificial mixtures, whereby\rone tree bringeth forthsundry fruits, and one and the same fruit of\rdivers colours and tastes,dallying as it were with nature and her\rcourse, as if her wholetrade were perfectly known unto them: of hard\rfruits they will maketender, of sour sweet, of sweet yet more\rdelicate, bereaving alsosome of their kernels, other of their cores,\rand finally enduing themwith the savour of musk, amber, or sweet\rspices, at theirpleasures. Divers also have written at large of these\rseveral practices, andsome of them how to convert the kernels of\rpeaches into almonds, ofsmall fruit to make far greater, and to\rremove or add superfluousor necessary moisture to the trees, with\rother things belonging totheir preservation, and with no less\rdiligence than ourphysicians do commonly show upon our own diseased\rbodies, which to me dothseem right strange. Whereby, and sundry\rother circumstances nothere to be remembered, I am persuaded that,\ralbeit the gardens of theHesperides were in times past so greatly\raccounted of, because oftheir delicacy, yet, if it were possible to\rhave such an equal judgeas by certain knowledge of both were able to\rpronounce upon them, Idoubt not but he would give the prize unto the\rgardens of our days, andgenerally over all Europe, in comparison of\rthose times wherein theold exceeded. Pliny and others speak of a rose\rthat had three scoreleaves growing upon one button: but if I should\rtell of one which bare atriple number unto that proportion, I know I\rshall not be believed, andno great matter though I were not; howbeit\rsuch a one was to be seenin Antwerp, 1585, as I have heard, and I\rknow who might have had aslip or stallon thereof, if he would have\rventured ten pounds uponthe growth of the same, which should have\rbeen but a tickle hazard,and therefore better undone, as I did always\rimagine. For mine ownpart, good reader, let me boast a little of my\rgarden, which is butsmall, and the whole area thereof little above\r300 foot of ground, andyet, such hath been my good luck in purchase\rof the variety of simples,that, notwithstanding my small ability,\rthere are very near threehundred of one sort and other contained\rtherein, no one of thembeing common or usually to be had. If\rtherefore my little plot,void of all cost in keeping, be so well\rfurnished, what shall wethink of those of Hampton Court, Nonsuch,\rTibaults, Cobham Garden,and sundry others appertaining to divers\rcitizens of London, whom Icould particularly name, if I should not\rseem to offend them bysuch my demeanour and dealing.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER IV\r \rOF FAIRS AND MARKETS\r \r[1577, Book II., Chapter11; 1587, Book II., Chapter 18.]\r \r \rThere are (as I take it)few great towns in England that have not\rtheir weekly markets, oneor more granted from the prince, in which\rall manner of provisionfor household is to be bought and sold, for\rease and benefit of thecountry round about. Whereby, as it cometh to\rpass that no buyer shallmake any great journey in the purveyance of\rhis necessities, so nooccupier shall have occasion to travel far off\rwith his commodities,except it be to seek for the highest prices,\rwhich commonly are nearunto great cities, where round[1] and\rspeediest utterance[2] isalways to be had. And, as these have been in\rtimes past erected for thebenefit of the realm, so are they in many\rplaces too, too muchabused: for the relief and ease of the buyer is\rnot so much intended inthem as the benefit of the seller. Neither are\rthe magistrates for themost part (as men loath to displease their\rneighbours for their oneyear\'s dignity) so careful in their offices\ras of right and duty theyshould be. For, in most of these markets,\rneither assizes of breadnor orders for goodness and sweetness of\rgrain and othercommodities that are brought thither to be sold are\rany whit looked unto, buteach one suffered to sell or set up what and\rhow himself listeth: andthis is one evident cause of dearth and\rscarcity in time of greatabundance.\r \r      [1] Direct.\r \r      [2] Market.\r \rI could (if I would)exemplify in many, but I will touch no one\rparticularly, sith it israre to see in any country town (as I said)\rthe assize of bread wellkept according to the statute; and yet, if\rany country baker happento come in among them on the market day with\rbread of better quantity,they find fault by-and-by with one thing or\rother in his stuff,whereby the honest poor man (whom the law of\rnations do commend, forthat he endeavoureth to live by any lawful\rmeans) is driven away, andno more to come there, upon some round\rpenalty, by virtue oftheir privileges. Howbeit, though they are so\rnice in the proportion oftheir bread, yet, in lieu of the same, there\ris such heady ale and beerin most of them as for the mightiness\rthereof among such as seekit out is commonly called "huffcap," "the\rmad dog,""Father Whoreson," "angels\' food," "dragon\'smilk,"\r"go-by-the-wall,""stride wide," and "lift leg," etc. And this is more\rto be noted, that when oneof late fell by God\'s providence into a\rtroubled conscience, afterhe had considered well of his reachless\rlife and dangerous estate,another, thinking belike to change his\rcolour and not his mind,carried him straight away to the strongest\rale, as to the nextphysician. It is incredible to say how our\rmalt-bugs lug at thisliquor, even as pigs should lie in a row lugging\rat their dame\'s teats,till they lie still again and be not able to\rwag. Neither did Romulusand Remus suck their she-wolf or shepherd\'s\rwife Lupa with such eagerand sharp devotion as these men hale at\r"huffcap," tillthey be red as cocks and little wiser than their\rcombs. But how am I fallenfrom the market into the ale-house? In\rreturning therefore untomy purpose, I find that in corn great abuse\ris daily suffered, to thegreat prejudice of the town and country,\respecially the poorartificer and householder, which tilleth no land,\rbut, labouring all theweek to buy a bushel or two of grain on the\rmarket day, can there havenone for his money: because bodgers,\rloaders, and commoncarriers of corn do not only buy up all, but give\rabove the price, to beserved of great quantities. Shall I go any\rfurther? Well, I will sayyet a little more, and somewhat by mine own\rexperience.\r \rAt Michaelmas time poormen must make money of their grain, that they\rmay pay their rents. Solong then as the poor man hath to sell, rich\rmen bring out none, butrather buy up that which the poor bring, under\rpretence of seed corn oralteration of grain, although they bring none\rof their own, because onewheat often sown without change of seed will\rsoon decay and beconverted into darnel. For this cause therefore they\rmust needs buy in themarkets, though they be twenty miles off, and\rwhere they be not known,promising there, if they happen to be espied\r(which, God wot, is veryseldom), to send so much to their next\rmarket, to be performed Iwot not when.\r \rIf this shift serve not(neither doth the fox use always one track for\rfear of a snare), theywill compound with some one of the town where\rthe market is holden, whofor a pot of "huffcap" or "merry-go-down,"\rwill not let to buy it forthem, and that in his own name. Or else\rthey wage one poor man orother to become a bodger, and thereto get\rhim a licence upon someforged surmise, which being done, they will\rfeed him with money to buyfor them till he hath filled their lofts,\rand then, if he can do anygood for himself, so it is; if not, they\rwill give him somewhat forhis pains at this time, and reserve him for\ranother year. How many ofthe like providers stumble upon blind creeks\rat the sea coast, I wotnot well; but that some have so done and yet\rdo under other men\'swings, the case is too, too plain. But who dare\rfind fault with them, whenthey have once a licence? yes, though it be\rbut to serve a meangentleman\'s house with corn, who hath cast up all\rhis tillage, because heboasteth how he can buy his grain in the\rmarket better cheap thanhe can sow his land, as the rich grazier\roften doth also upon thelike device, because grazing requireth a\rsmaller household and lessattendance and charge. If any man come to\rbuy a bushel or two forhis expenses unto the market cross, answer is\rmade: "Forsooth, herewas one even now that bade me money for it, and\rI hope he will haveit." And to say the truth, these bodgers are fair\rchapmen; for there are nomore words with them, but _"Let me see it!\rWhat shall I give you?Knit it up!
