I will have it--go carry it to such\ra chamber, and if youbring in twenty_ seme[3] _more in the weekday to\rsuch an inn or sollar[4]where I lay my corn, I will have it, and give\ryou (   ) pence or more in every bushel for sixweeks\' day of payment\rthan another will."_Thus the bodgers bear away all, so that the poor\rartificer and labourercannot make his provision in the markets, sith\rthey will hardly nowadayssell by the bushel, nor break their measure;\rand so much the rather forthat the buyer will look (as they say) for\rso much over measure inthe bushel as the bodger will do in a quarter.\rNay, the poor man cannotoft get any of the farmer at home, because he\rprovideth altogether toserve the bodger, or hath an hope, grounded\rupon a greedy andinsatiable desire of gain, that the sale will be\rbetter in the market, sothat he must give twopence or a groat more in\rthe bushel at his housethan the last market craved, or else go\rwithout it, and sleep witha hungry belly. Of the common carriage of\rcorn over unto the partsbeyond the seas I speak not; or at the\rleastwise, if I should, Icould not touch it alone, but needs must\rjoin other provisionwithal, whereby not only our friends abroad, but\ralso many of ouradversaries and countrymen, the papists, are\rabundantly relieved (asthe report goeth); but sith I see it not, I\rwill not so trust mineears as to write it for a truth. But to return\rto our markets again.\r \r      [3] Horse-loads.\r \r      [4] Loft.\r \rBy this time the pooroccupier hath sold all his crop for need of\rmoney, being readyperadventure to buy again ere long. And now is the\rwhole sale of corn in thegreat occupiers\' hands, who hitherto have\rthreshed little or none oftheir own, but bought up of other men as\rmuch as they could comeby. Henceforth also they begin to sell, not by\rthe quarter or load at thefirst (for marring the market) but by the\rbushel or two, or ahorseload at the most, thereby to be seen to keep\rthe cross, either for ashow, or to make men eager to buy, and so, as\rthey may have it formoney, not to regard what they pay. And thus corn\rwaxeth dear; but it willbe dearer the next market day. It is possible\ralso that they mislike theprice in the beginning for the whole year\rensuing, as men supposingthat corn will be little worth for this and\rof better price the nextyear. For they have certain superstitious\robservations whereby theywill give a guess at the sale of corn for\rthe year following. Andour countrymen do use commonly for barley,\rwhere I dwell, to judgeafter the price at Baldock upon St. Matthew\'s\rday; and for wheat, as itis sold in seed time. They take in like sort\rexperiment by sight of thefirst flocks of cranes that flee southward\rin winter, the age of themoon in the beginning of January, and such\rother apish toys as bylaying twelve corns upon the hot hearth for the\rtwelve months, etc.,whereby they shew themselves to be scant good\rChristians; but what carethey, so that they come by money? Hereupon\ralso will they thresh outthree parts of the old corn, towards the\rlatter end of the summer,when new cometh apace to hand, and cast the\rsame in the fourthunthreshed, where it shall lie until the next\rspring, or peradventuretill it must and putrify. Certes it is not\rdainty to see musty cornin many of our great markets of England which\rthese great occupiersbring forth when they can keep it no longer. But\ras they are enforcedoftentimes upon this one occasion somewhat to\rabate the price, so aplague is not seldom engendered thereby among\rthe poorer sort that ofnecessity must buy the same, whereby many\rthousands of all degreesare consumed, of whose death (in mine\ropinion) these farmers arenot unguilty. But to proceed. If they lay\rnot up their grain orwheat in this manner, they have yet another\rpolicy, whereby they willseem to have but small store left in their\rbarns: for else they willgird their sheaves by the band, and stack it\rup anew in less room, tothe end it may not only seem less in\rquantity, but also giveplace to the corn that is yet to come into the\rbarn or growing in thefield. If there happen to be such plenty in the\rmarket on any market daythat they cannot sell at their own price,\rthen will they set it upin some friend\'s house, against another on\rthe third day, and notbring it forth till they like of the sale. If\rthey sell any at home,beside harder measure, it shall be dearer to\rthe poor man that buyethit by twopence or a groat in a bushel than\rthey may sell it in themarket. But, as these things are worthy\rredress, so I wish thatGod would once open their eyes that deal thus\rto see their own errors:for as yet some of them little care how many\rpoor men suffer extremity,so that they fill their purses and carry\raway the gain.\r \rIt is a world also to seehow most places of the realm are pestered\rwith purveyors, who takeup eggs, butter, cheese, pigs, capons, hens,\rchickens, hogs, bacon,etc., in one market under pretence of their\rcommissions, and suffertheir wives to sell the same in another, or to\rpoulterers of London. Ifthese chapmen be absent but two or three\rmarket days then we mayperfectly see these wares to be more\rreasonably sold, andthereunto the crosses sufficiently furnished of\rall things. In like sort,since the number of buttermen have so much\rincreased, and since theytravel in such wise that they come to men\'s\rhouses for their butterfaster than they can make it, it is almost\rincredible to see how theprice of butter is augmented: whereas when\rthe owners were enforcedto bring it to the market towns, and fewer of\rthese butter buyers werestirring, our butter was scarcely worth\reighteen pence the gallonthat now is worth three shillings fourpence\rand perhaps fiveshillings. Whereby also I gather that the maintenance\rof a superfluous number ofdealers in most trades, tillage always\rexcepted, is one of thegreatest causes why the prices of things\rbecame excessive: for oneof them do commonly use to outbid another.\rAnd whilst our countrycommodities are commonly bought and sold at our\rprivate houses, I neverlook to see this enormity redressed or the\rmarkets well furnished.\r \rI could say more, but thisis even enough, and more peradventure than\rI shall be well thankedfor: yet true it is, though some think it no\rtrespass. This moreover isto be lamented, that one general measure is\rnot in use throughout allEngland, but every market town hath in\rmanner a several bushel;and the lesser it be, the more sellers it\rdraweth to resort unto thesame. Such also is the covetousness of many\rclerks of the market, thatin taking a view of measures they will\ralways so provide that oneand the same bushel shall be either too big\ror too little at theirnext coming, and yet not depart without a fee\rat the first so that whatby their mending at one time, and impairing\rthe same at another, thecountry is greatly charged, and few just\rmeasures to be had in anysteed. It is oft found likewise that divers\runconscionable dealershave one measure to sell by and another to buy\rwithal; the like is alsoin weights, and yet all sealed and branded.\rWherefore it were verygood that these two were reduced unto one\rstandard, that is, onebushel, one pound, one quarter, one hundred,\rone tale, one number: soshould things in time fall into better order\rand fewer causes ofcontention be moved in this land. Of the complaint\rof such poor tenants aspay rent corn unto their landlords, I speak\rnot, who are often dealtwithal very hardly. For, beside that in\rmeasuring of ten quartersfor the most part they lose one through the\riniquity of the bushel(such is the greediness of the appointed\rreceivers thereof), faultis found also with the goodness and\rcleanness of the grain.Whereby some piece of money must needs pass\runto their purses to stoptheir mouths withal, or else "My lord will\rnot like of thecorn," "Thou art worthy to lose thy lease," etc. Or,\rif it be cheaper in themarket than the rate allowed for it is in\rtheir rents, then mustthey pay money and no corn, which is no small\rextremity. And thereby wemay see how each one of us endeavoureth to\rfleece and eat up another.\r \rAnother thing there is inour markets worthy to be looked into, and\rthat is the recarriage ofgrain from the same into lofts and cellars,\rof which before I gavesome intimation; wherefore if it were ordered\rthat every seller shouldmake his market by an hour, or else the\rbailey or clerk of thesaid market to make sale thereof, according to\rhis discretion, withoutliberty to the farmers to set up their corn in\rhouses and chambers, I ampersuaded that the prices of our grain would\rsoon be abated. Again, ifit were enacted that each one should keep\rhis next market with hisgrain (and not to run six, eight, ten,\rfourteen, or twenty milesfrom home to sell his corn where he doth\rfind the highest price,and thereby leaveth his neighbours\runfurnished), I do notthink but that our markets would be far better\rserved than at thispresent they are. Finally, if men\'s barns might be\rindifferently viewedimmediately after harvest, and a note gathered by\ran estimate, and kept bysome appointed and trusty person for that\rpurpose, we should havemuch more plenty of corn in our town crosses\rthan as yet is commonlyseen: because each one hideth and hoardeth\rwhat he may, upon purposeeither that it will be dearer, or that he\rshall have some privy veinby bodgers, who do accustomably so deal\rthat the sea doth loadaway no small part thereof into other countries\rand our enemies, to thegreat hindrance of our commonwealth at home,\rand more likely yet to be,except some remedy be found. But what do I\rtalk of these things, ordesire the suppression of bodgers, being a\rminister? Certes I mayspeak of them right well as feeling the harm in\rthat I am a buyer,nevertheless I speak generally in each of them.\r \rTo conclude therefore, inour markets all things are to be sold\rnecessary for man\'s use;and there is our provision made commonly for\rall the week ensuing.Therefore, as there are no great towns without\rone weekly market atleast, so there are very few of them that have\rnot one or two fairs ormore within the compass of the year, assigned\runto them by the princeAnd albeit that some of them are not much\rbetter than Louse fair,[5]or the common kirkemesses,[6] beyond the\rsea, yet there are diversnot inferior to the greatest marts in\rEurope, as Stourbridgefair near to Cambridge, Bristow fair,\rBartholomew fair atLondon, Lynn mart, Cold fair at Newport pond for\rcattle, and divers other,all which, or at leastwise the greatest part\rof them (to the end I maywith the more ease to the reader and less\rtravel to myself fulfil mytask in their recital), I have set down\raccording to the names ofthe months wherein they are holden at the\rend of this book, whereyou shall find them at large as I borrowed the\rsame from J. Stow and thereports of others.\r \r      [5] The ancient London counterpart of themore modern "Rag\r      Fair" known to literary fame.--W.\r \r      [6] The Kermess, or literally,"Church mass," so famous in\r      "Faust."--W.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER V\r \rOF THE ANCIENT AND PRESENTESTATE OF THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND\r \r[1577, Book II., Chapter5, 1585, Book II., Chapter 1.]\r \r \rThere are now twoprovinces only in England, of which the first and\rgreatest is subject to thesee of Canterbury, comprehending a part of\rLhoegres, whole Cambria,and also Ireland, which in time past were\rseveral, and brought intoone by the archbishop of the said see, and\rassistance of the pope,who, in respect of meed, did yield unto the\rambitious desires ofsundry archbishops of Canterbury, as I have\relsewhere declared. Thesecond province is under the see of York. And,\rof these, each hath herarchbishop resident commonly within her own\rlimits, who hath not onlythe chief dealing in matters appertaining to\rthe hierarchy andjurisdiction of the church, but also great authority\rin civil affairs touchingthe government of the commonwealth, so far\rforth as their commissionsand several circuits do extend.\r \rIn old time there werethree archbishops, and so many provinces in\rthis isle, of which onekept at London, another at York, and the third\rat Caerleon upon Usk. Butas that of London was translated to\rCanterbury by Augustine,and that of York remaineth (notwithstanding\rthat the greatest part ofhis jurisdiction is now bereft him and given\rto the Scottisharchbishop), so that of Caerleon is utterly\rextinguished, and thegovernment of the country united to that of\rCanterbury in spiritualcases, after it was once before removed to St.\rDavid\'s in Wales, byDavid, successor to Dubritius, and uncle to King\rArthur, in the 519 ofGrace, to the end that he and his clerks might\rbe further off from thecruelty of the Saxons, where it remained till\rthe time of the Bastard,and for a season after, before it was annexed\rto the see of Canterbury.\r \rThe Archbishop ofCanterbury is commonly called the Primate of all\rEngland; and in thecoronations of the kings of this land, and all\rother times wherein itshall please the prince to wear and put on his\rcrown, his office is toset it upon their heads. They bear also the\rname of their highchaplains continually, although not a few of them\rhave presumed (in timepast) to be their equals, and void of\rsubjection unto them. Thatthis is true, it may easily appear by their\rown acts yet kept inrecord, beside their epistles and answers written\ror in print, wherein theyhave sought not only to match but also to\rmate[1] them with greatrigour and more than open tyranny. Our\radversaries willperadventure deny this absolutely, as they do many\rother things apparent,though not without shameless impudence, or at\rthe leastwise defend it asjust and not swerving from common equity,\rbecause they imagine everyarchbishop to be the king\'s equal in his\rown province. But how welltheir doing herein agreeth with the saying\rof Peter and examples ofthe primitive church it may easily appear.\rSome examples also oftheir demeanour--I mean in the time of popery--I\rwill not let to remember,lest they should say I speak of malice, and\rwithout all ground oflikelihood.\r \r      [1] Overcome.\r \rOf their practices withmean persons I speak not, neither will I begin\rat Dunstan, the author ofall their pride and presumption here in\rEngland....\r \rWherefore I refer you tothose reports of Anselm and Becket\rsufficiently penned byother, the which Anselm also making a shew as\rif he had been veryunwilling to be placed in the see of Canterbury,\rgave this answer to theletters of such his friends as did make\rrequest unto him to takethe charge upon him--\r \r    _"Secularia negotia, nescio, quiascire nolo, eorum námque\r    occupationes horreo, liberum affectansanimum. Voluntati sacrarum\r    intendo scripturarum, vos dissonantiamfacitis, verendumque est né\r    aratrum sancta ecclesia, quod in Anglia duoboves validi et pari\r    fortitudine, ad bonum certantes, id est,rex et archepiscopus,\r    debeant trahere nunc ove verula cum tauroindomito jugata,\r    distorqueatur a recto. Ego ovis verula, quisi quietus essem,\r    verbi Dei lacte, et operinento lanæ,aliquibus possèm fortassis\r    non ingratus esse, sed si me cum hoc tauroconiungitis, videbitis\r    pro disparilitate trahentium, aratrum nonrectè procedere,"_ etc.\r \rWhich is in English thus--\r \r    "Of secular affairs I have no skill,because I will not know them;\r    for I even abhor the troubles that riseabout them, as one that\r    desireth to have his mind at liberty. Iapply my whole endeavour\r    to the rule of the Scriptures; you lead meto the contrary; and it\r    is to be feared lest the plough of holychurch, which two strong\r    oxen of equal force, and both like earnestto contend unto that\r    which is good (that is, the king and thearchbishop), ought to\r    draw, should thereby now swerve from theright furrow, by matching\r    of an old sheep with a wild, untamed bull.I am that old sheep,\r    who, if I might be quiet, couldperadventure shew myself not\r    altogether ungrateful to some, by feedingthem with the milk of\r    the Word of God, and covering them withwool: but if you match me\r    with this bull, you shall see that, throughwant of equality in\r    draught, the plough will not go toright," etc.\r \rAs followeth in theprocess of his letters. The said Thomas Becket was\rso proud that he wrote toKing Henry the Second, as to his lord, to\rhis king, and to his son,offering him his counsel, his reverence, and\rdue correction, etc.Others in like sort have protested that they owed\rnothing to the kings ofthis land, but their council only, reserving\rall obedience unto the seeof Rome, whereby we may easily see the\rpride and ambition of theclergy in the blind time of ignorance.\r \rAnd as the old cock ofCanterbury did crow in this behalf, so the\ryoung cockerels of othersees did imitate his demeanour, as may be\rseen by this one examplealso in King Stephen\'s time, worthy to be\rremembered; unto whom theBishop of London would not so much as swear\rto be true subject:wherein also he was maintained by the pope....\r \rThus we see that kingswere to rule no further than it pleased the\rpope to like of; neitherto challenge more obedience of their subjects\rthan stood also with theirgood will and pleasure. He wrote in like\rsort unto Queen Maud aboutthe same matter, making her "Samson\'s\rcalf"[2] (the betterto bring his purpose to pass)....\r \r      [2] A fool or dupe.\r \rIs it not strange that apeevish order of religion (devised by man)\rshould break the expresslaw of God, who commandeth all men to honour\rand obey their kings andprinces, in whom some part of the power of\rGod is manifest and laidopen unto us? And even unto this end the\rcardinal of Hostia alsowrote to the canons of Paul\'s after this\rmanner, covertlyencouraging them to stand to their election of the\rsaid Robert, who was nomore willing to give over his new bishopric\rthan they careful tooffend the king, but rather imagined which way to\rkeep it still, maugre hisdispleasure, and yet not to swear obedience\runto him for all that heshould be able to do or perform unto the\rcontrary....\r \rHereby you see how KingStephen was dealt withal. And albeit the\rArchbishop of Canterburyis not openly to be touched herewith, yet it\ris not to be doubted buthe was a doer in it, so far as might tend to\rthe maintenance of theright and prerogative of holy church. And even\rno less unquietness hadanother of our princes with Thomas of Arundel,\rwho fled to Rome for fearof his head, and caused the pope to write an\rambitious and contumeliousletter unto his sovereign about his\rrestitution. But when (bythe king\'s letters yet extant, and beginning\rthus: _"Thomasproditionis non expers nostræ regiæ majestati insidias\rfabricavit"_[3]) thepope understood the bottom of the matter, he was\rcontented that Thomasshould be deprived, and another archbishop\rchosen in his stead.\r \r      [3] "Thomas, not innocent oftreason, has intrigued against\r      the majesty of our court."\r \rNeither did this pridestay at archbishops and bishops, but descended\rlower, even to therake-hells of the clergy and puddles of all\rungodliness. For, besidethe injury received of their superiors, how\rwas King John dealt withalby the vile Cistertians at Lincoln in the\rsecond of his reign?Certes when he had (upon just occasion) conceived\rsome grudge against themfor their ambitious demeanour, and upon\rdenial to pay such sums ofmoney as were allotted unto them, he had\rcaused seizure to be madeof such horses, swine, neat, and other\rthings of theirs as weremaintained in his forests, they denounced him\ras fast amongst themselveswith bell, book, and candle, to be accursed\rand excommunicated.Thereunto they so handled the matter with the pope\rand their friends that theking was fain to yield to their good\rgraces, insomuch that ameeting for pacification was appointed between\rthem at Lincoln, by meansof the present Archbishop of Canterbury, who\rwent off between him andthe Cistertian commissioners before the\rmatter could be finished.In the end the king himself came also unto\rthe said commissioners asthey sat in their chapterhouse, and there\rwith tears fell down attheir feet, craving pardon for his trespasses\ragainst them, and heartilyrequiring that they would (from henceforth)\rcommend him and his realmin their prayers unto the protection of the\rAlmighty, and receive himinto their fraternity, promising moreover\rfull satisfaction of theirdamages sustained, and to build an house of\rtheir order in whatsoeverplace of England it should please them to\rassign. And this heconfirmed by charter bearing date the\rseven-and-twentieth ofNovember, after the Scottish king was returned\rinto Scotland, anddeparted from the king. Whereby (and by other the\rlike, as between JohnStratford and Edward the Third, etc.) a man may\reasily conceive how proudthe clergymen have been in former times, as\rwholly presuming upon theprimacy of their pope. More matter could I\rallege of these and thelike broils, not to be found among our common\rhistoriographers. Howbeit,reserving the same unto places more\rconvenient, I will ceaseto speak of them at this time, and go forward\rwith such other things asmy purpose is to speak of. At the first,\rtherefore, there was likeand equal authority in both our archbishops,\rbut as he of Canterburyhath long since obtained the prerogative above\rYork (although I say notwithout great trouble, suit, some bloodshed,\rand contention), so theArchbishop of York is nevertheless written\rPrimate of England, as onecontenting himself with a piece of a title\rat the least, when allcould not be gotten. And as he of Canterbury\rcrowneth the king, so thisof York doth the like to the queen, whose\rperpetual chaplain he is,and hath been from time to time, since the\rdetermination of thiscontroversy, as writers do report. The first\ralso hath under hisjurisdiction to the number of one-and-twenty\rinferior bishops; theother hath only four, by reason that the\rchurches of Scotland arenow removed from his obedience unto an\rarchbishop of their own,whereby the greatness and circuit of the\rjurisdiction of York isnot a little diminished. In like sort, each of\rthese seven-and-twentysees have their cathedral churches, wherein the\rdeans (a calling not knownin England before the Conquest) do bear the\rchief rule, being menespecially chosen to that vocation, both for\rtheir learning andgodliness, so near as can be possible. These\rcathedral churches have inlike manner other dignities and canonries\rstill remaining unto them,as heretofore under the popish regiment.\rHowbeit those that arechosen to the same are no idle and unprofitable\rpersons (as in times pastthey have been when most of these livings\rwere either furnished withstrangers, especially out of Italy, boys,\ror such idiots as hadleast skill of all in discharging of those\rfunctions whereunto theywere called by virtue of these stipends), but\rsuch as by preaching andteaching can and do learnedly set forth the\rglory of God, and furtherthe overthrow of anti-Christ to the\ruttermost of their powers.\r \rThese churches are calledcathedral, because the bishops dwell or lie\rnear unto the same, asbound to keep continual residence within their\rjurisdictions for thebetter oversight and governance of the same, the\rword being derived _acathedra_--that is to say, a chair or seat where\rhe resteth, and for themost part abideth. At the first there was but\rone church in everyjurisdiction, whereinto no man entered to pray but\rwith some oblation orother toward the maintenance of the pastor. For\ras it was reputed aninfamy to pass by any of them without visitation,\rso it was no less reproachto appear empty before the Lord. And for\rthis occasion also theywere builded very huge and great; for\rotherwise they were notcapable to such multitude as came daily unto\rthem to hear the Word andreceive the sacraments.\r \rBut as the number ofChristians increased, so first monasteries, then\rfinally parish churches,were builded in every jurisdiction: from\rwhence I take our deanerychurches to have their original (now called\r"motherchurches," and their incumbents, archpriests), the rest being\radded since the Conquest,either by the lords of every town, or\rzealous men, loth totravel far, and willing to have some ease by\rbuilding them near hand.Unto these deanery churches also the clergy\rin old time of the samedeanery were appointed to repair at sundry\rseasons, there to receivewholesome ordinances, and to consult upon\rthe necessary affairs ofthe whole jurisdiction if necessity so\rrequired; and some imagehereof is yet to be seen in the north parts.\rBut as the number ofchurches increased, so the repair of the faithful\runto the cathedrals diddiminish; whereby they now become, especially\rin their nether parts,rather markets and shops for merchandise than\rsolemn places of prayer,whereunto they were first erected. Moreover,\rin the said cathedralchurches upon Sundays and festival days the\rcanons do make certainordinary sermons by course, whereunto great\rnumbers of all estates doorderly resort; and upon the working days,\rthrice in the week, one ofthe said canons (or some other in his\rstead) doth read andexpound some piece of holy Scripture, whereunto\rthe people do veryreverently repair. The bishops themselves in like\rsort are not idle in theircallings; for, being now exempt from court\rand council, which is one(and a no small) piece of their felicity\r(although RichardArchbishop of Canterbury thought otherwise, as yet\rappeareth by his lettersto Pope Alexander, Epistola 44, Petri\rBlesensis, where he saith,because the clergy of his time were\rsomewhat narrowly lookedunto, _"Supra dorsum ecclesiæ fabricant\rpeccatores,"etc._),[4] they so apply their minds to the setting forth\rof the Word that there arevery few of them which do not every Sunday\ror oftener resort to someplace or other within their jurisdictions\rwhere they expound theScriptures with much gravity and skill, and yet\rnot without the greatmisliking and contempt of such as hate the Word.\rOf their manifoldtranslations from one see to another I will say\rnothing, which is not nowdone for the benefit of the flock as the\rpreferment of the partyfavoured and advantage unto the prince, a\rmatter in time past muchdoubted of--to wit, whether a bishop or\rpastor might be translatedfrom one see to another, and left undecided\rtill prescription by royalauthority made it good. For, among princes,\ra thing once done is welldone, and to be done oftentimes, though no\rwarrant be to be foundtherefore.\r \r      [4] "Sinners build on the back ofthe church."\r \rThey have under them alsotheir archdeacons, some one, divers two, and\rmany four or more, astheir circuits are in quantity, which\rarchdeacons are termed inlaw the bishops\' eyes; and these (beside\rtheir ordinary courts,which are holden within so many or more of\rtheir several deaneries bythemselves or their officials once in a\rmonth at the least) dokeep yearly two visitations or synods (as the\rbishop doth in every thirdyear, wherein he confirmeth some children,\rthough most care but alittle for that ceremony), in which they make\rdiligent inquisition andsearch, as well for the doctrine and\rbehaviour of the ministersas the orderly dealing of the parishioners\rin resorting to their parishchurches and conformity unto religion.\rThey punish also withgreat severity all such trespassers, either in\rperson or by the purse(where permutation of penance is thought more\rgrievous to the offender),as are presented unto them; or, if the\rcause be of the moreweight, as in cases of heresy, pertinacy,\rcontempt, and such like,they refer them either to the bishop of the\rdiocese, or hischancellor, or else to sundry grave persons set in\rauthority, by virtue of anhigh commission directed unto them from the\rprince to that end, who invery courteous manner do see the offenders\rgently reformed or elseseverely punished if necessity so enforce.\r \rBeside this, in many ofour archdeaconries, we have an exercise lately\rbegun which for the mostpart is called a _prophecy_ or _conference_,\rand erected only for theexamination or trial of the diligence of the\rclergy in their study ofholy Scriptures. Howbeit, such is the thirsty\rdesire of the people inthese days to hear the Word of God that they\ralso have as it were withzealous violence intruded themselves among\rthem (but as hearers only)to come by more knowledge through their\rpresence at the same.Herein also (for the most part) two of the\ryounger sort of ministersdo expound each after other some piece of\rthe Scriptures ordinarilyappointed unto them in their courses\r(wherein they orderly gothrough with some one of the Evangelists, or\rof the Epistles, as itpleaseth the whole assembly to choose at the\rfirst in every of theseconferences); and when they have spent an hour\ror a little more betweenthem, then cometh one of the better learned\rsort, who, being agraduate for the most part, or known to be a\rpreacher sufficientlyauthorised and of a sound judgment, supplieth\rthe room of a moderator,making first a brief rehearsal of their\rdiscourses, and thenadding what him thinketh good of his own\rknowledge, whereby twohours are thus commonly spent at this most\rprofitable meeting. Whenall is done, if the first speakers have\rshewed any piece ofdiligence, they are commended for their travel,\rand encouraged to goforward. If they have been found to be slack, or\rnot sound in delivery oftheir doctrine, their negligence and error is\ropenly reproved before alltheir brethren, who go aside of purpose\rfrom the laity after theexercise ended to judge of these matters, and\rconsult of the nextspeakers and quantity of the text to be handled in\rthat place. The laitynever speak, of course (except some vain and\rbusy head will now andthen intrude themselves with offence), but are\ronly hearers; and, as itis used in some places weekly, in other once\rin fourteen days, indivers monthly, and elsewhere twice in a year, so\ris it a notable spur untoall the ministers thereby to apply their\rbooks, which otherwise (asin times past) would give themselves to\rhawking, hunting, tables,cards, dice, tippling at the alehouse,\rshooting of matches, andother like vanities, nothing commendable in\rsuch as should be godlyand zealous stewards of the good gifts of God,\rfaithful distributors ofhis Word unto the people, and diligent\rpastors according to theircalling.\r \rBut alas! as Sathan, theauthor of all mischief, hath in sundry\rmanners heretoforehindered the erection and maintenance of many good\rthings, so in this he hathstirred up adversaries of late unto this\rmost profitable exercise,who, not regarding the commodity that riseth\rthereby so well to thehearers as speakers, but either stumbling (I\rcannot tell how) at wordsand terms, or at the leastwise not liking to\rhear of the reprehensionof vice, or peradventure taking a misliking\rat the slender demeanoursof such negligent ministers as now and then\rin their course do occupythe rooms, have either by their own\rpractice, their sinisterinformation, or suggestions made upon\rsurmises unto other,procured the suppression of these conferences,\rcondemning them ashurtful, pernicious, and daily breeders of no small\rhurt and inconvenience.But hereof let God be judge, unto the cause\rbelongeth.\r \rOur elders or ministersand deacons (for subdeacons and the other\rinferior orders sometimeused in popish church we have not) are made\raccording to a certainform of consecration concluded upon in the time\rof King Edward the Sixthby the clergy of England, and soon after\rconfirmed by the threeestates of the realm in the high court of\rparliament. And out of thefirst sort--that is to say, of such as are\rcalled to the ministry(without respect whether they be married or\rnot)--are bishops, deans,archdeacons, and such as have the higher\rplaces in the hierarchy ofthe church elected; and these also, as all\rthe rest, at the firstcoming unto any spiritual promotion do yield\runto the prince the entiretax of that their living for one whole\ryear, if it amount invalue unto ten pounds and upwards, and this\runder the name and titleof first fruits.\r \rWith us also it ispermitted that a sufficient man may (by\rdispensation from theprince) hold two livings, not distant either\rfrom other above thirtymiles; whereby it cometh to pass that, as her\rMajesty doth reap somecommodity by the faculty, so that the unition\rof two in one man dothbring oftentimes more benefit to one of them in\ra month (I mean fordoctrine) than they have had before peradventure\rin many years.\r \rMany exclaim against suchfaculties, as if there were more good\rpreachers that wantmaintenance than livings to maintain them. Indeed\rwhen a living is voidthere are so many suitors for it that a man\rwould think the report tobe true, and most certain; but when it\rcometh to the trial (whoare sufficient and who not, who are staid men\rin conversation, judgment,and learning), of that great number you\rshall hardly find one ortwo such as they ought to be, and yet none\rmore earnest to make suit,to promise largely, bear a better shew, or\rfind fault with the stageof things than they. Nevertheless I do not\rthink that theirexclamations, if they were wisely handled, are\raltogether grounded uponrumours or ambitious minds, if you respect\rthe state of the thingitself, and not the necessity growing through\rwant of able men tofurnish out all the cures in England, which both\rour universities are neverable to perform. For if you observe what\rnumbers of preachersCambridge and Oxford do yearly send forth, and\rhow many new compositionsare made in the Court of First Fruits by the\rdeaths of the lastincumbents, you shall soon see a difference.\rWherefore, if in countrytowns and cities, yea even in London itself,\rfour or five of the littlechurches were brought into one, the\rinconvenience would ingreat part be redressed and amended.\r \rAnd, to say truth, onemost commonly of those small livings is of so\rlittle value that it isnot able to maintain a mean scholar, much less\ra learned man, as notbeing above ten, twelve, sixteen, seventeen,\rtwenty, or thirty poundsat the most, toward their charges, which now\r(more than before time) dogo out of the same. I say more than before,\rbecause every smalltrifle, nobleman\'s request, or courtesy craved by\rthe bishop, doth imposeand command a twentieth part, a three score\rpart, or twopence in thepound, etc., out of the livings, which\rhitherto hath not beenusually granted, but by the consent of a synod,\rwherein things weredecided according to equity, and the poorer sort\rconsidered of, which noware equally burdened.\r \rWe pay also the tenths ofour livings to the prince yearly, according\rto such valuation of eachof them as hath been lately made: which\rnevertheless in time pastwere not annual, but voluntary, and paid at\rrequest of king orpope.[5]...\r \r      [5] Here follows a story about thebootless errand of a pope\'s\r      legate in 1452.--W.\r \rBut to return to ourtenths, a payment first as devised by the pope,\rand afterward taken up asby the prescription of the king, whereunto\rwe may join also our firstfruits, which is one whole year\'s commodity\rof our living, due at ourentrance into the same, the tenths abated\runto the prince\'s coffers,and paid commonly in two years. For the\rreceipt also of these twopayments an especial office or court is\rerected, which bearethname of First Fruits and Tenths, whereunto, if\rthe party to be preferreddo not make his dutiful repair by an\rappointed time afterpossession taken, there to compound for the\rpayment of his saidfruits, he incurreth the danger of a great\rpenalty, limited by acertain statute provided in that behalf against\rsuch as do intrude intothe ecclesiastical function and refuse to pay\rthe accustomed dutiesbelonging to the same.\r \rThey pay likewisesubsidies with the temporalty, but in such sort that\rif these pay after fourshillings for land, the clergy contribute\rcommonly after sixshillings of the pound, so that of a benefice of\rtwenty pounds by the yearthe incumbent thinketh himself well\racquitted if, all ordinarypayments being discharged, he may reserve\rthirteen pounds sixshillings eightpence towards his own sustentation\ror maintenance of hisfamily. Seldom also are they without the compass\rof a subsidy; for if theybe one year clear from this payment (a thing\rnot often seen of late years),they are like in the next to hear of\ranother grant: so that Isay again they are seldom without the limit\rof a subsidy. Herein alsothey somewhat find themselves grieved that\rthe laity may at everytaxation help themselves, and so they do,\rthrough consideration hadof their decay and hindrance, and yet their\rimpoverishment cannot buttouch also the parson or vicar, unto whom\rsuch liberty is denied, asis daily to be seen in their accounts and\rtithings.\r \rSome of them also, afterthe marriages of their children, will have\rtheir proportionsqualified, or by friendship get themselves quite out\rof the book. But whatstand I upon these things, who have rather to\rcomplain of the injuryoffered by some of our neighbours of the laity,\rwhich daily endeavour tobring us also within the compass of their\rfifteens or taxes fortheir own ease, whereas the tax of the whole\rrealm, which is commonlygreater in the champagne than woodland soil,\ramounteth only to 37,930pounds ninepence halfpenny, is a burden easy\renough to be borne upon somany shoulders, without the help of the\rclergy, whose tenths andsubsidies make up commonly a double, if not\rtreble sum unto theiraforesaid payments? Sometimes also we are\rthreatened with a _Meliusinquirendum_, as if our livings were not\rracked high enoughalready. But if a man should seek out where all\rthose church lands whichin time past did contribute unto the old sum\rrequired or to be made up,no doubt no small number of the laity of\rall states should becontributors also with us, the prince not\rdefrauded of herexpectation and right. We are also charged with\rarmour and munitions fromthirty pounds upwards, a thing more needful\rthan divers other chargesimposed upon us are convenient, by which and\rother burdens our easegroweth to be more heavy by a great deal\r(notwithstanding ourimmunity from temporal services) than that of the\rlaity, and, for aught thatI see, not likely to be diminished, as if\rthe church were now becomethe ass whereon every market man is to ride\rand cast his wallet.\r \rThe other payments dueunto the archbishop and bishop at their several\rvisitations (of which thefirst is double to the latter), and such\ralso as the archdeaconreceive that his synods, etc., remain still as\rthey did without anyalteration. Only this I think he added within\rmemory of man, that at thecoming of every prince his appointed\rofficers do commonly visitthe whole realm under the form of an\recclesiasticalinquisition, in which the clergy do usually pay double\rfees, as unto thearchbishop.\r \rHereby then, and by thosealready remembered, it is found that the\rChurch of England is noless commodious to the prince\'s coffers than\rthe state of the laity, ifit do not far exceed the same, since their\rpayments are certain,continual, and seldom abated, howsoever they\rgather up their own dutieswith grudging, murmuring, suit, and\rslanderous speeches of thepayers, or have their livings otherwise\rhardly valued unto theuttermost farthing, or shrewdly cancelled by\rthe covetousness of the patrons,of whom some do bestow advowsons of\rbenefices upon theirbakers, butlers, cooks, good archers, falconers,\rand horsekeepers, insteadof other recompense, for their long and\rfaithful service, whichthey employ afterward unto the most advantage.\r \rCertes here they resemblethe pope very much; for, as he sendeth out\rhis idols, so do theytheir parasites, pages, chamberlains, stewards,\rgrooms, and lackeys; andyet these be the men that first exclaim of\rthe insufficiency of theministers, as hoping thereby in due time to\rget also their glebes andgrounds into their hands. In times past\rbishoprics went almostafter the same manner under the lay princes,\rand then under the pope,so that he which helped a clerk unto a see\rwas sure to have a presentor purse fine, if not an annual pension,\rbesides that which went tothe pope\'s coffers, and was thought to be\rvery good merchandise.\r \rTo proceed therefore withthe rest, I think it good also to remember\rthat the names usuallygiven unto such as feed the flock remain in\rlike sort as in timespast, so that these words, _parson, vicar,\rcurate_, and such, are notyet abolished more than the canon law\ritself, which is dailypleaded, as I have said elsewhere, although the\rstatutes of the realm havegreatly infringed the large scope and\rbrought the exercise ofthe same into some narrower limits. There is\rnothing read in ourchurches but the canonical Scriptures, whereby it\rcometh to pass that thePsalter is said over once in thirty days, the\rNew Testament four times,and the Old Testament once in the year. And\rhereunto, if the curate beadjudged by the bishop or his deputies\rsufficiently instructed inthe holy Scriptures, and therewithal able\rto teach, he permittethhim to make some exposition or exhortation in\rhis parish unto amendmentof life. And for so much as our churches and\runiversities have been sospoiled in time of error, as there cannot\ryet be had such number ofable pastors as may suffice for every parish\rto have one, there are(beside four sermons appointed by public order\rin the year) certainsermons or homilies (devised by sundry learned\rmen, confirmed for sounddoctrine by consent of the divines, and\rpublic authority of theprince), and those appointed to be read by the\rcurates of meanunderstanding (which homilies do comprehend the\rprincipal parts ofChristian doctrine, as of original sin, of\rjustification by faith, ofcharity, and such like) upon the Sabbath\rdays unto thecongregation. And, after a certain number of psalms\rread, which are limitedaccording to the dates of the month, for\rmorning and evening prayerwe have two lessons, whereof the first is\rtaken out of the OldTestament, the second out of the New; and of\rthese latter, that in themorning is out of the Gospels, the other in\rthe afternoon out of someone of the Epistles. After morning prayer\ralso, we have the Litanyand suffrages, an invocation in mine opinion\rnot devised without thegreat assistance of the Spirit of God,\ralthough many curiousmind-sick persons utterly condemn it as\rsuperstitious, andsavouring of conjuration and sorcery.\r \rThis being done, weproceed unto the communion, if any communicants be\rto receive the Eucharist;if not, we read the Decalogue, Epistle, and\rGospel, with the NiceneCreed (of some in derision called the "dry\rcommunion"), and thenproceed unto an homily or sermon, which hath a\rpsalm before and after it,and finally unto the baptism of such\rinfants as on everySabbath day (if occasion so require) are brought\runto the churches; andthus is the forenoon bestowed. In the afternoon\rlikewise we meet again,and, after the psalms and lessons ended, we\rhave commonly a sermon, orat the leastwise our youth catechised by\rthe space of an hour. Andthus do we spend the Sabbath day in good and\rgodly exercises, all donein our vulgar tongue, that each one present\rmay hear and understandthe same, which also in cathedral and\rcollegiate churches is soordered that the psalms only are sung by\rnote, the rest being read(as in common parish churches) by the\rminister with a loudvoice, saving that in the administration of the\rcommunion the choirsingeth the answers, the creed, and sundry other\rthings appointed, but inso plain, I say, and distinct manner that\reach one present mayunderstand what they sing, every word having but\rone note, though the wholeHarmony consist of many parts, and those\rvery cunningly set by theskilful in that science.\r \rCertes this translation ofthe service of the church into the vulgar\rtongue hath not a littleoffended the pope almost in every age, as a\rthing very often attemptedby divers princes, but never generally\robtained, for fear lestthe consenting thereunto might breed the\roverthrow (as it wouldindeed) of all his religion and hierarchy;\rnevertheless, in someplaces where the kings and princes dwelled not\runder his nose, it wasperformed maugre his resistance. Wratislaus,\rDuke of Bohemia, wouldlong since have done the like also in his\rkingdom; but, not daringto venture so far without the consent of the\rpope, he wrote unto himthereof, and received his answer inhibitory\runto all his proceeding inthe same....\r \rI would set down two orthree more of the like instruments passed from\rthat see unto the likeend, but this shall suffice, being less common\rthan the other, which areto be had more plentifully.\r \rAs for our churchesthemselves, bells and times of morning and evening\rprayer remain as in timespast, saving that all images, shrines,\rtabernacles, rood-lofts,and monuments of idolatry are removed, taken\rdown, and defaced, onlythe stories in glass windows excepted, which,\rfor want of sufficientstore of new stuff, and by reason of extreme\rcharge that should grow bythe alteration of the same into white panes\rthroughout the realm, arenot altogether abolished in most places at\ronce, but by little andlittle suffered to decay, that white glass may\rbe provided and set up intheir rooms. Finally, whereas there was wont\rto be a great partitionbetween the choir and the body of the church,\rnow it is either verysmall or none at all, and (to say the truth)\raltogether needless, siththe minister saith his service commonly in\rthe body of the church,with his face toward the people, in a little\rtabernacle of wainscotprovided for the purpose, by which means the\rignorant do not only learndivers of the psalms and usual prayers by\rheart, but also such ascan read do pray together with him, so that\rthe whole congregation atone instant pour out their petitions unto\rthe living God for thewhole estate of His church in most earnest and\rfervent manner. Our holyand festival days are very well reduced also\runto a less number; forwhereas (not long since) we had under the pope\rfour score and fifteen,called festival, and thirty _profesti_, beside\rthe Sundays, they are allbrought unto seven and twenty, and, with\rthem, the superfluousnumbers of idle wakes, guilds, fraternities,\rchurch-ales, help-ales,and soul-ales, called also dirge-ales, with\rthe heathenish rioting atbride-ales, are well diminished and laid\raside. And no great matterwere it if the feasts of all our apostles,\revangelists, and martyrs,with that of all saints, were brought to the\rholy days that follow uponChristmas, Easter, and Whitsuntide, and\rthose of the Virgin Mary,with the rest, utterly removed from the\rcalendars, as neithernecessary nor commendable in a reformed church.\r \rThe apparel in like sortof our clergymen is comely, and, in truth,\rmore decent than ever itwas in the popish church, before the\runiversities bound theirgraduates unto a stable attire, afterward\rusurped also even by theblind Sir Johns. For, if you peruse well my\rChronology ensuing, youshall find that they went either in divers\rcolours like players, orin garments of light hue, as yellow, red,\rgreen, etc., with theirshoes piked, their hair crisped, their girdles\rarmed with silver, theirshoes, spurs, bridles, etc., buckled with\rlike metal, their apparel(for the most part) of silk, and richly\rfurred, their caps lacedand buttoned with gold, so that to meet a\rpriest in those days wasto behold a peacock that spreadeth his tail\rwhen he danceth before thehen, which now (I say) is well reformed.\rTouching hospitality,there was never any greater used in England,\rsith by reason thatmarriage is permitted to him that will choose that\rkind of life, their meatand drink is more orderly and frugally\rdressed, their furnitureof household more convenient and better\rlooked unto, and the pooroftener fed generally than heretofore they\rhave been, when only a fewbishops and double or treble beneficed men\rdid make good cheer atChristmas only, or otherwise kept great houses\rfor the entertainment ofthe rich, which did often see and visit them.\rIt is thought muchperadventure that some bishops, etc., in our time\rdo come short of theancient gluttony and prodigality of their\rpredecessors; but to suchas do consider of the curtailing of their\rlivings, or excessiveprices whereunto things are grown, and how their\rcourse is limited by law,and estate looked into on every side, the\rcause of their so doing iswell enough perceived. This also offended\rmany, that they should,after their deaths, leave their substances to\rtheir wives and children,whereas they consider not that in old time\rsuch as had no lemans norbastards (very few were there, God wot, of\rthis sort) did leave theirgoods and possessions to their brethren and\rkinsfolks, whereby (as Ican shew by good record) many houses of\rgentility have grown andbeen erected. If in any age some one of them\rdid found a college,almshouse, or school, if you look unto these our\rtimes, you shall see nofewer deeds of charity done, nor better\rgrounded upon the rightstub of piety than before. If you say that\rtheir wives be fond, afterthe decease of their husbands, and bestow\rthemselves not soadvisedly as their calling requireth (which, God\rknoweth, these curioussurveyors make small account of truth, further\rthan thereby to gathermatter of reprehension), I beseech you then to\rlook into all states ofthe laity, and tell me whether some duchesses,\rcountesses, barons\' orknights\' wives, do not fully so often offend in\rthe like as they? For Evewill be Eve, though Adam would say nay. Not\ra few also find fault withour threadbare gowns, as if not our patrons\rbut our wives were causesof our woe. But if it were known to all that\rI know to have beenperformed of late in Essex, where a minister\rtaking a benefice (of lessthan twenty pounds in the Queen\'s books, so\rfar as I remember) wasenforced to pay to his patron twenty quarters\rof oats, ten quarters ofwheat, and sixteen yearly of barley (which he\rcalled _hawks\' meat_), andanother let the like in farm to his patron\rfor ten pounds by the yearwhich is well worth forty at the least, the\rcause of our threadbaregowns would easily appear: for such patrons do\rscrape the wool from ourcloaks. Wherefore I may well say that such a\rthreadbare minister iseither an ill man or hath an ill patron, or\rboth; and when such cooksand cobbling shifters shall be removed and\rweeded out of theministry, I doubt not but our patrons will prove\rbetter men, and bereformed whether they will or not, or else the\rsingle-minded bishopsshall see the living bestowed upon such as do\rdeserve it. When thePragmatic Sanction took place first in France, it\rwas supposed that theseenormities should utterly have ceased; but\rwhen the elections ofbishops came once into the hands of the canons\rand spiritual men, it grewto be far worse. For they also, within a\rwhile waxing covetous, bytheir own experience learned aforehand,\rraised the markets, andsought after new gains by the gifts of the\rgreatest livings in thatcountry, wherein (as Machiavelli writeth) are\reighteen archbishoprics,one hundred forty and five bishoprics, 740\rabbeys, elevenuniversities, 1,000,700 steeples (if his report be\rsound). Some are of theopinion that, if sufficient men in every town\rmight be sent for from theuniversities, this mischief would soon be\rremedied; but I am cleanof another mind. For, when I consider\rwhereunto the gifts offellowships in some places are grown, the\rprofit that ariseth atsundry elections of scholars out of grammar\rschools to the posers,schoolmasters, and preferers of them to our\runiversities, the gifts ofa great number of almshouses builded for\rthe maimed and impotentsoldiers by princes and good men heretofore\rmoved with a pitifulconsideration of the poor distressed, how\rrewards, pensions, andannuities also do reign in other cases whereby\rthe giver is broughtsometimes into extreme misery, and that not so\rmuch as the room of acommon soldier is not obtained oftentimes\rwithout a _"What willyou give me?"_ I am brought into such a mistrust\rof the sequel of thisdevice that I dare pronounce (almost for\rcertain) that, if Homerwere now alive, it should be said to him:\r \r    "Tuque licet venias musis comitatusHomere,\r    Si nihil attuleris, ibis Homereforas!"\r \rMore I could say, and moreI would say, of these and other things,\rwere it not that in mineown judgment I have said enough already for\rthe advertisement of suchas be wise. Nevertheless, before I finish\rthis chapter, I will add aword or two (so briefly as I can) of the\rold estate of cathedralchurches, which I have collected together here\rand there among thewriters, and whereby it shall easily be seen what\rthey were, and how nearthe government of ours do in these days\rapproach unto them; forthat there is an irreconcilable odds between\rthem and those of thePapists. I hope there is no learned man indeed\rbut will acknowledge andyield unto it.\r \rWe find therefore in thetime of the primitive church that there was\rin every see orjurisdiction one school at the least, whereunto such\ras were catechists inChristian religion did resort. And hereof, as we\rmay find great testimonyfor Alexandria, Antioch, Rome, and Jerusalem,\rso no small notice is leftof the like in the inferior sort, if the\rnames of such as taught inthem be called to mind, and the histories\rwell read which makereport of the same. These schools were under the\rjurisdiction of thebishops, and from thence did they and the rest of\rthe elders choose out suchas were the ripest scholars, and willing to\rserve in the ministry,whom they placed also in their cathedral\rchurches, there not onlyto be further instructed in the knowledge of\rthe world, but also to inurethem to the delivery of the same unto the\rpeople in sound manner, tominister the sacraments, to visit the sick\rand brethren imprisoned,and to perform such other duties as then\rbelonged to their charges.The bishop himself and elders of the church\rwere also hearers andexaminers of their doctrine; and, being in\rprocess of time found meetworkmen for the Lord\'s harvest, they were\rforthwith sent abroad(after imposition of hands and prayer generally\rmade for their goodproceeding) to some place or other then destitute\rof her pastor, and othertaken from the school also placed in their\rrooms. What number of suchclerks belonged now and then to some one\rsee, the Chronologyfollowing shall easily declare; and, in like sort,\rwhat officers, widows, andother persons were daily maintained in\rthose seasons by theofferings and oblations of the faithful it is\rincredible to be reported,if we compare the same with the decays and\roblations seen andpractised at this present. But what is that in all\rthe world which avariceand negligence will not corrupt and impair?\rAnd, as this is a patternof the estate of the cathedral churches in\rthose times, so I wishthat the like order of government might once\ragain be restored unto thesame, which may be done with ease, sith the\rschools are alreadybuilded in every diocese, the universities, places\rof their preferment untofurther knowledge, and the cathedral churches\rgreat enough to receive somany as shall come from thence to be\rinstructed unto doctrine.But one hindrance of this is already and\rmore and more to be lookedfor (beside the plucking and snatching\rcommonly seen from suchhouses and the church), and that is, the\rgeneral contempt of theministry, and small consideration of their\rformer pains taken,whereby less and less hope of competent\rmaintenance by preachingthe word is likely to ensue. Wherefore the\rgreatest part of the moreexcellent wits choose rather to employ their\rstudies unto physic andthe laws, utterly giving over the study of the\rScriptures, for fear lestthey should in time not get their bread by\rthe same. By this meansalso the stalls in their choirs would be\rbetter filled, which now(for the most part) are empty, and prebends\rshould be prebends indeed,there to live till they were preferred to\rsome ecclesiasticalfunction, and then other men chosen to succeed\rthem in their rooms,whereas now prebends are but superfluous\radditiments unto formerexcesses, and perpetual commodities unto the\rowners, which before timewere but temporal (as I have said before).\rBut as I have good leisureto wish for these things, so it shall be a\rlonger time before it willbe brought to pass. Nevertheless, as I will\rpray for a reformation inthis behold, so will I here conclude my\rdiscourse on the estate ofour churches.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER VI\r \rOF THE FOOD AND DIET OFTHE ENGLISH\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapter1; 1587, Book II., Chapter 6.]\r \r \rThe situation of ourregion, lying near unto the north, doth cause the\rheat of our stomachs to beof somewhat greater force: therefore our\rbodies do crave a littlemore ample nourishment than the inhabitants\rof the hotter regions areaccustomed withal, whose digestive force is\rnot altogether sovehement, because their internal heat is not so\rstrong as ours, which iskept in by the coldness of the air that from\rtime to time (especiallyin winter) doth environ our bodies.\r \rIt is no marvel thereforethat our tables are oftentimes more\rplentifully garnished thanthose of other nations, and this trade hath\rcontinued with us evensince the very beginning. For, before the\rRomans found out and knewthe way unto our country, our predecessors\rfed largely upon flesh andmilk, whereof there was great abundance in\rthis isle, because theyapplied their chief studies unto pasturage and\rfeeding. After this manneralso did our Welsh Britons order themselves\rin their diet so long asthey lived of themselves, but after they\rbecame to be united andmade equal with the English they framed their\rappetites to live afterour manner, so that at this day there is very\rlittle difference betweenus in our diets.\r \rIn Scotland likewise theyhave given themselves (of late years to\rspeak of) unto very ampleand large diet, wherein as for some respect\rnature doth make themequal with us, so otherwise they far exceed us\rin over much anddistemperate gormandise, and so ingross their bodies\rthat divers of them do oftbecome unapt to any other purpose than to\rspend their times in largetabling and belly cheer. Against this\rpampering of theircarcasses doth Hector Boethius in his description\rof the country verysharply inveigh in the first chapter of that\rtreatise. Henry Wardlawalso, bishop of St. Andrews, noting their\rvehement alteration fromcompetent frugality into excessive gluttony\rto be brought out ofEngland with James the First (who had been long\rtime prisoner there underthe fourth and fifth Henries, and at his\rreturn carried diversEnglish gentlemen into his country with him,\rwhom he very honourablypreferred there), doth vehemently exclaim\ragainst the same in openParliament holden at Perth, 1433, before the\rthree estates, and sobringeth his purpose to pass in the end, by\rforce of his learnedpersuasions, that a law was presently made there\rfor the restraint ofsuperfluous diet; amongst other things, baked\rmeats (dishes never beforethis man\'s days seen in Scotland) were\rgenerally so provided forby virtue of this Act that it was not lawful\rfor any to eat of the sameunder the degree of a gentleman, and those\ronly but on high andfestival days. But, alas, it was soon forgotten!\r \rIn old time these northBritons did give themselves universally to\rgreat abstinence, and intime of wars their soldiers would often feed\rbut once or twice at themost in two or three days (especially if they\rheld themselves in secret,or could have no issue out of their bogs\rand marshes, through thepresence of the enemy), and in this distress\rthey used to eat a certainkind of confection, whereof so much as a\rbean would qualify theirhunger above common expectation. In woods\rmoreover they lived withherbs and roots, or, if these shifts served\rnot through want of suchprovision at hand, then used they to creep\rinto the water or saidmoorish plots up unto the chins, and there\rremain a long time, onlyto qualify the heats of their stomachs by\rviolence, which otherwisewould have wrought and been ready to oppress\rthem for hunger and wantof sustenance. In those days likewise it was\rtaken for a great offenceover all to eat either goose, hare, or hen,\rbecause of a certainsuperstitious opinion which they had conceived of\rthose three creatures;howbeit after that the Romans, I say, had once\rfound an entrance intothis island it was not long ere open shipwreck\rwas made of this religiousobservation, so that in process of time so\rwell the north and southBritons as the Romans gave over to make such\rdifference in meats asthey had done before.\r \rFrom thenceforth also untoour days, and even in this season wherein\rwe live, there is norestraint of any meat either for religious sake\ror public order inEngland, but it is lawful for every man to feed\rupon whatsoever he is ableto purchase, except it be upon those days\rwhereon eating of flesh isespecially forbidden by the laws of the\rrealm, which order istaken only to the end our numbers of cattle may\rbe the better increasedand that abundance of fish which the sea\ryieldeth more generallyreceived. Besides this, there is great\rconsideration had inmaking this law for the preservation of the navy\rand maintenance ofconvenient numbers of seafaring men, both which\rwould otherwise greatlydecay if some means were not found whereby\rthey might be increased.But, howsoever this case standeth, white\rmeats, milk, butter, andcheese (which were never so dear as in my\rtime, and wont to beaccounted of as one of the chief stays throughout\rthe island) are nowreputed as food appertinent only to the inferior\rsort, whilst such as aremore wealthy do feed upon the flesh of all\rkinds of cattle accustomedto be eaten, all sorts of fish taken upon\rour coasts and in ourfresh rivers, and such diversity of wild and\rtame fowls as are eitherbred in our island or brought over unto us\rfrom other countries ofthe main.\r \rIn number of dishes andchange of meat the nobility of England (whose\rcooks are for the mostpart musical-headed Frenchmen and strangers) do\rmost exceed, sith there isno day in manner that passeth over their\rheads wherein they havenot only beef, mutton, veal, lamb, kid, pork,\rcony, capon, pig, or somany of these as the season yieldeth, but also\rsome portion of the red orfallow deer, beside great variety of fish\rand wild fowl, and theretosundry other delicates wherein the sweet\rhand of the seafaringPortugal is not wanting: so that for a man to\rdine with one of them, andto taste of every dish that standeth before\rhim (which few used to do,but each one feedeth upon that meat him\rbest liketh for the time,the beginning of every dish notwithstanding\rbeing reserved unto thegreatest personage that sitteth at the table,\rto whom it is drawn upstill by the waiters as order requireth, and\rfrom whom it descendethagain even to the lower end, whereby each one\rmay taste thereof), israther to yield unto a conspiracy with a great\rdeal of meat for thespeedy suppression of natural health than the use\rof a necessary mean tosatisfy himself with a competent repast to\rsustain his body withal.But, as this large feeding is not seen in\rtheir guests, no more isit in their own persons; for, sith they have\rdaily much resort untotheir tables (and many times unlooked for), and\rthereto retain greatnumbers of servants, it is very requisite and\rexpedient for them to besomewhat plentiful in this behalf.\r \rThe chief part likewise oftheir daily provision is brought in before\rthem (commonly in silvervessels, if they be of the degree of barons,\rbishops, and upwards) andplaced on their tables, whereof, when they\rhave taken what itpleaseth them, the rest is reserved, and afterwards\rsent down to their servingmen and waiters, who feed thereon in like\rsort with convenientmoderation, their reversion also being bestowed\rupon the poor which lieready at their gates in great numbers to\rreceive the same. This isspoken of the principal tables whereat the\rnobleman, his lady, andguests are accustomed to sit; besides which\rthey have a certainordinary allowance daily appointed for their\rhalls, where the chiefofficers and household servants (for all are\rnot permitted by custom towait upon their master), and with them such\rinferior guests do feed asare not of calling to associate the\rnobleman himself; so that,besides those afore-mentioned, which are\rcalled to the principaltable, there are commonly forty or three score\rpersons fed in thosehalls, to the great relief of such poor suitors\rand strangers also as oftbe partakers thereof and otherwise like to\rdine hardly. As for drink,it is usually filled in pots, goblets,\rjugs, bowls of silver, innoblemen\'s houses; also in fine Venice\rglasses of all forms; and,for want of these elsewhere, in pots of\rearth of sundry coloursand moulds, whereof many are garnished with\rsilver, or at theleastwise in pewter, all which notwithstanding are\rseldom set on the table,but each one, as necessity urgeth, calleth\rfor a cup of such drink ashim listeth to have, so that, when he has\rtasted of it, he deliveredthe cup again to some one of the standers\rby, who, making it cleanby pouring out the drink that remaineth,\rrestoreth it to thecupboard from whence he fetched the same. By this\rdevice (a thing brought upat the first by Mnesitheus of Athens, in\rconservation of the honourof Orestes, who had not yet made expiation\rfor the death of hisadulterous parents, Aegisthus and Clytemnestra)\rmuch idle tippling isfurthermore cut off; for, if the full pots\rshould continually standat the elbow or near the trencher, divers\rwould always be dealingwith them, whereas now they drink seldom, and\ronly when necessityurgeth, and so avoid the note of great drinking,\ror often troubling of theservitors with filling of their bowls.\rNevertheless in thenoblemen\'s halls this order is not used, neither\ris any man\'s housecommonly under the degree of a knight or esquire of\rgreat revenues. It is aworld to see in these our days, wherein gold\rand silver most aboundeth,how that our gentility, as loathing those\rmetals (because of theplenty) do now generally choose rather the\rVenice glasses, both forour wine and beer, than any of those metals\ror stone wherein beforetime we have been accustomed to drink; but\rsuch is the nature of mangenerally that it most coveteth things\rdifficult to be attained;and such is the estimation of this stuff\rthat many become rich onlywith their new trade unto Murana (a town\rnear to Venice, situate onthe Adriatic Sea), from whence the very\rbest are daily to be had,and such as for beauty do well near match\rthe crystal or the ancient_murrhina vasa_ whereof now no man hath\rknowledge. And as this isseen in the gentility, so in the wealthy\rcommunalty the like desireof glass is not neglected, whereby the gain\rgotten by their purchaseis yet much more increased to the benefit of\rthe merchant. The poorestalso will have glass if they may; but, sith\rthe Venetian is somewhattoo dear for them, they content themselves\rwith such as are made athome of fern and burned stone; but in fine\rall go one way--that is,to shards at the last, so that our great\rexpenses in glasses(beside that they breed much strife toward such as\rhave the charge of them)are worst of all bestowed in mine opinion,\rbecause their pieces doturn unto no profit. If the philosopher\'s\rstone were once found, andone part hereof mixed with forty of molten\rglass, it would inducesuch a metallical toughness thereunto that a\rfall should nothing hurtit in such manner; yet it might peradventure\rbunch or batter it;nevertheless that inconvenience were quickly to be\rredressed by the hammer.But whither am I slipped?\r \rThe gentlemen andmerchants keep much about one rate, and each of them\rcontenteth himself withfour, five, or six dishes, when they have but\rsmall resort, or peradventurewith one, or two, or three at the most,\rwhen they have nostrangers to accompany them at their tables. And yet\rtheir servants have theirordinary diet assigned, beside such as is\rleft at their master\'sboards, and not appointed to be brought thither\rthe second time, whichnevertheless is often seen, generally in\rvenison, lamb, or someespecial dish, whereon the merchantman himself\rliketh to feed when it iscold, or peradventure for sundry causes\rincident to the feeder isbetter so than if it were warm or hot. To be\rshort, at such times asthe merchants do make their ordinary or\rvoluntary feasts, it is aworld to see what great provision is made of\rall manner of delicatemeats, from every quarter of the country,\rwherein, beside that theyare often comparable herein to the nobility\rof the land, they willseldom regard anything that the butcher usually\rkilleth, but reject thesame as not worthy to come in place. In such\rcases also jellies of allcolours, mixed with a variety in the\rrepresentation of sundryflowers, herbs, trees, forms of beasts, fish,\rfowls, and fruits, andthereunto marchpane wrought with no small\rcuriosity, tarts of divershues, and sundry denominations, conserves\rof old fruits, foreign andhome-bred, suckets, codinacs, marmalades,\rmarchpane, sugar-bread,gingerbread, florentines, wild fowls, venison\rof all sorts, and sundryoutlandish confections, altogether seasoned\rwith sugar (which Plinycalleth _mel ex arundinibus_, a device not\rcommon nor greatly used inold time at the table, but only in\rmedicine, although it grewin Arabia, India, and Sicilia), do\rgenerally bear the sway,besides infinite devices of our own not\rpossible for me toremember. Of the potato, and such venerous roots as\rare brought out of Spain,Portugal, and the Indies to furnish up our\rbanquets, I speak not,wherein our mures[1] of no less force, and to\rbe had aboutCrosby-Ravenswath, do now begin to have place.\r \r      [1] Sweet cicely, sometimes miscalledmyrrh. Mure is the Saxon\r      word. At one time the plant was notuncommon as a salad.--W.\r \rBut among all these, thekind of meat which is obtained with most\rdifficulty and costs, iscommonly taken for the most delicate, and\rthereupon each guest willsoonest desire to feed. And as all estates\rdo exceed herein, I meanfor strangeness and number of costly dishes,\rso these forget not to usethe like excess in wine, insomuch as there\ris no kind to be had,neither anywhere more store of all sorts than in\rEngland, although we havenone growing with us but yearly to the\rproportion of 20,000 of30,000 tun and upwards, notwithstanding the\rdaily restraints of thesame brought over unto us, whereof at great\rmeetings there is not somestore to be had. Neither do I mean this of\rsmall wines only, asclaret, white, red, French, etc., which amount to\rabout fifty-six sorts,according to the number of regions from whence\rthey came, but also of thethirty kinds of Italian, Grecian, Spanish,\rCanarian, etc., whereofvernage, catepument, raspis, muscadell,\rromnie, bastard lire, osycaprie, clary, and malmesey, are not least\rof all accompted of,because of their strength and valour. For, as I\rhave said in meat, so, thestronger the wine is, the more it is\rdesired, by means whereof,in old time, the best was called\r_theologicum_, because itwas had from the clergy and religious men,\runto whose houses many ofthe laity would often send for bottles\rfilled with the same,being sure they would neither drink nor be\rserved of the worst, orsuch as was any ways mingled or brewed by the\rvinterer: nay, themerchant would have thought that his soul should\rhave gone straightway tothe devil if he should have served them with\rother than the best.Furthermore, when these have had their course\rwhich nature yieldeth,sundry sorts of artificial stuff as ypocras and\rwormwood wine must in likemanner succeed in their turns, beside stale\rale and strong beer, whichnevertheless bear the greatest brunt in\rdrinking, and are of somany sorts and ages as it pleaseth the brewer\rto make them.\r \rThe beer that is used atnoblemen\'s tables in their fixed and standing\rhouses is commonly a yearold, or peradventure of two years\' tunning\ror more; but this is notgeneral. It is also brewed in March, and\rtherefore called Marchbeer; but, for the household, it is usually not\runder a month\'s age, eachone coveting to have the same stale as he\rmay, so that it be notsour, and his bread new as is possible, so that\rit be not hot.\r \rThe artificer andhusbandman makes greatest account of such meat as\rthey may soonest come by,and have it quickliest ready, except it be\rin London when thecompanies of every trade do meet on their quarter\rdays, at which time theybe nothing inferior to the nobility. Their\rfood also consistethprincipally in beef, and such meat as the butcher\rselleth--that is to say,mutton, veal, lamb, pork, etc., whereof he\rfindeth great store in themarkets adjoining, beside sows, brawn,\rbacon, fruit, pies offruit, fowls of sundry sorts, cheese, butter,\reggs, etc., as the otherwanteth it not at home, by his own provision\rwhich is at the best hand,and commonly least charge. In feasting\ralso, this latter sort, Imean the husbandmen, do exceed after their\rmanner, especially atbridals, purifications of women, and such odd\rmeetings, where it isincredible to tell what meat is consumed and\rspent, each one bringingsuch a dish, or so many with him, as his wife\rand he do consult upon,but always with this consideration, that the\rlesser friend shall havethe better provision. This also is commonly\rseen at these banquets,that the good man of the house is not charged\rwith anything savingbread, drink, sauce, house-room, and fire. But\rthe artificers in citiesand good towns do deal far otherwise; for,\ralbeit that some of themdo suffer their jaws to go oft before their\rclaws, and divers of them,by making good cheer, do hinder themselves\rand other men, yet thewiser sort can handle the matter well enough in\rthese junketings, andtherefore their frugality deserveth\rcommendation. To conclude,both the artificer and the husbandman are\rsufficiently liberal, andvery friendly at their tables; and, when\rthey meet, they are somerry without malice, and plain without inward\rItalian or French craftand subtlety, that it would do a man good to\rbe in company among them.Herein only are the inferior sort somewhat\rto be blamed, that, beingthus assembled, their talk is now and then\rsuch as savoureth ofscurrility and ribaldry, a thing naturally\rincident to carters andclowns, who think themselves not to be merry\rand welcome if theirfoolish veins in this behalf be never so little\rrestrained. This ismoreover to be added in these meetings, that if\rthey happen to stumbleupon a piece of venison and a cup of wine or\rvery strong beer or ale(which latter they commonly provide against\rtheir appointed days),they think their cheer so great, and themselves\rto have fared so well, asthe Lord Mayor of London, with whom, when\rtheir bellies be full,they will not often stick to make comparison,\rbecause that of a subjectthere is no public officer of any city in\rEurope that may compare inport and countenance with him during the\rtime of his office.\r \rI might here talk somewhatof the great silence that is used at the\rtables of the honourableand wiser sort generally over all the realm\r(albeit that too muchdeserveth no commendation, for it belongeth to\rguests neither to be_muti_ nor _loquaces_[2]), likewise of the\rmoderate eating anddrinking that is daily seen, and finally of the\rregard that each one hathto keep himself from the note of surfeiting\rand drunkenness (for whichcause salt meat, except beef, bacon, and\rpork, are not any whitesteemed, and yet these three may not be much\rpowdered); but, as inrehearsal thereof I should commend the nobleman,\rmerchant, and frugal artificer,so I could not clear the meaner sort\rof husbandmen and countryinhabitants of very much babbling (except it\rbe here and there some oddyeoman), with whom he is thought to be the\rmerriest that talketh ofmost ribaldry or the wisest man that speaketh\rfastest among them, andnow and then surfeiting and drunkenness which\rthey rather fall into forwant of heed taking than wilfully following\ror delighting in thoseerrors of set mind and purpose. It may be that\rdivers of them living athome, with hard and pinching diet, small\rdrink, and some of themhaving scarce enough of that, are soonest\rovertaken when they comeinto such banquets, howbeit they take it\rgenerally as no smalldisgrace if they happen to be cupshotten, so\rthat it is a grief untothem, though now sans remedy, sith the thing\ris done and past. If thefriends also of the wealthier sort come to\rtheir houses from far,they are commonly so welcome till they depart\ras upon the first day oftheir coming; whereas in good towns and\rcities, as London, etc.,men oftentimes complain of little room, and,\rin reward of a fat caponor plenty of beef and mutton largely bestowed\rupon them in the country,a cup of wine or beer with a napkin to wipe\rtheir lips and an"You are heartily welcome!" is thought to be a great\rentertainment; andtherefore the old country clerks have framed this\rsaying in that behalf, Imean upon the entertainment of townsmen and\rLondoners after the daysof their abode, in this manner:\r \r    "Primus jucundus, tollerabilis estquesecundus,\r    Tertius est vanus, sed fetetquatriduanus."\r \r      [2] Neither "silent" nor"garrulous."\r \rThe bread throughout theland is made of such grain as the soil\ryieldeth; nevertheless thegentility commonly provide themselves\rsufficiently of wheat fortheir own tables, whilst their household and\rpoor neighbours in someshires are forced to content themselves with\rrye, or barley, yea, andin time of dearth, many with bread made\reither of beans, peas, ofoats, or of altogether and some acorns\ramong, of which scourgethe poorest do soonest taste, sith they are\rleast able to providethemselves of better. I will not say that this\rextremity is oft so wellto be seen in time of plenty as of dearth,\rbut, if I should, I couldeasily bring my trial.
