For, albeit that\rthere be much more groundeared now almost in every place than hath\rbeen of late years, yetsuch a price of corn continueth in each town\rand market without anyjust cause (except it be that landlords do get\rlicences to carry corn outof the land only to keep up the prices for\rtheir own private gainsand ruin of the commonwealth), that the\rartificer and poorlabouring man is not able to reach unto it, but is\rdriven to content himselfwith horse corn--I mean beans, peas, oats,\rtares, and lentils: andtherefore it is a true proverb, and never so\rwell verified as now, that"Hunger setteth his first foot into the\rhorse-manger."[3] Ifthe world last awhile after this rate, wheat and\rrye will be no grain forpoor men to feed on; and some caterpillars\rthere are that can say somuch already.\r \r      [3] A famine at hand is first seen in thehorse-manger, when\r      the poor do fall to horse corn.--H.\r \rOf bread made of wheat wehave sundry sorts daily brought to the\rtable, whereof the firstand most excellent is the manchet, which we\rcommonly call white bread,in Latin _primarius panis_, whereof Budeus\ralso speaketh, in hisfirst book _De asse_; and our good workmen\rdeliver commonly suchproportion that of the flour of one bushel with\ranother they make fortycast of manchet, of which every loaf weigheth\reight ounces into theoven, and six ounces out, as I have been\rinformed. The second isthe cheat or wheaten bread, so named because\rthe colour thereofresembleth the grey or yellowish wheat, being clean\rand well dressed, and outof this is the coarsest of the bran (usually\rcalled gurgeons orpollard) taken. The ravelled is a kind of cheat\rbread also, but itretaineth more of the gross, and less of the pure\rsubstance of the wheat;and this, being more slightly wrought up, is\rused in the halls of thenobility and gentry only, whereas the other\reither is or should bebaked in cities and good towns of an appointed\rsize (according to suchprice as the corn doth bear), and by a statute\rprovided by King John inthat behalf.[4] The ravelled cheat therefore\ris generally so made thatout of one bushel of meal, after two and\rtwenty pounds of bran besifted and taken from it (whereunto they add\rthe gurgeons that risefrom the manchet), they make thirty cast, every\rloaf weighing eighteenounces into the oven, and sixteen ounces out;\rand, beside this, they sohandle the matter that to every bushel of\rmeal they add only two andtwenty, or three and twenty, pound of\rwater, washing also (insome houses) their corn before it go to the\rmill, whereby theirmanchet bread is more excellent in colour, and\rpleasing to the eye, thanotherwise it would be. The next sort is\rnamed brown bread, of thecolour of which we have two sorts one baked\rup as it cometh from themill, so that neither the bran nor the flour\rare any whit diminished;this, Celsus called _autopirus panis_, lib.\r2, and putteth it in thesecond place of nourishment. The other hath\rlittle or no flour lefttherein at all, howbeit he calleth it _Panem\rCibarium_, and it is notonly the worst and weakest of all the other\rsorts, but also appointedin old time for servants, slaves, and the\rinferior kind of people tofeed upon. Hereunto likewise, because it is\rdry and brickle in theworking (for it will hardly be made up\rhandsomely into loaves),some add a portion of rye meal in our time,\rwhereby the rough drynessor dry roughness thereof is somewhat\rqualified, and then it isnamed _miscelin_, that is, bread made of\rmingled corn, albeit thatdivers do sow or mingle wheat and rye of set\rpurpose at the mill, orbefore it come there, and sell the same at the\rmarkets under theaforesaid name.\r \r      [4] The size of bread is very ill kept ornot at all looked\r      unto in the country towns or markets.--H.\r \rIn champaign countriesmuch rye and barley bread is eaten, but\respecially where wheat isscant and geson. As for the difference that\rit is between the summerand winter wheat, most husbandmen know it\rnot, sith they are neitheracquainted with summer wheat nor winter\rbarley; yet here and thereI find of both sorts, specially in the\rnorth and about Kendal,where they call it March wheat, and also of\rsummer rye, but in sosmall quantities as that I dare not pronounce\rthem to be greatly commonamong us.\r \rOur drink, whose force andcontinuance is partly touched already, is\rmade of barley, water, andhops, sodden and mingled together, by the\rindustry of our brewers ina certain exact proportion. But, before our\rbarley do come into theirhands, it sustaineth great alteration, and\ris converted into malt,the making whereof I will here set down in\rsuch order as my skilltherein may extend unto (for I am scarce a good\rmaltster), chiefly forthat foreign writers have attempted to describe\rthe same, and the makingof our beer, wherein they have shot so far\rwide, as the quantity ofground was between themselves and their mark.\rIn the meantime bear withme, gentle reader (I beseech thee), that\rlead thee from thedescription of the plentiful diet of our country\runto the fond report of aservile trade, or rather from a table\rdelicately furnished intoa musty malt-house; but such is now thy hap,\rwherefore I pray thee becontented.\r \rOur malt is made all theyear long in some great towns; but in\rgentlemen\'s and yeomen\'shouses, who commonly make sufficient for\rtheir own expenses only,the winter half is thought most meet for that\rcommodity: howbeit themalt that is made when the willow doth bud is\rcommonly worst of all.Nevertheless each one endeavoureth to make it\rof the best barley, whichis steeped in a cistern, in greater or less\rquantity, by the space ofthree days and three nights, until it be\rthoroughly soaked. Thisbeing done, the water is drained from it by\rlittle and little, till itbe quite gone. Afterward they take it out,\rand, laying it upon theclean floor on a round heap, it resteth so\runtil it be ready to shootat the root end, which maltsters call\r_combing_. When itbeginneth therefore to shoot in this manner, they\rsay it is come, and thenforthwith they spread it abroad, first thick,\rand afterwards thinner andthinner upon the said floor (as it\r_combeth_), and there itlieth (with turning every day four or five\rtimes) by the space of oneand twenty days at the least, the workmen\rnot suffering it in anywise to take any heat, whereby the bud end\rshould spire, thatbringeth forth the blade, and by which oversight or\rhurt of the stuff itselfthe malt would be spoiled and turn small\rcommodity to the brewer.When it hath gone, or been turned, so long\rupon the floor, they carryit to a kiln covered with hair cloth, where\rthey give it gentle heats(after they have spread it there very thin\rabroad) till it be dry,and in the meanwhile they turn it often, that\rit may be uniformly dried.For the more it be dried (yet must it be\rdone with soft fire) thesweeter and better the malt is, and the\rlonger it will continue,whereas, if it be not dried down (as they\rcall it), but slacklyhandled, it will breed a kind of worm called a\rweevil, which groweth inthe flour of the corn, and in process of time\rwill so eat out itselfthat nothing shall remain of the grain but even\rthe very rind or husk.\r \rThe best malt is tried bythe hardness and colour; for, if it look\rfresh with a yellow hue,and thereto will write like a piece of chalk,\rafter you have bitten akernel in sunder in the midst, then you may\rassure yourself that it isdried down. In some places it is dried at\rleisure with wood alone orstraw alone, in others with wood and straw\rtogether; but, of all, thestraw dried is the most excellent. For the\rwood-dried malt when it isbrewed, beside that the drink is higher of\rcolour, it doth hurt andannoy the head of him that is not used\rthereto, because of thesmoke. Such also as use both indifferently do\rbark, cleave, and drytheir wood in an oven, thereby to remove all\rmoisture that shouldprocure the fume; and this malt is in the second\rplace, and, with the samelikewise, that which is made with dried\rfurze, broom, etc.:whereas, if they also be occupied green, they are\rin manner so prejudicialto the corn as is the moist wood. And thus\rmuch of our malts, inbrewing whereof some grind the same somewhat\rgrossly, and, in seethingwell the liquor that shall be put into it,\rthey add to every ninequarters of malt one of headcorn (which\rconsisteth of sundrygrain, as wheat and oats ground). But what have I\rto do with this matter, orrather so great a quantity, wherewith I am\rnot acquainted?Nevertheless, sith I have taken occasion to speak of\rbrewing, I will exemplifyin such a proportion as I am best skilled\rin, because it is theusual rate for mine own family, and once in a\rmonth practised by my wifeand her maid-servants, who proceed withal\rafter this manner, as shehath oft informed me.\r \rHaving therefore groundeight bushels of good malt upon our quern,\rwhere the toll is saved,she addeth unto it half a bushel of wheat\rmeal, and so much of oatssmall ground, and so tempereth or mixeth\rthem with the malt thatyou cannot easily discern the one from the\rother; otherwise theselatter would clunter, fall into lumps, and\rthereby becomeunprofitable. The first liquor (which is full eighty\rgallons, according to theproportion of our furnace) she maketh\rboiling hot, and thenpoureth it softly into the malt, where it\rresteth (but withoutstirring) until her second liquor be almost ready\rto boil. This done, sheletteth her mash run till the malt be left\rwithout liquor, or at theleastwise the greatest part of the moisture,\rwhich she perceiveth bythe stay and soft issue thereof; and by this\rtime her second liquor inthe furnace is ready to seethe, which is put\ralso to the malt, as thefirst woort also again into the furnace,\rwhereunto she addeth twopounds of the best English hops, and so\rletteth them seethetogether by the space of two hours in summer or an\rhour and a half in winter,whereby it getteth an excellent colour, and\rcontinuance withoutimpeachment or any superfluous tartness. But,\rbefore she putteth herfirst woort into the furnace, or mingleth it\rwith the hops, she takethout a vessel full, of eight or nine gallons,\rwhich she shutteth upclose, and suffereth no air to come into it till\rit become yellow, and thisshe reserveth by itself unto further use,\ras shall appear hereafter,calling it _brackwoort_ or _charwoort_,\rand, as she saith, itaddeth also to the colour of the drink, whereby\rit yieldeth not unto amberor fine gold in hue unto the eye. By this\rtime also her second woortis let run; and, the first being taken out\rof the furnace, and placedto cool, she returneth the middle woort\runto the furnace, where itis stricken over, or from whence it is\rtaken again, when itbeginneth to boil, and mashed the second time,\rwhilst the third liquor isheat (for there are three liquors), and\rthis last put into thefurnace, when the second is mashed again. When\rshe hath mashed also thelast liquor (and set the second to cool by\rthe first), she letteth itrun, and then seetheth it again with a\rpound and a half of newhops, or peradventure two pounds, as she seeth\rcause by the goodness orbaseness of the hops, and, when it hath\rsodden, in summer twohours, and in winter an hour and a half, she\rstriketh it also, andreserveth it unto mixture with the rest when\rtime doth serve therefore.Finally, when she setteth her drink\rtogether, she addeth toher brackwoort or charwoort half an ounce of\rarras, and half a quarterof an ounce of bayberries, finely powdered,\rand then, putting the sameinto her woort, with a handful of wheat\rflour, she proceedeth insuch usual order as common brewing requireth,\rSome, instead of arras andbays, add so much long pepper only, but, in\rher opinion and my liking,it is not so good as the first, and hereof\rwe make three hogsheads ofgood beer, such (I mean) as is meet for\rpoor men as I am to livewithal, whoso small maintenance (for what\rgreat thing is fortypounds a year, _computatis computandis_, able to\rperform?) may endure nodeeper cut, the charges whereof groweth in\rthis manner. I value mymalt at ten shillings, my wood at four\rshillings (which I buy),my hops at twenty pence, the spice at\rtwopence, servants\' wagestwo shillings sixpence, with meat and drink,\rand the wearing of myvessel at twenty pence, so that for my twenty\rshillings I have ten scoregallons of beer or more, notwithstanding\rthe loss in seething,which some, being loth to forego, do not observe\rthe time, and thereforespeed thereafter in their success, and\rworthily. The continuanceof the drink is always determined after the\rquantity of the hops, sothat being well _hopt_ it lasteth longer. For\rit feedeth upon the hop,and holdeth out so long as the force of the\rsame continueth, whichbeing extinguished, the drink must be spent, or\relse it dieth and becomethof no value.\r \rIn this trade also ourbrewers observe very diligently the nature of\rthe water, which theydaily occupy, and soil through which it passeth,\rfor all waters are not oflike goodness, sith the fattest standing\rwater is always the best;for, although the waters that run by chalk\ror cledgy soils be good,and next unto the Thames water, which is the\rmost excellent, yet thewater that standeth in either of these is the\rbest for us that dwell inthe country, as whereon the sun lieth\rlongest, and fattest fishis bred. But, of all other, the fenny and\rmarsh is the worst, andthe clearest spring water next unto it. In\rthis business thereforethe skilful workman doth redeem the iniquity\rof that element, bychanging of his proportions, which trouble in ale\r(sometime our only, butnow taken with many for old and sick men\'s\rdrink) is never seen norheard of. Howbeit, as the beer well sodden in\rthe brewing, and stale, isclear and well coloured as muscadel or\rmalvesey, or rather yellowas the gold noble, as our pot-knights call\rit, so our ale, which isnot at all or very little sodden, and without\rhops, is more thick,fulsome, and of no such continuance, which are\rthree notable things to beconsidered in that liquor. But what for\rthat? Certes I know someale-knights so much addicted thereunto that\rthey will not cease frommorrow until even to visit the same,\rcleansing house afterhouse, till they defile themselves, and either\rfall quite under theboard, or else, not daring to stir from their\rstools, sit still pinkingwith their narrow eyes, as half sleeping,\rtill the fume of theiradversary be digested that he may go to it\rafresh. Such slights alsohave the ale-wives for the utterance of this\rdrink that they will mixit with rosen and salt; but if you heat a\rknife red-hot, and quenchit in the ale so near the bottom of the pot\ras you can put it, youshall see the rosen come forth hanging on the\rknife. As for the force ofsalt, it is well known by the effect, for\rthe more the drinkertippleth, the more he may, and so doth he carry\roff a dry drunken noll tobed with him, except his luck be the better.\rBut to my purpose.\r \rIn some places of Englandthere is a kind of drink made of apples\rwhich they call cider orpomage, but that of pears is called perry,\rand both are ground andpressed in presses made for the nonce. Certes\rthese two are very commonin Sussex, Kent, Worcester, and other steeds\rwhere these sorts of fruitdo abound, howbeit they are not their only\rdrink at all times, butreferred unto the delicate sorts of drink, as\rmetheglin is in Wales,whereof the Welshmen make no less account (and\rnot without cause, if itbe well handled) than the Greeks did of their\rambrosia or nectar, whichfor the pleasantness thereof was supposed to\rbe such as the godsthemselves did delight in. There is a kind of\rswish-swash made also inEssex, and divers other places, with\rhoneycombs and water,which the homely country wives, putting some\rpepper and a little otherspice among, call mead, very good in mine\ropinion for such as loveto be loose bodied at large, or a little\reased of the cough.Otherwise it differeth so much from the true\rmetheglin as chalk fromcheese. Truly it is nothing else but the\rwashing of the combs, whenthe honey is wrung out, and one of the best\rthings that I knowbelonging thereto is that they spend but little\rlabour, and less cost, inmaking of the same, and therefore no great\rloss if it were neveroccupied. Hitherto of the diet of my countrymen,\rand somewhat more at largeperadventure than many men will like of,\rwherefore I think good nowto finish this tractation, and so will I\rwhen I have added a fewother things incident unto that which goeth\rbefore, whereby the wholeprocess of the same shall fully be\rdelivered, and my promiseto my friend[5] in this behalf performed.\r \r      [5] Holinshed. This occurs in the last ofHarrison\'s prefatory\r      matter.--W.\r \rHeretofore there hath beenmuch more time spent in eating and\rdrinking than commonly isin these days; for whereas of old we had\rbreakfast in the forenoon,beverages or nunchions[6] after dinner,\rand thereto rear suppersgenerally when it was time to go to rest (a\rtoy brought into Englandby hardy Canutus, and a custom whereof\rAthenaeus also speaketh,lib. 1, albeit Hippocrates speaks but of\rtwice at the most, lib. 2,_De rat vict. in feb ac_). Now, these odd\rrepasts--thanked beGod!--are very well left, and each one in manner\r(except here and theresome young, hungry stomach that cannot fast\rtill dinner-time)contenteth himself with dinner and supper only. The\rNormans, misliking thegormandise of Canutus, ordained after their\rarrival that no tableshould be covered above once in the day, which\rHuntingdon imputeth totheir avarice; but in the end, either waxing\rweary of their ownfrugality, or suffering the cockle of old custom\rto overgrow the good cornof their new constitution, they fell to\rsuch liberty that inoften-feeding they surmounted Canutus surnamed\rthe Hardy. For, whereas hecovered his table but three or four times\rin the day, these spreadtheir cloths five or six times, and in such\rwise as I beforerehearsed. They brought in also the custom of long\rand stately sitting atmeat, whereby their feasts resembled those\rancient pontificalbanquets whereof Macrobius speaketh (lib. 3, cap.\r13), and Pliny (lib. 10,cap. 10), and which for sumptuousness of\rfare, long sitting, andcuriosity shewed in the same, exceeded all\rother men\'s feasting;which fondness is not yet left with us,\rnotwithstanding that itproveth very beneficial for the physicians,\rwho most abound where mostexcess and misgovernment of our bodies do\rappear, although it be agreat expense of time, and worthy of\rreprehension. For thenobility, gentlemen, and merchantmen,\respecially at greatmeetings, do sit commonly till two or three of\rthe clock at afternoon, sothat with many it is a hard matter to rise\rfrom the table to go toevening prayer, and return from thence to\rcome time enough tosupper.[7]...\r \r      [6] This word is not obsolete. Southcoast countrymen still\r      eat _nuntions_ and not _luncheons_.--W.\r \r      [7] Here follows a disquisition upon thetable practices of\r      the ancients.--W.\r \rWith us the nobility,gentry, and students do ordinarily go to dinner\rat eleven before noon, andto supper at five, or between five and six\rat afternoon. Themerchants dine and sup seldom before twelve at noon,\rand six at night,especially in London. The husbandmen dine also at\rhigh noon as they call it,and sup at seven or eight; but out of the\rterm in our universitiesthe scholars dine at ten. As for the poorest\rsort they generally dineand sup when they may, so that to talk of\rtheir order of repast itwere but a needless matter. I might here take\roccasion also to set downthe variety used by antiquity in their\rbeginnings of their diets,wherein almost every nation had a several\rfashion, some beginning ofcustom (as we do in summer time) with\rsalads at supper, and someending with lettuce, some making their\rentry with eggs, andshutting up their tables with mulberries, as we\rdo with fruit and conceitsof all sorts. Divers (as the old Romans)\rbegan with a few crops ofrue, as the Venetians did with the fish\rcalled gobius; the Belgreswith butter, or (as we do yet also) with\rbutter and eggs upon fishdays. But whereas we commonly begin with the\rmost gross food, and endwith the most delicate, the Scot, thinking\rmuch to leave the best forhis menial servants, maketh his entrance at\rthe best, so that he issure thereby to leave the worst. We use also\rour wines by degrees, sothat the hostess cometh last to the table:\rbut to stand upon suchtoys would spend much time, and turn to small\rprofit. Wherefore I willdeal with other things more necessary for\rthis turn.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER VII\r \rOF OUR APPAREL AND ATTIRE\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapter2; 1587, Book II., Chapter 7.]\r \r \rAn Englishman,endeavouring sometime to write of our attire, made\rsundry platforms for hispurpose, supposing by some of them to find\rout one steadfast groundwhereon to build the sum of his discourse.\rBut in the end (like anorator long without exercise), when he saw\rwhat a difficult piece ofwork he had taken in hand, he gave over his\rtravel, and only drew thepicture of a naked man[1], unto whom he\rgave a pair of shears inthe one hand and a piece of cloth in the\rother, to the end heshould shape his apparel after such fashion as\rhimself liked, sith hecould find no kind of garment that could\rplease him any whiletogether; and this he called an Englishman.\rCertes this writer(otherwise being a lewd popish hypocrite and\rungracious priest) shewedhimself herein not to be altogether void of\rjudgment, sith thephantastical folly of our nation (even from the\rcourtier to the carter) issuch that no form of apparel liketh us\rlonger than the firstgarment is in the wearing, if it continue so\rlong, and be not laidaside to receive some other trinket newly\rdevised by thefickle-headed tailors, who covet to have several\rtricks in cutting, therebyto draw fond customers to more expense of\rmoney. For my part, I cantell better how to inveigh against this\renormity than describe anycertainty of our attire; sithence such is\rour mutability that to-daythere is none to the Spanish guise,\rto-morrow the French toysare most fine and delectable, ere long no\rsuch apparel as that whichis after the high Almaine fashion,\rby-and-by the Turkishmanner is generally best liked of, otherwise\rthe Morisco gowns, theBarbarian fleeces, the mandilion worn to\rColley-Weston ward, andthe short French breeches make such a comely\rvesture that, except itwere a dog in a doublet, you shall not see\rany so disguised as are mycountrymen of England. And as these\rfashions are diverse, solikewise it is a world to see the costliness\rand the curiosity, theexcess and the vanity, the pomp and the\rbravery, the change andthe variety, and finally the fickleness and\rthe folly, that is in alldegrees, insomuch that nothing is more\rconstant in England thaninconstancy of attire. Oh, how much cost is\rbestowed nowadays upon ourbodies, and how little upon our souls! How\rmany suits of apparel haththe one, and how little furniture hath the\rother! How long time isasked in decking up of the first, and how\rlittle space left whereinto feed the latter! How curious, how nice\ralso, are a number of menand women, and how hardly can the tailor\rplease them in making itfit for their bodies! How many times must it\rbe sent back again to himthat made it! What chafing, what fretting,\rwhat reproachful language,doth the poor workman bear away! And many\rtimes when he doth nothingto it at all, yet when it is brought home\ragain it is very fit andhandsome; then must we put it on, then must\rthe long seams of our hosebe set by a plumb-line, then we puff, then\rwe blow, and finally sweattill we drop, that our clothes may stand\rwell upon us. I will saynothing of our heads, which sometimes are\rpolled, sometimes curled,or suffered to grow at length like woman\'s\rlocks, many times cut off,above or under the ears, round as by a\rwooden dish. Neither willI meddle with our variety of beards, of\rwhich some are shaven fromthe chin like those of Turks, not a few\rcut short like to thebeard of Marquess Otto, some made round like a\rrubbing brush, others witha _pique de vant_ (O! fine fashion!), or\rnow and then suffered togrow long, the barbers being grown to be so\rcunning in this behalf asthe tailors. And therefore if a man have a\rlean and straight face, aMarquess Otton\'s cut will make it broad and\rlarge; if it beplatter-like, a long, slender beard will make it seem\rthe narrower; if he beweasel-becked, then much hair left on the\rcheeks will make the ownerlook big like a bowdled hen, and as grim\ras a goose, if Cornells ofChelmersford say true. Many old men do\rwear no beards at all.Some lusty courtiers also and gentlemen of\rcourage do wear eitherrings of gold, stones, or pearl, in their ears,\rwhereby they imagine theworkmanship of God not to be a little\ramended. But herein theyrather disgrace than adorn their persons, as\rby their niceness inapparel, for which I say most nations do not\runjustly deride us, asalso for that we do seem to imitate all nations\rround about us, wherein webe like to the polypus or chameleon; and\rthereunto bestow most costupon our arses, and much more than upon all\rthe rest of our bodies, aswomen do likewise upon their heads and\rshoulders. In women also,it is most to be lamented, that they do now\rfar exceed the lightnessof our men (who nevertheless are transformed\rfrom the cap even to thevery shoe), and such staring attire as in\rtime past was supposedmeet for none but light housewives only is now\rbecome a habit for chasteand sober matrons. What should I say of\rtheir doublets withpendant codpieces on the breast full of jags and\rcuts, and sleeves ofsundry colours? Their galligascons to bear out\rtheir bums and make their attireto fit plum round (as they term it)\rabout them. Theirfardingals, and diversely coloured nether stocks of\rsilk, jerdsey, and suchlike, whereby their bodies are rather deformed\rthan commended? I have metwith some of these trulls in London so\rdisguised that it hathpassed my skill to discern whether they were\rmen or women.\r \r      [1] (COS.)\r \r        "I am an English man and naked Istand here,\r        Musying in my mynde what rayment Ishall were;\r        For now I will were thys, and now Iwill were that;\r        Now I will were I cannot tell what.\r        All new fashyons be plesaunt in me;\r        I wyl haue them, whether I thryve orthee."\r \r      From Andrew Boorde\'s _Introduction_(1541), and _Dyetary_ (1542),\r      edited by F.J.F. for Early English TextSociety, 1870, p. 116. (A\r      most quaint and interesting volume,though I say so.)--Furnivall.\r \rThus it is now come topass, that women are become men, and men\rtransformed into monsters;and those good gifts which Almighty God\rhath given unto us torelieve our necessities withal (as a nation\rturning altogether thegrace of God into wantonness, for\r \r  "Luxuriant animi rebus plerunquefecundis,")\r \rnot otherwise bestowedthan in all excess, as if we wist not\rotherwise how to consumeand waste them. I pray God that in this\rbehalf our sin be not likeunto that of Sodom and Gomorrah, whose\rerrors were pride, excessof diet, and abuse of God\'s benefits\rabundantly bestowed uponthem, beside want of charity towards the\rpoor, and certain otherpoints which the prophet shutteth up in\rsilence. Certes thecommonwealth cannot be said to nourish where\rthese abuses reign, but israther oppressed by unreasonable exactions\rmade upon rich farmers,and of poor tenants, wherewith to maintain\rthe same. Neither was itever merrier with England than when an\rEnglishman was knownabroad by his own cloth, and contented himself\rat home with his finecarsey hosen, and a mean slop; his coat, gown,\rand cloak of brown, blue,or puke, with some pretty furniture of\rvelvet or fur, and adoublet of sad tawny, or black velvet, or other\rcomely silk, without suchcuts and garish colours as are worn in\rthese days, and neverbrought in but by the consent of the French,\rwho think themselves thegayest men when they have most diversities\rof jags and change ofcolours about them. Certes of all estates our\rmerchants do least altertheir attire, and therefore are most to be\rcommended; for albeit thatwhich they wear be very fine and costly,\ryet in form and colour itrepresenteth a great piece of the ancient\rgravity appertaining tocitizens and burgesses, albeit the younger\rsort of their wives, bothin attire and costly housekeeping, cannot\rtell when and how to makean end, as being women indeed in whom all\rkind of curiosity is to befound and seen, and in far greater measure\rthan in women of highercalling. I might here name a sort of hues\rdevised for the nonce,wherewith to please fantastical heads, as\rgoose-turd green,peas-porridge tawny, popingay blue, lusty gallant,\rthe devil-in-the-head (Ishould say the hedge), and such like; but I\rpass them over, thinkingit sufficient to have said thus much of\rapparel generally, whennothing can particularly be spoken of any\rconstancy thereof.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER VIII\r \rOF THE MANNER OF BUILDINGAND FURNITURE OF OUR HOUSES\r \r[1577, Book II., Chapter10; 1587, Book II., Chapter 12.]\r \r \rThe greatest part of ourbuilding in the cities and good towns of\rEngland consisteth only oftimber, for as yet few of the houses of\rthe communalty (excepthere and there in the West-country towns) are\rmade of stone, althoughthey may (in my opinion) in divers other\rplaces be builded so goodcheap of the one as of the other. In old\rtime the houses of theBritons were slightly set up with a few posts\rand many raddles, with stableand all offices under one roof, the\rlike whereof almost is tobe seen in the fenny countries and northern\rparts unto this day, wherefor lack of wood they are enforced to\rcontinue this ancientmanner of building. It is not in vain,\rtherefore, in speaking ofbuilding, to make a distinction between the\rplain and woody soils; foras in these, our houses are commonly\rstrong and well-timbered(so that in many places there are not above\rfour, six, or nine inchesbetween stud and stud), so in the open\rchampaign countries theyare forced, for want of stuff, to use no\rstuds at all, but onlyfrankposts, raisins, beams, prickposts,\rgroundsels, summers (ordormants), transoms, and such principals,\rwith here and there agirding, whereunto they fasten their splints or\rraddles, and then cast itall over with thick clay to keep out the\rwind, which otherwisewould annoy them. Certes this rude kind of\rbuilding made theSpaniards in Queen Mary\'s days to wonder, but\rchiefly when they saw whatlarge diet was used in many of these so\rhomely cottages; insomuchthat one of no small reputation amongst\rthem said after thismanner--"These English (quoth he) have their\rhouses made of sticks anddirt, but they fare commonly so well as the\rking." Whereby itappeareth that he liked better of our good fare in\rsuch coarse cabins than oftheir own thin diet in their prince-like\rhabitations and palaces.In like sort as every country house is thus\rapparelled on the outside,so is it inwardly divided into sundry\rrooms above and beneath;and, where plenty of wood is, they cover\rthem with tiles, otherwisewith straw, sedge, or reed, except some\rquarry of slate be nearhand, from whence they have for their money\rmuch as may suffice them.The clay wherewith our houses are\rimpannelled is eitherwhite, red, or blue; and of these the first\rdoth participate very muchof the nature of our chalk; the second is\rcalled loam; but the thirdeftsoons changeth colour as soon as it is\rwrought, notwithstandingthat it looks blue when it is thrown out of\rthe pit. Of chalk also wehave our excellent asbestos or white lime,\rmade in most places,wherewith being quenched, we strike over our\rclay works and stonewalls, in cities, good towns, rich farmers\' and\rgentlemen\'s houses:otherwise, instead of chalk (where it wanteth,\rfor it is so scant that insome places it is sold by the pound), they\rare compelled to burn acertain kind of red stone, as in Wales, and\relsewhere other stones andshells of oysters and like fish found upon\rthe sea coast, which,being converted into lime, doth naturally (as\rthe other) abhor andeschew water, whereby it is dissolved, and\rnevertheless desire oil,wherewith it is easily mixed, as I have seen\rby experience. Withintheir doors also, such as are of ability do oft\rmake their floors andparget of fine alabaster burned, which they\rcall plaster of Paris,whereof in some places we have great plenty,\rand that very profitableagainst the rage of fire. In plastering\rlikewise of our fairesthouses over our heads, we use to lay first a\rline or two of whitemortar, tempered with hair, upon laths, which\rare nailed one by another(or sometimes upon reed of wickers more\rdangerous for fire, andmake fast here and there saplaths for falling\rdown), and finally coverall with the aforesaid plaster, which,\rbeside the delectablewhiteness of the stuff itself, is laid on so\reven and smoothly asnothing in my judgment can be done with more\rexactness. The walls ofour houses on the inner sides in like sort be\reither hanged withtapestry, arras work, or painted cloths, wherein\reither divers histories,or herbs, beasts, knots, and such like are\rstained, or else they areceiled with oak of our own, or wainscot\rbrought hither out of theeast countries, whereby the rooms are not a\rlittle commended, madewarm, and much more close than otherwise they\rwould be. As for stoves,we have not hitherto used them greatly, yet\rdo they now begin to bemade in divers houses of the gentry and\rwealthy citizens, whobuild them not to work and feed in, as in\rGermany and elsewhere, butnow and then to sweat in, as occasion and\rneed shall require it.\r \rThis also hath been commonin England, contrary to the customs of all\rother nations, and yet tobe seen (for example, in most streets of\rLondon), that many of ourgreatest houses have outwardly been very\rsimple and plain to sight,which inwardly have been able to receive a\rduke with his whole train,and lodge them at their ease. Hereby,\rmoreover, it is come topass that the fronts of our streets have not\rbeen so uniform andorderly builded as those of foreign cities, where\r(to say truth) the outerside of their mansions and dwellings have\roft more cost bestowedupon them than all the rest of the house,\rwhich are often verysimple and uneasy within, as experience doth\rconfirm. Of old time, ourcountry houses, instead of glass, did use\rmuch lattice, and thatmade either of wicker or fine rifts of oak in\rcheckerwise. I read alsothat some of the better sort, in and before\rthe times of the Saxons(who notwithstanding used some glass also\rsince the time of BenedictBiscop, the monk that brought the feat of\rglazing first into thisland), did make panels of horn instead of\rglass, and fix them inwooden calmes. But as horn in windows is now\rquite laid down in everyplace, so our lattices are also grown into\rless use, because glass iscome to be so plentiful, and within a very\rlittle so good cheap, ifnot better than the other. I find obscure\rmention of the specularstone also to have been found and applied to\rthis use in England, butin such doubtful sort as I dare not affirm\rit for certain.Nevertheless certain it is that antiquity used it\rbefore glass was known,under the name of _selenites_. And how glass\rwas first found I care notgreatly to remember, even at this present,\ralthough it be directlybeside my purposed matter. In Syria Phenices,\rwhich bordereth uponJewry, and near to the foot of Mount Carmel,\rthere is a moor or marshwhereout riseth a brook called sometime\rBelus, and falleth intothe sea near to Ptolemais. This river was\rfondly ascribed unto Baal,and also honoured under that name by the\rinfidels long time beforethere was any king in Israel. It came to\rpass also, as a certainmerchant sailed that way, loaden with nitrum,\rthe passengers went toland for to repose themselves, and to take in\rsome store of fresh waterinto their vessel. Being also on the shore,\rthey kindled a fire andmade provision for their dinner, but (because\rthey wanted trevets orstones whereon to set their kettles on) ran by\rchance into the ship, andbrought great pieces of nitrum with them,\rwhich served their turnfor that present. To be short, the said\rsubstance being hot, andbeginning to melt, it mixed by chance with\rthe gravel that lay underit, and so brought forth that shining\rsubstance which now iscalled glass, and about the time of Semiramis.\rWhen the company saw this,they made no small accompt of their\rsuccess, and forthwithbegan to practise the like in other mixtures,\rwhereby great variety ofthe said stuff did also ensue. Certes for\rthe time this history maywell be true, for I read of glass in Job;\rbut, for the rest, I referme to the common opinion conceived by\rwriters. Now, to turnagain to our windows. Heretofore also the\rhouses of our princes andnoblemen were often glazed with beryl (an\rexample whereof is yet tobe seen in Sudeley Castle) and in divers\rother places with finecrystal, but this especially in the time of\rthe Romans, whereof alsosome fragments have been taken up in old\rruins. But now these arenot in use, so that only the clearest glass\ris most esteemed: for wehave divers sorts, some brought out of\rBurgundy, some out ofNormandy, much out of Flanders, beside that\rwhich is made in England,which would be so good as the best if we\rwere diligent and carefulto bestow more cost upon it, and yet as it\ris each one that may willhave it for his building. Moreover the\rmansion houses of ourcountry towns and villages (which in champaign\rground stand altogether bystreets, and joining one to another, but\rin woodland soilsdispersed here and there, each one upon the several\rgrounds of their owners)are builded in such sort generally as that\rthey have neither dairy,stable, nor brew-house annexed unto them\runder the same roof (as inmany places beyond the sea and some of the\rnorth parts of ourcountry), but all separate from the first, and one\rof them from another. Andyet, for all this, they are not so far\rdistant in sunder but thatthe goodman lying in his bed may lightly\rhear what is done in eachof them with ease, and call quickly unto\rhis many if any dangershould attack him.\r \rThe ancient manors andhouses of our gentlemen are yet and for the\rmost part of strongtimber, in framing whereof our carpenters have\rbeen and are worthilypreferred before those of like science among\rall other nations. Howbeitsuch as be lately builded are commonly\reither of brick or hardstone, or both, their rooms large and comely,\rand houses of officefurther distant from their lodgings. Those of\rthe nobility are likewisewrought with brick and hard stone, as\rprovision may best bemade, but so magnificent and stately as the\rbasest house of a barondoth often match in our days with some\rhonours of a princes inold time. So that, if ever curious building\rdid flourish in England,it is in these our years wherein our workmen\rexcel and are in mannercomparable in skill with old Vitruvius, Leo\rBaptista, and Serlo.Nevertheless their estimation, more than their\rgreedy and servilecovetousness, joined with a lingering humour,\rcauseth them often to berejected, and strangers preferred to greater\rbargains, who are morereasonable in their takings, and less wasters\rof time by a great dealthan our own.\r \rThe furniture of ourhouses also exceedeth, and is grown in manner\reven to passing delicacy:and herein I do not speak of the nobility\rand gentry only, butlikewise of the lowest sort in most places of\rour south country thathave anything at all to take to. Certes in\rnoblemen\'s houses it isnot rare to see abundance of arras, rich\rhangings of tapestry,silver vessels, and so much other plate as may\rfurnish sundry cupboardsto the sum oftentimes of a thousand or two\rthousand pounds at theleast, whereby the value of this and the rest\rof their stuff doth growto be almost inestimable. Likewise in the\rhouses of knights,gentlemen, merchantmen, and some other wealthy\rcitizens, it is not gesonto behold generally their great provision\rof tapestry, Turkey work,pewter, brass, fine linen, and thereto\rcostly cupboards of plate,worth five or six hundred or a thousand\rpounds to be deemed byestimation. But, as herein all these sorts do\rfar exceed their eldersand predecessors, and in neatness and\rcuriosity the merchant allother, so in times past the costly\rfurniture stayed there,whereas now it is descended yet lower even\runto the inferiorartificers and many farmers, who, by virtue of\rtheir old and not of theirnew leases, have, for the most part,\rlearned also to garnishtheir cupboards with plate, their joined beds\rwith tapestry and silkhangings, and their tables with carpets and\rfine napery, whereby thewealth of our country (God be praised\rtherefore, and give usgrace to employ it well) doth infinitely\rappear. Neither do I speakthis in reproach of any man, God is my\rjudge, but to shew that Ido rejoice rather to see how God hath\rblessed us with his goodgifts; and whilst, I behold how (in a time\rwherein all things aregrown to most excessive prices, and what\rcommodity so ever is to behad is daily plucked from the communalty\rby such as look into everytrade) we do yet find the means to obtain\rand achieve such furnitureas heretofore hath been unpossible.\r \rThere are old men yetdwelling in the village where I remain which\rhave noted three things tobe marvellously altered in England within\rtheir sound remembrance,and other three things too too much\rincreased.\r \rOne is the multitude ofchimneys lately erected, whereas in their\ryoung days there were notabove two or three, if so many, in most\ruplandish towns of therealm (the religious houses and manor places\rof their lords alwaysexcepted, and peradventure some great\rpersonages), but each onemade his fire against a reredos in the\rhall, where he dined anddressed his meat.\r \rThe second is the great(although not general) amendment of lodging;\rfor, said they, ourfathers, yea and we ourselves also, have lain\rfull oft upon strawpallets, on rough mats covered only with a sheet,\runder coverlets made ofdagswain or hopharlots (I use their own\rterms), and a good roundlog under their heads instead of a bolster\ror pillow. If it were sothat our fathers--or the good man of the\rhouse had within sevenyears after his marriage purchased a mattress\ror flock bed, and theretoa stack of chaff to rest his head upon, he\rthought himself to be aswell lodged as the lord of the town, that\rperadventure lay seldom ina bed of down or whole feathers, so well\rwere they content, andwith such base kind of furniture: which also\ris not very much amendedas yet in some parts of Bedfordshire, and\relsewhere, further offfrom our southern parts. Pillows (said they)\rwere thought meet only forwomen in childbed. As for servants, if\rthey had any sheet abovethem, it was well, for seldom had they any\runder their bodies to keepthem from the pricking straws that ran oft\rthrough the canvas of thepallet and rased their hardened hides.\r \rThe third thing they tellof is the exchange of vessel, as of treen\rplatters into pewter, andwooden spoons into silver or tin. For so\rcommon were all sorts oftreen stuff in old time that a man should\rhardly find four pieces ofpewter (of which one was peradventure a\rsalt) in a good farmer\'shouse, and yet for all this frugality (if it\rmay so be justly called)they were scarce able to live and pay their\rrents at their dayswithout selling of a cow, or a horse or more,[1]\ralthough they paid butfour pounds at the uttermost by the year. Such\ralso was their povertythat, if some one odd farmer or husbandman had\rbeen at the ale-house, athing greatly used in those days, amongst six\ror seven of hisneighbours, and there in a bravery, to shew what store\rhe had, did cast down hispurse, and therein a noble or six shillings\rin silver, unto them (forfew such men then cared for gold, because it\rwas not so ready payment,and they were oft enforced to give a penny\rfor the exchange of anangel), it was very likely that all the rest\rcould not lay down so muchagainst it; whereas in my time, although\rperadventure four poundsof old rent be improved to forty, fifty, or a\rhundred pounds, yet willthe farmer, as another palm of date tree,\rthink his gains very smalltoward the end of his term if he have not\rsix or seven years\' rentlying by him, therewith to purchase a new\rlease, beside a fairgarnish of pewter oft his cupboard, with so much\rmore in odd vessel goingabout the house, three or four feather beds,\rso many coverlids andcarpets of tapestry, a silver salt, a bowl for\rwine (if not a wholeneast), and a dozen of spoons to furnish up the\rsuit. This also he takesto be his own clear, for what stock of money\rsoever he gathereth andlayeth up in all his years it is often seen\rthat the landlord willtake such order with him for the same when he\rreneweth his lease, whichis commonly eight or six years before the\rold be expired (sith it isnow grown almost to a custom that if he\rcome not to his lord solong before another shall step in for a\rreversion, and so defeathim outright), that it shall never trouble\rhim more than the hair ofhis beard when the barber hath washed and\rshaved it from his chin.\r \r      [1] This was in the time of generalidleness.--H.\r \rAnd as they commend these,so (beside the decay of housekeeping\rwhereby the poor have beenrelieved) they speak also of three things\rthat are grown to be verygrevious unto them--to wit, the enhancing\rof rents, latelymentioned; the daily oppression of copyholders,\rwhose lords seek to bringtheir poor tenants almost into plain\rservitude and misery,daily devising new means, and seeking up all\rthe old, how to cut themshorter and shorter, doubling, trebling, and\rnow and then seven timesincreasing their fines, driving them also\rfor every trifle to loseand forfeit their tenures (by whom the\rgreatest part of the realmdoth stand and is maintained), to the end\rthey may fleece them yetmore, which is a lamentable hearing. The\rthird thing they talk ofis usury, a trade brought in by the Jews,\rnow perfectly practisedalmost by every Christian, and so commonly\rthat he is accompted butfor a fool that doth lend his money for\rnothing. In time past itwas _sors pro sorte_--that is, the principal\ronly for the principal;but now, beside that which is above the\rprincipal properly called_Usura_, we challenge _Foenus_--that is,\rcommodity of soil andfruits of the earth, If not the ground itself.\rIn time past also one ofthe hundred was much; from thence it rose\runto two, called in Latin_Usura, Ex sextante_; three, to wit _Ex\rquadrante_; then to four,to wit, _Ex triente_; then to five, which\ris _Ex quincunce_; then tosix, called _Ex semisse_, etc. As the\raccompt of the _Assis_ariseth, and coming at the last unto _Usura ex\rasse_, it amounteth totwelve in the hundred, and therefore the\rLatins call it_Centesima_, for that in the hundred month it doubleth\rthe principal; but more ofthis elsewhere. See Cicero against Verres,\rDemosthenes againstAphobus, and Athenaeus, lib. 13, in fine; and,\rwhen thou hast read themwell, help I pray thee in lawful manner to\rhang up such as take_Centum pro cento_, for they are no better\rworthy as I do judge inconscience. Forget not also such landlords as\rused to value their leasesat a secret estimation given of the wealth\rand credit of the taker,whereby they seem (as it were) to eat them\rup, and deal with bondmen,so that if the lessee be thought to be\rworth a hundred pounds heshall pay no less for his new term, or else\ranother to enter with hardand doubtful covenants. I am sorry to\rreport it, much moregrieved to understand of the practice, but most\rsorrowful of all tounderstand that men of great port and countenance\rare so far from sufferingtheir farmers to have any gain at all that\rthey themselves becomegraziers, butchers, tanners, sheepmasters,\rwoodmen, and _denique quidnon_, thereby to enrich themselves, and\rbring all the wealth ofthe country into their own hands, leaving the\rcommunalty weak, or as anidol with broken or feeble arms, which may\rin a time of peace have aplausible shew, but when necessity shall\renforce have a heavy andbitter sequel.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER IX\r \rOF PROVISION MADE FOR THEPOOR\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapter5; 1587, Book II., Chapter 10.]\r \r \rThere is no commonwealthat this day in Europe wherein there is not\rgreat store of poorpeople, and those necessarily to be relieved by\rthe wealthier sort, whichotherwise would starve and come to utter\rconfusion. With us thepoor is commonly divided into three sorts, so\rthat some are poor byimpotence, as the fatherless child, the aged,\rblind, and lame, and thediseased person that is judged to be\rincurable; the second arepoor by casualty, as the wounded soldier,\rthe decayed householder,and the sick person visited with grievous\rand painful diseases; thethird consisteth of thriftless poor, as the\rrioter that hath consumedall, the vagabond that will abide nowhere,\rbut runneth up and downfrom place to place (as it were seeking work\rand finding none), andfinally the rogue and the strumpet, which are\rnot possible to be dividedin sunder, but run to and fro over all the\rrealm, chiefly keeping thechampaign soils in summer to avoid the\rscorching heat, and thewoodland grounds in winter to eschew the\rblustering winds.\r \rFor the first two sorts(that is to say, the poor by impotence and\rpoor by casualty, whichare the true poor indeed, and for whom the\rWord doth bind us to makesome daily provision), there is order taken\rthroughout every parish inthe realm that weekly collection shall be\rmade for their help andsustentation--to the end they shall not\rscatter abroad, and, bybegging here and there, annoy both town and\rcountry. Authority also isgiven unto the justices in every county\r(and great penaltiesappointed for such as make default) to see that\rthe intent of the statutein this behalf be truly executed according\rto the purpose and meaningof the same, so that these two sorts are\rsufficiently provided for;and such as can live within the limits of\rtheir allowance (as eachone will do that is godly and well disposed)\rmay well forbear to roamand range about. But if they refuse to be\rsupported by this benefitof the law, and will rather endeavour by\rgoing to and fro tomaintain their idle trades, then are they adjudged\rto be parcel of the thirdsort, and so, instead of courteous\rrefreshing at home, areoften corrected with sharp execution and whip\rof justice abroad. Manythere are which, notwithstanding the rigour of\rthe laws provided in thatbehalf, yield rather with this liberty (as\rthey call it) to be dailyunder the fear and terror of the whip than,\rby abiding where they wereborn or bred, to be provided for by the\rdevotion of the parishes.I found not long since a note of these\rlatter sort, the effectwhereof ensueth. Idle beggars are such either\rthrough other men\'soccasion or through their own default--by other\rmen\'s occasion (as one wayfor example) when some covetous man (such,\rI mean, as have the castor right vein daily to make beggars enough\rwhereby to pester theland, espying a further commodity in their\rcommons, holds, andtenures) doth find such means as thereby to wipe\rmany out of theiroccupyings and turn the same unto his private\rgains.[1] Hereupon itfolloweth that, although the wise and\rbetter-minded do eitherforsake the realm for altogether, and seek to\rlive in other countries,as France, Germany, Barbary, India, Muscovia,\rand very Calcutta,complaining of no room to be left for them at home,\rdo so behave themselvesthat they are worthily to be accounted among\rthe second sort, yet thegreater part, commonly having nothing to stay\rupon, are wilful, andthereupon do either prove idle beggars or else\rcontinue stark thievestill the gallows do eat them up, which is a\rlamentable case. Certes insome men\'s judgment these things are but\rtrifles, and not worthythe regarding. Some also do grudge at the\rgreat increase of peoplein these days, thinking a necessary brood of\rcattle far better than asuperfluous augmentation of mankind. But I\rcan liken such men best ofall unto the pope and the devil, who\rpractise the hindrance ofthe furniture of the number of the elect to\rtheir uttermost, to theend the authority of the one upon the earth,\rthe deferring of thelocking up of the other in everlasting chains,\rand the great gains of thefirst, may continue and endure the longer.\rBut if it should come topass that any foreign invasion should be\rmade--which the Lord Godforbid for his mercies\' sake!--then should\rthese men find that a wallof men is far better than stacks of corn\rand bags of money, andcomplain of the want when it is too late to\rseek remedy. The likeoccasion caused the Romans to devise their law\r_Agraria_: but the rich,not liking of it, and the covetous, utterly\rcondemning it as rigorousand unprofitable, never ceased to practise\rdisturbance till it wasquite abolished. But to proceed with my\rpurpose.\r \r      [1] At whose hands shall the blood ofthese men be required?--H.\r \r \rSuch as are idle beggarsthrough their own default are of two sorts,\rand continue their estateseither by casual or mere voluntary means:\rthose that are such bycasual means are in the beginning justly to be\rreferred either to thefirst or second sort of poor aforementioned,\rbut, degenerating into thethriftless sort, they do what they can to\rcontinue their misery,and, with such impediments as they have, to\rstray and wander about, ascreatures abhorring all labour and every\rhonest exercise. Certes Icall these casual means, not in the respect\rof the original of allpoverty, but of the continuance of the same,\rfrom whence they will notbe delivered, such is their own ungracious\rlewdness and frowarddisposition. The voluntary means proceed from\routward causes, as bymaking of corrosives, and applying the same to\rthe more fleshy parts oftheir bodies, and also laying of ratsbane,\rspearwort, crowfoot, andsuch like unto their whole members, thereby\rto raise pitiful andodious sores, and move the hearts of the\rgoers-by such places wherethey lie, to yearn at their misery, and\rthereupon bestow largealms upon them. How artificially they beg,\rwhat forcible speech, andhow they select and choose out words of\rvehemence, whereby they doin manner conjure or adjure the goer-by to\rpity their cases, I passover to remember, as judging the name of God\rand Christ to be moreconversant in the mouths of none and yet the\rpresence of the Heavenly Majestyfurther off from no men than from\rthis ungracious company.Which maketh me to think that punishment is\rfar meeter for them thanliberality or alms, and sith Christ willeth\rus chiefly to have aregard to Himself and his poor members.\r \rUnto this nest is anothersort to be referred, more sturdy than the\rrest, which, having soundand perfect limbs, do yet notwithstanding\rsometime counterfeit thepossession of all sorts of diseases. Divers\rtimes in their apparelalso they will be like serving men or\rlabourers: oftentimes theycan play the mariners, and seek for ships\rwhich they never lost. Butin fine they are all thieves and\rcaterpillars in thecommonwealth, and by the Word of God not\rpermitted to eat, siththey do but lick the sweat from the true\rlabourers\' brows, andbereave the godly poor of that which is due\runto them, to maintaintheir excess, consuming the charity of\rwell-disposed peoplebestowed upon them, after a most wicked and\rdetestable manner.\r \rIt is not yet fullthreescore years since this trade began: but how\rit hath prospered sincethat time it is easy to judge, for they are\rnow supposed, of one sexand another, to amount unto above 10,000\rpersons, as I have heardreported. Moreover, in counterfeiting the\rEgyptian rogues, they havedevised a language among themselves, which\rthey name"Canting," but others, "pedler\'s French," a speech compact\rthirty years since, ofEnglish and a great number of odd words of\rtheir own devising,without all order or reason, and yet such is it\ras none but themselves areable to understand. The first deviser\rthereof was hanged by theneck--a just reward, no doubt, for his\rdeserts, and a common endto all of that profession.\r \rA gentleman also of latehath taken great pains to search out the\rsecret practices of thisungracious rabble. And among other things he\rsetteth down anddescribeth three and twenty sorts of them, whose\rnames it shall not beamiss to remember whereby each one may take\roccasion to read and knowas also by his industry what wicked people\rthey are, and whatvillainy remaineth in them.\r \r_The several disorders anddegrees amongst our idle vagabonds_.\r \r 1. Rufflers.\r 2. Uprightmen.\r 3. Hookers or anglers.\r 4. Rogues.\r 5. Wild rogues.\r 6. Priggers or pransers.\r 7. Palliards.\r 8. Fraters.\r 9. Abrams.\r10. Freshwater mariners orwhipjacks.\r11. Drummerers.\r12. Drunken tinkers.\r13. Swadders or pedlers.\r14. Jarkemen or patricoes.\r \r_Of the women kind_.\r \r1. Demanders for glimmaror fire.\r2. Bawdy-baskets.\r3. Mortes.\r4. Autem mortem.\r5. Walking mortes.\r6. Doxies.\r7. Dells.\r8. Kinching mortes.\r9. Kinching cooes.\r \rThe punishment that isordained for this kind of people is very sharp,\rand yet it cannot restrainthem from their gadding: wherefore the end\rmust needs be martiallaw,[2] to be exercised upon them, as upon\rthieves, robbers,despisers of all laws, and enemies to the\rcommonwealth and welfareof the land. What notable robberies,\rpilferies, murders, rapes,and stealings of young children, burning,\rbreaking, and disfiguringtheir limbs to make them pitiful in the\rsight of the people, Ineed not to rehearse; but for their idle\rrogueing about thecountry, the law ordaineth this manner of\rcorrection. The roguebeing apprehended, committed to prison, and\rtried in the next assizes(whether they be of gaol delivery or\rsessions of the peace), ifhe happen to be convicted for a vagabond,\reither by inquest ofoffice or the testimony of two honest and\rcredible witnesses upontheir oaths, he is then immediately adjudged\rto be grievously whippedand burned through the gristle of the right\rear with a hot iron of thecompass of an inch about, as a\rmanifestation of hiswicked life, and due punishment received for the\rsame. And this judgment isto be executed upon him except some honest\rperson worth five poundsin the queen\'s books in goods, or twenty\rshillings in land, or somerich householder to be allowed by the\rjustices, will be bound inrecognisance to retain him in his service\rfor one whole year. If hebe taken the second time, and proved to have\rforsaken his said service,he shall then be whipped again, bored\rlikewise through the otherear, and set to service: from whence if he\rdepart before a year beexpired, and happen afterwards to be attached\ragain, he is condemned tosuffer pains of death as a felon (except\rbefore excepted) withoutbenefit of clergy or sanctuary, as by the\rstatute doth appear. Amongrogues and idle persons, finally, we find\rto be comprised allproctors that go up and down with counterfeit\rlicences, cozeners, andsuch as gad about the country, using unlawful\rgames, practisers ofphysiogonomy and palmestry, tellers of fortunes,\rfencers, players,minstrels, jugglers, pedlers, tinkers, pretended\rscholars, shipmen,prisoners gathering for fees, and others so oft as\rthey be taken without sufficientlicence. From among which company our\rbearwards are notexcepted, and just cause: for I have read that they\rhave, either voluntarilyor for want of power to master their savage\rbeasts, been occasion ofthe death and devouration of many children in\rsundry countries by whichthey have passed, whose parents never knew\rwhat was become of them.And for that cause there is and have been\rmany sharp laws made forbearwards in Germany, whereof you may read in\rother. But to our rogues.Each one also that harboureth or aideth them\rwith meat or money istaxed and compelled to fine with the queen\'s\rmajesty for every timethat he doth succour them as it shall please\rthe justices of peace toassign, so that the taxation exceed not\rtwenty, as I have beeninformed. And thus much of the poor and such\rprovision as is appointedfor them within the realm of England.\r \r      [2] Law of the Marshal.--Furnivall.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER X\r \rOF THE AIR AND SOIL ANDCOMMODITIES OF THIS ISLAND\r \r[1577, Book I., Chapter13; 1587, Book I., Chapter 18.]\r \r \rThe air (for the mostpart) throughout the island is such as by\rreason in manner ofcontinual clouds is reputed to be gross, and\rnothing so pleasant asthat of the main. Howbeit, as they which\raffirm these things haveonly respect to the impediment or hindrance\rof the sunbeams by theinterposition of the clouds and of ingrossed\rair, so experienceteacheth us that it is no less pure, wholesome,\rand commodious than isthat of other countries, and (as Caesar\rhimself hereto addeth)much more temperate in summer than that of the\rGauls, from whom headventured hither. Neither is there any thing\rfound in the air of ourregion that is not usually seen amongst other\rnations lying beyond theseas. Wherefore we must needs confess that\rthe situation of ourisland (for benefit of the heavens) is nothing\rinferior to that of anycountry of the main, wheresoever it lie under\rthe open firmament. Andthis Plutarch knew full well, who affirmeth a\rpart of the Elysian Fieldsto be found in Britain, and the isles that\rare situated about it inthe ocean.\r \rThe soil of Britain issuch as by the testimonies and reports both of\rthe old and new writers,and experience also of such as now inhabit\rthe same, is veryfruitful, and such indeed as bringeth forth many\rcommodities, whereof othercountries have need, and yet itself (if\rfond niceness wereabolished) needless of those that are daily\rbrought from other places.Nevertheless it is more inclined to\rfeeding and grazing thanprofitable for tillage and bearing of corn,\rby reason whereof thecountry is wonderfully replenished with neat\rand all kind of cattle;and such store is there also of the same in\revery place that thefourth part of the land is scarcely manured for\rthe provision andmaintenance of grain. Certes this fruitfulness was\rnot unknown unto theBritons long before Caesar\'s time, which was the\rcause wherefore ourpredecessors living in those days in manner\rneglected tillage andlived by feeding and grazing only. The graziers\rthemselves also thendwelled in movable villages by companies, whose\rcustom was to divide theground amongst them, and each one not to\rdepart from the placewhere his lot lay (a thing much like the Irish\rCriacht) till, by eatingup of the country about him, he was enforced\rto remove further and seekfor better pasture. And this was the\rBritish custom, as Ilearn, at first. It hath been commonly reported\rthat the ground of Walesis neither so fruitful as that of England,\rneither the soil ofScotland so bountiful as that of Wales, which is\rtrue for corn and for themost part; otherwise there is so good\rground in some parts ofWales as is in England, albeit the best of\rScotland be scarcelycomparable to the mean of either of both.\rHowbeit, as the bounty ofthe Scotch doth fail in some respect, so\rdoth it surmount in other,God and nature having not appointed all\rcountries to yield forthlike commodities.\r \rBut where our ground isnot so good as we would wish, we have--if\rneed be--sufficient helpto cherish our ground withal, and to make it\rmore fruitful. For, besidethe compest that is carried out of the\rhusbandmen\'s yards,ditches, ponds, dung-houses, or cities and great\rtowns, we have with us akind of white marl which is of so great\rforce that if it be castover a piece of land but once in threescore\ryears it shall not need ofany further compesting. Hereof also doth\rPliny speak (lib. 17, cap.6, 7, 8), where he affirmeth that our marl\rendureth upon the earth bythe space of fourscore years: insomuch\rthat it is laid upon thesame but once in a man\'s life, whereby the\rowner shall not need totravel twice in procuring to commend and\rbetter his soil. Hecalleth it _marga_, and, making divers kinds\rthereof, he finallycommendeth ours, and that of France, above all\rother, which liethsometime a hundred foot deep, and far better than\rthe scattering of chalkupon the same, as the Hedui and Pictones did\rin his time, or as some ofour days also do practise: albeit divers\rdo like better to cast onlime, but it will not so long endure, as I\rhave heard reported.\r \rThere are also in thisisland great plenty of fresh rivers and\rstreams, as you have heardalready, and these thoroughly fraught with\rall kinds of delicate fishaccustomed to be found in rivers. The\rwhole isle likewise isvery full of hills, of which some (though not\rvery many) are ofexceeding height, and divers extending themselves\rvery far from thebeginning; as we may see by Shooter\'s Hill, which,\rrising east of London andnot far from the Thames, runneth along the\rsouth side of the island westwarduntil it come to Cornwall. Like\runto these also are theCrowdon Hills, which, though under divers\rnames (as also the otherfrom the Peak), do run into the borders of\rScotland. What should Ispeak of the Cheviot Hills, which reach\rtwenty miles in length? ofthe Black Mountains in Wales, which go\rfrom ([1]) to ([1]) milesat the least in length? of the Clee Hills\rin Shropshire, which comewithin four miles of Ludlow, and are\rdivided from some part ofWorcester by the Leme? of the Crames in\rScotland, and of ourChiltern, which are eighteen miles at the least\rfrom one end of them,which reach from Henley in Oxfordshire to\rDunstable in Bedfordshire,and are very well replenished with wood\rand corn, notwithstandingthat the most part yield a sweet short\rgrass, profitable forsheep? Wherein albeit they of Scotland do\rsomewhat come behind us,yet their outward defect is inwardly\rrecompensed, not only withplenty of quarries (and those of sundry\rkinds of marble, hardstone, and fine alabaster), but also rich mines\rof metal, as shall beshewed hereafter.\r \r      [1] Here lacks.--H.\r \rIn this island the windsare commonly more strong and fierce than in\rany other places of themain (which Cardane also espied): and that is\roften seen upon the nakedhills not guarded with trees to bear and\rkeep it off. That grievousinconvenience also enforceth our nobility,\rgentry, and communality tobuild their houses in the valleys, leaving\rthe high grounds untotheir corn and cattle, lest the cold and stormy\rblasts of winter shouldbreed them greater annoyance; whereas in other\rregions each one desirethto set his house aloft on the hill, not only\rto be seen afar off, andcast forth his beams of stately and curious\rworkmanship into everyquarter of the country, but also (in hot\rhabitations) for coldnesssake of the air, sith the heat is never so\rvehement on the hill-topas in the valley, because the reverberation\rof the sun\'s beams eitherreacheth not so far as the highest, or else\rbecometh not so strong aswhen it is reflected upon the lower soil.\r \rBut to leave our buildingsunto the purposed place (which\rnotwithstanding have verymuch increased, I mean for curiosity and\rcost, in England, Wales,and Scotland, within these few years) and to\rreturn to the soil again.Certainly it is even now in these our days\rgrown to be much morefruitful than it hath been in times past. The\rcause is for that ourcountrymen are grown to be more painful,\rskilful, and carefulthrough recompense of gain, than heretofore they\rhave been: insomuch thatmy _synchroni_ or time fellows can reap at\rthis present greatcommodity in a little room; whereas of late years\ra great compass hathyielded but small profit, and this only through\rthe idle and negligentoccupation of such as daily manured and had\rthe same in occupying. Imight set down examples of these things out\rof all the parts of thisisland--that is to say, many of England,\rmore out of Scotland, butmost of all out of Wales; in which two last\rrehearsed, very otherlittle food and livelihood was wont to be\rlooked for (beside flesh)more than the soil of itself and the cow\rgave, the people in themeantime living idly, dissolutely, and by\rpicking and stealing onefrom another. All which vices are now (for\rthe most part)relinquished, so that each nation manureth her own\rwith triple commodity tothat it was before time.\r \rThe pasture of this islandis according to the nature and bounty of\rthe soil, whereby in mostplaces it is plentiful, very fine, batable,\rand such as either fattethour cattle with speed or yieldeth great\rabundance of milk andcream whereof the yellowest butter and finest\rcheese are made. But wherethe blue clay aboundeth (which hardly\rdrinketh up the winter\'swater in long season) there the grass is\rspeary, rough, and veryapt for bushes: by which occasion it becometh\rnothing so profitable untothe owner as the other. The best pasture\rground of all England isin Wales, and of all the pasture in Wales\rthat of Cardigan is thechief. I speak of the same which is to be\rfound in the mountainsthere, where the hundredth part of the grass\rgrowing is not eaten, butsuffered to rot on the ground, whereby the\rsoil becometh matted anddivers bogs and quickmoors made withal in\rlong continuance: becauseall the cattle in the country are not able\rto eat it down. If it beaccounted good soil on which a man may lay a\rwand over night and on themorrow find it hidden and overgrown with\rgrass, it is not hard tofind plenty thereof in many places of this\rland. Nevertheless such isthe fruitfulness of the aforesaid county\rthat it far surmounteththis proportion, whereby it may be compared\rfor batableness withItaly, which in my time is called the paradise\rof the world, although byreason of the wickedness of such as dwell\rtherein it may be calledthe sink and drain of hell; so that whereas\rthey were wont to say ofus that our land is good but our people\revil, they did but onlyspeak it; whereas we know by experience that\rthe soil of Italy is anoble soil, but the dwellers therein far off\rany virtue or goodness.\r \rOur meadows are eitherbottoms (whereof we have great store, and\rthose very large, becauseour soil is hilly) or else such as we call\rland meads, and borrowedfrom the best and fattest pasturages. The\rfirst of them are yearlyand often overflown by the rising of such\rstreams as pass throughthe same, or violent falls of land-waters,\rthat descend from thehills about them. The other are seldom or never\roverflown, and that is thecause wherefore their grass is shorter\rthan that of the bottoms,and yet is it far more fine, wholesome, and\rbatable, sith the hay ofour low meadows is not only full of sandy\rcinder, which breedethsundry diseases in our cattle, but also more\rrowty, foggy, and full offlags, and therefore not so profitable for\rstore and forrage as thehigher meads be. The difference furthermore\rin their commodities isgreat; for, whereas in our land meadows we\rhave not often above onegood load of hay, or peradventure a little\rmore in an acre of ground(I use the word _carrucata_, or _carruca_,\rwhich is a wain load, and,as I remember, used by Pliny, lib. 33,\rcap. 2), in low meadows wehave sometimes three, but commonly two or\rupwards, as experiencehath oft confirmed.\r \rOf such as are twice mowedI speak not, sith their later math is not\rso wholesome for cattle asthe first; although in the mouth more\rpleasant for the time: forthereby they become oftentimes to be\rrotten, or to increase sofast in blood, that the garget and other\rdiseases do consume manyof them before the owners can seek out any\rremedy, by phlebotomy orotherwise. Some superstitious fools suppose\rthat they which die of thegarget are ridden with the nightmare, and\rtherefore they hang upstones which naturally have holes in them, and\rmust be found unlookedfor; as if such a stone were an apt cockshot\rfor the devil to runthrough and solace himself withal, while the\rcattle go scot-free andare not molested by him! But if I should set\rdown but half the toysthat superstition hath brought into our\rhusbandmen\'s heads in thisand other behalf, it would ask a greater\rvolume than is convenientfor such a purpose, wherefore it shall\rsuffice to have said thusmuch of these things.\r \rThe yield of ourcorn-ground is also much after this rate following.\rThroughout the land (ifyou please to make an estimate thereof by the\racre) in mean andindifferent years, wherein each acre of rye or\rwheat, well tilled anddressed, will yield commonly sixteen or twenty\rbushels, an acre of barleysix-and-thirty bushels, of oats and such\rlike four or fivequarters, which proportion is notwithstanding oft\rabated toward the north,as it is oftentimes surmounted in the south.\rOf mixed corn, as peas andbeans, sown together, tares and oats\r(which they call bulmong),rye and wheat (named miscelin), here is no\rplace to speak, yet theiryield is nevertheless much after this\rproportion, as I haveoften marked. And yet is not this our great\rfoison comparable to thatof hotter countries of the main. But, of\rall that I ever read, theincrease which Eldred Danus writeth of in\rhis _De imperie Judaeorumin Aethiopia_ surmounteth, where he saith\rthat in the field near tothe Sabbatike river, called in old time\rGosan, the ground is sofertile that every grain of barley growing\rdoth yield an hundredkernels at the least unto the owner.\r \rOf late years also we havefound and taken up a great trade in\rplanting of hops, whereofour moory hitherto and unprofitable grounds\rdo yield such plenty andincrease that there are few farmers or\roccupiers in the countrywhich have not gardens and hops growing of\rtheir own, and those farbetter than do come from Flanders unto us.\rCertes the corruptionsused by the Flemings, and forgery daily\rpractised in this kind ofware, gave us occasion to plant them here\rat home; so that now wemay spare and send many over unto them. And\rthis I know by experience,that some one man by conversion of his\rmoory grounds intohopyards, whereof before he had no commodity, doth\rraise yearly by so littleas twelve acres in compass two hundred\rmarks--all charges bornetowards the maintenance of his family. Which\rindustry God continue!though some secret friends of Flemings let not\rto exclaim against thiscommodity, as a spoil of wood, by reason of\rthe poles, whichnevertheless after three years do also come to the\rfire, and spare theirother fuel.\r \rThe cattle which we breedare commonly such as for greatness of bone,\rsweetness of flesh, andother benefits to be reaped by the same, give\rplace unto none other; asmay appear first by our oxen, whose\rlargeness, height, weight,tallow, hides, and horns are such as none\rof any other nation docommonly or may easily exceed them. Our sheep\rlikewise, for good tasteof flesh, quantity of limbs, fineness of\rfleece, caused by theirhardness of pasturage and abundance of\rincrease (for in manyplaces they bring forth two or three at an\rcaning), give no placeunto any, more than do our goats, who in like\rsort do follow the sameorder, and our deer come not behind. As for\rour conies, I have seenthem so fat in some soils, especially about\rMeall and Disnege, thatthe grease of one being weighed hath peised\rvery near six or sevenounces. All which benefits we first refer to\rthe grace and goodness ofGod, and next of all unto the bounty of our\rsoil, which he hath enduedwith so notable and commodious\rfruitfulness.\r \rBut, as I mean to intreatof these things more largely hereafter, so\rwill I touch in this placeone benefit which our nation wanteth, and\rthat is wine, the faultwhereof is not in our soil, but the\rnegligence of ourcountrymen (especially of the south parts), who do\rnot inure the same to thiscommodity, and which by reason of long\rdiscontinuance is nowbecome inapt to bear any grapes almost for\rpleasure and shadow, muchless then the plain fields or several\rvineyards for advantageand commodity. Yet of late time some have\ressayed to deal for wine(as to your lordship also is right well\rknown). But sith thatliquor, when it cometh to the drinking, hath\rbeen found more hard thanthat which is brought from beyond the sea,\rand the cost of plantingand keeping thereof so chargeable that they\rmay buy it far bettercheap from other countries, they have given\rover their enterpriseswithout any consideration that, as in all\rother things, so neitherthe ground itself in the beginning, nor\rsuccess of their travel,can answer their expectation at the first,\runtil such time as thesoil be brought as it were into acquaintance\rwith this commodity, andthat provision may be made for the more\reasiness of charge to beemployed upon the same.\r \rIf it be true that wherewine doth last and endure well there it will\rgrow no worse, I muse nota little wherefore the planting of vines\rshould be neglected inEngland. That this liquor might have grown in\rthis island heretofore,first the charter that Probus the Emperor\rgave equally to us, theGauls, and Spaniards, is one sufficient\rtestimony. And that it didgrow here (beside the testimony of Beda,\rlib. 1., cap. 1) the oldnotes of tithes for wine that yet remain in\rthe accounts of someparsons and vicars in Kent, elsewhere, besides\rthe records of sundrysuits, commenced in divers ecclesiastical\rcourts, both in Kent,Surrey, etc., also the enclosed parcels almost\rin every abbey yet calledthe vineyards, may be a notable witness, as\ralso the plot which we nowcall East Smithfield in London, given by\rCanutus, sometime king ofthis land, with other soil thereabout, unto\rcertain of his knights,with the liberty of a Guild which thereof was\rcalled Knighton Guild. Thetruth is (saith John Stow, our countryman\rand diligent traveller inthe old estate of this my native city) that\rit is now named PortsokenWard, and given in time past to the\rreligious house withinAldgate. Howbeit first Otwell, the archovel,\rOtto, and finally GeffreyEarl of Essex, constables of the of London,\rwithheld that portion fromthe said house until the reign of King\rStephen, and thereof madea vineyard to their great commodity and\rlucre.
