The Isle of Elyalso was in the first times of the Normans\rcalled Le Ile des Vignes.And good record appeareth that the bishop\rthere had yearly three orfour tun at the least given him _nomine\rdecimæ_, beside whatsoeverover-sum of the liquor did accrue to him\rby leases and otherexcheats whereof also I have seen mention.\rWherefore our soil is notto be blamed, as though our nights were so\rexceeding short that inAugust and September the moon, which is lady\rof moisture and chiefripener of this liquor, cannot in any wise\rshine long enough upon thesame: a very mere toy and fable, right\rworthy to be suppressed,because experience convinceth the upholders\rthereof even in theRhenish wines.\r \rThe time hath been alsothat woad, wherewith our countrymen dyed\rtheir faces (as Cæsarsaith), that they might seem terrible to their\renemies in the field (andalso women and their daughters-in-law did\rstain their bodies and gonaked, in that pickle, to the sacrifices of\rtheir gods, coveting toresemble therein the Ethiopians, as Pliny\rsaith, [lib. 22, cap. 1]),and also madder have been (next unto our\rtin and wools) the chiefcommodities and merchandise of this realm, I\rfind also that rape oilhath been made within this land. But now our\rsoil either will not, orat the leastwise may not, bear either woad\ror madder. I say not thatthe ground is not able so to do, but that\rwe are negligent, afraidof the pilling of our grounds, and careless\rof our own profits, as menrather willing to buy the same of others\rthan take any pain toplant them here at home. The like I may say of\rflax, which by law oughtto be sown in every country town in England,\rmore or less; but I see nosuccess of that good and wholesome law;\rsith it is rathercontemptuously rejected than otherwise dutifully\rkept in any place inEngland.\r \rSome say that our greatnumber of laws do breed a general negligence\rand contempt of all goodorder, because we have so many that no\rsubject can live withoutthe transgression of some of them, and that\rthe often alteration ofour ordinances doth much harm in this\rrespect, which (afterAristotle) doth seem to carry some reason\rwithal, for (as CorneliusGallus hath)--\r \r  _"Eventus varios res nova semperhabet."_[1]\r \r      [1] "An innovation, has always mixedeffects."\r \rBut very many let not toaffirm that the greedy corruption of the\rpromoters on the one side,facility in dispensing with good laws and\rfirst breach of the samein the lawmakers and superiors and private\rrespects of theirestablishment on the other, are the greatest causes\rwhy the inferiors regardno good order, being always so ready to\roffend without any facultyone way as they are otherwise to presume\rupon the examples of theirbetters when any hold is to be taken. But\ras in these things I haveno skill, so I wish that fewer licences for\rthe private commodity butof a few were granted (not that thereby I\rdeny the maintenance ofthe prerogative royal, but rather would with\rall my heart that it mightbe yet more honourably increased), and\rthat every one which byfee\'d friendship (or otherwise) doth attempt\rto procure ought from theprince that may profit but few and prove\rhurtful to many might beat open assizes and sessions denounced enemy\rto his country andcommonwealth of the land.\r \rGlass also hath been madehere in great plenty before, and in the\rtime of the Romans; andthe said stuff also, beside fine scissors,\rshears, collars of goldand silver for women\'s necks, cruises and\rcups of amber, were aparcel of the tribute which Augustus in his\rdays laid upon thisisland. In like sort he charged the Britons with\rcertain implements andvessels of ivory (as Strabo saith); whereby it\rappeareth that in old timeour countrymen were far more industrious\rand painful in the use andapplication of the benefits of their\rcountry than either afterthe coming of the Saxons or Normans, in\rwhich they gave themselvesmore to idleness and following of the\rwars.\r \rIf it were requisite thatI should speak of the sundry kinds of mould,\ras the cledgy, or clay,whereof are divers sorts (red, blue, black,\rand white), also the redor white sandy, the loamy, roselly, gravelly,\rchalky, or black, I couldsay that there are so many divers veins in\rBritain as elsewhere inany quarter of like quantity in the world.\rHowbeit this I must needconfess, that the sand and clay do bear great\rsway: but clay most ofall, as hath been and yet is always seen and\rfelt through plenty anddearth of corn. For if this latter (I mean the\rclay) do yield her fullincrease (which it doth commonly in dry years\rfor wheat), then is theregeneral plenty: whereas if it fail, then\rhave we scarcity,according to the old rude verse set down of England,\rbut to be understood ofthe whole island, as experience doth confirm--\r \r  "_When the sand doth serve the clay,\r  Then may we sing well-away;\r  But when the clay doth serve the sand,\r  Then is it merry with England_."\r \rI might here intreat ofthe famous valleys in England, of which one\ris called the Vale ofWhite Horse, another of Evesham (commonly taken\rfor the granary ofWorcestershire), the third of Aylesbury, that\rgoeth by Thame, the rootsof Chiltern Hills, to Dunstable, Newport\rPagnel, Stony Stratford,Buckingham, Birstane Park, etc. Likewise of\rthe fourth, of Whitehartor Blackmoor in Dorsetshire. The fifth, of\rRingdale or Renidale,corruptly called Kingtaile, that lieth (as mine\rauthor saith) upon theedge of Essex and Cambridgeshire, and also the\rMarshwood Vale: but,forsomuch as I know not well their several\rlimits, I give over to goany further in their description. In like\rsort it should not beamiss to speak of our fens, although our\rcountry be not so full ofthis kind of soil as the parts beyond the\rseas (to wit, Narbonne,etc.), and thereto of other pleasant bottoms,\rthe which are not onlyendued with excellent rivers and great store\rof corn and fine fodderfor neat and horses in time of the year\r(whereby they areexceeding beneficial unto their owners), but also\rof no small compass andquantity in ground. For some of our fens are\rwell known to be either often, twelve, sixteen, twenty, or thirty\rmiles in length, that ofthe Girwies yet passing all the rest, which\ris full sixty (as I haveoften read). Wherein also Ely, the famous\risle, standeth, which isseven miles every way, and whereunto there\ris no access but by threecausies, whose inhabitants in like sort by\ran old privilege may takewood, sedge turf, etc., to burn, likewise\rhay for their cattle andthatch for their houses of custom, and each\roccupier in his appointedquantity throughout the isle; albeit that\rcovetousness hath nowbegun somewhat to abridge this large\rbenevolence and commodity,as well in the said isle as most other\rplaces of this land.\r \rFinally, I might discoursein like order of the large commons, laid\rout heretofore by thelords of the soil for the benefit of such poor\ras inhabit within thecompass of their manors. But, as the true\rintent of the givers isnow in most places defrauded, insomuch that\rnot the poor tenantsinhabitating upon the same, but their landlords,\rhave all the commodity andgain. Wherefore I mean not at this present\rto deal withal, butreserve the same wholly unto the due place,\rwhilst I go forward withthe rest, setting down nevertheless by the\rway a general commendationof the whole island, which I find in an\rancient monument, muchunto this effect--\r \r  "Illa quidem longè celebris splendore,beata,\r  Glebis, lacte, favis, supereminet insulacunctis,\r  Quas regit ille Deus, spumanti cujus ab oro\r  Proffuit oceanus," etc.\r \rAnd a little after--\r \r  "Testis Lundoniurntibus, WintoniaBaccho,\r  Herefordia grege, Worcestria frugeredundans,\r  Batha lacu, Salabyra feris, Cantuarin pisce,\r  Eboraca sylvis, Excestria clara metallis,\r  Norwicum Dacis hybernis, Cestria Gallis,\r  Cicestrum Norwagenis, Dunelmia præpinguia,\r  Testis Lincolnia gens infinita decore,\r  Testis Ell formosa situ, Doncastriavisu," etc.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER XI\r \rOF SUNDRY MINERALS ANDMETALS\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapters16 and 18; 1587, Book III., Chapters\r10 and 11.]\r \r \rWith how great benefitsthis island of ours hath been endued from the\rbeginning I hope there isno godly man but will readily confess, and\ryield unto the Lord Godhis due honour for the same. For we are\rblessed every way, andthere is no temporal commodity necessary to be\rhad or craved by anynation at God\'s hand that he hath not in most\rabundant manner bestowedupon us Englishmen, if we could see to use\rit, and be thankful forthe same. But alas! (as said in the chapter\rprecedent) we love toenrich them that care not for us, but for our\rgreat commodities: and onetrifling toy not worth the carriage,\rcoming (as the proverbsaith) in three ships from beyond the sea, is\rmore worth with us than aright good jewel easy to be had at home.\rThey have also the cast toteach us to neglect our own things; for,\rif they see that we beginto make any account of our commodities (if\rit be so that they havealso the like in their own countries) they\rwill suddenly abase thesame to so low a price that our gain not\rbeing worthy our travel,and the same commodity with less cost ready\rto be had at home fromother countries (though but for a while), it\rcauseth us to give overour endeavours and as it were by-and-by to\rforget the matterwhereabout we went before, to obtain them at their\rhands. And this is theonly cause wherefore our commodities are oft\rso little esteemed of.Some of them can say, without any teacher,\rthat they will buy thecase of a fox of an Englishman for a groat,\rand make him afterwardsgive twelve pence for the tail. Would to God\rwe might once wax wiser,and each one endeavour that the commonwealth\rof England may nourishagain in her old rate, and that our\rcommodities may be fullywrought at home (as cloth if you will for an\rexample) and not carriedout to be shorn and dressed abroad, while\rour clothworkers here dostarve and beg their bread, and for lack of\rdaily practice utterlyneglect to be skilful in this science! But to\rmy purpose.\r \rWe have in England greatplenty of quicksilver, antimony, sulphur,\rblack lead, and orpimentred and yellow. We have also the finest alum\r(wherein the diligence ofone of the greatest favourers of the\rcommonwealth of England ofa subject[1] hath been of late egregriously\rabused, and even almostwith barbarous incivility) and of no less\rforce against fire, if itwere used in our parietings, than that of\rLipari, which only was inuse sometime amongst the Asians and Romans\rand whereof Sylla had suchtrial that when he meant to have burned a\rtower of wood erected byArchelaus, the lieutenant of Mithridates, he\rcould by no means set iton fire in a long time, because it was washed\rover with alum, as werealso the gates of the temple of Jerusalem with\rlike effect, and perceivedwhen Titus commanded fire to be put unto\rthe same. Besides this, wehave also the natural cinnabarum or\rvermillion, the sulphurousglebe called bitumen in old time, for\rmortar, and yet burned inlamps where oil is scant and geson; the\rchrysocolla, copperas, andmineral stone, whereof petriolum is made,\rand that which is moststrange, the mineral pearl, which as they are\rfor greatness and colourmost excellent of all other, so are they\rdigged out of the mainland and in sundry places far distant from the\rshore. Certes the westernpart of the land hath in times past greatly\rabounded with these andmany other rare and excellent commodities, but\rnow they are washed awayby the violence of the sea, which hath\rdevoured the greatest partof Cornwall and Devonshire on either side;\rand it doth appear yet bygood record that, whereas now there is a\rgreat distance between theScilly Isles and the point of the Land\'s\rEnd, there was of lateyears to speak of scarcely a brook or drain of\rone fathom water betweenthem, if so much, as by those evidences\rappeareth, and are yet tobe seen in the hands of the lord and chief\rowner of those isles. Butto proceed.\r \r      [1] The Lord Mountjoy.--H.\r \rOf coal-mines we have suchplenty in the north and western parts of\rour island as may sufficefor all the realm of England; and so must\rthey do hereafter indeed,if wood be not better cherished than it is\rat this present. And sosay the truth, notwithstanding that very many\rof them are carried intoother countries of the main, yet their\rgreatest trade beginnethnow to grow from the forge into the kitchen\rand hall, as may appearalready in most cities and towns that lie\rabout the coast, wherethey have but little other fuel except it be\rturf and hassock. I marvelnot a little that there is no trade of\rthese into Sussex andSouthamptonshire, for want thereof the smiths\rdo work their iron withcharcoal. I think that far carriage be the\ronly cause, which is but aslender excuse to enforce us to carry them\rinto the main from hence.\r \rBesides our coal-mines, wehave pits in like sort of white plaster,\rand of fat and white andother coloured marble, wherewith in many\rplaces the inhabitors docompest their soil, and which doth benefit\rtheir land in ample mannerfor many years to come. We have saltpetre\rfor our ordinance and saltsoda for our glass, and thereto in one\rplace a kind of earth (inSouthery; as I ween, hard by Codington, and\rsometime in the tenure ofone Croxton of London) which is so fine to\rmake moulds for goldsmithsand casters of metal, that a load of it\rwas worth five shillingsthirty years ago; none such again they say\rin England. But whetherthere be or not, let us not be unthankful to\rGod, for these and otherhis benefits bestowed upon us, whereby he\rsheweth himself a lovingand merciful father unto us, which\rcontrariwise return untohim in lieu of humility and obedience\rnothing but wickedness,avarice, mere contempt of his will, pride,\rexcess, atheism, and noless than Jewish ingratitude.[2]\r \r      [2] Here ends the chapter entitled"Minerals," and the one\r      on "Metals" begins.--W.\r \rAll metals receive theirbeginning of quicksilver and sulphur, which\rare as mother and fatherto them. And such is the purpose of nature in\rtheir generations that shetendeth always to the procreation of gold;\rnevertheless she seldomreacheth unto that her end, because of the\runequal mixture andproportion of these two in the substance\rengendered, wherebyimpediment and corruption is induced, which as it\ris more or less doth shewitself in the metal that is produced....\r \rAnd albeit that we have nosuch abundance of these (as some other\rcountries do yield), yethave my rich countrymen store enough of both\rin their purses, where intime past they were wont to have least,\rbecause the garnishing ofour churches, tabernacles, images, shrines,\rand apparel of the priestsconsumed the greatest part, as experience\rhath confirmed.\r \rOf late my countrymen havefound out I wot not what voyage into the\rWest Indies, from whencethey have brought some gold, whereby our\rcountry is enriched; butof all that ever adventured into those\rparts, none have spedbetter than Sir Francis Drake, whose success\r(1582) hath far passedeven his own expectation. One John Frobisher\rin like manner, attemptingto seek out a shorter cut by the northerly\rregions into the peaceablesea and kingdom of Cathay, happened (1577)\rupon certain islands bythe way, wherein great plenty of much gold\rappeared, and so much thatsome letted not to give out for certainty\rthat Solomon had his goldfrom thence, wherewith he builded the\rtemple. This golden shewmade him so desirous also of like success\rthat he left off hisformer voyage and returned home to bring news of\rsuch things as he hadseen. But, when after another voyage it was\rfound to be but dross, hegave over both the enterprises, and now\rkeepeth home without anydesire at all to seek into far countries. In\rtruth, such was the plentyof ore there seen and to be had that, if\rit had holden perfect,might have furnished all the world with\rabundance of that metal;the journey also was short and performed in\rfour or five months, whichwas a notable encouragement. But to\rproceed.\r \rTin and lead, metals whichStrabo noteth in his time to be carried\runto Marsilis from hence,as Diodorus also confirmeth, are very\rplentiful with us, the onein Cornwall, Devonshire, and elsewhere in\rthe north, the other inDerbyshire, Weredale, and sundry places of\rthis island; whereby mycountrymen do reap no small commodity, but\respecially our pewterers,who in times past employed the use of\rpewter only upon dishes,pots, and a few other trifles for service\rhere at home, whereas nowthey are grown unto such exquisite cunning\rthat they can in mannerimitate by infusion any form or fashion of\rcup, dish, salt bowl, orgoblet, which is made by goldsmiths\' craft,\rthough they be never socurious, exquisite, and artificially forged.\rSuch furniture ofhousehold of this metal as we commonly call by the\rname of _vessel_ is soldusually by the garnish, which doth contain\rtwelve platters, twelvedishes, twelve saucers, and those are either\rof silver fashion or elsewith broad or narrow brims, and bought by\rthe pound, which is nowvalued at six or seven pence, or peradventure\rat eight pence. Ofporringers, pots, and other like, I speak not,\ralbeit that in the makingof all these things there is such exquisite\rdiligence used, I mean forthe mixture of the metal and true making\rof this commodity (byreason of sharp laws provided in that behalf),\ras the like is not to befound in any other trade. I have been also\rinformed that itconsisteth of a composition which hath thirty pounds\rof kettle brass to athousand pounds of tin, whereunto they add three\ror four pounds oftin-glass; but as too much of this doth make the\rstuff brickle, so the morethe brass be, the better is the pewter,\rand more profitable untohim that doth buy and purchase the same. But\rto proceed.\r \rIn some places beyond thesea a garnish of good flat English pewter\rof an ordinary making (Isay flat, because dishes and platters in my\rtime begin to be made deeplike basins, and are indeed more\rconvenient both for sauce,broth, and keeping the meat warm) is\resteemed almost soprecious as the like number of vessels that are\rmade of fine silver, andin manner no less desired amongst the great\restates, whose workmen arenothing so skilful in that trade as ours,\rneither their metal sogood, nor plenty so great, as we have here in\rEngland. The Romans madeexcellent looking-glasses of our English\rtin, howbeit our workmenwere not then so exquisite in that feat as\rthe Brundusians, whereforethe wrought metal was carried over unto\rthem by way ofmerchandise, and very highly were those glasses\resteemed of till silvercame generally in place, which in the end\rbrought the tin into suchcontempt that in manner every dishwasher\rrefused to look in otherthan silver glasses for the attiring of her\rhead. Howbeit the makingof silver glasses had been in use before\rBritain was known unto theRomans, for I read that one Praxiteles\rdevised them in the youngtime of Pompey, which was before the coming\rof Caesar into thisisland.\r \rThere were mines of leadsometimes also in Wales, which endured so\rlong till the people hadconsumed all their wood by melting of the\rsame (as they did also atComeriswith, six miles from Stradfleur),\rand I suppose that inPliny\'s time the abundance of lead (whereof he\rspeaketh) was to be foundin those parts, in the seventeenth of his\rthirty-fourth book; alsohe affirmeth that it lay in the very sward\rof the earth, and dailygotten in such plenty that the Romans made a\rrestraint of the carriagethereof to Rome, limiting how much should\ryearly be wrought andtransported over the sea.[3]\r \r      [3] Here follow two stories about crowsand miners.--W.\r \rIron is found in manyplaces, as in Sussex, Kent, Weredale, Mendip,\rWalshall, as also inShropshire, but chiefly in the woods betwixt\rBelvos and Willock (orWicberry) near Manchester, and elsewhere in\rWales. Of which minesdivers do bring forth so fine and good stuff as\rany that cometh frombeyond the sea, beside the infinite gains to the\rowners, if we would soaccept it, or bestow a little more cost in the\rrefining of it. It is alsoof such toughness, that it yieldeth to the\rmaking of claricord wirein some places of the realm. Nevertheless, it\rwas better cheap with uswhen strangers only brought it hither; for it\ris our quality when we getany commodity to use it with extremity\rtowards our own nation,after we have once found the means to shut out\rforeigners from thebringing in of the like. It breedeth in like\rmanner great expense andwaste of wood, as doth the making of our pots\rand table vessels ofglass, wherein is much loss, sith it is so\rquickly broken; and yet(as I think) easy to be made tougher, if our\ralchemists could once findthe true birth or production of the red\rman, whose mixture wouldinduce a metallic toughness unto it, whereby\rit should abide thehammer.\r \rCopper is lately notfound, but rather restored again to light. For I\rhave read of copper tohave been heretofore gotten in our island;\rhowbeit as strangers havemost commonly the governance of our mines,\rso they hitherto makesmall gains of this in hand in the north parts;\rfor (as I am informed) theprofit doth very hardly countervail the\rcharges, whereat wise mendo not a little marvel, considering the\rabundance which that minedoth seem to offer, and, as it were, at\rhand. Leland, ourcountryman, noteth sundry great likelihoods of\rnatural copper mines to beeastwards, as between Dudman and Trewardth,\rin the sea cliffs, besideother places, whereof divers are noted here\rand there in sundry placesof this book already, and therefore it\rshall be but in vain torepeat them here again. As for that which is\rgotten out of themarchasite, I speak not of it, sith it is not\rincident to my purpose. InDorsetshire also a copper mine lately found\ris brought to goodperfection.\r \rAs for our steel, it isnot so good for edge-tools as that of Cologne,\rand yet the one is oftensold for the other, and like talc used in\rboth, that is to say,thirty gads to the sheaf, and twelve sheaves to\rthe burden.\r \rOur alchemy is artificial,and thereof our spoons and some salts are\rcommonly made andpreferred before our pewter with some,[4] albeit in\rtruth it be much subjectto corruption, putrefaction, more heavy and\rfoul to handle than ourpewter; yet some ignorant persons affirm it to\rbe a metal more natural,and the very same which Encelius calleth\r_plumbum cincreum_, theGermans _wisemute, mithan_, and _counterfeie_,\radding that where itgroweth silver cannot be far off. Nevertheless it\ris known to be a mixtureof brass, lead, and tin (of which this latter\roccupieth the one-half),but after another proportion than is used in\rpewter. But alas, I ampersuaded that neither the old Arabians nor new\ralchemists of our time didever hear of it, albeit that the name\rthereof do seem to comeout of their forge. For the common sort indeed\rdo call it alchemy, anunwholesome metal (God wot) and worthy to be\rbanished and driven out ofthe land. And thus I conclude with this\rdiscourse, as having nomore to say of the metals of my country,\rexcept I should talk ofbrass, bell metal, and such as are brought\rover for merchandise fromother countries; and yet I cannot but say\rthat there is some brassfound also in England, but so small is the\rquantity that it is notgreatly to be esteemed or accounted for.\r \r      [4] Some tell me that it is a mixture ofbrass, lead, and\r      tin.--H.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER XII\r \rOF CATTLE KEPT FOR PROFIT\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapter8; 1587, Book III., Chapter 1.]\r \r \rThere is no kind of tamecattle usually to be seen in these parts of\rthe world whereof we havenot some, and that great store, in England,\ras horses, oxen, sheep,goats, swine, and far surmounting the like in\rother countries, as may beproved with ease. For where are oxen\rcommonly made more largeof bone, horses more decent and pleasant in\rpace, kine more commodiousfor the pail, sheep more profitable for\rwool, swine more wholesomeof flesh, and goats more gainful to their\rkeepers than here with usin England? But, to speak of them\rpeculiarly, I suppose thatour kine are so abundant in yield of milk,\rwhereof we make our butterand cheese, as the like any where else, and\rso apt for the plough indivers places as either our horses or oxen.\rAnd, albeit they now andthen twin, yet herein they seem to come short\rof that commodity which islooked for in other countries, to wit, in\rthat they bring forth mostcommonly but one calf at once. The gains\ralso gotten by a cow (allcharges borne) hath been valued at twenty\rshillings yearly; but now,as land is enhanced, this proportion of\rgain is much abated, andlikely to decay more and more, if ground\rarise to be yetdearer--which God forbid, if it be His will and\rpleasure. I heard of lateof a cow in Warwickshire, belonging to\rThomas Breuer of Studley,which in six years had sixteen calves, that\ris four at once in threecalvings and twice twins, which unto many may\rseem a thing incredible.In like manner our oxen are such as the like\rare not to be found in anycountry of Europe, both for greatness of\rbody and sweetness offlesh or else would not the Roman writers have\rpreferred them beforethose of Liguria. In most places our graziers\rare now grown to be socunning that if they do but see an ox or\rbullock, and come to thefeeling of him, they will give a guess at his\rweight, and how many scoreor stone of flesh and tallow he beareth,\rhow the butcher may liveby the sale, and what he may have for the\rskin and tallow, which isa point of skill not commonly practised\rheretofore. Some suchgraziers also are reported to ride with velvet\rcoats and chains of goldabout them and in their absence their wives\rwill not let to supplythose turns with no less skill than their\rhusbands: which is a hardwork for the poor butcher, sith he through\rthis means can seldom berich or wealthy by his trade. In like sort\rthe flesh of our oxen andkine is sold both by hand and by weight as\rthe buyer will; but inyoung ware rather by weight especially for the\rsteer and heifer, sith thefiner beef is the lightest, whereas the\rflesh of bulls and oldkine, etc., is of sadder substance, and\rtherefore much heavier asit lieth in the scale. Their horns also are\rknown to be more fair andlarge in England than in any other places,\rexcept those which are tobe seen among the Paeones, which quality,\ralbeit that it be given toour breed generally by nature, yet it is\rnow and then helped alsoby art. For, when they be very young, many\rgraziers will oftentimesanoint their budding horns or tender tips\rwith honey, whichmollifieth the natural hardness of that substance,\rand thereby maketh them togrow unto a notable greatness. Certes it is\rnot strange in England tosee oxen whose horns have the length of a\ryard or three feet betweenthe tips, and they themselves thereto so\rtall as the height of aman of mean and indifferent stature is scarce\requal unto them.Nevertheless it is much to be lamented that our\rgeneral breed of cattle isnot better looked unto; for the greatest\roccupiers wean leaststore, because they can buy them (as they say)\rfar better cheap than toraise and bring them up. In my time a cow\rhath risen from fournobles to four marks by this means, which\rnotwithstanding were nogreat price if they did yearly bring forth\rmore than one calf apiece, as I hear they do in other countries.\r \rOur horses, moreover, arehigh, and, although not commonly of such\rhuge greatness as in otherplaces of the main, yet, if you respect the\reasiness of their pace, itis hard to say where their like are to be\rhad. Our land doth yieldno asses, and therefore we want the\rgeneration also of mulesand somers, and therefore the most part of\rour carriages is made bythese, which, remaining stoned, are either\rreserved for the cart orappointed to bear such burdens as are\rconvenient for them. Ourcart or plough horses (for we use them\rindifferently) arecommonly so strong that five or six of them (at the\rmost) will draw threethousand weight of the greatest tale with ease\rfor a long journey,although it be not a load of common usage, which\rconsisteth only of twothousand, or fifty foot of timber, forty\rbushels of white salt, orsix-and-thirty of bay, of five quarters of\rwheat, experience dailyteacheth, and I have elsewhere remembered.\rSuch as are kept also forburden will carry four hundredweight\rcommonly without any hurtor hindrance. This furthermore is to be\rnoted, that our princesand the nobility have their carriage commonly\rmade by carts, whereby itcometh to pass that when the queen\'s majesty\rdoth remove from any oneplace to another, there are usually 400\rcarewares, which amount tothe sum of 2400 horses, appointed out of\rthe countries adjoining,whereby her carriage is conveyed safely unto\rthe appointed place.Hereby also the ancient use of somers and sumpter\rhorses is in mannerutterly relinquished, which causeth the trains of\rour princes in theirprogresses to shew far less than those of the\rkings of other nations.\r \rSuch as serve for thesaddle are commonly gelded, and now grew to be\rvery dear among us,especially if they be well coloured, justly\rlimbed, and have theretoan easy ambling pace. For our countrymen,\rseeking their ease inevery corner where it is to be had, delight very\rmuch in those qualities,but chiefly in their excellent paces, which,\rbesides that it is inmanner peculiar unto horses of our soil, and not\rhurtful to the rider orowner sitting on their backs, it is moreover\rvery pleasant anddelectable in his ears, in that the noise of their\rwell-proportioned pacedoth yield comfortable sound as he travelleth\rby the way. Yet is thereno greater deceit used anywhere than among\rour horsekeepers,horsecoursers, and hostlers; for such is the subtle\rknavery of a great sort ofthem (without exception of any of them be\rit spoken which deal forprivate gain) that an honest-meaning man\rshall have very good luckamong them if he be not deceived by some\rfalse trick or other.\r \rThere are certain notablemarkets wherein great plenty of horses and\rcolts is bought and sold,and whereunto such as have need resort\ryearly to buy and maketheir necessary provision of them, as Ripon,\rNewport Pond, Wolfpit,Harboro\', and divers others. But, as most\rdrovers are very diligentto bring great store of these unto those\rplaces, so many of themare too too lewd in abusing such as buy them.\rFor they have a custom, tomake them look fair to the eye, when they\rcome within two days\'journey of the market to drive them till they\rsweat, and for the spaceof eight or twelve hours, which, being done,\rthey turn them all overthe backs into some water, where they stand\rfor a season, and then goforward with them to the place appointed,\rwhere they make sale oftheir infected ware, and such as by this means\rdo fall into many diseasesand maladies. Of such outlandish horses as\rare daily brought overunto us I speak not, as the jennet of Spain,\rthe courser of Naples, thehobby of Ireland, the Flemish roile and the\rScottish nag, because thatfurther speech of them cometh not within\rthe compass of thistreatise, and for whose breed and maintenance\r(especially of thegreatest sort) King Henry the Eighth erected a\rnoble studdery, and for atime had very good success with them, till\rthe officers, waxingweary, procured a mixed brood of bastard races,\rwhereby his good purposecame to little effect. Sir Nicholas Arnold of\rlate hath bred the besthorses in England, and written of the manner\rof their production: wouldto God his compass of ground were like to\rthat of Pella in Syria,wherein the king of that nation had usually a\rstuddery of 30,000 maresand 300 stallions, as Strabo doth remember,\rlib. 16. But to leavethis, let us see what may be said of sheep.\r \rOur sheep are veryexcellent, sith for sweetness of flesh they pass\rall other. And so much areour wools to be preferred before those of\rMilesia and other placesthat if Jason had known the value of them\rthat are bred and to behad in Britain he would never have gone to\rColchis to look for anythere. For, as Dionysius Alexandrinus saith in\rhis _De situ Orbis_, itmay by spinning be made comparable to the\rspider\'s web. What foolsthen are our countrymen, in that they seek to\rbereave themselves of thiscommodity by practising daily how to\rtransfer the same to othernations, in carrying over their rams and\rewes to breed and increaseamong them! The first example hereof was\rgiven under Edward theFourth, who, not understanding the bottom of\rthe suit of sundrytraítorous merchants that sought a present gain\rwith the perpetualhindrance of their country licensed them to carry\rover certain numbers ofthem into Spain, who, having licence but for a\rfew, shipped very many: athing practised in other commodities also,\rwhereby the prince and hisland are not seldom times defrauded. But\rsuch is our nature, and soblind are we indeed, that we see no\rinconvenience before wefeel it; and for a present gain we regard not\rwhat damage may ensue toour posterity. Hereto some other man would\radd also the desire thatwe have to benefit other countries and to\rimpeach our own. And itis, so sure as God liveth, that every trifle\rwhich cometh from beyondthe sea, though it be not worth threepence,\ris more esteemed than acontinual commodity at home with us, which far\rexceedeth that value. Intime past the use of this commodity\rconsisteth (for the mostpart) in cloth and woolsteds; but now, by\rmeans of strangerssuccoured here from domestic persecution, the same\rhath been employed untosundry other uses, as mockados, bays,\rvellures, grograines,etc., whereby the makers have reaped no small\rcommodity. It isfurthermore to be noted, for the low countries of\rBelgie know it, and dailyexperience (notwithstanding the sharpness of\rour laws to the contrary)doth yet confirm it, that, although our rams\rand wethers do go thitherfrom us never so well headed according to\rtheir kind, yet after theyhave remained there a while they cast there\rtheir heads, and fromthenceforth they remain polled without any horns\rat all. Certes this kindof cattle is more cherished in England than\rstandeth well with thecommodity of the commons or prosperity of\rdivers towns, whereof someare wholly converted to their feeding; yet\rsuch a profitablesweetness is their fleece, such necessity in their\rflesh, and so great abenefit in the manuring of barren soil with\rtheir dung and piss, thattheir superfluous members are the better\rborn withal. And there isnever a husbandman (for now I speak not of\rour great sheepmasters, ofwhom some one man hath 20,000) but hath\rmore or less of thiscattle feeding on his fallows and short grounds,\rwhich yield the finerfleece.\r \rNevertheless the sheep ofour country are often troubled with the rot\r(as are our swine with themeasles, though never so generally), and\rmany men are now and thengreat losers by the same; but, after the\rcalamity is over, if theycan recover and keep their new stock sound\rfor seven years together,the former loss will easily be recompensed\rwith double commodity.Cardan writeth that our waters are hurtful to\rour sheep; howbeit this isbut his conjecture, for we know that our\rsheep are infected bygoing to the water, and take the same as a sure\rand certain token that arot hath gotten hold of them, their livers\rand lights being alreadydistempered through excessive heat, which\renforceth them the ratherto seek unto the water. Certes there is no\rparcel of the main whereina man shall generally find more fine and\rwholesome water than inEngland; and therefore it is impossible that\rour sheep should decay bytasting of the same. Wherefore the hindrance\rby rot is rather to beascribed to the unseasonableness and moisture\rof the weather in summer,also their licking in of mildews, gossamire,\rrowtie fogs, and rankgrass, full of superfluous juice, but especially\r(I say) to over moistweather, whereby the continual rain piercing\rinto their hollow fellssoaketh forthwith into their flesh, which\rbringeth them to theirbaines. Certes I find among the writers\rthat the milk of a goat isnext in estimation to that of the woman,\rfor that it helpeth thestomach, removeth oppilations and stoppings of\rthe liver, and looseth thebelly. Some place also next unto it the\rmilk of the ewe, andthirdly that of the cow. It is made commonly of the fore part\rof a tame boar, set up forthe purpose by the space of a whole year or\rtwo, especially ingentlemen\'s houses (for the husbandmen and farmers\rnever frank them for theirown use above three or four months, or half\ra year at the most), inwhich time he is dieted with oats and peason,\rand lodged on the bareplanks of an uneasy coat, till his fat be\rhardened sufficiently fortheir purpose: afterward he is killed,\rscalded, and cut out, andthen of his former parts is our brawn made.\rThe rest is nothing sofat, and therefore it beareth the name of sowse\ronly, and is commonlyreserved for the serving-man and hind, except it\rplease the owner to haveany part thereof baked, which are then\rhandled of custom afterthis manner: the hinder parts being cut off,\rthey are first drawn withlard, and then sodden; being sodden, they\rare soused in claret wineand vinegar a certain space, and afterward\rbaked in pasties, andeaten of many instead of the wild boar, and\rtruly it is very goodmeat: the pestles may be hanged up a while to\rdry before they be drawnwith lard, if you will, and thereby prove the\rbetter. But hereof enough,and therefore to come again unto our brawn.\rThe neck pieces, being cutoff round, are called collars of brawn, the\rshoulders are namedshilds, only the ribs retain the former\rdenomination, so thatthese aforesaid pieces deserve the name of\rbrawn: the bowels of thebeast are commonly cast away because of their\rrankness, and so werelikewise his stones, till a foolish fantasy got\rhold of late amongst somedelicate dames, who have now found the means\rto dress them also withgreat cost for a dainty dish, and bring them\rto the board as a serviceamong other of like sort, though not without\rnote of their desire tothe provocation of fleshly lust which by this\rtheir fond curiosity isnot a little revealed. Some use to make brawn of great\rbarrow hogs, and seethethem, and souse the whole as they do that of\rthe boar; and in myjudgment it is the better of both, and more easy\rof digestion. But of brawnthus much, and so much may seem sufficient.\r \r      [1] Tape.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER XIII\r \rOF WILD AND TAME FOWLS\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapters9 and 11; 1587, Book III., Chapters\r2 and 5.]\r \r \rOrder requireth that Ispeak somewhat of the fowls also of England,\rwhich I may easily divideinto the wild and tame; but, alas! such is\rmy small skill in fowlsthat, to say the truth, I can neither recite\rtheir numbers nor welldistinguish one kind of them from another. Certes this enormity bred great troubles\rin King John\'s days,insomuch that, going in progress about the tenth\rof his reign, he foundlittle or no game wherewith to solace himself\ror exercise his falcons.Wherefore, being at Bristow in the Christmas\rensuing, he restrained allmanner of hawking or taking of wild fowl\rthroughout England for aseason, whereby the land within few years was\rthoroughly replenishedagain. As for egrets,\rpawpers, and such like,they are daily brought unto us from beyond the\rsea, as if all the fowl ofour country could not suffice to satisfy\rour delicate appetites.\r \r      [1] The proper English name of the birdwhich vulgar acceptance\r      forces us to now call _bittern_.--W.\r \rOur tame fowl are such(for the most part) as are common both to us\rand to other countries, ascocks, hens, geese, ducks, peacocks of Ind,\rpigeons, now a hurtfulfowl by reason of their multitudes, and number\rof houses daily erectedfor their increase (which the boors of the\rcountry call in scornalmshouses, and dens of thieves, and such like),\rwhereof there is greatplenty in every farmer\'s yard. They are kept\rthere also to be soldeither for ready money in the open markets, or\relse to be spent at homein good company amongst their neighbours\rwithout reprehension orfines. Neither are we so miserable in England\r(a thing only granted untous by the especial grace of God and liberty\rof our princes) as to dineor sup with a quarter of a hen, or to make\ras great a repast with acock\'s comb as they do in some other\rcountries; but, ifoccasion serve, the whole carcases of many capons,\rhens, pigeons, and suchlike do oft go to wrack, beside beef, mutton,\rveal, and lamb, all ofwhich at every feast are taken for necessary\rdishes amongst thecommunalty of England.\r \rThe gelding of cocks,whereby capons are made, Is an ancient practice\rbrought in old time by theRomans when they dwelt here in this land;\rbut the gelding of turkeysor Indian peacocks is a newer device, and\rcertainly not used amiss,sith the rankness of that bird is very much\rabated thereby and thestrong taste of the flesh is sundry wise\ramended. The happy andfortunate want of these beasts in England is\runiversally ascribed tothe politic government of King Edgar.[1]...\r \r      [1] Here follows an account of theextermination of wolves,\r      and a reference to lions and wild bullsrampant in Scotland of\r      old.--W.\r \rOf foxes we have some, butno great store, and also badgers in our\rsandy and light grounds,where woods, furze, broom, and plenty of\rshrubs are to shroud themin when they be from their burrows, and\rthereunto warrens ofconies at hand to feed upon at will. This ends the\r      chapter on "savage beasts."--W.\r \rIf I should go about tomake any long discourse of venomous beasts or\rworms bred in England, Ishould attempt more than occasion itself\rwould readily offer, sithwe have very few worms, but no beasts at\rall, that are thought bytheir natural qualities to be either venomous\ror hurtful. First of all,therefore, we have the adder (in our old\rSaxon tongue called anatter), which some men do not rashly take to be\rthe viper. Certes, if itbe so, then is not the viper author of the\rdeath of her[3] parents,as some histories affirm, and thereto\rEncelius, a late writer,in his _De re Metallica_, lib. 3, cap. 38,\rwhere he maketh mention ofa she adder which he saw in Sala, whose\rwomb (as he saith) waseaten out after a like fashion, her young ones\rlying by her in thesunshine, as if they had been earthworms.\rNevertheless, as he nameththem _viperas_, so he calleth the male\r_echis_. and the female_echidna_, concluding in the end that _echis_\ris the same serpent whichhis countrymen to this day call _ein atter_,\ras I have also notedbefore out of a Saxon dictionary. Ouradders lie in winter under stones, as\rAristotle also saith ofthe viper (lib. 8, cap. 15), and in holes of\rthe earth, rotten stubs oftrees, and amongst the dead leaves; but in\rthe heat of the summerthey come abroad, and lie either round in heaps\ror at length upon somehillock, or elsewhere in the grass. The cut or girt\rwaisted (for so I Englishthe word _insecta_) are the hornets, wasps,\rbees, and such like,whereof we have great store, and of which an\ropinion is conceived thatthe first do breed of the corruption of dead\rhorses, the second ofpears and apples corrupted, and the last of kine\rand oxen: which may betrue, especially the first and latter in some\rparts of the beast, andnot their whole substances, as also in the\rsecond, sith we have neverwasps but when our fruit beginneth to wax\rripe. Indeed Virgil andothers speak of a generation of bees by\rkilling or smothering abruised bullock or calf and laying his bowels\ror his flesh wrapped up inhis hide in a close house for a certain\rseason; but how true itis, hitherto I have not tried. Yet sure I am\rof this, that no oneliving creature corrupteth without the production\rof another, as we may seeby ourselves, whose flesh doth alter into\rlice, and also in sheepfor excessive numbers of flesh flies, if they\rbe suffered to lieunburied or uneaten by the dogs and swine, who\roften and happily presentsuch needless generations.\r \rAs concerning bees, Ithink it good to remember that, whereas some\rancient writers affirm itto be a commodity wanting in our island, it\ris now found to be nothingso. In old times peradventure we had none\rindeed; but in my daysthere is such plenty of them in manner\reverywhere that in someuplandish towns there are one hundred or two\rhundred hives of them,although the said hives are not so huge as\rthose of the east country,but far less, and not able to contain above\rone bushel of corn or fivepecks at the most. Pliny (a man that of set\rpurpose delighteth towrite of wonders), speaking of honey, noteth\rthat in the north regionsthe hives in his time were of such quantity\rthat some one combcontained eight foot in length, and yet (as it\rshould seem) he speakethnot of the greatest. For in Podolia, which is\rnow subject to the King ofPoland, their hives are so great, and combs\rso abundant, that hugeboars, overturning and falling into them, are\rdrowned in the honeybefore they can recover and find the means to\rcome out.\r \rOur honey also is takenand reputed to be the best, because it is\rharder, better wrought,and cleanlier vesselled up, than that which\rcometh from beyond thesea, where they stamp and strain their combs,\rbees, and young blowingsaltogether into the stuff, as I have been\rinformed. In use also ofmedicine our physicians and apothecaries\reschew the foreign,especially that of Spain and Pontus, by reason of\ra venomous qualitynaturally planted in the same, as some write, and\rchoose the home-made: notonly by reason of our soil (which hath no\rless plenty of wild thymegrowing therein than in Sicilia and about\rAthens, and maketh thebest stuff) as also for that it breedeth (being\rgotten in harvest time)less choler, and which is oftentimes (as I\rhave seen by experience)so white as sugar, and corned as if it were\rsalt. Our hives are madecommonly of rye straw and wattled about with\rbramble quarters; but somemake the same of wicker, and cast them over\rwith clay. We cherish nonein trees, but set our hives somewhere on\rthe warmest side of thehouse, providing that they may stand dry and\rwithout danger both of themouse and the moth. This furthermore is to\rbe noted, that whereas invessels of oil that which is nearest the top\ris counted the finest andof wine that in the middest, so of honey the\rbest which is heaviest andmoistest is always next the bottom, and\revermore casteth anddriveth his dregs upward toward the very top,\rcontrary to the nature ofother liquid substances, whose grounds and\rleeze do generally settledownwards. And thus much as by the way of\rour bees and Englishhoney.\r \rAs for the whole-bodied,as the _cantharides_, and such venomous\rcreatures of the samekind, to be abundantly found in other countries,\rwe hear not of them: yethave we beetles, horseflies, turdbugs or dors\r(called in Latin_scarabei_), the locust or the grasshopper (which to\rme do seem to be onething, as I will anon declare), and such like,\rwhereof let other intreatthat make an exercise in catching of flies,\rbut a far greater sport inoffering them to spiders, as did Domitian\rsometime, and anotherprince yet living who delighted so much to see\rthe jolly combats betwixta stout fly and an old spider that divers\rmen have had great rewardsgiven them for their painful provision of\rflies made only for thispurpose. Some parasites also, in the time of\rthe aforesaid emperor(when they were disposed to laugh at his folly,\rand yet would seem inappearance to gratify his fantastical head with\rsome shew of dutifuldemeanour), could devise to set their lord on\rwork by letting a fleshfly privily into his chamber, which he\rforthwith would eagerlyhave hunted (all other business set apart) and\rnever ceased till he hadcaught her into his fingers, wherewith arose\rthe proverb, "_Nemusca quidem_" uttered first by Vibius Priscus, who\rbeing asked whetheranybody was with Domitian, answered "_Ne musca\rquidem_" whereby henoted his folly. There are some cockscombs here\rand there in England,learning it abroad as men transregionate, which\rmake account also of thispastime, as of a notable matter, telling\rwhat a sight is seenbetween them, if either of them be lusty and\rcourageous in his kind.One also hath made a book of the spider and\rthe fly, wherein hedealeth so profoundly, and beyond all measure of\rskill that neither hehimself that made it nor any one that readeth it\rcan reach unto the meaningthereof. But if those jolly fellows,\rinstead of the straw thatthey must thrust into the fly\'s tail (a\rgreat injury no doubt tosuch a noble champion), would bestow the cost\rto set a fool\'s cap upontheir own heads, then might they with more\rsecurity and lessreprehension behold these notable battles.\r \rNow, as concerning thelocust, I am led by divers of my country, who\r(as they say) were eitherin Germany, Italy, or Pannonia, 1542, when\rthose nations were greatlyannoyed with that kind of fly, and affirm\rvery constantly that theysaw none other creature than the grasshopper\rduring the time of thatannoyance, which was said to come to them from\rthe Meotides. In most ofour translations also of the Bible the word\r_locusta_ is Englished agrasshopper, and thereunto (Leviticus xi.) it\ris reputed among the cleanfood, otherwise John the Baptist would\rnever have lived with themin the wilderness. In Barbary, Numidia, and\rsundry other places ofAfrica, as they have been,[6] so are they eaten\rto this day powdered inbarrels, and therefore the people of those\rparts are called_Acedophagi_: nevertheless they shorten the life of\rthe eaters, by theproduction at the last of an irksome and filthy\rdisease. In India they arethree foot long, in Ethiopia much shorter,\rbut in England seldomabove an inch. As for the cricket, called in\rLatin _cicada_, he hathsome likelihood, but not very great, with the\rgrasshopper, and thereforehe is not to be brought in as an umpire in\rthis case. Finally,Matthiolus and so many as describe the locust do\rset down none other formthan that of our grasshopper, which maketh me\rso much the more to restupon my former imagination, which is that the\rlocust and the grasshopperare one.\r \r      [6] See Diodorus Siculus.--H.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER XV\r \rOF OUR ENGLISH DOGS ANDTHEIR QUALITIES\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapter13; 1587, Book III., Chapter 7.]\r \r \rThere is no country thatmay (as I take it) compare with ours in\rnumber, excellency, anddiversity of dogs.\r \rThe first sort thereforehe divideth either into such as rouse the\rbeast, and continue thechase, or springeth the bird, and bewrayeth\rher flight by pursuit. Andas these are commonly called spaniels, so\rthe other are namedhounds, whereof he maketh eight sorts, of which\rthe foremost excelleth inperfect smelling, the second in quick\respying, the third inswiftness and quickness, the fourth in smelling\rand nimbleness, etc., andthe last in subtlety and deceitfulness.\rThese (saith Strabo) aremost apt for game, and called Sagaces by a\rgeneral name, not onlybecause of their skill in hunting, but also for\rthat they know their ownand the names of their fellows most exactly.\rFor if the hunter see anyone to follow skilfully, and with likelihood\rof good success, hebiddeth the rest to hark and follow such a dog,\rand they eftsoones obey sosoon as they hear his name. The first kind\rof these are often calledharriers, whose game is the fox, the hare,\rthe wolf (if we had any),hart, buck, badger, otter, polecat,\rlopstart, weasel, conie,etc.: the second height a terrier and it\rhunteth the badger andgrey only: the third a bloodhound, whose office\ris to follow the fierce,and now and then to pursue a thief or beast\rby his dry foot: thefourth height a gazehound, who hunteth by the\reye: the fifth agreyhound, cherished for his strength and swiftness\rand stature, commended byBratius in his _De Venatione_, and not\runremembered by HerculesStroza in a like treatise, and above all\rother those of Britain,where he saith: "Magna spectandi mole\rBritanni;" also byNemesianus, libro Cynegeticón, where he saith:\r"Divisa Britanniamittit Veloces nostrique orbis venatibus aptos," of\rwhich sort also some besmooth, of sundry colours, and some\rshake-haired: the sixth aliemer, that excelleth in smelling and\rswift-running: the seventha tumbler: and the eighth a thief whose\roffices (I mean of thelatter two) incline only to deceit, wherein\rthey are oft so skilfulthat few men would think so mischievous a wit\rto remain in such sillycreatures. Having made this enumeration of\rdogs which are apt for thechase and hunting, he cometh next to such\ras serve the falcons intheir time, whereof he maketh also two sorts.\rOne that findeth his gameon the land, another that putteth up such\rfowl as keepeth in thewater: and of these this is commonly most usual\rfor the net or train, theother for the hawk, as he doth shew at\rlarge. Of the first hesaith that they have no peculiar names assigned\rto them severally, buteach of them is called after the bird which by\rnatural appointment he isalloted to hunt or serve, for which\rconsideration some benamed dogs for the pheasant, some for the\rfalcon, and some for the partridge.Howbeit the common name for all is\rspaniel (saith he), andthereupon alluded as if these kinds of dogs\rhad been brought hitherout of Spain. In like sort we have of water\rspaniels in their kind.The third sort of dogs of the gentle kind is\rthe spaniel gentle, orcomforter, or (as the common term is) the\rfistinghound, and thoseare called Melitei, of the Island Malta, from\rwhence they were broughthither. These are little and pretty, proper\rand fine, and sought outfar and near to falsify the nice delicacy of\rdainty dames, and wantonwomen\'s wills, instruments of folly to play\rand dally withal, intrifling away the treasure of time, to withdraw\rtheir minds from morecommendable exercises, and to content their\rcorrupt concupiscenceswith vain disport--a silly poor shift to shun\rtheir irksome idleness.The Sybaritical puppies the smaller they be\r(and thereto if they havea hole in the fore parts of their heads) the\rbetter they are accepted,the more pleasure also they provoke, as meet\rplayfellows for mincingmistresses to bear in their bosoms, to keep\rcompany withal in theirchambers, to succour with sleep in bed, and\rnourish with meat atboard, to lie in their laps, and lick their lips\ras they lie (like youngDianas) in their waggons and coaches. And good\rreason it should be so,for coarseness with fineness hath no\rfellowship, but featnesswith neatness hath neighbourhood enough. That\rplausible proverbtherefore versified sometime upon a tyrant--namely,\rthat he loved his sowbetter than his son--may well be applied to some\rof this kind of people,who delight more in their dogs, that are\rdeprived of allpossibility of reason, than they do in children that\rare capable of wisdom andjudgment. Yea, they oft feed them of the\rbest where the poor man\'s childat their doors can hardly come by the\rworst. But the formerabuse peradventure reigneth where there hath\rbeen long want of issue,else where barrenness is the best blossom of\rbeauty: or, finally, wherepoor men\'s children for want of their own\rissue are not ready to behad. It is thought of some that it is very\rwholesome for a weakstomach to bear such a dog in the bosom, as it is\rfor him that hath thepalsy to feel the daily smell and savour of a\rfox. But how truly this isaffirmed let the learned judge: only it\rshall suffice for DoctorCaius to have said thus much of spaniels and\rdogs of the gentle kind.\r \rDogs of the homely kindare either shepherd\'s curs or mastiffs. The\rfirst are so common thatit needeth me not to speak of them. Their use\ralso is so well known inkeeping the herd together (either when they\rgrass or go before theshepherd) that it should be but in vain to\rspend any time about them.Wherefore I will leave this cur unto his\rown kind, and go in handwith the mastiff, tie dog, or band dog, so\rcalled because many ofthem are tied up in chains and strong bonds in\rthe daytime, for doinghurt abroad, which is a huge dog, stubborn,\rugly, eager, burthenous ofbody (and therefore of but little\rswiftness), terrible andfearful to behold, and oftentimes more fierce\rand fell than anyArchadian or Corsican cur. Our Englishmen, to the\rextent that these dogs maybe more cruel and fierce, assist nature\rwith some art, use, andcustom. For although this kind of dog be\rcapable of courage,violent, valiant, stout, and bold: yet will they\rincrease these theirstomachs by teaching them to bait the bear, the\rbull, the lion, and othersuch like cruel and bloody beasts (either\rbrought over or kept up athome for the same purpose), without any\rcollar to defend theirthroats, and oftentimes there too they train\rthem up in fighting andwrestling with a man (having for the safeguard\rof his life either apikestaff, club, sword, privy coat), whereby they\rbecome the more fierce andcruel unto strangers. The Caspians make so\rmuch account sometimes ofsuch great dogs that every able man would\rnourish sundry of them inhis house of set purpose, to the end they\rshould devour theircarcases after their deaths thinking the dog\'s\rbellies to be the mosthonourable sepulchres. The common people also\rfollowed the same rate,and therefore there were tie dogs kept up by\rpublic ordinance, todevour them after their deaths: by means whereof\rthese beasts became themore eager, and with great difficulty after a\rwhile restrained fromfalling upon the living. But whither am I\rdigressed? In returningtherefore to our own, I say that of mastiffs,\rsome bark only with fierceand open mouth but will not bite; but the\rcruelest do either notbark at all or bite before they bark, and\rtherefore are more to befeared than any of the other. They take also\rtheir name of the word"mase" and "thief" (or "master-thief" if you\rwill), because they oftenstound and put such persons to their shifts\rin towns and villages, andare the principal causes of their\rapprehension and taking.The force which is in them surmounteth all\rbelief, and the fast holdwhich they take with their teeth exceedeth\rall credit: for three ofthem against a bear, four against a lion, are\rsufficient to try mastrieswith them. King Henry the Seventh, as the\rreport goeth, commandedall such curs to be hanged, because they durst\rpresume to fight againstthe lion, who is their king and sovereign.\rThe like he did with anexcellent falcon, as some say, because he\rfeared not hand-to-handmatch with an eagle, willing his falconers in\rhis own presence to pluckoff his head after he was taken down, saying\rthat it was not meet forany subject to offer such wrong unto his lord\rand superior, wherein hehad a further meaning. But if King Henry the\rSeventh had lived in ourtime what would he have done to our English\rmastiff, which alone andwithout any help at all pulled down first a\rhuge bear, then a pard,and last of all a lion, each after other\rbefore the French king inone day, when the Lord Buckhurst was\rambassador unto him, andwhereof if I should write the circumstances,\rthat is, how he took hisadvantage being let loose unto them, and\rfinally drave them intosuch exceeding fear, that they were all glad\rto run away when he wastaken from them, I should take much pains, and\ryet reap but small credit:wherefore it shall suffice to have said\rthus much thereof. Some ofour mastiffs will rage only in the night,\rsome are to be tied upboth day and night. Such also as are suffered\rto go loose about thehouse and yard are so gentle in the daytime that\rchildren may ride on theirbacks and play with them at their\rpleasures. Divers of themlikewise are of such jealousy over their\rmaster and whosoever ofhis household, that if a stranger do embrace\ror touch any of them, theywill fall fiercely upon them, unto their\rextreme mischief if theirfury be not prevented. Such a one was the\rdog of Nichomedes, kingsometime of Bithynia, who seeing Consigne the\rqueen to embrace and kissher husband as they walked together in a\rgarden, did tear her allto pieces, maugre his resistance and the\rpresent aid of such asattended on them. Some of them moreover will\rsuffer a stranger to comein and walk about the house or yard where he\rlisteth, without givingover to follow him: but if he put forth his\rhand to touch anything,then will they fly upon them and kill them if\rthey may. I had one myselfonce, which would not suffer any man to\rbring in his weaponfurther than my gate: neither those that were of\rmy house to be touched inhis presence. Or if I had beaten any of my\rchildren, he would gentlyhave essayed to catch the rod in his teeth\rand take it out of my handor else pluck down their clothes to save\rthem from the stripes:which in my opinion is not unworthy to be\rnoted.\r \rThe last sort of dogsconsisteth of the currish kind meet for many\rtoys, of which the whappetor prick-eared cur is one. Some men call\rthem warners, because theyare good for nothing else but to bark and\rgive warning when anybodydoth stir or lie in wait about the house in\rthe night season. Certesit is impossible to describe these curs in\rany order, because theyhave no one kind proper unto themselves, but\rare a confused companymixed of all the rest. The second sort of them\rare called turnspits,whose office is not unknown to any. And as these\rare only reserved for thispurpose, so in many places our mastiffs\r(beside the use whichtinkers have of them in carrying their heavy\rbudgets) are made to drawwater in great wheels out of deep wells,\rgoing much like unto thosewhich are framed for our turnspits, as is\rto be seen at Roiston,where this feat is often practised. Besides\rthese also we have sholtsor curs daily brought out of Ireland, and\rmade much of among us,because of their sauciness and quarrelling.\rMoreover they bite verysore, and love candles exceedingly, as do the\rmen and women of theircountry; but I may say no more of them, because\rthey are not bred with us.Yet this will I make report of by the way,\rfor pastime\'s sake, thatwhen a great man of those parts came of late\rinto one of our shipswhich went thither for fish, to see the form and\rfashion of the same, hiswife apparelled in fine sables, abiding on\rthe deck whilst herhusband was under the hatches with the mariners,\respied a pound or two ofcandles hanging on the mast, and being loath\rto stand there idle alone,she fell to and eat them up every one,\rsupposing herself to havebeen at a jolly banquet, and shewing very\rpleasant gesture when herhusband came up again unto her.\r \rThe last kind of toyishcurs are named dancers, and those being of a\rmongrel sort also, aretaught and exercised to dance in measure at the\rmusical sound of aninstrument, as at the just stroke of a drum, sweet\raccent of the citharne,and pleasant harmony of the harp, shewing many\rtricks by the gesture oftheir bodies: as to stand bolt upright, to\rlie flat on the ground, toturn round as a ring holding their tails in\rtheir teeth, to saw andbeg for meat, to take a man\'s cap from his\rhead, and sundry suchproperties, which they learn of their idle\rroguish masters, whoseinstruments they are to gather gain, as old\rapes clothed in motley andcoloured short-waisted jackets are for the\rlike vagabonds, who seekno better living than that which they may get\rby fond pastime andidleness. I might here intreat of other dogs, as\rof those which are bredbetween a bitch and a wolf, also between a\rbitch and a fox, or a bearand a mastiff. But as we utterly want the\rfirst sort, except they bebrought unto us: so it happeneth sometimes\rthat the other two areengendered and seen at home amongst us. But all\rthe rest heretoforeremembered in this chapter there is none more ugly\rand odious in sight, crueland fierce in deed, nor untractable in\rhand, than that which isbegotten between the bear and the bandog. For\rwhatsoever he catchethhold of he taketh it so fast that a man may\rsooner tear and rend hisbody in sunder than get open his mouth to\rseparate his chaps. Certeshe regardeth neither wolf, bear, nor lion,\rand therefore may well becompared with those two dogs which were sent\rto Alexander out of India(and procreated as it is thought between a\rmastiff and a male tiger,as be those also of Hircania), or to them\rthat are bred in Archadia,where copulation is oft seen between lions\rand bitches, as the lionis in France (as I said) between she wolves\rand dogs, whereof let thissuffice, sith the further tractation of\rthem doth not concern mypurpose, more than the confutation of\rCardan\'s talk, _De subt._,lib. 10, who saith that after many\rgenerations dogs do becomewolves, and contrariwise, which if it were\rtrue, then could notEngland be without many wolves: but nature hath\rset a difference betweenthem, not only in outward form, but also\rinward disposition oftheir bones, whereof it is impossible that his\rassertion can be sound.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER XVI\r \rOF THE NAVY OF ENGLAND\r \r[1577, Book II., Chapter13; 1587, Book II., Chapter 17.]\r \r \rThere is nothing that hathbrought me into more admiration of the\rpower and force ofantiquity than their diligence and care had of\rtheir navies: wherein,whether I consider their speedy building, or\rgreat number of shipswhich some one kingdom or region possessed at\rone instant, it giveth mestill occasion either to suspect the\rhistory, or to think thatin our times we come very far behind\rthem.[1]...\r \r      [1] Here follows an account of Roman andCarthaginian galleys\r      which "did not only match, but farexceed" in capacity our ships\r      and galleys of 1587.--W.\r \rI must needs confesstherefore that the ancient vessels far exceeded\rours for capacity,nevertheless if you regard the form, and the\rassurance from peril ofthe sea, and therewithal the strength and\rnimbleness of such as aremade in our time, you shall easily find that\rours are of more valuethan theirs: for as the greatest vessel is not\ralways the fastest, sothat of most huge capacity is not always the\raptest to shift and brookthe seas: as might be seen by the _Great\rHenry_, the hugest vesselthat ever England framed in our times.\rNeither were the ships ofold like unto ours in mould and manner of\rbuilding above the water(for of low galleys in our seas we make small\raccount) nor so full ofease within, since time hath engendered more\rskill in the wrights, andbrought all things to more perfection than\rthey had in the beginning.And now to come unto our purpose at the\rfirst intended.\r \rThe navy of England may bedivided into three sorts, of which the one\rserveth for the wars, theother for burden, and the third for\rfishermen which get theirliving by fishing on the sea. How many of\rthe first order aremaintained within the realm it passeth my cunning\rto express; yet, since itmay be parted into the navy royal and common\rfleet, I think good tospeak of those that belong unto the prince, and\rso much the rather, forthat their number is certain and well known to\rvery many. Certainly thereis no prince in Europe that hath a more\rbeautiful or gallant sortof ships than the queen\'s majesty of England\rat this present, and thosegenerally are of such exceeding force that\rtwo of them, being wellappointed and furnished as they ought, will\rnot let to encounter withthree or four of those of other countries,\rand either bowge them orput them to flight, if they may not bring\rthem home.\r \rNeither are the moulds ofany foreign barks so conveniently made, to\rbrook so well one sea asanother lying upon the shore of any part of\rthe continent, as those ofEngland. And therefore the common report\rthat strangers make of ourships amongst themselves is daily confirmed\rto be true, which is, thatfor strength, assurance, nimbleness, and\rswiftness of sailing,there are no vessels in the world to be compared\rwith ours. And all theseare committed to the regiment and safe\rcustody of the admiral,who is so called (as some imagine) of the\rGreek word _almiros_, acaptain on the sea; for so saith Zonaras in\r_Basilio Macedone_ and_Basilio Porphyriogenito_, though others fetch\rit from _ad mare_, theLatin words, another sort from _Amyras_, the\rSaracen magistrate, orfrom some French derivation: but these things\rare not for this place,and therefore I pass them over. The queen\'s\rhighness hath at thispresent (which is the four-and-twentieth of her\rreign) already made andfurnished, to the number of four or\rfive-and-twenty greatships, which lie for the most part in Gillingham\rRoad, beside threegalleys, of whose particular names and furniture\r(so far forth as I cancome by them) it shall not be amiss to make\rreport at this time.\r \r_The names of so manyships belonging to her majesty as I could come\rby at this present_.\r \rThe Bonadventure.      White Bear.\rElizabeth Jonas.[2]    Philip and Mary.\rTriumph.               Aid.\rBull.                  Handmaid.\rTiger.[3]              Dreadnought.\rAntelope.              Swallow.\rHope.                  Genet.\rLion.                  Bark of Bullen.\rVictory.               Achates.\rMary Rose.             Falcon.\rForesight.             George.\rSwiftsure.             Revenge.\r \r      [2] A name devised by her grace inremembrance of her own\r      deliverance from the fury of her enemies,from which in one\r      respect she was no less miraculouslypreserved than was the\r      prophet Jonas from the belly of thewhale.--H.\r \r      [3] So called of her exceeding nimblenessin sailing and\r      swiftness of course.--H.\r \rIt is said that as kingsand princes have in the young days of the\rworld, and long since,framed themselves to erect every year a city in\rsome one place or other oftheir kingdom (and no small wonder that\rSardanapalus should beginand finish two, to wit, Anchialus and\rTarsus, in one day), soher grace doth yearly build one ship or other\rto the better defence ofher frontiers from the enemy. But, as of this\rreport I have no assuredcertainty, so it shall suffice to have said\rso much of these things;yet this I think worthy further to be added,\rthat if they should all bedriven to service at one instance (which\rGod forbid) she shouldhave a power by sea of about nine or ten\rthousand men, which were anotable company, beside the supply of other\rvessels appertaining toher subjects to furnish up her voyage.\r \rBeside these, her gracehath other in hand also, of whom hereafter, as\rtheir turns do come about,I will not let to leave some further\rremembrance. She hathlikewise three notable galleys: the Speedwell,\rthe Try Right, and theBlack Galley, with the sight whereof, and the\rrest of the navy royal, itis incredible to say how greatly her grace\ris delighted: and notwithout great cause (I say) since by their means\rher coasts are kept inquiet, and sundry foreign enemies put back,\rwhich otherwise wouldinvade us. The number of those that serve for\rburden with the other,whereof I have made mention already and whose\ruse is daily seen, asoccasion serveth in time of the wars, is to me\rutterly unknown.
