Of these also there are some\rof the queen\'s majesty\'ssubjects that have two or three; some, four\ror six; and (as I heard oflate) one man, whose name I suppress for\rmodesty\'s sake, hath beenknown not long since to have had sixteen or\rseventeen, and employedthem wholly to the wafting in and out of our\rmerchants, whereby he hathreaped no small commodity and gain. I might\rtake occasion to tell ofthe notable and difficult voyages made into\rstrange countries byEnglishmen, and of their daily success there; but\ras these things arenothing incident to my purpose, so I surcease to\rspeak of them. Only thiswill I add, to the end all men shall\runderstand somewhat of thegreat masses of treasure daily employed\rupon our navy, how thereare few of those ships, of the first and\rsecond sort, that, beingapparelled and made ready to sail, are not\rworth one thousand pounds,or three thousand ducats at the least, if\rthey should presently besold. What shall we think then of the\rgreater, but especially ofthe navy royal, of which some one vessel is\rworth two of the other, asthe shipwrights have often told me? It is\rpossible that somecovetous person, hearing this report, will either\rnot credit it at all, orsuppose money so employed to be nothing\rprofitable to the queen\'scoffers: as a good husband said once when he\rheard there should be aprovision made for armour, wishing the queen\'s\rmoney to be rather laidout to some speedier return of gain unto her\rgrace, "because therealm (saith he) is in case good enough," and so\rperadventure he thought.But if, as by store of armour for the defence\rof the country, he had likewiseunderstanded that the good keeping of\rthe sea is the safeguardof our land, he would have altered his\rcensure, and soon givenover his judgment. For in times past, when our\rnation made small accountof navigation, how soon did the Romans, then\rthe Saxons, and last ofall the Danes, invade this island? whose\rcruelty in the endenforced our countrymen, as it were even against\rtheir wills, to providefor ships from other places, and build at home\rof their own whereby theirenemies were oftentimes distressed. But\rmost of all were theNormans therein to be commended. For, in a short\rprocess of time after theconquest of this island, and good\rconsideration had for thewell-keeping of the same, they supposed\rnothing more commodiousfor the defence of the country than the\rmaintenance of a strongnavy, which they speedily provided,\rmaintained, and therebyreaped in the end their wished security,\rwherewith before theirtimes this island was never acquainted. Before\rthe coming of the Romans Ido not read that we had any ships at all,\rexcept a few made ofwicker and covered with buffalo hides, like unto\rwhich there are some to beseen at this present in Scotland (as I\rhear), although there be alittle (I wot not well what) difference\rbetween them. Of the samealso Solinus speaketh, so far as I remember:\rnevertheless it may begathered from his words how the upper parts of\rthem above the water onlywere framed of the said wickers, and that\rthe Britons did use tofast all the whiles they went to the sea in\rthem; but whether it weredone for policy or superstition, as yet I do\rnot read.\r \rIn the beginning of theSaxons\' regiment we had some ships also; but\ras their number and mouldwas little, and nothing to the purpose, so\rEgbert was the firstprince that ever thoroughly began to know this\rnecessity of a navy anduse the service thereof in the defence of his\rcountry. After him alsoother princes, as Alfred, Edgar, Ethelred,\retc., endeavoured more andmore to store themselves at the full with\rships of all quantities,but chiefly Edgar, for he provided a navy of\r1600 _aliàs_ 3600 sail,which he divided into four parts, and sent\rthem to abide upon foursundry coasts of the land, to keep the same\rfrom pirates. Next untohim (and worthy to be remembered) is Ethelred,\rwho made a law that everyman that hold 310 hidelands should find a\rship furnished to servehim in the wars. Howbeit, as I said before,\rwhen all their navy was atthe greatest, it was not comparable for\rforce and sure building tothat which afterward the Normans provided,\rneither that of theNormans anything like to the same that is to be\rseen now in these ourdays. For the journeys also of our ships, you\rshall understand that awell-builded vessel will run or sail commonly\rthree hundred leagues ornine hundred miles in a week, or peradventure\rsome will go 2200 leaguesin six weeks and a half. And surely, if\rtheir lading be readyagainst they come thither, there be of them that\rwill be here, at the WestIndies, and home again in twelve or thirteen\rweeks from Colchester,although the said Indies be eight hundred\rleagues from the cape orpoint of Cornwall, as I have been informed.\rThis also I understand byreport of some travellers, that, if any of\rour vessels happen to makea voyage to Hispaniola or New Spain (called\rin time past Quinquegiaand Haiti), which lieth between the north\rtropic and the Equator,after they have once touched at the Canaries\r(which are eight days\'sailing or two hundred and fifty leagues from\rSt. Lucas de Barameda, inSpain) they will be there in thirty or forty\rdays, and home again inCornwall in other eight weeks, which is a\rgoodly matter, beside thesafety and quietness in the passage, but\rmore of this elsewhere.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER XVII\r \rOF SUNDRY KINDS OFPUNISHMENT APPOINTED FOR OFFENDERS\r \r[1577, Book III., Chapter6; 1587, Book II., Chapter 11.]\r \r \rIn cases of felony,manslaughter, robbery, murder, rape, piracy, and\rsuch capital crimes as arenot reputed for treason or hurt of the\restate, our sentencepronounced upon the offender is, to hang till he\rbe dead. For of otherpunishments used in other countries we have no\rknowledge or use; and yetso few grievous crimes committed with us as\relsewhere in the world. Touse torment also or question by pain and\rtorture in these common caseswith us is greatly abhorred, since we\rare found always to besuch as despise death, and yet abhor to be\rtormented, choosing ratherfrankly to open our minds than to yield our\rbodies unto such servilehaulings and tearings as are used in other\rcountries. And this is onecause wherefore our condemned persons do go\rso cheerfully to theirdeaths; for our nation is free, stout, haughty,\rprodigal of life andblood, as Sir Thomas Smith saith, lib. 2, cap.\r25, _De Republica_, andtherefore cannot in any wise digest to be used\ras villains and slaves, insuffering continually beating, servitude,\rand servile torments. No,our gaolers are guilty of felony, by an old\rlaw of the land, if theytorment any prisoner committed to their\rcustody for the revealingof his accomplices.\r \rThe greatest and mostgrievous punishment used in England for such as\roffend against the Stateis drawing from the prison to the place of\rexecution upon an hurdleor sled, where they are hanged till they be\rhalf dead, and then takendown, and quartered alive; after that, their\rmembers and bowels are cutfrom their bodies, and thrown into a fire,\rprovided near hand andwithin their own sight, even for the same\rpurpose.\r \rSometimes, if the trespassbe not the more heinous, they are suffered\rto hang till they be quitedead. And whensoever any of the nobility\rare convicted of hightreason by their peers, that is to say, equals\r(for an inquest of yeomenpasseth not upon them, but only of the lords\rof parliament), thismanner of their death is converted into the loss\rof their heads only,notwithstanding that the sentence do run after\rthe former order. In trialof cases concerning treason, felony, or any\rother grievous crime notconfessed, the party accused doth yield, if\rhe be a noble man, to betried by an inquest (as I have said) and his\rpeers; if a gentleman, bygentlemen; and an inferior, by God and by\rthe country, to wit, theyeomanry (for combat or battle is not greatly\rin use), and, beingcondemned of felony, manslaughter, etc., he is\reftsoons hanged by theneck till he be dead, and then cut down and\rburied. But if he beconvicted of wilful murder, done either upon\rpretended malice or in anynotable robbery, he is either hanged alive\rin chains near the placewhere the fact was committed (or else upon\rcompassion taken, firststrangled with a rope), and so continueth till\rhis bones consume tonothing. We have use neither of the wheel nor of\rthe bar, as in othercountries; but, when wilful manslaughter is\rperpetrated, besidehanging, the offender hath his right hand commonly\rstricken off before ornear unto the place where the act was done,\rafter which he is ledforth to the place of execution, and there put\rto death according to thelaw.\r \rThe word felon is derivedof the Saxon words _fell_ and _one_, that is\rto say, an evil and wickedone, a one of untameable nature and\rlewdness not to besuffered for fear of evil example and the\rcorruption of others. Inlike sort in the word _felony_ are many\rgrievous crimes contained,as breach of prison (Ann. I of Edward the\rSecond), disfigurers ofthe prince\'s liege people (Ann. 5 of Henry the\rFourth), hunting by nightwith painted faces and visors (Ann. I of\rHenry the Seventh), rape,or stealing of women and maidens (Ann. 3 of\rHenry Eight), conspiraciesagainst the person of the prince (Ann. 3 of\rHenry the Seventh),embezzling of goods committed by the master to the\rservant above the value offorty shillings (Ann. 17 of Henry the\rEighth), carrying ofhorses or mares into Scotland (Ann. 23 of Henry\rEight), sodomy and buggery(Ann. 25 of Henry the Eighth), conjuring,\rforgery, witchcraft, anddigging up of crosses (Ann. 33 of Henry\rEight), prophesying uponarms, cognisances, names, and badges (Ann. 33\rof Henry Eight), castingof slanderous bills (Ann. 37, Henry Eight),\rwilful killing by poison(Ann. 1 of Edward the Sixth), departure of a\rsoldier from the field(Ann. 2 of Edward the Sixth), diminution of\rcoin, all offences withincase of premunire, embezzling of records,\rgoods taken from dead menby their servants, stealing of whatsoever\rcattle, robbing by thehigh way, upon the sea, or of dwelling houses,\rletting out of ponds,cutting of purses, stealing of deer by night,\rcounterfeits of coin,evidences charters, and writings, and divers\rother needless to beremembered. If a woman poison her husband, she is\rburned alive; if theservant kill his master, he is to be executed for\rpetty treason; he thatpoisoneth a man is to be boiled to death in\rwater or lead, althoughthe party die not of the practice; in cases of\rmurder, all theaccessories are to suffer pains of death accordingly.\rPerjury is punished by thepillory, burning in the forehead with the\rletter P, the rewalting ofthe trees growing upon the grounds of the\roffenders, and loss of allhis movables. Many trespasses also are\rpunished by the cuttingoff of one or both ears from the head of the\roffender, as the utteranceof seditious words against the magistrates,\rfraymakers, petty robbers,etc. Rogues are burned through the ears;\rcarriers of sheep out ofthe land, by the loss of their hands; such as\rkill by poison are eitherboiled or scalded to death in lead or\rseething water. Hereticsare burned quick; harlots and their mates, by\rcarting, ducking, anddoing of open penance in sheets in churches and\rmarket steeds, are oftenput to rebuke. Howbeit, as this is counted\rwith some either as nopunishment at all to speak of, or but little\rregarded of the offenders,so I would with adultery and fornication to\rhave some sharper law. Forwhat great smart is it to be turned out of\rhot sheet into a cold, orafter a little washing in the water to be\rlet loose again unto theirformer trades? Howbeit the dragging of some\rof them over the Thamesbetween Lambeth and Westminster at the tail of\ra boat is a punishmentthat most terrifieth them which are condemned\rthereto; but this isinflicted upon them by none other than the knight\rmarshall, and that withinthe compass of his jurisdiction and limits\ronly. Canutus was thefirst that gave authority to the clergy to\rpunish whoredom, who atthat time found fault with the former laws as\rbeing too severe in thisbehalf. For, before the time of the said\rCanutus, the adultererforfeited all his goods to the king and his\rbody to be at hispleasure; and the adulteress was to lose her eyes or\rnose, or both if the casewere more than common: whereby it appears of\rwhat estimation marriagewas amongst them, since the breakers of that\rholy estate were sogrievously rewarded. But afterward the clergy\rdealt more favourably withthem, shooting rather at the punishments of\rsuch priests and clerks aswere married than the reformation of\radultery and fornication,wherein you shall find no example that any\rseverity was shewed exceptupon such lay men as had defiled their\rnuns. As in thefttherefore, so in adultery and whoredom, I would wish\rthe parties trespassing tobe made bond or slaves unto those that\rreceived the injury, tosell and give where they listed, or to be\rcondemned to the galleys:for that punishment would prove more bitter\rto them thanhalf-an-hour\'s hanging, or than standing in a sheet,\rthough the weather benever so cold.\r \rManslaughter in time pastwas punished by the purse, wherein the\rquantity or quality of thepunishment was rated after the state and\rcalling of the partykilled: so that one was valued sometime at 1200,\ranother at 600, or 200shillings. And by a statute made under Henry\rthe First, a citizen ofLondon at 100, whereof elsewhere I have spoken\rmore at large. Such askill themselves are buried in the field with a\rstake driven through theirbodies.\r \rWitches are hanged, orsometimes burned; but thieves are hanged (as I\rsaid before) generally onthe gibbet or gallows, saving in Halifax,\rwhere they are beheadedafter a strange manner, and whereof I find\rthis report. There is andhas been of ancient time a law, or rather a\rcustom, at Halifax, thatwhosoever does commit any felony, and is taken\rwith the same, orconfesses the fact upon examination, if it be valued\rby four constables toamount to the sum of thirteenpence-halfpenny, he\ris forthwith beheaded uponone of the next market days (which fall\rusually upon the Tuesdays,Thursdays, and Saturdays), or else upon the\rsame day that he is soconvicted, if market be then holden. The engine\rwherewith the execution isdone is a square block of wood of the\rlength of four feet and ahalf, which does ride up and down in a slot,\rrabbet, or regall, betweentwo pieces of timber, that are framed and\rset upright, of five yardsin height. In the nether end of the sliding\rblock is an axe, keyed orfastened with an iron into the wood, which\rbeing drawn up to the topof the frame is there fastened by a wooden\rpin (with a notch madeinto the same, after the manner of a Samson\'s\rpost), unto the midst ofwhich pin also there is a long rope fastened\rthat cometh down among thepeople, so that, when the offender hath\rmade his confession andhath laid his neck over the nethermost block,\revery man there presentdoth either take hold of the rope (or putteth\rforth his arm so near tothe same as he can get, in token that he is\rwilling to see truejustice executed), and, pulling out the pin in\rthis manner, thehead-block wherein the axe is fastened doth fall down\rwith such a violence that,if the neck of the transgressor were as big\ras that of a bull, itshould be cut in sunder at a stroke and roll\rfrom the body by a hugedistance. If it be so that the offender be\rapprehended for an ox,oxen, sheep, kine, horse, or any such cattle,\rthe self beast or other ofthe same kind shall have the end of the\rrope tied somewhere untothem, so that they, being driven, do draw out\rthe pin, whereby theoffender is executed. Thus much of Halifax law,\rwhich I set down only toshew the custom of that country in this\rbehalf.\r \rRogues and vagabonds areoften stocked and whipped; scolds are ducked\rupon cucking-stools in thewater. Such felons as stand mute, and speak\rnot at their arraignment,are pressed to death by huge weights laid\rupon a board, that liethover their breast, and a sharp stone under\rtheir backs; and thesecommonly held their peace, thereby to save\rtheir goods unto theirwives and children, which, if they were\rcondemned, should beconfiscated to the prince. Thieves that are saved\rby their books and clergy,for the first offence, if they have stolen\rnothing else but oxen,sheep, money, or such like, which be no open\rrobberies, as by thehighway side, or assailing of any man\'s house in\rthe night, without puttinghim in fear of his life, or breaking up his\rwalls or doors, are burnedin the left hand, upon the brawn of the\rthumb, with a hot iron, sothat, if they be apprehended again, that\rmark betrayeth them tohave been arraigned of felony before, whereby\rthey are sure at that timeto have no mercy. I do not read that this\rcustom of saving by thebook is used anywhere else than in England;\rneither do I find (aftermuch diligent enquiry) what Saxon prince\rordained that law. Howbeitthis I generally gather thereof, that it\rwas devised to train theinhabitants of this land to the love of\rlearning, which beforecontemned letters and all good knowledge, as\rmen only giving themselvesto husbandry and the wars: the like whereof\rI read to have beenamongst the Goths and Vandals, who for a time\rwould not suffer eventheir princes to be learned, for weakening of\rtheir courage, nor anylearned men to remain in the council house, but\rby open proclamation wouldcommand them to avoid whensoever anything\rtouching the state of theland was to be consulted upon. Pirates and\rrobbers by sea arecondemned in the Court of the Admiralty, and hanged\ron the shore at low-watermark, where they are left till three tides\rhave overwashed them.Finally, such as having walls and banks near\runto the sea, and dosuffer the same to decay (after convenient\radmonition), whereby thewater entereth and drowneth up the country,\rare by a certain ancientcustom apprehended, condemned, and staked in\rthe breach, where theyremain for ever as parcel of the foundation of\rthe new wall that is to bemade upon them, as I have heard reported.\r \rAnd thus much in part ofthe administration of justice used in our\rcountry, wherein,notwithstanding that we do not often hear of\rhorrible, merciless, andwilful murders (such I mean as are not seldom\rseen in the countries ofthe main), yet now and then some manslaughter\rand bloody robberies areperpetrated and committed, contrary to the\rlaws, which be severelypunished, and in such wise as I have before\rreported. Certes there isno greater mischief done in England than by\rrobberies, the first byyoung shifting gentlemen, which oftentimes do\rbear more port than theyare able to maintain. Secondly by\rserving-men, whose wagescannot suffice so much as to find them\rbreeches; wherefore theyare now and then constrained either to keep\rhighways, and break intothe wealthy men\'s houses with the first sort,\ror else to walk up anddown in gentlemen\'s and rich farmers\' pastures,\rthere to see and viewwhich horses feed best, whereby they many times\rget something, althoughwith hard adventure: it hath been known by\rtheir confession at thegallows that some one such chapman hath had\rforty, fifty, or sixtystolen horses at pasture here and there abroad\rin the country at a time,which they have sold at fairs and markets\rfar off, they themselvesin the mean season being taken about home for\rhonest yeomen, and verywealthy drovers, till their dealings have been\rbetrayed. It is not longsince one of this company was apprehended,\rwho was before timereputed for a very honest and wealthy townsman; he\ruttered also more horsesthan any of his trade, because he sold a\rreasonable pennyworth andwas a fairspoken man. It was his custom\rlikewise to say, if anyman hucked hard with him about the price of a\rgelding, "So God helpme, gentlemen (or sir), either he did cost me so\rmuch, or else, by Jesus, Istole him!" Which talk was plain enough;\rand yet such was hisestimation that each believed the first part of\rhis tale, and made noaccount of the latter, which was truer indeed.\r \rOur third annoyers of thecommonwealth are rogues, which do very great\rmischief in all placeswhere they become. For, whereas the rich only\rsuffer injury by the firsttwo, these spare neither rich nor poor;\rbut, whether it be greatgain or small, all is fish that cometh to net\rwith them. And yet, I say,both they and the rest are trussed up\rapace. For there is notone year commonly wherein three hundred or\rfour hundred of them arenot devoured and eaten up by the gallows in\rone place and other. Itappeareth by Cardan (who writeth it upon the\rreport of the bishop ofLexovia), in the geniture of King Edward the\rSixth, how Henry theEighth, executing his laws very severely against\rsuch idle persons, I meangreat thieves, petty thieves, and rogues,\rdid hang up threescore andtwelve thousand of them in his time. He\rseemed for a while greatlyto have terrified the rest; but since his\rdeath the number of themis so increased, yea, although we have had no\rwars, which are a greatoccasion of their breed (for it is the custom\rof the more idle sort,having once served, or but seen the other side\rof the sea under colour ofservice, to shake hand with labour for\rever, thinking it adisgrace for himself to return unto his former\rtrade), that, except somebetter order be taken, or the laws already\rmade be better executed,such as dwell in uplandish towns and little\rvillages shall live but insmall safety and rest. For the better\rapprehension also ofthieves and mankillers, there is an old law in\rEngland very well providedwhereby it is ordered that, if he that is\rrobbed (or any man)complain and give warning of slaughter or murder\rcommitted, the constableof the village whereunto he cometh and crieth\rfor succour is to raisethe parish about him, and to search woods,\rgroves, and all suspectedhouses and places, where the trespasser may\rbe, or is supposed tolurk; and not finding him there, he is to give\rwarning unto the nextconstable, and so one constable, after search\rmade, to advertise anotherfrom parish to parish, till they come to\rthe same where theoffender is harboured and found. It is also\rprovided that, if anyparish in this business do not her duty, but\rsuffereth the thief (forthe avoiding of trouble sake) in carrying him\rto the gaol, if he shouldbe apprehended, or other letting of their\rwork to escape, the sameparish is not only to make fine to the king,\rbut also the same, withthe whole hundred wherein it standeth, to\rrepay the party robbed hisdamages, and leave his estate harmless.\rCertainly this is a goodlaw; howbeit I have known by my own\rexperience felons beingtaken to have escaped out of the stocks, being\rrescued by other for wantof watch and guard, that thieves have been\rlet pass, because thecovetous and greedy parishioners would neither\rtake the pains nor be atthe charge, to carry them to prison, if it\rwere far off; that whenhue and cry have been made even to the faces\rof some constables, theyhave said: "God restore your loss! I have\rother business at thistime." And by such means the meaning of many a\rgood law is leftunexecuted, malefactors emboldened, and many a poor\rman turned out of thatwhich he hath sweat and taken great pains\rtoward the maintenance ofhimself and his poor children and family.\r \r \r \r \rCHAPTER XVIII\r \rOF UNIVERSITIES\r \r[1577, Book II., Chapter6; 1587, Book II., Chapter 3.]\r \r \rThere have beenheretofore, and at sundry times, divers famous\runiversities in thisisland, and those even in my days not altogether\rforgotten, as one atBangor, erected by Lucius, and afterward\rconverted into amonastery, not by Congellus (as some write), but by\rPelagius the monk. Thesecond at Caerleon-upon-Usk, near to the place\rwhere the river doth fallinto the Severn, founded by King Arthur. The\rthird at Thetford, whereinwere six hundred students, in the time of\rone Rond, sometime king ofthat region. The fourth at Stamford,\rsuppressed by Augustinethe monk. And likewise other in other places,\ras Salisbury, Eridon orCricklade, Lachlade, Reading, and Northampton;\ralbeit that the two lastrehearsed were not authorised, but only arose\rto that name by thedeparture of the students from Oxford in time of\rcivil dissension unto thesaid towns, where also they continued but\rfor a little season. Whenthat of Salisbury began I cannot tell; but\rthat it flourished mostunder Henry the Third and Edward the First I\rfind good testimony by thewriters, as also by the discord which fell,\r1278, between thechancellor for the scholars there on the one part\rand William the archdeaconon the other, whereof you shall see more in\rthe chronology herefollowing. In my time there are three noble\runiversities inEngland--to wit, one at Oxford, the second at\rCambridge, and the thirdin London; of which the first two are the\rmost famous, I meanCambridge and Oxford, for that in them the use of\rthe tongues, philosophy,and the liberal sciences, besides the\rprofound studies of thecivil law, physic, and theology, are daily\rtaught and had: whereas inthe latter the laws of the realm are only\rread and learned by suchas give their minds unto the knowledge of the\rsame. In the first thereare not only divers goodly houses builded\rfour square for the mostpart of hard freestone or brick, with great\rnumbers of lodgings andchambers in the same for students, after a\rsumptuous sort, throughthe exceeding liberality of kings, queens,\rbishops, noblemen andladies of the land; but also large livings and\rgreat revenues bestowedupon them (the like whereof is not to be seen\rin any other region, asPeter Martyr did oft affirm) to the\rmaintenance only of suchconvenient numbers of poor men\'s sons as the\rseveral stipends bestowedupon the said houses are able to\rsupport.[1]...\r \r      [1] Here follows a paragraph about thelegendary foundation\r      of the universities.--W.\r \rOf these two, that ofOxford (which lieth west and by north from\rLondon) standeth mostpleasantly, being environed in manner round\rabout with woods on thehills aloft, and goodly rivers in the bottoms\rand valleys beneath, whosecourses would breed no small commodity to\rthat city and countryabout if such impediments were removed as\rgreatly annoy the same andhinder the carriage which might be made\rthither also from London.That of Cambridge is distant from London\rabout forty and six milesnorth and by east, and standeth very well,\rsaving that it is somewhatnear unto the fens, whereby the\rwholesomeness of the airis not a little corrupted. It is excellently\rwell served with all kindsof provisions, but especially of fresh\rwater fish and wild fowl,by reason of the river that passeth thereby;\rand thereto the Isle ofEly, which is so near at hand. Only wood is\rthe chief want to such asstudy there, wherefore this kind of\rprovision is brought themeither from Essex and other places\rthereabouts, as is alsotheir coal, or otherwise the necessity thereof\ris supplied with gall (abastard kind of mirtus as I take it) and\rseacoal, whereof they havegreat plenty led thither by the Grant.\rMoreover it hath not suchstore of meadow ground as may suffice for\rthe ordinary expenses ofthe town and university, wherefore the\rinhabitants are enforcedin like sort to provide their hay from other\rvillages about, whichminister the same unto them in very great\rabundance.\r \rOxford is supposed tocontain in longitude eighteen degrees and eight\rand twenty minutes, and inlatitude one and fifty degrees and fifty\rminutes: whereas that ofCambridge standing more northerly, hath\rtwenty degrees and twentyminutes in longitude, and thereunto fifty\rand two degrees andfifteen minutes in latitude, as by exact\rsupputation is easy to befound.\r \rThe colleges of Oxford,for curious workmanship and private\rcommodities, are much morestately, magnificent, and commodious than\rthose of Cambridge: andthereunto the streets of the town for the most\rpart are more large andcomely. But for uniformity of building,\rorderly compaction, andpolitic regiment, the town of Cambridge, as\rthe newer workmanship,[2]exceeds that of Oxford (which otherwise is,\rand hath been, the greaterof the two) by many a fold (as I guess),\ralthough I know diversthat are of the contrary opinion. This also is\rcertain, that whatsoeverthe difference be in building of the town\rstreets, the townsmen ofboth are glad when they may match and annoy\rthe students, byencroaching upon their liberties, and keep them bare\rby extreme sale of theirwares, whereby many of them become rich for a\rtime, but afterward fallagain into poverty, because that goods evil\rgotten do seldom longendure.[3]...\r \r      [2] Cambridge burned not long since.--H.\r \r      [3] Here follows an account of Oxford andCambridge castles, and\r      the legend of the building of Osney Abbeyby Robert and Edith\r      D\'Oyley.--W.\r \rIn each of theseuniversities also is likewise a church dedicated to\rthe Virgin Mary, whereinonce in the year--to wit, in July--the\rscholars are holden, andin which such as have been called to any\rdegree in the yearprecedent do there receive the accomplishment of\rthe same, in solemn andsumptuous manner. In Oxford this solemnity is\rcalled an Act, but inCambridge they use the French word\r_Commencement_; and suchresort is made yearly unto the same from all\rparts of the land by thefriends of those who do proceed that all the\rtown is hardly able toreceive and lodge those guests. When and by\rwhom the churchesaforesaid were built I have elsewhere made relation.\rThat of Oxford also wasrepaired in the time of Edward the Fourth and\rHenry the Seventh, whenDoctor Fitz James, a great helper in that\rwork, was warden of MertonCollege; but ere long, after it was\rfinished, one tempest in anight so defaced the same that it left few\rpinnacles standing aboutthe church and steeple, which since that time\rhave never been repaired.There were sometime four and twenty parish\rchurches in the town andsuburbs; but now there are scarcely sixteen.\rThere have been also 1200burgesses, of which 400 dwelt in the\rsuburbs; and so manystudents were there in the time of Henry the\rThird that he allowed themtwenty miles compass about the town for\rtheir provision ofvictuals.\r \rThe common schools ofCambridge also are far more beautiful than those\rof Oxford, only theDivinity School of Oxford excepted, which for fine\rand excellent workmanshipcometh next the mould of the King\'s Chapel\rin Cambridge, than thewhich two, with the Chapel that King Henry the\rSeventh did build atWestminster, there are not (in my opinion) made\rof lime and stone threemore notable piles within the compass of\rEurope.\r \rIn all the other thingsthere is so great equality between these two\runiversities as no man canimagine how to set down any greater, so\rthat they seem to be thebody of one well-ordered commonwealth, only\rdivided by distance ofplace and not in friendly consent and orders.\rIn speaking therefore ofthe one I cannot but describe the other; and\rin commendation of thefirst I cannot but extol the latter; and, so\rmuch the rather, for thatthey are both so dear unto me as that I\rcannot readily tell untowhether of them I owe the most good-will.\rWould to God my knowledgewere such as that neither of them might have\rcause to be ashamed oftheir pupil, or my power so great that I might\rworthily requite them bothfor those manifold kindnesses that I have\rreceived of them! But toleave these things, and proceed with other\rmore convenient to mypurpose.\r \rThe manner to live inthese universities is not as in some other of\rforeign countries we seedaily to happen, where the students are\renforced for want of suchhouses to dwell in common inns, and taverns,\rwithout all order ordiscipline. But in these our colleges we live in\rsuch exact order, andunder so precise rules of government, as that\rthe famous learned manErasmus of Rotterdam, being here among us fifty\ryears passed, did not letto compare the trades in living of students\rin these two places, evenwith the very rules and orders of the\rancient monks, affirmingmoreover, in flat words, our orders to be\rsuch as not only came nearunto, but rather far exceeded, all the\rmonastical institutionsthat ever were devised.\r \rIn most of our collegesthere are also great numbers of students, of\rwhich many are found bythe revenues of the houses and other by the\rpurveyances and help oftheir rich friends, whereby in some one\rcollege you shall have twohundred scholars, in others an hundred and\rfifty, in divers a hundredand forty, and in the rest less numbers, as\rthe capacity of the saidhouses is able to receive: so that at this\rpresent, of one sort andother, there are about three thousand\rstudents nourished in themboth (as by a late survey it manifestly\rappeared). They wereerected by their founders at the first only for\rpoor men\'s sons, whoseparents were not able to bring them up unto\rlearning; but now theyhave the least benefit of them, by reason the\rrich do so encroach uponthem. And so far has this inconvenience\rspread itself that it isin my time a hard matter for a poor man\'s\rchild to come by afellowship (though he be never so good a scholar\rand worthy of that room).Such packing also is used at elections that\rnot he which bestdeserveth, but he that has most friends, though he\rbe the worst scholar, isalways surest to speed, which will turn in\rthe end to the overthrowof learning. That some gentlemen also whose\rfriends have been in timespast benefactors to certain of those houses\rdo intrude into thedisposition of their estates without all respect\rof order or statutesdevised by the founders, only thereby to place\rwhom they think good (andnot without some hope of gain), the case is\rtoo too evident: and theirattempt would soon take place if their\rsuperiors did not provideto bridle their endeavours. In some grammar\rschools likewise whichsend scholars to these universities, it is\rlamentable to see whatbribery is used; for, ere the scholar can be\rpreferred, such bribage ismade that poor men\'s children are commonly\rshut out, and the richersort received (who in time past thought it\rdishonour to live as itwere upon alms), and yet, being placed, most\rof them study little otherthan histories, tables, dice, and trifles,\ras men that make not theliving by their study the end of their\rpurposes, which is alamentable hearing. Beside this, being for the\rmost part either gentlemenor rich men\'s sons, they often bring the\runiversities into muchslander. For, standing upon their reputation\rand liberty, they ruffleand roist it out, exceeding in apparel, and\rbanting riotous company(which draweth them from their books unto\ranother trade), and forexcuse, when they are charged with breach of\rall good order, think itsufficient to say that they be gentlemen,\rwhich grieveth many not alittle. But to proceed with the rest.\r \rEvery one of thesecolleges have in like manner their professors or\rreaders of the tongues andseveral sciences, as they call them, which\rdaily trade up the youththere abiding privately in their halls, to\rthe end they may be ableafterward (when their turn cometh about,\rwhich is after twelveterms) to shew themselves abroad, by going from\rthence into the commonschools and public disputations (as it were\r"_In aream_")there to try their skill, and declare how they have\rprofited since theircoming thither.\r \rMoreover, in the publicschools of both the universities, there are\rfound at the prince\'scharge (and that very largely) fine professors\rand readers, that is tosay, of divinity, of the civil law, physic,\rthe Hebrew and the Greektongues. And for the other lectures, as of\rphilosophy, logic,rhetoric, and the quadrivials (although the latter,\rI mean arithmetic, music,geometry, and astronomy, and with them all\rskill in the perspectives,are now smally regarded in either of them),\rthe universitiesthemselves do allow competent stipends to such as\rread the same, wherebythey are sufficiently provided for, touching\rthe maintenance of theirestates, and no less encouraged to be\rdiligent in theirfunctions.\r \rThese professors in likesort have all the rule of disputations and\rother school exerciseswhich are daily used in common schools\rseverally assigned to eachof them, and such of their hearers as by\rtheir skill shewed in thesaid disputations are thought to have\rattained to any convenientripeness of knowledge according to the\rcustom of otheruniversities (although not in like order) are\rpermitted solemnly to taketheir deserved degrees of school in the\rsame science and facultywherein they have spent their travel. From\rthat time forward alsothey use such difference in apparel as becometh\rtheir callings, tendethunto gravity, and maketh them known to be\rcalled to somecountenance.\r \rThe first degree is thatof the general sophisters, from whence, when\rthey have learned moresufficiently the rules of logic, rhetoric, and\robtained thereto competentskill in philosophy, and in the\rmathematicals, they ascendhigher unto the estate of bachelors of art,\rafter four years of theirentrance into their sophistry. From thence\ralso, giving their mindsto more perfect knowledge in some or all the\rother liberal sciences andthe tongues, they rise at the last (to wit,\rafter other three or fouryears) to be called masters of art, each of\rthem being at that timereputed for a doctor in his faculty, if he\rprofess but one of thesaid sciences (besides philosophy), or for his\rgeneral skill, if he beexercised in them all. After this they are\rpermitted to choose whatother of the higher studies them liketh to\rfollow, whether it bedivinity, law, or physic, so that, being once\rmasters of art, the nextdegree, if they follow physic, is the\rdoctorship belonging tothat profession; and likewise in the study of\rthe law, if they bendtheir minds to the knowledge of the same. But,\rif they mean to go forwardwith divinity, this is the order used in\rthat profession. First,after they have necessarily proceeded masters\rof art, they preach onesermon to the people in English, and another\rto the university inLatin. They answer all comers also in their own\rpersons unto two severalquestions of divinity in the open schools at\rone time for the space oftwo hours, and afterward reply twice against\rsome other man upon a likenumber and on two several dates in the same\rplace, which being donewith commendation, he receiveth the fourth\rdegree, that is, bachelorof divinity, but not before he has been\rmaster of arts by thespace of seven years, according to their\rstatutes.\r \rThe next, and last degreeof all, is the doctorship, after other three\ryears, for the which hemust once again perform all such exercises and\racts as are beforeremembered; and then is he reputed able to govern\rand teach others, andlikewise taken for a doctor. I have read that\rJohn of Beverley was thefirst doctor that ever was in Oxford, as Beda\rwas in Cambridge. But Isuppose herein that the word "doctor" is not\rso strictly to be taken inthis report as it is now used, since every\rteacher is in Latin calledby that name, as also such in the primitive\rchurch as kept schools ofcatechists, wherein they were trained up in\rthe rudiments andprinciples of religion, either before they were\radmitted unto baptism orany office in the Church.\r \rThus we see that from ourentrance into the university unto the last\rdegree received iscommonly eighteen or twenty years, in which time,\rif a student has notobtained sufficient learning thereby to serve his\rown turn and benefit hiscommonwealth, let him never look by tarrying\rlonger to come by anymore. For after this time, and forty years of\rage, the most part ofstudents do commonly give over their wonted\rdiligence, and live likedrone bees on the fat of colleges,\rwithholding better witsfrom the possession of their places, and yet\rdoing little good in theirown vocation and calling. I could rehearse\ra number (if I listed) ofthis sort, as well in one university as the\rother. But this shallsuffice instead of a large report, that long\rcontinuance in thoseplaces is either a sign of lack of friends, or of\rlearning, or of good andupright life, as Bishop Fox[4] sometime\rnoted, who thought itsacrilege for a man to tarry any longer at\rOxford than he had adesire to profit.\r \r      [4] This Fox builded Corpus ChristiCollege, in Oxford.--H.\r \rA man may (if he will)begin his study with the law, or physic (of\rwhich this giveth wealth,the other honour), so soon as he cometh to\rthe university, if hisknowledge in the tongues and ripeness of\rjudgment serve therefor:which if he do, then his first degree is\rbachelor of law, orphysic; and for the same he must perform such acts\rin his own science as thebachelors or doctors of divinity do for\rtheir parts, the onlysermons except, which belong not to his calling.\rFinally, this will I say,that the professors of either of those\rfaculties come to suchperfection in both universities as the best\rstudents beyond the sea doin their own or elsewhere. One thing only I\rmislike in them, and thatis their usual going into Italy, from whence\rvery few without specialgrace do return good men whatsoever they\rpretend of conference orpractice, chiefly the physicians[5] who under\rpretence of seeking offoreign simples do oftentimes learn the framing\rof such compositions aswere better unknown than practised, as I have\rheard often alleged, andtherefore it is most true that Doctor Turner\rsaid: "Italy is notto be seen without a guide, that is, without\rspecial grace given fromGod, because of the licentious and corrupt\rbehaviour of thepeople."\r \r      [5] So much also may be inferred oflawyers.--H.\r \rThere is moreover in everyhouse a master or provost, who has under\rhim a president andcertain censors or deans, appointed to look to the\rbehaviour and manners ofthe students there, whom they punish very\rseverely if they make anydefault, according to the quantity and\rquality of their trespass.And these are the usual names of governors\rin Cambridge. Howbeit inOxford the heads of houses are now and then\rcalled presidents inrespect of such bishops as are their visitors and\rfounders. In each of thesealso they have one or more treasurers, whom\rthey call _bursarios_ orbursars, beside other officers whose charge\ris to see unto the welfareand maintenance of these houses. Over each\runiversity also there is aseveral chancellor, whose offices are\rperpetual, howbeit theirsubstitutes, whom we call vice-chancellors,\rare changed every year, asare also the proctors, taskers, masters of\rthe streets, and otherofficers, for the better maintenance of their\rpolicy and estate.\r \rAnd thus much at this timeof our two universities, in each of which I\rhave received such degreeas they have vouchsafed--rather of their\rfavour than my desert--toyield and bestow upon me, and unto whose\rstudents I wish one thing,the execution whereof cannot be prejudicial\rto any that meaneth well,as I am resolutely persuaded, and the case\rnow standeth in these ourdays. When any benefice therefor becometh\rvoid it were good that thepatron did signify the vacation thereof to\rthe bishop, and the bishopthe act of the patron to one of the\runiversities, with requestthat the vice-chancellor with his\rassistants might providesome such able man to succeed in the place as\rshould by their judgmentbe meet to take the charge upon him.\rCertainly if this orderwere taken, then should the church be provided\rof good pastors, by whomGod should be glorified, the universities\rbetter stored, thesimoniacal practices of a number of patrons utterly\rabolished, and the peoplebetter trained to live in obedience toward\rGod and their prince,which were a happier estate.\r \rTo these two also we mayin like sort add the third, which is at\rLondon (serving only forsuch as study the laws of the realm) where\rthere are sundry famoushouses, of which three are called by the name\rof Inns of the Court, therest of the Chancery, and all built before\rtime for the furtheranceand commodity of such as apply their minds to\rour common laws. Out ofthese also come many scholars of great fame,\rwhereof the most part haveheretofore been brought up in one of the\raforesaid universities,and prove such commonly as in process of time\rrise up (only throughtheir profound skill) to great honour in the\rcommonwealth of England.They have also degrees of learning among\rthemselves, and rules ofdiscipline, under which they live most\rcivilly in their houses,albeit that the younger of them abroad in the\rstreets are scarcely ableto be bridled by any good order at all.\rCertainly this error waswont also greatly to reign in Cambridge and\rOxford, between thestudents and the burgesses; but, as it is well\rleft in these two places,so in foreign countries it cannot yet be\rsuppressed.\r \rBesides theseuniversities, also there are great number of grammar\rschools throughout therealm, and those very liberally endowed, for\rthe better relief of poorscholars, so that there are not many\rcorporate towns now underthe Queen\'s dominion that have not one\rgrammar school at theleast, with a sufficient living for a master and\rusher appointed to thesame.\r \rThere are in like mannerdivers collegiate churches, as Windsor,\rWinchester, Eton,Westminster (in which I was some time an\runprofitable grammarianunder the reverend father Master Nowell, now\rdean of Paul\'s), and inthose a great number of poor scholars, daily\rmaintained by theliberality of the founders, with meat, books, and\rapparel, from whence,after they have been well entered in the\rknowledge of the Latin andGreek tongues, and rules of versifying (the\rtrial whereof is made bycertain apposers yearly appointed to examine\rthem), they are sent tocertain special houses in each university,\rwhere they are receivedand trained up in the points of higher\rknowledge in their privatehalls, till they be adjudged meet to shew\rtheir face\'s in theschools as I have said already.\r \rAnd thus much have Ithought good to note of our universities, and\rlikewise of colleges inthe same, whose names I will also set down\rhere, with those of theirfounders, to the end the zeal which they\rbare unto learning mayappear, and their remembrance never perish from\ramong the wise andlearned.\r \rOF THE COLLEGES OFCAMBRIDGE WITH THEIR FOUNDERS\r \rYears of the\rFoundation     Colleges        Founders\r \r1546   1 Trinity In my opinion the\rlivers in these are verylike to those that are of the inns in the\rchancery, their names alsoare these so far as I now remember:\r \rBrodegates.            St. Mary Hall.\rHart Hall.             White Hall.\rMagdalen Hall.         New Inn.\rAlburne Hall.          Edmond Hall.\rPostminster Hall.\r \rThe students also thatremain in them are called hostlers or halliers.\rHereof it came of late topass that the right Reverend Father in God,\rThomas, late archbishop ofCanterbury, being brought up in such an\rhouse at Cambridge, was ofthe ignorant sort of Londoners called an\r"Hostler,"supposing that he had served with some inn-holder in the\rstable, and therefore, indespite, divers hung up bottles of hay at\rhis gate when he began topreach the gospel, whereas indeed he was a\rgentleman born of anancient house, and in the end a faithful witness\rof Jesus Christ, in whosequarrel he refused not to shed his blood,\rand yield up his life,unto the fury of his adversaries.\r \rBesides these there ismention and record of divers other halls or\rhostels that have beenthere in times past, as Beef Hall, Mutton Hall,\retc., whose ruins yetappear: so that if antiquity be to be judged by\rthe shew of ancientbuildings which is very plentiful in Oxford to be\rseen, it should be an easymatter to conclude that Oxford is the elder\runiversity. Therein arealso many dwelling-houses of stone yet\rstanding that have beenhalls for students, of very antique\rworkmanship, besides theold walls of sundry others, whose plots have\rbeen converted intogardens since colleges were erected.\r \rIn London also the housesof students at the Common Law are these:\r \rSergeant\'s Inn.        Furnival\'s Inn.\rGray\'s Inn.            Clifford\'s Inn.\rThe Temple.            Clement\'s Inn.\rLincoln\'s Inn.         Lion\'s Inn.\rDavid\'s Inn.           Barnard\'s Inn.\rStaple Inn.            Newmann.\r \rAnd thus much in generalof our noble universities, whose lands some\rgreedy gripers do gapewide for, and of late have (as I hear)\rpropounded sundry reasonswhereby they supposed to have prevailed in\rtheir purposes. But whoare those that have attempted this suit, other\rthan such as either hatelearning, piety, and wisdom, or else have\rspent all their own, andknow not otherwise than by encroaching upon\rother men how to maintainthemselves? When such a motion was made by\rsome unto King Henry theEighth, he could answer them in this manner:\r"Ah, sirra! Iperceive the Abbey lands have fleshed you, and set your\rteeth on edge, to ask alsothose colleges. And, whereas we had a\rregard only to pull downsin by defacing the monasteries, you have a\rdesire also to overthrowall goodness, by subversion of colleges. I\rtell you, sirs, that Ijudge no land in England better bestowed than\rthat which is given to ouruniversities; for by their maintenance our\rrealm shall be wellgoverned when we be dead and rotten. As you love\ryour welfares therefore,follow no more this vein, but content\ryourselves with that youhave already, or else seek honest means\rwhereby to increase yourlivelihoods; for I love not learning so ill\rthat I will impair therevenues of any one house by a penny, whereby\rit may be upholden."In King Edward\'s days likewise the same suit was\ronce again attempted (as Ihave heard), but in vain; for, saith the\rDuke of Somerset, amongother speeches tending to that end--who also\rmade answer thereunto inthe king\'s presence by his assignation: "If\rlearning decay, which ofwild men maketh civil; of blockish and rash\rpersons, wise and goodlycounsellors; of obstinate rebels, obedient\rsubjects; and of evil men,good and godly Christians; what shall we\rlook for else butbarbarism and tumult? For when the lands of colleges\rbe gone, it shall be hardto say whose staff shall stand next the\rdoor; for then I doubt notbut the state of bishops, rich farmers,\rmerchants, and thenobility, shall be assailed, by such as live to\rspend all, and think thatwhatsoever another man hath is more meet for\rthem and to be at theircommandment than for the proper owner that has\rsweat and laboured forit." In Queen Mary\'s days the weather was too\rwarm for any such courseto be taken in hand; but in the time of our\rgracious Queen Elizabeth Ihear that it was after a sort in talk the\rthird time, but withoutsuccess, as moved also out of season; and so I\rhope it shall continue forever. For what comfort should it be for any\rgood man to see hiscountry brought into the estate of the old Goths\rand Vandals, who made lawsagainst learning, and would not suffer any\rskilful man to come intotheir council-house: by means whereof those\rpeople became savagetyrants and merciless hell-hounds, till they\rrestored learning againand thereby fell to civility.\r \r_Planned and Designed atThe Collier Press\rBy William Patten_\r \r \r \r \r \r \r \r*** END OF THE PROJECTGUTENBERG EBOOK CHRONICLE AND ROMANCE: FROISSART, MALORY, HOLINSHED ***\r \r \r    \r \rUpdated editions willreplace the previous one—the old editions will\rbe renamed.\r \rCreating the works fromprint editions not protected by U.S. copyright\rlaw means that no one ownsa United States copyright in these works,\rso the Foundation (andyou!) can copy and distribute it in the United\rStates without permissionand without paying copyright\rroyalties. CAMPBELL\r \r                 WITH AN INTRODUCTION BY JAMESMURDOCH\r          LATE SECRETARY TO THE BOARD OFNORTHERN LIGHTHOUSES\r \r                             [Illustration]\r \r                EDINBURGH: DAVID DOUGLAS,CASTLE STREET\r \r                                  1904\r \r \r \r \r                                PREFACE.\r \r \rThese desultory notes wereoriginally undertaken at the instigation of\ran invalid friend,desirous of a closer acquaintance with our lonely\renvironments.\r \rAt the termination of anine years’ residence on the Rock, I have been\radvised to publish them inbook form, and being fortunate in securing\rthe services of a generouspublisher, they are now collected from the\rcolumns of the local pressand issued in this form in the hope that\rthey may interest the generalreader.\r \rI have to thank theEditors of _The Arbroath Guide_ and _Chambers’s\rJournal_ for theircourtesy.\r \r                                           J.M. CAMPBELL,\r                                               _Assistant Lightkeeper_.\r \r  BELL ROCK LIGHTHOUSE,\r       _May 1904_.\r \r \r \r \r                             INTRODUCTION.\r \r \rIn consequence probably ofmy connection of more than fifty years\rwith the NorthernLighthouse Board, and of the almost equally long\rservice of my father, Ihave been requested, and with much diffidence\rhave complied with therequest, to write, by way of Introduction to\rthese very interesting andinstructive “Notes from the Bell Rock,” a\rfew words regardingLighthouses, and a short account of the Northern\rLighthouse Service and itsLightkeepers. My love for that service,\rand the esteem I have forthose responsible and patient watchmen of\rthe night, whose duty itis to keep their lights burning to guard\rthe mariner from some ofthe dangers to which he is exposed, and to\rguide him on his way overthe vasty deep, may possibly enable me to\rsay something to interestreaders of the Notes in a service whose\rappropriate motto is “INSALUTEM OMNIUM.”\r \rThe origin, as well as theearly history, of lighthouses is involved in\rmuch obscurity, althoughwe learn from ancient writers that lights of\rsome sort, or beaconfires, were used for guiding vessels or warning\rthem of danger at leastthree hundred years before the Christian era.\rThe Colossus of Rhodes andthe Pharos of Alexandria are those that\rwe first read of, but verylittle authentic information is to be got\rregarding them. At a muchlater date we know that sea lights for such\rpurposes were produced bythe burning of wood and coal in chauffers on\rcoasts where they could bewell seen. One such beacon fire was shown\rfrom a tower on the Isleof May, at the entrance to the Firth of Forth,\rfrom the year 1635 till1816, when the present lighthouse was built,\rand is supposed to havebeen the first sea light on the coast of\rScotland. It is notunlikely, however, that long before that date some\rof the most dangerousparts of the Mediterranean were lighted in a like\rprimitive manner.\r \rThe first lighthouse ofany note of which we have authentic record\ris the Tour de Corduan,near the mouth of the river Garonne, in the\rsouth-west of France,which was founded in 1584, but not completed\rand lighted till 1610. Onaccount of the style and grandeur of its\rarchitecture, it was longregarded as one of the wonders of the world,\rthe Pharos of Alexandriahaving been regarded as another. Its lightroom\rwas originally constructedfor the combustion of wood in a kind of\rchauffer raised six feetabove the floor of the lantern; but it has\rundergone many alterationsand improvements since then, to bring it\rinto keeping with theprogressing and modern system of lighthouse\rillumination, which hasmade great strides during the last half-century.\r \rWinstanley’s woodenstructure to mark the Eddystone Rock off Plymouth\rwas probably the next workof importance in lighthouse building. It was\rlighted in 1698, butwashed away in a storm about five years afterwards\rwhen Winstanley, who hadgone there with some workmen to execute\rcertain repairs, and thelightkeepers all perished. A subsequent\rlighthouse, also of wood,on the Eddystone, was accidentally burned\rdown about fifty yearslater, after which Smeaton’s structure of stone\rwas placed on it. Thisbuilding stood until a few years ago, when it\rwas seen the sea wasmaking such serious inroads on the rock on which\rit was founded, that itwas deemed advisable to take it down and have\ranother built on adifferent part of the reef. The success of Smeaton’s\rlighthouse having beenassured, attention was directed at the beginning\rof last century to theBell Rock, which was a source of great danger\rto vessels navigating theEast Coast of Scotland, and particularly to\rthose sailing to or fromthe Firths of Forth and Tay, many of them\rbeing lost on it.\r \rThe Commissioners ofNorthern Lighthouses accordingly resolved to erect\ra lighthouse there,somewhat after the model of Smeaton’s Eddystone,\rbut the work proved to bea much more difficult and arduous undertaking\rowing to the Rock beingalways covered by the sea, except for a short\rtime at low water, whereasthe Eddystone was never altogether covered,\reven at high water. TheBell Rock is a low flat lying reef, the surface\rof which becomes uncoveredto any extent only at low water of spring\rtides, but on which athigh water there is a depth of from twelve to\rsixteen feet. Its extentis about 1400 or 1500 feet in length, with a\rbreadth of about 300 feet.In olden times it was known as the Inchcape\rRock. Tradition has itthat at one time an Abbot of Aberbrothock being\rimpressed with its danger,and anxious to avert to some extent, if\rpossible, the loss of lifewhich often occurred on it by shipwrecks,\rmoored thereon a buoy orlog of wood, having a bell attached to it,\rwhich the action of thesea tolled continuously, thus giving warning\rof danger. It afterwardsbecame known as the Bell Rock. Tradition also\rsays that a pirate knownas Ralph the Rover, who frequented these seas,\rfinding that the bellinterfered with his nefarious occupation, removed\rit. Retribution, however,was not long of overtaking him, for it is\rsaid that his vesselshortly afterwards struck on the reef and was lost\rwith all on board.Southey’s graphic ballad, descriptive of the legend,\rentitled “Sir Ralph theRover,” is so well known that it is quite\runnecessary to do morethan refer to it here.\r \rThe sanction of Governmenthaving to be procured before the erection of\rthe lighthouse could beproceeded with, considerable time was occupied\rwith the necessarynegotiations, but in 1807, Mr Robert Stevenson,\rthe Engineer to theNorthern Lighthouse Board, was allowed to\rcommence operations, andafter encountering and overcoming innumerable\rdifficulties by hisindomitable skill, energy, and perseverance, he at\rlast completed the work,and had a light shown from it on 1st February\r1811. It is verysatisfactory to be able to state as testifying to the\rexcellency of thematerials used in its construction, as well as to\rthe careful and welldevised scheme and execution of the workmanship,\rthat the tower as yetshows no symptoms of decay, and stands as strong\rto-day as when newlyerected.\r \rIn a highly interestinglecture which the writer of the Notes delivered\rat Arbroath, about a yearago, he thus described the lightroom and\rlighting apparatus, whichhad just been renewed, not on account of tear\rand wear, but to bring itup to present day standard:--\r \r“In the centre of thefloor stands the revolving machinery enclosed\rin a heavy metal case,upon which the huge lens, with its supporting\rcarriage, revolves. Thelens itself--a marvel of the glassmaker’s\rart--is the production ofa French firm. Imagine a huge saucer, twelve\rfeet in diameter, composedof twenty concentric prisms of purest glass,\reach with a diameteralmost as much as a man may enclose with both\rhands, terminatingcentrally in a sixteen inch plano-convex lens or\rbull’s-eye. Suppose therim of this saucer to the extent of four prisms\rbe turned sharply inwards,the whole set vertically on edge--convexity\routwards--and a verticalsection--in which the bull’s-eye and three\radjoining prisms are aloneintact--projected a foot further forward,\rone may gain some idea ofthat particular portion of the lens allotted\rto the red flash, thecolour of which is attained by means of sheets of\rred glass attached insidethe central section and on the outside of the\radjoining wings. On theopposite side of the lens, and in a line with\rthe central red section,is a similar section--minus the adjoining\rwings and the redmedia--through which the white flash is transmitted.\rBoth flashes are intendedto equal each other in intensity, which\raccounts for the muchsmaller portion of the lens allotted to the\rwhite. A belt ofhorizontal prisms, three feet wide, connects the\rwings of the red sectionwith the white on either side, and reflects\rthe rays of light equallyto both sections. Stooping underneath this\rbelt, access is obtainedto a fixed circular platform in the interior\rof the lens. In the centreof this platform, upon an iron pedestal, is\rplaced the source ofillumination, a large six-wick lamp. Between this\rplatform and the top ofthe machine case, the circular carriage upon\rwhich the superstructureof the lens is erected revolves upon twelve\rfive-inch steel rollerstravelling upon a circular metal pathway.\rAttached to the under sideof this carriage is a heavy gun-metal\rring, six feet indiameter, toothed on its inner circumference, which\rengages with a horizontalpinion wheel rising from the corner of the\rmachine case, and throughwhich the driving power is transmitted. The\rmachine--an exaggeratedform of clockwork--is driven by a weight of\r400 lbs. travelling in thecentre of the spiral stair on the first\rflat. The speed of themachine is regulated by adjustable fans; and a\rspeed indicator, furnishedwith an alarm bell, intimates the periods of\rwinding--an operationnecessitating two minutes’ stiff winding every\rhalf-hour. The entirelens, with its supporting carriage, is estimated\rto weigh about six tons.The lamp, as I have already stated, is placed\rupon an iron pedestal inthe centre of the platform, or service table,\ras it is called, in theinterior of the lens. It is fitted with what\ris known as the steppedDoty burner, and carries six concentric wicks,\reach slightly elevatedabove the other towards the centre. The burner\ris six inches in diameter,and consumes paraffin oil at the rate of\reighteen gills per hour.To maintain this supply, a forty gallon tank\rof polished brass isplaced on the lightroom floor; and a small force\rpump, with tripleplungers, working in conjunction with the revolving\rmachine, maintains aconstant supply of oil, which is kept cool by\rcirculating within an inchof the burning edge of the wicks, the\rsurplus oil returning tothe pump-tank. The flash, on being transmitted\rthrough the lens, isreckoned to be equal to 60,000 candles; and the\rcharacteristic of thelight--a red and white flash alternately every\rhalf-minute--visibletwenty miles distant.”\r \rA description of the workof renewal of the lighting apparatus and the\rerection of a new andenlarged lantern to hold it on the top of the\rtower, is also given inthe Notes; and no further reference to it is\rneeded than to say thatthe light, which has the same characteristic as\rbefore, is now, by meansof the new apparatus, made much stronger and\rmore brilliant.\r \rSuch an erection as thislighthouse--standing, as it were, a pillar in\rthe ocean, with a stormysea raging round it--may surely be described\ras one of the noblest andmost wonderful works of man. As no ship has\rbeen wrecked on the Rocksince the light was first exhibited, it is\rincalculable how manyvaluable lives may have been saved by it. Sir\rWalter Scott, on theoccasion of his visiting the Bell Rock as the\rguest of the Commissionerson their annual tour of inspection in 1814,\rgave beautiful expressionto his feelings in the following appropriate\rlines, which he wrote inthe Lighthouse Album:--\r \r         PHAROS LOQUITUR.\r \r    Far in the bosom of the deep,\r    O’er these wild shelves my watch I keep,\r    A ruddy gem of changeful light\r    Bound on the dusky brow of night;\r    The seaman bids my lustre hail\r    And scorns to strike his timorous sail.\r \rThe Eddystone and the BellRock Lighthouses having been, as it were,\rthe forerunners of theclass of lighthouse that required to be built\ron rocks exposed to the fullfetch of heavy seas, many more of the\rsame sort have since beenerected off the coasts of Great Britain and\rIreland. That ofSkerryvore, which is situated in the Atlantic, west of\rthe Island of Tiree inArgyllshire, is regarded as probably the finest\rspecimen of lighthousearchitecture in the world. This lighthouse was\rthe creation of AlanStevenson, who succeeded his father, Robert, as\rEngineer to the NorthernLighthouse Board, and it is interesting to\rknow that the designingand engineering of the Northern Lighthouses has\rnow been in the hands ofthe Stevenson family for more than a hundred\ryears, Mr David AlanStevenson, one of the grandsons of Robert, now\rholding the position ofEngineer to the Board. But the family is not\raltogether indebted tolighthouse engineering for its fame, as the late\rtalented and lamentedwriter and novelist, Robert Louis Stevenson, who\rmade a world-wide name forhimself, was another grandson of the Bell\rRock Engineer.\r \rIt is not necessary to saymore about lighthouses, but I considered\rit desirable to give ashort description of one or two of the most\rnotable, including that ofthe Bell Rock, in which these Notes were\rwritten, to show from whatlimited sources a man of intelligence and\rkeen observation canprocure subjects of surpassing interest to engage\rhis attention, as well asto instruct and amuse others.\r \rThe Lighthouse Authoritiesof the United Kingdom are the Trinity\rHouse for England, theCommissioners of Northern Lighthouses for\rScotland, and the Commissionersof Irish Lights for Ireland. The\rTrinity House exerts acertain control over the Scottish and Irish\rBoards, particularly as tothe site and character of lights proposed\rby them, and the Board ofTrade holds the financial control of all\rthree. The Boards are notall similarly constituted, the members of\rthe Trinity House beingmostly men of nautical knowledge, while those\rcomposing the Irish Boardare mostly connected with the Corporation\rof Dublin. TheCommissioners of Northern Lighthouses are the Lord\rAdvocate and theSolicitor-General for Scotland, the Lord Provosts of\rEdinburgh, Glasgow,Aberdeen, and Dundee; the Provosts of Greenock,\rInverness, Campbeltown,and Leith; the eldest Bailies of Edinburgh and\rGlasgow--and the Sheriffsof the maritime counties of Scotland. The\rorigin of the Board datesfrom 1786, and it was incorporated by an Act\rof Parliament passed in1798. The primary and general object of the\rthree Boards is theerection and maintenance of lighthouses and other\rsea marks, such as beaconsand buoys, for the security of navigation\rand the saving of life andproperty. The funds for these objects are\rgot by levying tolls onshipping.\r \rIn 1815 the NorthernLighthouse Commissioners acquired the right to\rerect lighthouses on theIsle of Man, which since then has been under\rtheir jurisdiction.\r \rIn olden times, manylighthouses in England and Ireland were the\rproperty of privateindividuals, who had the power of charging dues\rfor their erection andmaintenance; but the Isle of May light was\rthe only one of that kindin Scotland, and it became the property of\rthe Commissioners ofNorthern Lighthouses by purchase in 1814. The\rtolls or dues have longbeen collected for the different Boards by\rthe Collectors of Customsat the various ports, and are now paid into\rwhat is called the“General Lighthouse Fund,” which is held by the\rBoard of Trade, and onwhich the Lighthouse Boards draw according to\rtheir requirements. Sixtyyears ago this tax, as it may be called,\ron shipping varied asregarded different lighthouses from a farthing\rto one-penny-halfpenny perton for each light passed, the rates on\rover-sea voyages beinggenerally double those for coasting voyages;\rbut since then they havefrequently been reduced, both in amount and\rin incidence. Ships of theNavy and all lighthouse vessels are, of\rcourse, exempt from suchdues. On 1st April 1899, an alteration was\rmade by which vessels wereno longer charged a rate per ton for each\rlight passed, but a rateper ton per voyage, and in some cases a rate\rper vessel; and adeduction was made when a number of similar voyages\rtook place during theyear. Very recently, a further reduction has been\rgranted by an abatement oftwelve-and-a-half per cent. on the total.\rThis, of course, is allpaid by the shipowners, who have long been,\rand still are,discontented at being charged for light dues at all,\rtheir contention beingthat all the expenditure necessary for erecting\rand maintaininglighthouses and other sea marks should be paid out\rof the Imperial taxationof the country. They also now desire to be\rrepresented on the threeBoards, and have a share in the management.\rI, who have seenhalf-a-century’s administration by the Commissioners\rof Northern Lighthouses,may be allowed to express an opinion that it\rwould be very difficult toconstruct a Board to do its work better than\rthe Northern LighthouseBoard. The Commissioners require no eulogy from\rme; but I cannot imagineany other body of men, be they scientific or\runscientific, nautical orcommercial, paid or unpaid--and be it noted\rthat the Commissioners areall unpaid--taking more interest in their\rwork, or devoting moretime and attention to it. The introduction of\rshipowners, who may haveconflicting interests to serve in the lighting\rof different parts of thecoast, might introduce an element of discord\rfrom which the presentBoard, so far as I am aware, has always been\rexempt.\r \rThe staff of the Boardconsists of an Engineer and a Secretary, who\ralso acts as GeneralManager, with an accountant, examiner of accounts,\rand five clerks. Thenthere is a superintending staff, consisting of a\rsuperintendent, with anassistant, and three district superintendents.\rFour small steamers, theproperty of the Board, deliver stores and oil,\rand fill with gas thelighted beacons and buoys, as well as relieve\rthe keepers at some of therock lighthouses. A number of boats also\rattend certain island andremote stations. There are more than 200\rlightkeepers attached toabout 80 lights, most of these lights being\rattended by two keepers,one acting as principal and the other as\rassistant. At rock and fogsignal stations, however, there are three\ror four keepers, accordingto requirement; such lighthouses as the\rBell Rock, Skerryvore, andseveral others of that class having four.\rAt the Isle of May, whichis an electric light station, there is an\rengineer in charge, withsix assistants. Besides these, there are also\ra number of small beaconand subsidiary lights which do not require\rthe personal attendance oflightkeepers. In the early part of last\rcentury lightkeepers weremostly chosen from the seafaring class, or\rfrom men who resided inthe district in which a lighthouse was placed,\rand age was considered nodetriment so long as they were able-bodied\rand of good character. TheScottish Board never employed women as\rlightkeepers, but not verylong ago it was customary in certain\rcases for lightkeepers’wives to act in this capacity in Ireland. As\rlighthouses increased innumber, applications to fill the post of\rlightkeepers also becamemore numerous, and now it is almost essential\rthat an applicant, inorder to get his name placed on the expectant\rlist, should be either amechanic or a seaman. Before receiving an\rappointment he has also toundergo a period of probation at one or two\rlighthouses, where he getsinstruction in his duties. There is now so\rmuch delicate andexpensive machinery in lightrooms that those placed\rin charge should not onlyhave skill to keep it in good working order,\rbut be able to executeslight repairs should accidents occur. It is\ralso found that seamen aremost suitable for rock or island stations,\rwhere there is muchboating or landing of stores and provisions, their\rearly training andfamiliarity with the sea giving expertness to\rtheir movements and aconfidence which few landsmen can ever acquire.\rThere is now an age limitfor entrance to the service, consequently\rall are young when firstappointed, and before getting an appointment\rrequire to pass anexamination in reading, writing, and arithmetic, and\rgive evidence of generalintelligence. They must also pass a medical\rexamination to prove thatthey are free from physical defects and have\ra sound constitution, andfreedom from colour blindness. At sixty years\rof age they may retire,and at sixty-five they must do so, pensions\rbeing awarded themaccording to their period of service. The day\rduties are light, exceptduring spells of fog, when at those stations\rwhere there are fogsignals, and the sirens require to be continually\rsounded, close attentionmust be given to the engines and machinery\rconnected with them. Thenight duties are divided into watches similar\rto those adopted on boardships. Lightkeepers are not allowed to\rread, write, or work whileon watch in the lightroom, as duty there\rrequires all the attentionthey can give to keep the lights burning\rbrightly, and at revolvinglights to watch and wind up the machinery\rperiodically. Then duringcertain states of the atmosphere the glass of\rthe lantern requirescleaning, more especially when snow is falling on\rit and obscuring thelight. A graphic description of this operation at\rthe Bell Rock is given inthe Notes.\r \rThe lives of alllightkeepers are insured, and much is done to make\rtheir position and that oftheir families a comfortable one. They have\ra liberal allowance ofholidays; and, if sickness overtakes them or\rany member of theirfamilies, medical attendance and medicines are\rfurnished by the Boardpractically free. Comfortable dwelling-houses,\rwith a certain amount offurniture, are supplied to all of them,\rwith uniform clothing,bedding, cooking utensils, coal, and oil for\rlighting purposes. Whenmen are doing duty on rock lighthouses, their\rfood and all their wantsare, as a matter of course, supplied. At\rstations remote fromschools, a boarding allowance is given to enable\rlightkeepers to get theirchildren boarded and educated elsewhere. Nor\rmust I omit to mentionthat all are liberally supplied with illustrated\rand other newspapers,monthly periodicals, and books of useful and\rgeneral literature.Lightkeepers and their families at most island\rstations have also meansafforded them for occasional attendance on\rDivine ordinances. Theyhave time to indulge in hobbies, such as\rhandicraft of variouskinds, from the making and mending of shoes to\rthe construction ofbeautiful models of lighthouses and ships, or, like\rthat of the writer of theNotes, the studying of the natural history of\rthe objects around them. Iknew one who, on the eve of his retirement,\rbuilt for himself a smallboat of plate iron, in which he afterwards\rused to go fishing.\r \rThe lights shown fromlighthouses have all special characteristics--such\ras fixed, flashing, or avariation in colour--to distinguish them\rfrom each other, and toenable the mariner when he sights them to\rknow exactly off what partof the coast he is. Unfortunately, this\rdoes not always preventshipwrecks occurring; for, although he should\rnot do so, sometimes themariner mistakes his light, and runs into\rdanger instead of out ofit; or fog may render a light invisible;\ror a storm may drive avessel on a lee shore in spite of any light.\rIt might be said thatwrecks should never occur from the first of\rthese causes, viz., amariner mistaking his light; but sailors are\rsometimes careless, likeother people, and only learn their lesson\rwhen too late. It isdifferent, however, when a master or officer has\rbeen storm tossed,probably for many days and nights, without seeing\rthe sun or stars to givehim an idea of his whereabouts. Suddenly the\rfog lifts a little and hesees a gleam of light which, in the anxious\rstate of his mind, hesupposes to be one which he thinks he ought to\rbe approaching, and thentaking, as he supposes, his correct course,\rruns on the rocks. Such acase occurred about five years ago, when the\rs.s. _Labrador_, boundfrom Halifax, Nova Scotia, to Liverpool, was\rlost on the Skerryvorereef. The captain had not been able for many\rdays to take anobservation owing to fog, and the tide had evidently\rcarried him further to thenorth than he reckoned on, when suddenly\rthe light of Skerryvoreappeared, and mistaking it for a light on the\rnorth coast of Ireland, heunfortunately altered his course, with the\rresult that the ship ranon a portion of the Skerryvore reef and became\ra total wreck.Fortunately, all on board were saved. Two boat-loads\rof crew and passengerswere picked up by a steamer and landed on the\rIsland of Mull; whileanother boat, containing the remainder, eighteen\rin all, reached the rockwhere the lighthouse stood, and, assisted by\rthe lightkeepers, landedand found shelter there, and had all their\rwants attended to till thelighthouse steamer _Hesperus_ went to their\rassistance and took themto Oban. Many acts of heroism since that\rof Grace Darling have beenperformed by lightkeepers in saving life\rfrom shipwreck, and havebeen suitably acknowledged by the Lifeboat\rInstitution or HumaneSociety. A short time ago, two daughters of the\rprincipal lightkeeper atKyleakin, observed a sailing boat struck by a\rsquall off the lighthouse,and its occupants (two men) thrown into the\rwater. The tide wasrunning fast, and as there was no time to lose,\rthey rushed down to theshore, and, getting into a boat, rowed out\rto where they saw one manstruggling in the water, and, after taking\rhim on board, rowed afterthe upturned boat, which had the other man\rclinging to it, and savedhim also.\r \rIn closing my shortIntroduction I cannot do better than refer to\ra visit paid to the BellRock Lighthouse by some fifty members of\rthe British Association in1850, and give a few quotations from a\rspeech made by DrRobinson, of Armagh, at a general meeting of that\rAssociation held inEdinburgh shortly afterwards, when he moved a\rvote of thanks to theCommissioners of Northern Lighthouses for their\rcourtesy in conveying theparty and showing them over the Lighthouse.\rHe said he had been led toan object which, almost from the days of his\rchildhood, engrossed hisattention, and which he had ever regarded as\rone of the wonders of theworld.\r \r“When I visited thatmarvellous, beautiful structure, rising up in\rits strength andloneliness out of the deep, I found that though the\rsea was calm and the windwas still, yet there was quite enough of\rdanger in the enterpriseof approaching it. Under these circumstances\rit enabled the mind tocall up for itself the terrors which must in\rformer years have besetthose who were unhappily entangled in that\rwilderness of rocks, whichthat noble structure now crowns as a\rbeacon.... It wasimpossible not to feel admiration for the beneficent\rcourage and the mechanicalskill of the late distinguished engineer,\rRobert Stevenson....
