WhenI thought of the extraordinary resources,\rboth of wealth and talent,that must have been accumulated to overcome\rsuch a tremendousdifficulty, I naturally looked to the nature of\rthe power by which suchmarvels had been achieved, and I found not a\rmere unenlightened body ofwhat are called practical men, of persons\rwho followed the road ofexperience, going always into the same old\rtrack, and incapable ofavailing themselves of the progress of the\rage to perfect theirfeeble endeavours. I found I was among men who\rwere able to teach me inmany important facts regarding which I had\rin vain sought forinformation for years, and which I learned in\rthat excursion.... When Iwas led to ask the question, Who are the\rcontrollers of thisadmirable system? I learned with surprise that\rthe Commissioners ofNorthern Lighthouses are not a set of salaried\rfunctionaries, whoseprofessional habits might have led them to\rinterest themselves inthese pursuits, but a body of lawyers and\rmunicipal magistrates.”\r \rDr Robinson’s appreciationof the Commissioners in the important\rservices they render tothe shipping interests is, I am sure, shared\rand endorsed by all whoknow or have known the Commissioners of any\rperiod.\r \r                                                        J. M.\r \rEDINBURGH, _August 1904_.\r \r \r \r \r                                 NOTES\r \r                                   ON\r \r                          THE NATURAL HISTORY\r \r                                   OF\r \r                             THE BELL ROCK.\r \r \r \r \r                             _APRIL 1901._\r \r \rI wonder how many peoplehave had the pleasure of a trip to the Bell\rRock Lighthouse. I don’tmean the customary trip per summer steamer,\rwhich keeps at a veryrespectable distance, and gives one but a faint\ridea of what the buildingis really like; but those who have made a\rlanding on the Rock, andspent an hour or two in admiring the ingenuity\rand skill displayed in theerection of this noble structure, which has\rso bravely stood the testof almost a century’s storms. It is not my\rintention to enter into adetailed description of the Lighthouse, but\rmerely to jot down inhaphazard fashion any little items which may\rserve to interest or amusethe general reader. The usual signs which\rto the landsman’s eyechronicle the passing seasons are here unknown;\rbut to us, the fish, shellfish, marine plants, migratory birds, etc.,\rconstitute an endlesscalendar. Early this month the flocks of eider\rand long-tailed ducks,which have been in close attendance since\rSeptember, have gonehousekeeping, and one belated pair of eiders alone\rremain, evidently asundecided as some of their human contemporaries\rabout taking the importantstep. The gulls, which have been levying\rblackmail from the ducksall winter, have almost all disappeared,\rand we miss their raucousvoices at our door, contending for the\rafter-dinner scraps. Onewould scarcely credit the swallowing capacity\rof these omnivorous birds.A piece of ham skin, nine inches long and\rthree inches broad, andabout the consistency of sole leather, was\rgreedily bolted by ablackback without apparent effort. These birds,\rthough not classed asdivers, I have frequently seen go completely\runder water to recover asinking tit-bit. I had an interesting view\rfrom the balcony the othermorning of a seal which was breakfasting off\ra full-sized cod which hehad just captured. Seizing the fish by the\rshoulders in his teeth,and pushing it from him with his fore flippers\rhe tore off a great stripclear to the tail. Elevating his head in the\rair, he gulped it over.Diving after the disappearing fish, he quickly\rhad it on the surfaceagain, and the pushing and tearing repeated till\rthere was nothing left butthe head and backbone. A couple of gulls\rkept circling andscreaming over him, picking up any strayed pieces\rwhich came their way, buthe took good care their share was small,\rand kept a wary eye ontheir movements, evidently suspecting they had\rdesigns on the fishitself. They, in turn, I noticed, always kept their\rwings elevated whenresting for a moment on the water awaiting his\rreappearance with thefish, prepared to shoot into the air should he\rattempt to rush at them.\r \rThe white whelk, whosenumbers here are legion, are now making their\rappearance from theirwinter quarters, where, in sheltered nooks and\rcrannies, they havesuccessfully resisted the winter’s gales. Unlike\rsome of their species,which subsist solely on marine plants, they\rare not vegetarians, but,spreading themselves over the Rock like a\rdevastating army, theydevour all animal matter they come across.\rArmed with a strongmuscular proboscis, containing within itself\rthe necessary boringapparatus, and which consists of a cylindrical\rimplement, the extremityof which forms the mouth of the animal, and\ris surrounded by twostrong muscular lips, enclosing a tongue, armed\rwith spines, they areable, by the joint action of tongue and lips, to\rperforate the hardestshells. Fixing itself on the defenceless mussel,\rthe boring operation iscarried on through the furrow on the one side\rof the rim of the whelk,and a neat cylindrical orifice, no bigger\rthan a pinhole, iseventually made in the mussel shell, through which\rthe tongue is thrust andthe contents gradually extracted. Two years\rago the Rock was literallycovered with patches of immature mussels,\rbut is now completelydenuded by these rapacious hordes. Some seasons\rthe mussel spawn is prettymuch in evidence here, but they never\rcome to maturity; thewhite whelk takes care of that; but apart from\rthat cause, it is doubtfulif they could manage to subsist in such a\rboisterous situation. Theworkmen, while employed here in the building\rof the Lighthouse, inorder to regale themselves with a fresh diet\roccasionally, made theexperiment of transplanting mussels from the\rshore, but withoutsuccess. The white whelk was evidently considered\rthe chief offender, asbarrels of them were collected and destroyed\rwithout any appreciablediminution of their numbers. The attempt was\rultimately abandoned indisgust.\r \r“All is not gold thatglitters,” neither does every whelk shell enclose\rits legitimate owner. Pickup that one which moves with such unusual\rspeed through this shallowpool, and you will find a pair of lobster\rlike claws dangling fromits mouth. Gently crack the shell--for you\rwill find it next toimpossible to extract him alive otherwise--and\ryou will see, what one maybe pardoned for supposing, a miniature\rlobster, but which inreality belongs to another distinct species,\rnamely, the hermit crab.Whether he has obtained occupancy by force\rof arms or merely throughdecease of the original tenant is a moot\rpoint, but the firstsupposition is highly probable, as he is a most\rbelligerent littlecustomer. An amusing sight may be witnessed by\rplacing several of them,deprived of the shells, in an ordinary soup\rplate, with a little seawater and some empty shells--fewer shells than\rcrabs. The fighting andstruggling to secure houses is ludicrous in the\rextreme. One may be seenalmost successful in mooring himself within\ra shell--which, by theway, is effected by means of the shelly plates\rat the extremity of hissoft, twisted tail--when another seizes him by\rthe nape of the neck, asit were, and he is dragged reluctantly forth.\rThe evictor still holdshim struggling at claw’s length, and not until\rhe himself is safelyensconced does he relinquish his grasp. Others,\ragain, may be seenprospecting the interior of a shell. Extended at\rfull length on the top ofthe shell, with their claws groping within,\rone is forcibly remindedof a person “guddling” for trout. Should there\rbe any portion of theoriginal whelk remaining in the shell, this,\rafter repeated tuggings,is cleared out. The tail is then inserted, and\rthe whole body withdrawninto the shell, providing it is large enough;\rif not, he stands a badchance of being evicted by the next pugnacious\rhouse-hunter.\r \r \r \r \r                              _MAY 1901._\r \r \rFlowery May! Well, notexactly. To us here this month generally spells\rfish, and is lookedforward to as a pleasant change from the usual\rregime. It may probablysurprise many to learn that though planted\rhere, right in the centreof the fishing grounds, our table for the\rgreater part of the yearis “fishless”; for, unlike Mahomet and the\rmountain, the fish mustcome to us, even to our very door--for from\rour doorway the most ofour fish are caught, save an occasional one\rtaken with rod and linefrom the deep pools left on the Rock by the\rreceding tide. Thecatching of fish from one’s doorstep will be easily\runderstood when it isknown that a stumble from our door at full\rtide means a sheer fall offifteen feet into two or three fathoms of\rwater. A stay fixed in thedoorway, with its outer end attached to the\rlanding-slip fifty feetfrom the tower, carries a weighted pulley, to\rwhich is attached thefishing line, while pending from the pulley is\rthe snid and hook. Thepulley is carried to the extremity of the stay\rby its own momentum, andis hauled back by means of the fishing line.\rThe most of ourfly-fishing is carried on with this apparatus, our\rlargest catches beinggenerally in the fall and consisting principally\rof poddlies, with anoccasional lithe or cod. Strangers often ask why\rwe do not keep a boathere; it might almost as reasonably be asked\rwhy we don’t keep a cow.Simply because we have not the necessary\raccommodation--that is,unless one could be devised with the properties\rof a limpet, and be nonethe worse for several hours’ immersion every\rtide. Besides, ourCommissioners have decreed that it would not be\radvisable, as thetemptation to wander might end in our being cast\raway, and the possibleresult of the Rock being left even for one\rnight without itscustomary warning light might be too horrible to\rcontemplate.\r \r_Cyclopterus lumpus_ isagain with us. This is not a new form of\rthe plague, but merely thetechnical term for the fish called the\rlump-sucker, better knownon the East Coast as the paidle-cock and\rpaidle-hen. Early thismonth they annually visit the Rock to deposit\rtheir ova. This the hendoes in some convenient angle of the Rock,\roften so ill-judged as toexpose the nest at low water. The ova is\rcemented into a compactmass, and adheres to the Rock by means of a\rgelatinous envelopesurrounding each egg. This operation performed, the\rhen evidently considersher share of the contract as finished, as she\rimmediately clears out todeep water, leaving the cock to mount guard\rover the nest. This dutyhe faithfully performs, as he is always to be\rseen with his nose closeup to the ova, and never seems to leave it for\ra moment. I havefrequently taken them away from the nest and placed\rthem in a different partof the pool, but they invariably returned to\rtheir post. A stick orother substance intruded in the vicinity of\rthe nursery is viciouslysnapped at. The ova seems to be considered a\rdesirable dainty by otherfishes, as the stomachs of the cod caught by\rus bear indisputableevidence of the cock’s inefficiency as guardian of\rhis embryonic progeny. Thehen is about eighteen inches long, and of a\rsomewhat repulsiveappearance. The cock is about half this size, and\rmore attractive, beingbrilliantly coloured, combining various shades\rof blue, purple, and richorange. A broad sucking disc between the\rpectoral fins enables thefish to moor itself to the rock and maintain\ran upright position. Thedorsal ridge somewhat resembles a cock’s comb,\rand is probably the originof the name paidle-cock.\r \r“Treasure-trove--Discoveryof Specie on the Bell Rock.” There is a\rheading for a sensationalarticle, recalling visions of that fictitious\rpersonage Ralph the Roverand his ill-gotten wealth. Well, many a yarn\ris built on a less slenderfoundation. Here are the facts:--The specie\rdid not consist of Spanishdollars stacked in massive oaken coffers,\rbut of a similar metalenclosed in a far more ingenious receptacle,\rsimply a shilling in alive mussel. The shilling appeared as crisp as\rif newly struck, and borethe date 1839. It had turned a dark brown\rcolour and had somefilaments of the byssus or “beard” of the mussel\radhering to it. The musselwas one of a quantity taken from underneath\rGranton Pier, and wasbeing opened here for bait purposes when the\r“discovery” was made.\r \rOn the evening of the 20thinst. we had a grand view of a flotilla of\rtorpedo destroyerssteaming south. Although the sea was comparatively\rcalm, they appeared to bemaking heavy weather of it; they literally\r“shovelled” the sea overthemselves, and the steersmen, being placed\rfurther forward than inordinary vessels, were being continually\rdrenched. The terrificspeed and the flames spurting from their short,\rstumpy funnels suggestedthe idea of their being on an errand of life\rand death rather than on apeaceful tour.\r \rWe have just completed asmall aquarium, by means of which we hope to\rbecome better acquaintedwith the more minute organisms with which\rthe Rock at this season ofthe year teems. Apart from the study\rof man himself, what canbe more interesting than to be an actual\reye-witness of the gradualevolution of the different forms in the\rgreat life-scheme of theCreator, from the simple nucleated speck of\rprotoplasm (_amœba_),which multiplies by simple division, to the more\rcomplex structure of themembers of the vertebrate kingdom?\r \r \r \r \r                              _JUNE 1901._\r \r \rA heavy, pounding,nor’-east swell in the early part of this month has\ralmost denuded the higherportions of the Rock of the young vegetation,\rthe tangles being ascleanly cut as if by a reaper. The paidle-cocks’\rnests also suffered, asnot a vestige of them was left. Several cocks\rhave been seen wanderingaimlessly about, their occupation evidently\rgone.\r \rOn the afternoon of the14th we had a heavy shower of hail, accompanied\rwith loud peals ofthunder; but on the whole the month has been fairly\rgood. At high water onseveral days the Rock was literally black with\rpoddlies feeding on youngsand eels, half-a-dozen terns and several\rsmall gulls joining in thefeast, while a number of gannets kept\rwheeling and diving in thevicinity, evidently picking up a decent\rliving. The continualsplashing of the fish in pursuit of their prey\rcould be distinctly heardby us through our open window while lying in\rbed. Strange to say, ourefforts to “take in” a few of them met with\rbut little success;probably the sufficiency of eels was the cause of\rtheir ignoring ourquestionable lure. The few that we caught were choke\rfull of eels, several ofwhich were disgorged in our doorway still\ralive.\r \rOn the 4th of the month wehad a visit from a carrier pigeon, which\rhad evidently strayed inthe haze. It carried no message, but was\rstamped on the wing, andhad a numbered rubber ring on its leg. After\rfeeding, it was liberatednext morning, with a message attached. We\roccasionally have similarvisitors. Last year one of them landed home\rin Warwickshire--the ownerthanking us and enclosing a consideration\rfor our kindness to thebird.\r \r“There’s nothing new underthe sun.” This much quoted aphorism was\rforcibly suggested to ourminds the other day while collecting\rspecimens for ouraquarium. In the first instance, a spider-crab,\rwhich, when stranded highand dry, appeared but an unsightly mass of\rtangled seaweed, whenplaced in the aquarium assumed all the beauties\rof a verdant grove. Fromevery available point on the upper surface of\rhis mossy-covered shellbeautiful variegated plants streamed and waved\rtheir delicately-featheredfronds. Conspicuous amongst this luxurious\rgrowth were specimens ofthe corallines or sea-firs, which a casual\robserver might easilysuppose to be miniature fir trees, but which in\rreality are plants only insemblance. Each of these delicate looking\rplants is actually ananimal; in fact, a colony of animals. Closely\rplaced along each side ofthe stem and delicate branches of other\rgrowths are slightprojections or nodules, each containing a separate\ranimal, which it surprisesone to learn is eventually destined to\rbecome a jelly fish. Thebenefits of this partnership between crab and\rcoralline is probablymutual, but the advantage to the crab in being\rthus arrayed is easilyseen, as he can remain completely concealed from\rhis enemies, and be ableto stalk his prey with greater certainty of\rsuccess. Shakespeare, inhis tragedy of “Macbeth,” caused an attacking\rforce to advance undercover of a wood they had cut down for that\rpurpose, but here inNature’s own arena similar tactics are being\rpursued, and probably wereages before “Birnam Wood came to Dunsinane,”\ror any of the _genus homo_ever saw the light.\r \rIn the second instance,our attention was centred in a small jelly-fish\rswimming about in a quietpool, its translucent body being scarcely\rdistinguishable but forthe beautiful flashes of iridescent light it\rwas continually giving offin the bright sunshine. This beautiful\robject might, withoutexaggeration, be truly termed a living gem.\rTransferring it to a glassof sea water for a closer inspection, our\rcuriosity was amplyrewarded. In shape and size similar to a nutmeg,\rits body was divided byeight equidistant bands running, as it were,\rfrom its North to itsSouth Pole. Two long filamentous tentacles\rstreamed from the lowerportion of the animal, and were constantly\rbeing shot forth andwithdrawn into its body, probably concerned in\rsome way in the animal’snutrition. Along one side of each tentacle\rwere ranged delicatefilaments, scarcely perceptible to the naked\reye, and were probably ofservice in entangling the minute food forms\rcontained in the water.Each of the eight vertical bands was seen to be\rfurnished with minuteplates overlapping each other like the plume of\ra feather. These plates,being continually in motion, were the means\rby which the animal waspropelled through the water; by reversing the\raction it moved backwards,and by moving those on one side only, a\rrotary motion wasobtained, the action of the plates producing the\rmost brilliant prismaticeffects. Call these plates paddles, and their\rdifferent movementsa-head, a-stern, port and starboard, and man’s\rwonderful invention thepaddle-wheel does not appear so very “new\runder the sun.” Thevarious motions man obtains by means of ponderous\rmachinery are here vestedin this simple, almost structureless animal,\rwhich has aptly beenlikened to a drop of animated sea water, and the\rfacility with which itrises to the surface or descends to any depth\rmight furnish hintstowards the solution of the submarine vessel,\rwhich is at present soengrossing the attention of naval authorities\rthe world over. Dwellersby the sea at this season of the year should\rhave little trouble inprocuring specimens of this most beautiful and\rinteresting animal, whichwould certainly prove to them “a thing of\rbeauty and a joyfor”--well, several days, if the water is renewed.\r \r \r \r \r                              _JULY 1901._\r \r \rExcessive heat, coupledwith an unusual continuance of fog, have been\rthe principle features ofthis month. The continual booming of our\rexplosive fog-signal everyfive minutes, night and day, would be rather\rapt to “get on” astranger’s nerves were he compelled to sleep within\ra few feet of it; as arule, it does not disturb us in the least, but\rwith such protractedspells as we have had this month it does become a\rtrifle irksome. The firstshot generally sends the beads of some of the\rwindow cases rattling downthe traps. This has a more disturbing effect\ron us when asleep than theactual shot itself, of which we are just\rdimly conscious.\r \rThe few boats which havebeen prosecuting the lobster fishing here for\rthe last three months havenow abandoned it. Although fairly successful\rat the commencement, theywere latterly reduced to a mere pittance.\rA return of four lobstersfor the hauling of fifty “sunks” is but a\rprecarious living.Anchored close to the Rock, in order to avoid being\rrun down by prowlingtrawlers, they often passed the night, sleeping\runderneath their sails.Their cooking range, consisting of an old\rmetal pail with holespunched through the sides, set on a stone slab,\rwhile an empty meat tindid duty as kettle, fish-pan, or tea-pot, as\roccasion required. It isonly within this year or two that the Rock has\ragain attracted theattention of the lobster fisher, after a lapse of\rmany years. Prior to thattime, we could always rely on an occasional\rlobster being found in theholes on the Rock at low water; while crabs,\rwhich could be had inabundance, are now extremely scarce, and the\rlobster, as far as we areconcerned, might well be as extinct as the\rDodo. We had rather asurprising catch in a lobster-creel one time\rhere. On hauling ourcreel, instead of the expectant lobster a huge\rconger-eel was found inpossession, his girth just barely admitting\rhim through the “funnel.”A further surprise, however, awaited us;\rfor, on being cut open, afull-grown lobster was found in his stomach.\rHow the biter in this caseescaped being bitten is a mystery, as one\rwould naturally supposethe lobster, with his powerful claws, would\rbe more than his match.This recalls an incident which happened the\rother day. A pretty littlefish, of a kind we had not yet seen, was,\rafter some manœuvring,placed in a bucket of water along with some\rother fish, sea weeds, andshells. On examining our catch a little\rlater, our pretty strangerwas nowhere visible; suspicion falling on\ran ugly-looking little“poach” complacently resting at the bottom of\rthe bucket, Jeddartjustice was summarily meted out to the suspected\rcannibal; a post-mortemconclusively established his guilt. That these\rfish are cannibals thereis not the slightest doubt. I picked up one\rabout a foot long on abeach in Orkney, which had partly succeeded in\rswallowing, tail first, abrother half his size, but had been choked\rin the attempt; the hornson either side of his victim’s head becoming\rembedded in his gullet, hecould neither entertain nor reject him.\rAmongst the numerous_aliases_ by which the “Poach” is known are the\rfollowing--Bullhead,Hardhead, Cobbler, Shoemaker, Gunflucker, Comper,\rand Johnny Mainland, thelatter being his Orcadian name.\r \rThe terns have increasedto over a hundred this month; from daylight to\rdark their creaking voicesare dinning in our ears. Most active little\rbirds, they are almostcontinually on the wing, wheeling and diving\rwith wonderful celerity.Their prey being surface-swimmers--chiefly\rherring-fry atpresent--necessitate a dive of only a few inches. The\ryoung birds, of whichthere is a goodly sprinkling, though almost as\rbig as the parents, havenot yet acquired the forked tail nor the\rpronounced plumage of theolder birds. Awanting also in dexterity, they\rare being frequently fedby their parents. It is amusing to witness\rthe chagrin of a youngsterwhen, as sometimes happens, an old one has\rmistaken it for its ownoffspring, and only discovers the error when\rabout to drop theglistening prize into its gaping mouth. Woe to the\rgull who dares invadetheir sphere of operations when following a shoal\rof “fry”; he is soon putto rout at the point of the bayonet--for their\rbills are quite as sharppointed. While stationed in Orkney I have,\rwhen in the vicinity oftheir nests, been “assaulted to the effusion\rof blood” as the policereports say, their bills easily penetrating my\rtweed cap. Horses andcattle are driven in mad flight before these bold\rlittle birds, they all thewhile pecking mercilessly till well clear of\rtheir nursery.\r \rThe pleasure steamerswhich formerly visited the Rock from Leith and\rDundee have this summerscarcely made an appearance, possibly the\rattractions of the GlasgowExhibition is the cause; as yet, only three\rvisits have been made, andthese from Dundee. An hour’s fishing is\rgenerally given thepassengers by the Dundee steamer. The diversity\rof tackle with which someof these amateur fishermen are equipped\ris fearful, andclock-weights, half-bricks, and scrap-iron of every\rconceivable shape take theplace of the ordinary sinker. Closely ranged\ralong the vessel’s sides,one can imagine the result of lines so\rdifferently weighted, andshould a fish be hooked confusion follows.\rIf the sea happens to be abit “choppy” many of them may be seen\rearnestly engaged incompulsorily contributing to the support of their\rerstwhile intended prey,each drawing his own line of demarcation down\rthe vessel’s side, as ifsuspicious of his neighbour encroaching on his\rterritory.\r \r \r \r \r                             _AUGUST 1901._\r \r \rThe extreme heat prevalentin the earlier part of this month was\rcharacterised by a numberof unusual visitors but ill adapted for\rany lengthened sojournhere. Butterflies, bees, wasps, and moths\rinnumerable were to beseen flitting about the rocks in the daytime\rand clinging to thelantern at night, numbers of them being drowned\revery time the rocks weresubmerged. Several daddy-longlegs and a\rsingle specimen of thebeautiful painted butterfly were seen among the\rill-fated host. Why theyshould have journeyed to such inhospitable\rquarters is not veryapparent, but possibly the steady westerly wind\rthen blowing wasresponsible for their presence here, and, finding\rthemselves unable to stemthe current, like many other unfortunates,\rthey followed the line ofleast resistance--then, _Facilis descensus\rAverni_, and there youare! We have frequent glimpses at present of an\rexportation of which thestatute-books take no cognisance. Quantities\rof thistledown are to beseen careering before the off-shore wind,\rprobably with Norway fortheir future home. What a wonderful provision\rof Nature that enablesthese mute messengers of the fleeting summer to\rvirtually wing their wayto pastures new! suggestive in their silent\rflight of the\r \r         ... whisper down the field,\r         Where the year has shot her yield,\r         And the ricks stand grey to the sun.\r \rThe sea in our vicinity isjust now actually alive with shoals of\rimmature fish, chieflysand-eels, herring-fry, and what appears to us\rto be finger-longwhitings. Incessant war is being continually waged\rupon them by the ternsfrom above and the poddlies from below. Watch\rthis particular shoal of“fry” as it swims with the current past our\rdoor; notice theorderliness which prevails amongst them, as of a\rdisciplined army. But frombelow the poddlies have sighted them, and\rswift as light they areamongst them with a deadly rush. Completely\rdisorganised, the “fry”scatter in every direction. Some seek shelter\rbeneath the glassy domesof the passing jelly fishes; others, twisting\rand doubling like harescoursed by hounds, spurt spasmodically\ralong the surface in theirfrantic endeavours to escape the enemies\rdestined by nature fortheir destruction. The successful raiders are\rseen scurrying about, withtheir glistening prizes dangling from\rtheir mouths, dodging thethieving attacks of their less successful\rbrethren in the foray. Butsuddenly a flash of bronze in the bright\rsunshine betokens the leapof the lordly lythe, as he in turn seizes\rhis victim from amongstthe attacking force and as quickly returns\rto his lurking-place amongthe luxuriant tangles. And so the war is\rwaged, the strong preyingupon the weak, right down the chain of life,\rtill the unaided eye canbut discern the destroyer alone. One is apt\rto experience a feeling ofrevulsion at the tactics pursued by the\rlythe in thus lurkingconcealed, while above him his prey sport in\rblissful ignorance of hispresence. On the other hand, with what little\rcompunction do weourselves, by every available means, harry their\rnumbers to supply ourtable, and a savoury dish they are at present;\rcooked when freshly caughtthey are simply delicious.\r \rOn Saturday the 10th wehad a heavy thunderstorm; the lightning was\rextremely vivid, andappeared to zig-zag from the sea to the zenith,\rwhile the thunder, atfirst resembling the rippling discharge of small\rarms, gradually increasedto the deep boom of heavy ordnance. The\rhitherto unbroken sea wasthreshed into white foam by the heaviest rain\rI have ever seen here. Thepoddlies, though busy amongst the “fry” at\rthe time, would not deignto look at our “fly,” and, though we tried\rour best, we did notsucceed in hooking a single one. A similar result\ris experienced during theoperation of our explosive fog-signal. As\ran instance how fish ofthe same kind may differ, there is a circular\rpool on the Rock at lowwater, a couple of fathoms deep and about four\rfathoms in diameter, namedNeill’s Pool, but which we have jocularly\rnicknamed “the hospital,”as the poddlies taken from there are, as a\rrule, extremely poor inflesh, often presenting queer abnormities.\rSome are twisted anddeformed; others have constrictions upon their\rbodies, where at someperiod of their existence they had been almost\rcut in two by the snap ofsome larger fish, probably a lythe; others,\ragain, have been takenwith hooks embedded in their jaws and gills,\rand, though in the laststages of emaciation, do not apparently profit\rby their formerexperience. The full-grown lythe may be truly termed\rthe poor man’s salmon, notfrom a food point of view--though in itself\rnot to be despised--but asa source of sport. Equipped with a rod such\ras fishermen use who fishfor a living, and for a lure preferably\ra fresh-water eel aboutsix or seven inches long, skinned from the\r“busking” downwards, astruggle with one of these lusty fish imparts\rmost of the pleasurablesensations of the salmon fisher. Possibly\rat the first cast yourlure is flipped clean out of the water by a\rvanishing tail, denotingthat his lordship has not quite made up his\rmind about yourinvitation. However, your next cast is almost sure to\rbe followed by a swiftrush, which carries him well out of the water,\rand your lure is off tothe bottom and possibly your tackle along with\rit, for, despite yourtriple gut, unless great care is exercised in\rthe first few mad rushes,there will be a dissolution of partnership.\rEasily fagged, once yousucceed in getting his head above the surface,\ra little judicious towingwill land your two-feet bronzed beauty at\ryour feet.\r \r \r \r \r                           _SEPTEMBER 1901._\r \r \rThe Rock has taken onquite a wintry appearance. The vegetation on the\rmore exposed portions hasentirely disappeared under the influence\rof the heavy seasexperienced during the greater part of this month.\rThe acorn barnacles withwhich the higher parts were encrusted are\rfollowing suit owing tothe ravages of the white whelk; the terns have\rdeserted us, and, tocomplete the prospect, on the morning of the 19th\rwe had the first visit ofour winter boarders, the eider duck. A chip\rof rock covered with acornbarnacles becomes an interesting object\rwhen placed in theaquarium. Each conical shell is packed as close as\rpossible to its neighbour,apex upwards. The apex is open, and fitted\rwith a lid composed offour shells. Under water these lid-shells are\rseen to separate, and abunch of “fingers” set on a stalk are thrust\rout, make a clutch, andare withdrawn. The “fingers” have extremely\rfine hair-like processesfixed at right angles to them, the whole\rforming a sort of netthrough which the water is filtered and the\rminute food-formsretained. It is interesting to know that although now\rfixed immovably to therock these animals began life as free swimmers,\rand, strange to say,closely resembled the young crab. Another object\rwe had under observationat the same time was one of the sea anemones,\rnamed the dahlia wartlet.A fleshy-looking disc studded with pieces\rof broken shell and sand,it appeared anything but attractive; but\rseen in the aquarium, theconnection with its floral namesake was at\ronce apparent. Unfoldingitself from an orifice in the centre, as\rone would “flype” astocking, rows of beautiful coloured tentacles\rwere disclosed. Thesetentacles have the property of adhering to any\robject they come incontact with, and contain within themselves some\rwonderful mechanism.Placing a fly on the extremity of one of the\rtentacles, it wasimmediately held fast. The whole of the tentacles\rthen curled inwards,carrying the fly with them, thus clearly showing\rtheir function.\r \rThe heavy easterly surfhas deprived us for the present of our fishing,\rforcing the fish off therock to deeper water. There are evidently\rplenty about, as thegannets are to be seen busy diving in the\rvicinity. It is extremelyinteresting to watch these birds pursuing\rtheir prey. Flitting nearthe surface, they enter the water at an angle\rof about twenty degrees;again, at a higher altitude, they drop like\ra plummet, describing anarc of bubbling foam from their entrance to\rwhere they emerge with abounce a few feet further ahead, beating the\rwater with their wings forseveral yards before being again fairly\ron the wing. The air cellspervading various parts of the body of a\rbird, and which contributeto its buoyancy, are probably vested in a\rgreater degree in thegannet, an extremely large one being situated in\rfront of the forked bone,or clavicles. Several instances are recorded\rwhere a bird which had itswindpipe temporarily obstructed was able,\rby means of these cells,to carry on the function of respiration\rthrough the wing bone, thebroken end of which protruded through the\rskin. The voluntarycompression of these cells, by expelling the air,\rdestroys the buoyancy ofthe bird, and explains the amazing rapidity\rof its descent. Anobjectionable method is practised in some places\rfor the capture of thesebirds. A submerged piece of planking with a\rherring fixed to its uppersurface is set adrift, or towed from a boat,\rin the vicinity of theirfishing grounds. Swooping from an altitude,\rsay, of a hundred feet,they apparently see but the herring alone,\rwith the result that theirnecks are dislocated by impact with the\rplank, the impetus oftheir descent being sometimes so great as to\rbury their bills to thebase in the wood. It is a common sight here,\rduring the breedingseason, to see these birds trooping past in Indian\rfile to their home on theBass Rock, in batches of a dozen or so,\reach preserving a regulardistance from his neighbour. Though I have\rfrequently watched thempursuing their vocation, I have never seen them\rbring their prey to thesurface, nor could I say whether their dive was\rsuccessful or not; butoccasionally they emerge from their dive with\ra satisfied “honk,” whichmay be translated “got ’im.” Gifted with an\rinsatiable appetite, theysometimes gorge themselves to such an extent\ras to be incapable ofrising from the water, when they may be easily\rcaptured, as they make noattempt to dive. An instance of this was\rwitnessed by a large crowdone Sunday, a few summers ago, in Arbroath\rHarbour. Some conceptionof the carrying capacity of these birds may be\rhad when it is known thata sitting mother bird has been seen to insert\rher bill into the invitingmouth of her returned partner and deftly\rextract, one by one, asmany as six full-grown herring.\r \rA “false alarm” wasoccasioned at the end of last month by\rtwo cormorants or scartsappropriating the signal poles as a\rroosting-place. One ofthese poles is fixed on either side of the\rbalcony, and projectshorizontally. When a signal is made from the\rRock, two-feet discs aresuspended from them in pre-arranged positions.\rA wire stay from thebalcony railing supports the extremity of each\rpole, and on this stay thebirds were seated, one at the outer end, the\rother in the middle. Discsin this position, but pendant from the pole,\rby our code reads “Sendboat,” and this the keeper on shore duty in\rArbroath construed it tobe and acted accordingly, with the result that\rwe were somewhat alarmedby the appearance of the harbour tug about\releven the same evening.Our impression was that something serious had\rhappened on shore, andthat one of our number was urgently wanted. On\rthe tug hailing us, andsaying they had been sent out in response to\rsignals shown from theRock that afternoon, our minds reverted to the\rbirds, and our fears setat rest. Considerable alarm prevailed amongst\rour families, and notuntil the tug returned with the news that “All\rwas well on the Rock” weretheir fears allayed.\r \rOn the morning of the 27ththe sea round the Rock was seen to be strewn\rwith apples, a few dozenof which we managed to secure. Their presence\rhere is a mystery, and wetrust has no connection with the long spell\rof fog we have had. On the24th we completed a fusillade of forty\rhours, a record run offog.\r \r \r \r \r                            _OCTOBER 1901._\r \r \rThe flock of eider duckswhich keep us company through the winter\rincreases daily, and nownumbers over thirty. Swimming and diving\ramongst the breakers fromdaylight till dark, it is astonishing how\rthey escape being smashedon the bare rocks. The receding wave may\rleave them almoststranded, and just as the incoming breaker is about\rto engulf them, they popthrough its base and come up on the other\rside in a smother of foam.They are sometimes quite close to the\rtower, and then we have aninteresting view of their proceedings. The\rdiving of one is generallythe signal for the remainder to follow,\rand the whole flock may beclearly seen, a couple of fathoms down,\rscurrying over the rocksin eager quest of the different dainties on\rtheir menu, consistingchiefly of small crabs. The capture of one of\rthese crabs by no meansensures that it will ultimately contribute\rto the duck’ssustenance--this is not intended as a reflection on\rtheir digestive power,which appears equal to anything short of\rnails, considering thequantity of hard-shelled crabs they assimilate\rduring a day’sfishing--for, on gaining the surface with his prize,\rhe may be immediatelyassailed by the marauding gulls and compelled\rto dive with his prey.This may be repeated several times, until he\rreluctantly surrenders thesucculent tit-bit, or is compelled to\rswallow it under water--aproceeding they are evidently averse to,\rotherwise the gulls wouldfare but poorly in their nefarious calling.\rThe uncertainty of thecrab’s final lodgment is again demonstrated\rin the case of thesuccessful “blackmailer.” Hastily swallowing his\rbooty to avoid beingplundered in turn by his fellows, he is again on\rwatch for the reappearanceof his unwilling providers. But retribution\roccasionally overtakes thedespoiler as it does his human prototype,\rwith the difference thatin default of imprisonment, he is mulcted\rin the contents of hisstomach, the nemesis in this case being the\rdusky-coated skua orrobber gull, who with his hawk-like flight easily\rheads him at every turn,and the chase terminates only when the\rcontents of the stomachare disgorged, or the excrement voided, either\rof which is adroitlycaught by this foul freebooter of the sea before\rit reaches the water.\r \rA hazy moonless night,with a sou’-easterly breeze and drizzling\rrain--given theseconditions, at this season of the year we have\rnumerous visits of variousbirds, members of the autumnal migratory\rflight. Making straightfor the light, they dash themselves against\rthe heavy plate-glass ofthe lantern; many of them are thus killed\rand swept by the wind intothe sea. Others, again, arrive with more\rcaution, and though takenin the hand and thrown clear of the tower\rinvariably return, andremain fluttering against the glass till\rdaylight reveals to themthe futility of their exertions in that\rdirection. The most numerousof these visitors are the redwings and\rfieldfares, butblackbirds, larks, starlings, wheatears, finches, tits,\retc., may be met with inthe course of the season. It is somewhat\rstartling, when on watchin the lightroom, to hear the thud with\rwhich they strike. Thewoodcock, owing to his rapid flight, strikes\rhardest of all, and theother extreme is met with in the smallest\rof our British birds, thetiny gold-crested wren, whose presence on\rthe lantern is announcedby a feeble tinkling sound, which a robust\rbutterfly might easilyimitate. The heavier birds do not always strike\rwith impunity; instanceshave occurred where ducks have gone clean\rthrough the lantern to thederangement of the revolving gear of the\rlight, the splinteredglass bringing the machinery to a dead stop.\rAn incident of this naturehappened a few years ago at Turnberry\rLighthouse, on theAyrshire coast, the intruder in this case being a\rcurlew or whaup. Astorm-pane is considered a necessary adjunct to\revery lightroom, and isalways held in readiness to be shipped in\rcase of such emergency. Atsome shore stations it is customary on the\rapproach of a favourablenight, during the migratory period, to keep\rthe cats indoors toprevent them mangling the expected catch. In one\rparticular instance thebirds collected of a morning filled an ordinary\rclothes-basket, and a fewnights later included five wild geese, which\rwere secured out of alarge flock that came to grief on the dome.\r \rAn hour before daybreak onthe 22nd it appeared as if we were about to\rsuffer a bombardment, andthat daylight was to witness the commencement\rof hostilities. No lessthan seven torpedo-boat destroyers were\rseen creeping close up tothe Rock, their low black hulls scarcely\rdiscernible in the feeblelight, and not until daylight disclosed\rthe white ensign were weassured of their intentions. A little later\rthey were joined by threegunboats and, after some clever manœuvring,\rformed into three lines,the gunboats occupying the centre. They then\rsteamed away in thedirection of the Firth of Forth. Two hours later\rother three gunboatspassed us, going in the same direction, escorted\rby four destroyers, andfollowed shortly after by a solitary gunboat.\rExtremely interesting itwas to witness the precision and dexterity of\rtheir movements as theyswung into their respective positions for the\radvance, their semaphoresall the while going like windmills. Again, on\rthe 24th, about 11 a.m., afleet of about a dozen battleships, headed\rby a dispatch boat, wasseen moving in stately procession from the Tay,\revidently bound for theForth.\r \rWe have had severalheliographic communications from our shore station\rin Arbroath during themonth, and providing there is sunshine there is\rnow no difficulty intransmitting messages to the Rock by this means.\rFour years ago the late DrRussell, Arbroath, while on a professional\rvisit to the shorestation, for which he was medical attendant,\rwitnessed our initialattempts in this direction, and, convinced of the\rfeasibility of the method,urged upon us, in his characteristically\rvigorous style, thenecessity for persevering in our attempts, at the\rsame time predicting thatit would ultimately prove successful. Little\rdid we then dream it wassoon to become the means of conveying the\rsorrowful intelligence ofthis estimable gentleman’s death.\r \r \r \r \r                            _NOVEMBER 1901._\r \r \rBoisterous weatherprevailing for the greater part of this month,\rwe have been closelyconfined to the house. Our connection with the\ramphibia being soextremely remote completely disqualifies us from\renjoying our usual“constitutional,” the grating, even at low water,\rbeing occasionally sweptby the heavy seas. Our winter boarders, the\reider ducks, have beenreinforced, on the morning of the 14th--somewhat\rlater than usual--by thearrival of a flock of long-tailed ducks.\rThese, with the eiders,will keep us company till April again calls\rtheir attention todomestic affairs. Our relief, which was due on the\rnight of the 11th, waseffected just in time; had it been delayed\ranother day a “missedrelief” would probably have been recorded. The\rmorning after brought asevere north-easterly gale, which precluded all\rpossibility of making alanding during the three succeeding days. That\ris usually the timeallotted by the steamer in the attempt. Should she\rfail to make a landing onthe third day, we are abandoned for another\rfortnight, minus the timeengaged in the attempt. As our stock of\rfresh provisions isgenerally consumed by the time the relief is due,\ra missed relief means afortnight’s _regime_ of “hard tack” and “beef\rembalmed,” of which duringthe winter months we have a three months’\rreserve stock on hand incase of such emergencies. Fortunately, this is\rnot of common occurrence;during the past six years but three reliefs\rhave been missed, and onlyone in the preceding ten. This speaks much\rfor the ability and skillof those concerned in the handling of the\rboats, for during thewinter months the landings were until recently\reffected in darkness, andan exciting scene it was to see the two boats\rbuffeting their waythrough the foaming channels, with jutting rocks\rso close on either sidethat an oar’s length deviation would entail\rserious disaster. Apowerful searchlight has of recent years been added\rto the equipment of therelieving steamer, and is of much advantage in\rthe guidance of the boats,though it has the peculiarity of grossly\rexaggerating thetempestuous appearance of the sea. The sea, which on\rthe evening of the reliefwas comparatively calm, was the next day\rrolling down on us like asolid wall, and viewed from the balcony in\rall its magnificentgrandeur what a puny, frail, unstable structure\rour habitation seemed incomparison. Each succeeding wave seemed\rimbued with the solemotive of accomplishing our destruction, and as\rthey struck and slicedaway on either side in two mighty crescents\rof hissing foam, blindedour kitchen windows seventy feet above the\rrock. Clashing togetheragain to leeward with a roar, as if incensed\rat our stubbornresistance, they drive their way furiously along the\rremaining portion of thereef in foam-capped ridges, and where the\rcross seas meet them thespray is flung high in the air from their\rpoints of intersection.The appearance of the reef at this stage, as\rseen from our elevation,is of a number of rectangular enclosures, each\rabout the size of anordinary bowling-green, with well-defined walls,\rthe whole under a heavycoating of snow, with each corner marked by\ra snow-laden tree. At highwater--the sea having flowed about twelve\ror fifteen feet on thebuilding by that time--the waves, generally\runbroken, slip pastharmlessly; an hour before or after high water is\rwhen we experience theheaviest shocks, for then the depth of water is\rsuch that the waves arearrested by the rock when close to the tower,\rand their whole volumeflung violently against the building. The effect\rof such weather on thetower must be felt to be understood. The nearest\rdescription I can give ofthe seas striking is as if a log of wood were\rhurled by each sea,striking end on, and a short, sharp, tremulous\rmotion--sufficient torattle the crockery in the kitchen cupboard--is\rimparted to the tower byeach impact. This tremor is more particularly\rfelt when the galesubsides and the heavy swell sets in, for when the\rgale is at its height, theseas are so broken and tossed about that\rtheir assaults are butfeeble in comparison with those of the long\rcurly-headed combers ofthe after-swell. The bell-shaped formation\rof the base of the toweris admirably adapted for withstanding the\rassaults of the sea, andis built solid to a height of thirty feet,\rabove which the seas neverstrike, though I have seen the spray\rcarried right over ourbalcony, a hundred feet from the rock. That the\rbuilding remains to allappearance as intact as when completed, almost\ra century ago, speaksvolumes for the skill and ingenuity displayed in\rits erection. In weathersuch as I have described we are as completely\rcut off from outsideassistance as though we were at the North Pole;\rindeed, it is doubtful ifthere is another situation--save similar\rones, of course--where mencould live so comfortable and unconcerned\rand yet remain for thetime being so completely “ungetatable.”\r \r \r \r \r                            _DECEMBER 1901._\r \r \rAs a consequence of thestormy weather which has been prevailing here\rof late, we have beenvisited by numerous “Travellers.” This may seem\rstrange considering theinclemency of the season, but stranger still\rwhen it is known that ourreception of them is fiercely hostile,\rand our duty onlyconsidered accomplished when we have completely\rannihilated them. Hugeboulders of hard red sandstone, sometimes\rweighing over three tons;these are our “Travellers,” and their\rappearance on the Rock isat once resented and their speedy removal\reffected by blasting andhammering whenever the tide and weather\rpermits. This isabsolutely necessary, for if allowed to remain\rlying in the boat tracksthey constitute a serious danger at relief\rtimes, besides thepossibility of their carrying away portions of our\rcast-iron grating, whichoccasionally does happen in spite of all\rprecautions. Where theycome from is a mystery; ever since the tower\rwas built they have beenin evidence. Although composed of the same\rmaterial, the Rock itselfdoes not suffer any apparent diminution, nor\rcan their original abodebe located even at the lowest tides. Many of\rthem carry a crop ofseaweed and tangles, and have their angularities\rrubbed down andwater-worn; none of them, however, bear any trace of\rrecent detachment, butprobably from their similarity of structure they\rat some remote periodformed a part of the reef. They generally effect\rtheir entrance from thesouth side of the reef during the prevalence of\ra heavy ground swell. Thisside of the reef forms a steep declivity,\rsloping to 35 fathoms at adistance of ¾ mile, while at a similar\rdistance on the north sidethe depth, though not exceeding 11 fathoms,\rpresents a moreprecipitous barrier to these wanderers of the deep. A\rdull, rumbling noise,distinctly audible in the light room, announces\rtheir presence at the baseof the tower, and at low water a dotted\rline of chips andabrasions marks their passage across the Rock to\rwhere they are againhurled to the depths. Others, again, may bring up\rin some sheltered corner,where, if not considered dangerous, they may\rremain a fixture foryears.\r \rAn instance occurredrecently where one was wheeled against our grating\rafter occupying a safeposition for many years. Those that take up\rpositions in the boattracks are of course assailed at the earliest\ropportunity, an operationwhich generally entails a bit of submarine\rmining on our part. Thereef consists of hard, red sandstone, arranged\rin irregular layers, witha dip of 15 degrees towards the south-east\rand extends in anorth-easterly and south-westerly direction, having\ran area of about 500 yardsby 100 yards considered dangerous to\rshipping. The north-eastend, on which the Lighthouse is built, is\rslightly higher, and hasan area of about 140 yards by 70 yards, the\rhighest portions of whichdo not exceed 10 feet above the lowest tides.\rThe geological formationof the Bell Rock is similar to that of the\rRedhead, in Forfarshire,and can be traced northward through Rossshire,\rwhile in the oppositedirection the shores of Berwick present the same\rfeatures, and continues asfar as Cumberland. Soundings prove the\rexistence of a ridge orshallower part of the sea bottom extending\ra considerable way inthese directions, and as the adjacent coasts\rpresent ample evidence ofthe sea having at some remote period in the\rworld’s history occupied amuch higher level, the theory that the Bell\rRock did not always occupythe isolated position it now does, but\rstretched continuouslyfrom the Red Head to Berwick, damming the waters\rof the Forth and Tay,appears highly tenable. Possibly our present day\r“Travellers” are, throughsome great seismic disturbance, wandering\revidences supporting thistheory.\r \rAn item of interest toArbroath Freemasons is the laying of the\rfoundation stone of theBell Rock Lighthouse, on the 10th July 1808,\rwith Masonic honours, bythe builder, Robert Stevenson, who, in\rhis own words, applied thesquare, the level, and the mallet, and\rpronounced the followingbenediction:--“May the Great Architect of\rthe Universe complete andbless this building,” on which three hearty\rcheers were given andsuccess to the future operations was drunk with\rthe greatest enthusiasm.Another interesting feature of that period\rwas the existence of the“Pressgang,” which, owing to our war with the\rNorthern Powers, wasconsidered necessary. Centres were established at\rDundee, Aberdeen, andArbroath, and were the means of rendering the\rLighthouse operationspopular with seamen, as they stood protected\rfrom impressment while inthat employment. Prior to this there was a\rtendency among seamen toshun the works on account of the hazardous\rnature of the undertaking.As the impress officers were exceedingly\ractive in their duty, itwas found necessary to furnish each seaman\rengaged in the operationsat the Rock with a “ticket,” descriptive of\rhis person, to which wasattached a silver medal, emblematical of the\rLighthouse Service. On oneside of the medal was a figure of the Bell\rRock Lighthouse, and onthe other the word “Medal,” referring to the\rAdmiralty protection, anda description of the person by the engineer.\rOne of these medals is atpresent in possession of an Arbroath\rgentleman, and is said tobe the only one in existence. The following\ris a copy of one of the“tickets,” taken from “Stevenson’s Bell Rock\rLighthouse”:--\r \r \r                                       BELLROCK WORKYARD,\r                                      Arbroath, 31st March 1808.\r \r     “John Pratt, seaman, in the service of theHonourable the\r     Commissioners of the Northern Lighthouses,aged 35 years,\r     5 feet 8 inches high, black complexion,and slightly marked\r     with the smallpox.”\r \r                                  (Signed)ROBERT STEVENSON,\r                               Engineer forNorthern Lighthouses.\r \r \r                              _Obverse._\r \r     “The Bearer, John Pratt, is serving onboard of the ‘Sir\r     Joseph Banks’ tender and craft, employedat the erection of\r     the Bell Rock Lighthouse.”\r \r     The signature of the Master of the tender.\r \r                                       (Signed) DAVID TAYLOR.\r              The signature of the bearer(Signed) JOHN PRATT.\r \rNotwithstanding theseprecautions, so rigorous were the impress\rofficers that theyactually pressed a Bell Rock seaman named George\rDall, while on a visit tosome friends near Dundee, in July 1810, and\rthis despite the fact ofhis having the protection medal and ticket\rin his possession. Theseproofs the officer chose to ignore, holding\rthat a seaman only stoodprotected on board the ship to which the\rAdmiralty protection hadbeen granted, or in a boat belonging to the\rship. This was absurd, asit was impossible for each man to carry the\rship’s protection withhim. However, Dall was kept a prisoner, and only\ron the representations ofthe Lighthouse Commissioners did the Dundee\rMagistrates order hisrelease.\r \r \r \r \r                            _JANUARY 1902._\r \r \rA ramble round the rocksat low water just now discloses a scene of\rbareness quite in keepingwith the season of the year. The upper\rsurface of the higherlying rocks is as bare as a street pavement, and\ronly an occasional patchof acorn barnacles remains of the encrustation\rwith which they wereinvested during the summer. The white whelk,\rso much in evidence here,have all gone into winter quarters, and\runderneath projectingledges and in sheltered nooks they may be seen in\rmyriads, their positionbeing so judiciously chosen as to be completely\rprotected from the heavynorth-east seas. So closely are they wedged\rtogether that were a givenspace to be cleared it would be found almost\rimpossible to replace themin the same area. Detaching one from its\ranchorage, it seems quitedormant and inert, and appears to have lost\rthe alacrity with which,in summer, they withdraw themselves into their\rshells, and only withapparent difficulty is the operculum or door\rof their domicile closedagainst intruders. To witness the continual\rthumping and pounding towhich the Rock is subjected during the winter,\rone is surprised to findthat life in any form should continue to\rexist under suchconditions. A close search reveals exceedingly minute\rforms of life. Here inthis stony basin, originally but a shallow\rdepression in which astone had lodged, and by the swirling action of\rthe seas converted to itspresent shape, with its sediment of broken\rshells, is a small crab,so small indeed that a split pea might easily\rconceal him. He is not ayoungster either, but fully adult, in proof of\rwhich we have frequentlyfound them, in the proper season, with their\rspawn attached. Deep inhis little pit he seems quite immune from the\rfurious seas that tumbleoverhead as the tide makes. Numbers of small\rwhite-banded whelks, whichone may easily crush between the fingers,\rmaintain their position onthe base of the tower, despite the constant\rswirl of waters, thoughthey may be detached with a flick of the finger.\r \rVegetation now exists onlyat low-water mark; above that, broken tangle\rroots, or, to be morecorrect, the claspers are seen still adhering\rto the rocks, the tanglesthemselves having been shorn clean from\rtheir moorings. Awaytowards the south-west, in the deeper water, a\rboat may float among wholegroves of storm-torn tangles as they flaunt\rtheir tattered banners inthe frosty sunlight, suggestive of leafless\rtrees in a winterlandscape. Over the recently emptied contents of the\rcook’s slop-pail a flockof gulls are circling and screaming, actually\rhustling each other intheir attempts to capture anything edible.\rA solitary “black-back” isseen amongst the noisy crowd, and as he\rswoops at some temptingmorsel, his black, beady eye watches our every\rmovement with suspicion.What a handsome bird he is as he swings past\rwithin a few feet of us,the back and wings presenting a dead black\rappearance in startlingcontrast with the immaculate whiteness of the\rfan-shaped tail and theremainder of the body. Despite his handsome\rappearance, he is averitable vulture, and nothing comes amiss to\rhim in the way of food, beit fish, flesh or fowl. Frequently I have\rseen them make a meal of awounded duck, and once witnessed in Orkney\ra tug-of-war between twoof them for the possession of a dead lamb,\rresulting, thanks to itsdecomposed state, in an equal division.\r \rMore gruesome meals arecredited to them by those who have witnessed\rtheir proceedings on awreck strewn shore where loss of life had been\rinvolved. A terror also onthe grouse moors, they devour both eggs and\ryoung, and even thesitting grouse herself is not safe from him. One\rcan scarcely credit such asweeping indictment against this handsome\rbird, but the proofs areall too plain. Consequently we find him\routside the pale of theWild Birds Protection Act, an Ishmael among\rhis kind, whom any man mayslay when and wherever found. Except when\rharrying the eider ducksof their legitimate spoil, he may be seen\rriding gracefully, head towind, in front of our kitchen window, with\rhis weather eye alwayslifting in our direction. A hand thrust from the\rwindow is sufficientinvitation, he is up at once, and the smallest\rmorsel tossing among thefoaming breakers does not escape his keen\reye. How gracefully hefloats back to his former position, lighting on\rthe surface like a fleckof foam. What a contrast to the eiders, who,\rwhen changing theirfishing ground, wing their way with such rapid\rwing beats as to give onethe impression that they are barely able\rto support themselves, andfinally strike the water with an awkward\rsplash, reminding one ofthe somewhat inelegant term with which boys\rdesignate a bad dive--a“gutser.” Should a flock of eiders be fishing\rto leeward of the tower,an amusing sight may be witnessed if advantage\rbe taken, while they areunder water, of pouring a little paraffin\roil from the balcony, sothat it will drift in their direction. No\rsooner does the head ofthe first emerge in the greasy track of the\roil than he is consciousof something unusual having taken place.\rFlippering hither andthither with outstretched neck, he becomes quite\rexcited, and each as hebounces to the surface joins in the commotion,\rfrequently colliding witheach other. Finally, with loud cacklings, the\rwhole flock takes wing,evidently in high dudgeon at the insult offered\rto their olfactory organs.\r \rSea pheasant is the nameby which the long tailed duck is known in\rsome localities, and as wewatch a flock of them crossing the reef in\rfull flight the synonym isat once apparent. In style of flight and\rshape, to the long tailfeathers, they are similar to the pheasant,\rbut only half the size,with beautiful plumage of black and white.\rHere they are known as“candlewicks,” their call notes needing but\rlittle stretch of theimagination to be rendered “Here’s a candlewick,”\rrepeated several times inshrill falsetto, which on a quiet day becomes\rsomewhat annoying as itclamorously floats through our bedroom window.\rSome queer visitors wehave here at times in the way of birds. Once\rwe captured a large owldosing sleepily in one of our windows. During\rthe week of his captivityhe would not deign to partake of any food\rwe offered him. Coming offwatch one night I took one of a flock of\rlarks which were makingsuicidal attempts to pierce the plate glass\rof the lantern. Placing itin the room where the owl was roosting, it\rfluttered to the window,when, like a flash of lightning and equally as\rnoiseless, from the otherside of the room the owl came crash against\rthe glass, a few featherslater on testifying his appreciation of this\rform of dietary.\r \r \r \r \r                            _FEBRUARY 1902._\r \r \rPiercing cold weather hereof late, with a good deal of frost and\roccasional snow showers.No matter how heavy the snowfall may be here\rwe only see it falling, asit does not lie long round _our_ doors, and\ronly when our gaze isdirected Arbroathwards--which, you may be sure,\ris not seldom--are wereminded of its occurrence. The close of last\rmonth saw our barometertaxed to its utmost intelligence, and though\ra tenth higher would haveseen its limit, nothing of a phenomenal\rnature was noted. Thesolan geese or gannets, which are pretty much in\revidence here during thebreeding season, foraging for their families\ron the Bass Rock,gradually disappeared, till during the month of\rNovember not one was to beseen. A solitary one was seen in the first\rweek of December, andsince then the number sighted has gradually\rincreased, till in themiddle of the present month, as many as eight\rin one string were countedwinging their way southward. The Bass Rock,\rAilsa Craig, and theoutlying stacks of lonely St Kilda, are said to be\rthe only breeding placesof these birds in Scotland. At the beginning\rof the past century theywere considered a dainty article of food by\rthe Edinburgh gentry, andthe Bass Rock was rented for the purpose of\rsupplying the market, thebirds selling at the rate of half-a-crown\ra-piece. I have seen itstated that the _modus operandi_ of these\rbirds when engaged infishing is to flit along the surface till fish\rare sighted, when theyrise to a high altitude, close their wings, and\rdrop hawk-like on theirprey. This, I venture to think, is scarcely\rcorrect. My experience isthat when flitting near the surface if fish\rare sighted they areinvariably struck at without rising to a higher\relevation. It is a wellknown fact that objects under water are more\reasily distinguished froma height than from near the surface, so that\rit may be taken for grantedthat the higher these birds are flying when\rin pursuit of prey thedeeper the fish are swimming. Again, when diving\rfrom a high altitude, thewings are kept rigidly outspread, and as the\rtail is never seen spreadrudder-like, as in the case of the hawk, any\rdeviation from their lineof descent is controlled by the long narrow\rwings, and only whennearing the “plunge” are they partially closed.\r \rFor the past fortnight wehave had the company of a solitary seal. His\rfishing does not seem tobe very successful, either in quantity or\rquality, as the only catchwe have seen him negotiating was a saithe\rthe length of a man’sforearm. Playing with it as a cat would a mouse,\rhe would allow it to swimfeebly for some distance, then diving he\rwould bring it to thesurface, till latterly, with a toss of his head\rand a thrust with his foreflipper, he quite disembowelled it, an act\rof charity which thescreaming gulls were not slow to appreciate.\rAlthough so long here hehas not been seen to rest on the rocks;\rindeed, I only once sawone ashore here, and as we had a somewhat\ramusing experience withhim it will perhaps bear relating. For several\rdays it was seen, as thetide fell, to rest in one particular place a\rfew yards from the base ofthe tower. Our outer door opens outwards,\rand is always closed atnight, not that we are afraid of burglars, but\rmerely to prevent theentrance of the seas, and for our own general\rcomfort. The opening ofthis door always alarmed the seal, and sent him\rinto the water_instanter_. Dropping a line from the balcony at low\rwater, we made the end ofit fast within a few feet of his accustomed\rresting place. Next day,as the tide fell and the rocks began to\rappear, he was seen totake up his former position, yawning lazily as\rhe rolled from side toside in the sunshine. Fixing a four ounce charge\rof tonite to our electriccable, we quietly lowered it down the line\rwe had already made fasttill within about six feet from where he lay,\rapparently in blissfulignorance of what was happening overhead. When\ryawning at his widest, we,by means of our magneto-exploder, fired the\rcharge, and, well--hestopped yawning and went away! and his going was\rabout the smartest thing Iever witnessed. The force of the explosion,\rbeing unconfined, merelytilted him on his side, but quickly recovering\rhimself he flopped intothe water and shot seaward through the gully\rlike a flash, a black lineunder water denoting his course. Rounding\rthe outer end of thegully, he doubled back on the outside of the reef,\rand when opposite hisoriginal position, made his appearance on the\rsurface, a very muchstartled seal. His aspect was quite comical as he\rstood, so to speak, on histip-toes evidently investigating the cause\rof his hurried departure.\r \rSeveral schools ofporpoises have been seen this month, presumably in\rpursuit of herring. Toanyone who has seen these animals gambolling\rin front of a ship’s bowswhen travelling at her best, the ease with\rwhich they maintain theirdistance is a matter of surprise--always on\rthe point of being rundown, but ever ahead, snorting playfully as\rif in derision at thepossibility of their being overtaken by their\rlumbering follower. Offthe island of Anticosta, in the Gulf of St\rLawrence--where theseanimals attain a size several times larger\rthan those of our homewaters, and are of a cream colour--I had an\rinteresting view of theirmanner of suckling their young. I have seen\rit stated that the motherby muscular compression expels the nutritive\rfluid, which is absorbedby the young one as it floats to the surface.\rThe operation appeared tome to be one of actual contact. The young\rone--which, by the way, isof a slatey-blue colour--snuggling as\rclose as possible to themother as she lay somewhat on her side on\rthe surface, all the whileexhibiting the tenderest solicitude for\rher offspring. Truly theone touch of nature which makes the whole\rworld kin. It issurprising to learn the evolution these animals\rhave undergone in order toaccommodate themselves to their altered\rcircumstances.Land-dwellers at one stage of the world’s history, but\racquiring a taste forfish, they gradually became aquatic in their\rhabits, dispensing withsuch portions of their anatomy as were no\rlonger necessary, whiledeveloping others more appropriate to their new\rsphere of existence, till,like their big brother the whale, from being\ra four-footed animal theybecame quite fish like in appearance, even to\rthe cultivation of adorsal fin, though still possessing rudimentary\rtraces of their formerconstruction. Change is apparent on every hand\rin the plan of nature;ages were necessary for the evolution of our\rpresent day horse from hisfive toed ancestors; and after all it does\rnot seem so very startlingwhen the transformation is enacted before\rour very eyes in a fewshort stages, as in the case of the common\rfrog, from the gillbreathing tadpole to the lung breathing adult.\rMore startling it is tolearn that man himself was at one time a gill\rbreather, and, asbiologists affirm, still exhibits traces of gill\rclefts at one stage of hisembryonic development.\r \r \r \r \r                             _MARCH 1902._\r \r \rSigns of uneasiness andunrest are now apparent amongst our winter\rboarders, the eiders andlong-tailed ducks. Taking wing on the\rslightest provocation,they wheel aimlessly round the Rock, and instead\rof their usual steadypersistence in diving for a living, they seem\rquite discontented withtheir lot, and plainly making up their minds\rto desert us for thesummer. Advances by the males are as yet met with\rscornful rebuffs by theirless showy plumaged partners, but soon a\rmutual understanding willbe arrived at, and before the month closes\rthey will have gonehouse-hunting, eiders possibly to the Isle of May,\rwhile the long-tails,being migratory, seek their homes in the frozen\rNorth. It seems a strangeanomaly that the less robust looking longtail\rshould choose suchrigorous latitudes for the rearing of its brood,\rwhile the sturdy “dunter,”swathed in his arctic coat, should elect to\rstay at home. On the otherhand, we have been visited on hazy nights by\rnumbers of larks andthrushes returning to our shores, after wintering\rin “Norroway ower thefaem.” These members of the spring migratory\rmovement often come togrief on our lantern, and when one considers\rthe number of lighthousesround our coasts, it will be understood that\rthe death-roll from thiscause alone must be extremely high. Designed\rto save life, weunwittingly lure our feathered friends to their\rdestruction.\r \rA couple of seals havebeen sporting round our door of late, and they\ralso exhibit signs ofexuberance in keeping with the season. At high\rwater they come quiteclose to the tower, and their antics are seen\rto advantage from ourbalcony. Rolling over each other, they make for\rthe bottom, gliding alongthe rocks like hounds hunting in couples;\rthen with a rush they areon the surface, floating bolt upright, with\rtheir muzzles almosttouching, staring with their large, expressive\reyes into each other’sface. An almost human touch was given to their\rplay by one taking thehead of the other between his fore-flippers, as\rif about to salute him, ormore likely her, in the orthodox fashion.\rOne was seen the othermorning in possession of a large fish, while\ra number of gulls sat at asafe distance round him, waiting for the\rfragments when the feastshould begin. By the way he glared at them, he\rwas evidently annoyed attheir presence. Sinking for a few seconds, he\rappeared on the surfaceminus the fish. This was evidently intended as\ra ruse, and meant to implythat he had lost it; but the gulls seemed to\rknow better, and kepttheir position. Diving, he made his appearance\rsome distance off, thistime with the fish in his mouth, only to find\rhimself, to his annoyance,again the centre of wistful expectations.\rPresuming these gulls tobe up-to-date birds, their exulting cacklings\rmight be literallyrendered--“You better begin, Mister Phoca; it’s no\ruse trying, you know; youcan’t possibly dewett us!” At least, the seal\rseemed to think so, for hethere and then opened the banquet with a rip\rof his teeth thatdistributed the offal amongst the hungry cordon.\r \rThe rocks become at thisseason of the year invested with a slippery\rcoating of algæ, whichrenders it extremely difficult to maintain one’s\rfooting, and alsonecessitates repeated applications of hot lime to our\rgratings in order torender them passable. Myriads of minute whelks, no\rlarger than turnip seed,strew the rocks and crunch under foot as we\rwalk, while great patchesof mussel spawn delight the heart of the more\rventuresome of the whitewhelks--a prospecting party who will doubtless\rcommunicate the promisingstate of the commissariat to their fellows\rstill in winter quarters.\r \rFishing in the Rock poolshas been tried for the first time this\rseason, and resulted inthe capture of a solitary “cobbler.” It may be\ra month hence before wemeet with any success.\r \rThis month has beenextremely mild, though the hills behind Arbroath\rare still seen to carryportions of their winter coat, while the\rhigher ranges inland arecompletely snow-capped. On a clear day our\rview is limited by TodHead, about twenty-five miles to the north,\rand St Abb’s Head thirtymiles south of us. The coast-line presents a\runiform flatness, whichbecomes monotonous in comparison with the more\rpicturesque raggedness ofthe West Coast. A most conspicuous feature\rin the landscape in thevicinity of Arbroath is the clump of trees on\rthe summit of the LawHill--a landmark well known to navigators, and\reasily discernible, as itstands sharply defined against the sky-line.\rArbroath, when notenveloped in smoke, is clearly seen, and with the\raid of our telescope theafter-church promenaders can be distinguished\ron the Protection Wall, orwending their way towards the Victoria Park.\r \r \r \r \r                             _APRIL 1902._\r \r \rThe extremely low tidesprevalent at the opening of the month enabled\rus to extend our huntinggrounds somewhat further than usual, and also\rto reach and demolishseveral “travellers” which the heavy seas had\rhurled into the boattracks, thus constituting a serious danger at\rrelief times. Quite aforest of luxuriant tangles now cover the lower\rlying portion of the reef.Their dripping blades appear on the surface,\rscintillating in thebrilliant sunshine like so many diamonds, till\rthe receding tide permitsthe warm sun to rob them of their freshness,\rtheir beauty vanishing ina perceptible vapour, leaving them flaccid\rand inert till thereturning tide restores their pristine beauty. The\rbadderlock or henware ishere also in great profusion, and usually\rselects a position thereverse of peaceful, being generally found\rwhere the wash of the seasis most constant. Of rapid growth, they\rattain a great length,some measuring fully sixteen feet; one we had\runder observation was seento increase a foot in length in six weeks\rtime. Owing to hazyweather we had a number of compulsory visitors to\rdinner yesterday. Seatedoutside our kitchen window was a party of\rfog-bound travellers,consisting of a pigeon, a starling, a wagtail,\ra robin, and a couple ofwheatears. The starling was sitting bunched\rup by himself, preservinga stolid indifference at his enforced\rdetention, and appeared totreat the animated expansion and flirting\rof the wheatears’ tails asundue levity, unbecoming their sorrowful\rpredicament. The beautifulblack-throated wagtail is all alertness, and\rthe slightest movement onour part sends him circling round the Rock\rtill, unable to sight theland, he is fain to regain his resting place.\rThe pigeon has been here aweek now, and evidently has no intention\rof leaving. Should thewindow be left open he makes bold enough to\renter, although but theother day he gave us a somewhat dramatic\rillustration of theproverbial hen on the hot “griddle” by rehearsing\ra fandango on the top ofour cooking range, a position from which he\rhad to be forciblyremoved. To-day, the 21st, he has been joined by a\rcompanion of his ownspecies, a red-chequered homer; but instead of the\rmutual demonstrations ofpleasure one would expect to witness at their\rmeeting in such isolation,they remained quite indifferent to each\rother’s presence, thenewcomer possibly from motives of disdain, as he\rappears to belong to the aristocracy,seeing he sports an aluminium\rbracelet, on which are theletters “U.B.” and the year 1901, besides\ra number composed of threefigures, which, unfortunately, I took no\rnote of. A strongsoutherly breeze on the 22nd deprived us of their\rcompany. Losing theshelter of the tower, they were unable to make\rheadway against the wind,and, fortunately for themselves, were driven\rlandwards.\r \rOn the 20th a small patchof paidle-fish spawn was seen cemented in\ra sheltered nook of therocks. This is unusually early for nesting\roperations, as it isgenerally May before they are much in evidence\rhere. The extremely smallquantity may denote a change of mind on the\rpart of the depositor;besides, the site is badly chosen, as the nest\ris a couple of feet abovelow water, and consequently without the\rcock’s guardianship forsome time each tide. Possibly the heavy seas\rprevalent during the pastfortnight may have warned the builder of\rbeing somewhat prematurein her operations.\r \rWe had oculardemonstration the other day concerning a matter of which\rdoubts have beenexpressed, namely, the skinning of their prey by\rseals. Not only do theyskin their fish, but each shred of skin is\rgreedily swallowed as soonas stripped. The skinning entails a good\rdeal of trouble, as thefish is pushed away from the seal at every\rmouthful, and consequentlysinks, so that a dive is necessary each time\rin order to resumeoperations. Why he should take all this trouble\ris not apparent, butpresumably he understands his own business\rbest. His operations atpresent are watched by us with longing eyes,\rfor though he appears tohave all he wants we are as yet fishless.\rHowever, the presence ofthe paidle spawn is a hopeful sign, and is\rthe first attraction forthe wandering cod, by whom it is greedily\rdevoured, providing theycan steal a march on the red-coated sentry--a\rdifficult matter, onewould think, considering how assiduous he is in\rthe protection of hischarge. The white whelks, presumably adopting\rthe promising report ofthe reconnoitring party sent out last month,\rhave turned out _enmasse_, and are now waging a one-sided war of\rextermination upon thedefenceless mussels.\r \rThe times change and wechange with them. Our present light is doomed,\rand what the assaults ofalmost a century’s gales have failed to\raccomplish will succumb tothe demands of modern innovation. Doubtless,\rthe presiding genius ofthe reef will be congratulating himself, as he\rbares his head each tideto witness the process of demolition, on the\rreturn of the palmy dayswhen as yet no meddling light interfered with\rthe working of his ownsweet will in dealing death and destruction to\rmany a stout ship.Happily, this view is only apparent, for by early\rautumn a much morepowerful light will be installed, and a new lease of\rlife granted to the grandold building which has so effectively served\rthe maritime world since1811.
