Probably but few on shore noticed the\rfirst appearance of thetemporary light on the evening of the 30th.\rOf weaker power, but presentingsimilar characteristics as the future\rlight, namely, red andwhite flashes alternately, with an interval of\rthirty seconds betweeneach flash, it will remain in use till ousted by\rits more powerfulsuccessor.\r \r \r \r \r                              _MAY 1902._\r \r \rDecember in May fitlydescribes the prevailing state of the weather\rduring this month.Chilling winds, accompanied by snow, hail, or sleet\rshowers, engender doubtsas to the veracity of the calendar, but the\rarrival of a number ofterns on the 18th dispels all doubts upon the\rmatter. Sojourning inAfrica since their departure in September, they\rinvariably make theirappearance here in May. At present there are\rabout thirty of theseenergetic little birds busy diving among the\rbreakers, picking up smallfry, among which is seen inch long sand\reels. A flock of kittiwakegulls also hunt alongside of them, while\rseveral gannets are to beseen further off, plunging in pursuit of\rlarger game. Clustered insheltering nooks of the rock are numerous\rpatches of ova, depositedby the white whelk. Closely resembling ears\rof wheat in size andshape, each is attached to the rock by a short\rfootstalk, terminating ina flattened disc. On being pressed, a milky\rfluid, somewhat granular,is exuded from the free end. The whelks\rthemselves are at presentfeasting on limpets, whose shells have been\rfractured by the debrisconsequent on the alterations in progress,\rthough at other times theydo not appear to attack the limpets, their\rthick shells possiblymaking the game not worth the candle.\r \rDespite the inclemency ofthe weather, the work in connection with\rthe alterations is beingrapidly pushed forward. The removal of the\rold lantern and parapetwall turned out a more laborious undertaking\rthan the erection of thenew ones. Strength and stability were the\routstanding features ofthe old erection, and were carried to such\ran extent as wouldprobably be considered superfluous in these days.\rThe stone parapet wallwould in itself be an eye-opener to our\rmodern jerrybuilders.Octagonal outside, circular within, the wall\rwas composed of fivecourses of Craigleith freestone, each course\rfeathered and grooved,while each stone dovetailed its entire depth\rinto its neighbour. Ateach point of the octagon holes were drilled\rfrom top to bottom of thewall to receive the two inch iron bolts which\rsecured the heavy castiron lantern to the parapet. It was necessary\rto reduce the stones tofragments before hurling them into the sea,\rin order to prevent themobstructing the boat tracks or damaging the\rgratings. Between theouter and inner linings of the copper dome a\rscrap of newspaper wasfound wrapped round what appeared to be a file\rhandle. The printed matterwas quite legible, and bore reference to\ran unfortunate episode,happily long since relegated to the realms\rof oblivion, namely, theinvestigation into the conduct of the then\rPrincess of Wales in 1806.In one of the ventilators which pierced the\rparapet wall on a levelwith the balcony, but long since disused, a\rperfectly desiccatedspecimen of a wren was found. Attracted probably\rby the light while on amigratory journey, it had evidently taken\rshelter in the ventilatingtube just prior to its being plugged up\rwith a wad of tow, amaterial which for many years has been superseded\rthroughout the service bycotton waste.\r \rThe ping-pong craze hascome our length, and in imitation of other\rmanlier sports a trophyhas been instituted for competition, the\rsaid trophy to become theproperty of the holder after being won\rthirteen consecutivetimes. The trophy takes the form of a handsome\rcup of silver, or, to bemore explicit, of a metal usually found in\rconjunction with silver,and is quite Grecian in its simplicity of\rdesign. It is consideredto be of foreign origin, and bears evidence\rof having at one time beenprofusely chased and engraved. A beautiful\rpastoral scene is depictedon the one side, while, on the other, two\rforeign words are barelydecipherable, namely, “Lait Concentré.” The\rtrophy generally gracesour tea table for some time prior to the\rcompetition, andmaterially aids in stimulating the flagging energies\rof the competitors.\r \r \r \r \r                              _JUNE 1902._\r \r \rOnly towards the end ofthis month did we experience anything like\rsummer weather. Belieingthe wintry weather we had been experiencing,\rthe fragrant odour of thehawthorn blossom borne on the off-shore wind\rimparts a pleasurablesensation, recalling scenes of earlier days\rwhen void of care we went“flourish” gathering, or later on disported\rourselves amongst the“hips and haws.” Here, no sylvan scenery greets\rthe tired eye nor givesrespite to the senses from the everlasting\rwaste of waters, with itsever-changing moods, from placid glassy\rcalm to the wildestturbulence, when blustering Boreas drives his\rteam amain, and thewhite-maned coursers charge down upon us like an\ravalanche. As the tidedrops, and the long lush tangles trail their\rtattered tops on thesurface, a dank heavy odour is perceptible,\rscarcely so pleasing tothe senses as that of the “hawthorn bud that\ropes in the month of May.”Equipped with a stout stick bearing an iron\rhook, an hour’scrab-hunting among the rocks brings one into contact\rwith many forms of lifeotherwise unnoticed. Groping underneath a\rprojecting ledge, toascertain if the inmate is at home, the eye is\rarrested by minute nodulesof scarlet jelly pendant from the roof, and\rdestined to become a closeimitation of their terrestrial namesake the\ranemone, or, in similarsituations, patches of white whelk ova appear\rlike so many grains ofwheat arranged as close as possible to each\rother.\r \rRecently a solitaryinstance was noticed of a whelk carrying the ova\rattached to the exteriorof its own shell. Many different species of\rwhelks are thus met with,some scarcely distinguishable by the naked\reye. The intrusion of thecrab-stick soon betrays the presence of the\rcrab. Gripping the “cleek”in his claws, he prepares for resistance by\rforcing his back againstthe roof of his domicile with all the power\rhis crooked legs arecapable of. Should he feel himself being drawn he\rimmediately releases hisgrip, and, if possible, “seeks his benmost\rbore.” Should the cleekfind a favourable hold, such as under the\rarmpit, so to speak, he issoon dislodged, but if the hole be somewhat\rcrooked it is extremelydifficult to move him, and even then he may\rmake his appearance insections, as he parts company with the different\rmembers of his body on theslightest provocation, a proceeding about\rwhich he has but littlecompunction, as he knows well others will soon\rsprout in their places, aconvenience which Nature might with advantage\rhave extended to the_genus homo_. Poachers, it is stated, have made\ruse of these crustaceanswhile “ferretting” rabbits, by sending them\rinto the burrows with astump of lighted candle stuck on their backs.\rOne can fancy the surprisewith which “bunny” would stand aghast at\rsuch a fearful apparition.\r \rScarcely a bird is to beseen in our vicinity at present, nesting\roperations calling themelsewhere. A few foraging gannets are seen\rdaily passing andrepassing, catering for their sitting mates on the\rBass Rock. The terns andgulls will probably have their wants supplied\rfrom the shores in theneighbourhood of their nurseries. The nest of\rthe tern is of thesimplest description--a slight depression on a\rgravelly beach or grassymound, or even the bare surface of a rock\ris considered sufficientfor their purpose, nest-building, in their\restimation, beingevidently considered superfluous. It is surprising\rthat the eggs remain insome of the positions in which they are\rdeposited. I havefrequently set them rolling along the rock surface\rby the action of mybreath. On their exit from the egg the young are\rimmediately led by theparents to a shingly beach, or other place of\rconcealment, where it isextremely difficult to detect them from their\rsurroundings. Here theyare fed with sand-eels and other small fry till\rsuch time as they are ableto wing their way to the fishing grounds\rthemselves, though eventhen they are frequently the recipients of the\rparents’ generosity, theirhunting powers being as yet inadequate to\rsupply their needs.\r \rThe work in connectionwith the alterations here progresses rapidly,\rand by the end of nextmonth it is expected but little will be left\rundone. To all externalappearance the work is already finished, but\rthe building of the hugelens and revolving machinery, along with the\rinternal fittings, haveyet to be completed.\r \r \r \r \r                              _JULY 1902._\r \r \rMyriads of medusae orjellyfishes are constantly streaming past our\rdoor, apparently withoutany powers of volition of their own, but\rhelplessly at the mercy ofthe tides. Of various sizes, shapes, and\rcolours, they impart quitea gay appearance to the seascape, somewhat\rresembling a grassy swardcarpeted with beautiful flowers--huge\rsunflowerspredominating--the whole moving silently just beneath\rthe green, glassy surface.Great tremulous discs, twelve inches in\rdiameter, trail theirstreaming tentacles several feet behind them;\rothers, again, no largerthan a pea possess the power of radiating,\rfrom the ciliary bandswith which they are furnished, all the colours\rof the rainbow. Strandedhigh and dry, what a contrast to their former\rglory, now an inert massof slobbery mucilage. At one period of their\rexistence they appearquite plant-like in their habits. Attached to the\rrocks, they closelyresemble miniature fir trees, each plant ultimately\rproducing whole coloniesof juvenile medusae. Fish have been fairly\rplentiful this month, butowing to the work at present in progress we\rhave but little time toavail ourselves of the opportunity. On the 6th\ra red chequered pigeon,stamped “J. B. Sollaway, Beeston,” on wing,\rwas released after anight’s detention. On Saturday the 12th, other\rtwo pigeons were capturedat 8.30 p.m. One a red chequered homer, with\raluminium ring on legmarked N.U. 01, H.A. 587, also rubber racing ring\ron other leg, marked 132outside and 263 Q inside; the other a blue\rchequered homer, with legring marked N.U. 99, C. 8953, and racing ring\rmarked Q 513 inside and174 outside; wing feathers stamped “Walter\rH. Walker, Bank House,Horsforth, Leeds.” Both pigeons, after being\rwatered and fed, werereleased at 11 a.m. on 13th, each steering a\rsou’-westerly course fromthe Rock.\r \rOn the evening of Sundaythe 27th our new light was exhibited for the\rfirst time, the covetedhonour of “first light” falling in the ordinary\rroutine of duty to thewriter. The new apparatus--a bewildering\rarrangement of massiveglass prisms--is in striking contrast with its\rpredecessor, the oldreflector system of lighting, a system, by the\rway, now almost obsolete.The following description of the new light is\rcopied from an engravedplate affixed to the new apparatus:--“Combined\rhyper-radiant and 1storder apparatus, with equiangular dioptric\relements and catadioptricback prisms; power of red flash and white\rflash equalised. White andred flashing light, showing white and\rred flashes alternatelyevery half minute, the period being one\rminute. Designed by MessrsStevenson, Civil Engineers, Edinburgh.\rContractors, Messrs Steven& Struthers, Glasgow, and Messrs Société Des\rEtablissements HenryLepaute, Paris. David A. Stevenson, Engineer to\rthe Board. Apparatus makesone revolution in one minute--1901.”\r \rOccasionally during theprogress of the alterations our population,\runlike that of Arbroath,increased to a somewhat alarming extent,\rmounting at times to agrand total of seven all told. Considering that\rthe majority of thepopulation were unaccustomed to life under such\r“cribbed, cabined, andconfined” conditions, it was surprising to\rwitness the cheerfulnessand good humour with which they accepted their\rsixteen weeks’ solitaryconfinement. At times the resources of our\rcommissariat were taxed totheir utmost. Beef, which is stored in our\rsafe on the balcony, andretains its freshness for a fortnight in cold\rweather, demands a liberalsalting at present, otherwise it does become\ra trifle “gamey,” but, onthe whole, it is preferable to its relative\rin tins--a relationship,by the way, extremely difficult to prove,\rand hopelessly so shouldthe label be missing. What though at times\ra transverse section ofour loaves disclosed a landscape in cerulean\rtints undreamt of by themost vivid impressionist, the transference to\r“hard tack” was acceptedwith better grace than when a similar move had\rto be made from the saltedmeat to the “embalmed commodity.”\r \r \r \r \r                             _AUGUST 1902._\r \r \rThe coating of acornbarnacles with which the higher surfaces of\rthe Rock and also the baseof the tower are whitened in summer is\rfast disappearing beforethe ravages of that ruthless destroyer the\rwhite whelk. Seen from thebalcony, this encrustation resembles\ra lime-hauled wall, andpresents a suitable background for the\robservation of movingobjects under water. These barnacles are\rfrequently mistaken by thecasual observer for young limpets, whereas,\runlike the limpet, whichmoves freely from place to place in quest of\rvegetable diet, the momentthe young barnacle settles to erect his\rlimey habitation, hepossesses a fixity of tenure which terminates\ronly with his existence.An outer wall, with razor edges, surrounds a\rhollow cone, his privateapartment, and probably guards his four-leaved\rdoor from injury. Thisopening, through which all business with the\router world is transacted,is scarcely discernible when above water;\rbut immediately the tidecovers it, the hollow cone is seen to fall\rapart in four verticalsections, a bunch of fingers is thrust forth\rand rhythmic clutches madeat invisible food. How little they resemble\rtheir relatives who swingby their pendulous stalks from ships’ bottoms\ror submerged wreckage, andsee the world without any exertion of their\rown. The ancients firmlybelieved that from these animals certain birds\rwere produced, probablyfrom the resemblance of their shelly casement\rto the beak of a bird, andthe bird known as the barnacle-goose owes\rhis name to this belief.Even to-day there are persons who solemnly\rdeclare that the NorthernDiver is so evolved.\r \rAnother fallacy commonamongst fishing communities on the West Coast\ris the attributing thedestructive effects of the _teredo navalis_,\ror ship-worm, to theinnocent barnacle, whose only fault is the\rresistance theirmultitudes offer to a ship’s progress through the\rwater. A log of wood whichhas been adrift at sea for a lengthened\rperiod will generally befound to have its surface clustered with\rpendulous barnacles. Theremoval of these disclose minute pin-holes on\rthe surface, which, in theinterior, assume the diameter of a man’s\rlittle finger, andpermeate the log from end to end like a honeycomb.\rEach little tunnel issmoothly enamelled with a deposit of lime by this\rindefatigable borer, the_teredo_. Though boring parallel with his\rneighbour, the thicknessof paper only separating them, they never, by\rany chance, encroach oneach other’s bore. Their tracks are seen to\rabruptly diverge when allbut into that of their neighbour, so that\rthey are evidentlycognisant of each other’s proximity, an interesting\rfact also apparent in ratson board wooden vessels, who, though they\rwill gnaw their waythrough any woodwork, instinctively refrain from\rsuicidal attempts on theouter skin of the ship.\r \rOn the memorable 9th wehad a bird’s-eye view of the Coronation\rcelebrations in Arbroath.With the aid of our telescope the crowds on\rthe Common were clearlyvisible, the ladies in white dresses being most\rconspicuous. The flash ofthe guns firing the royal salute was seen\rfifty-five seconds beforethe report reached us. In the afternoon the\rsports in the VictoriaPark occupied our attention, and the white-clad\rcompetitors in the highjump could be seen taking their preliminary run\rand rising over theobstacle. Parties straying on the beach had only\rtheir heads visible, andas they neared the margin appeared to vanish\runder water. The progressof the bonfire on the Common at night was\ralso watched, and themoving figures could be plainly seen silhouetted\rin the glare. Probably butfew noticed our attempt to celebrate the\roccasion. Two strings offlags from the balcony to the rocks fluttered\rgaily in the breeze, whilethe balcony railing was similarly decked.\rAmongst those suspendedfrom the rail was a flag of peculiar interest,\rnamely, one which had beensewn by Miss Stevenson, a sister of the\rbuilder, Robert Stevenson,almost a hundred years ago. The central\rsubject depicted on thewhite ground is the Bell Rock Lighthouse;\ron the right, the patronsaint of Scotland with his cross; while a\rship under full sailoccupies the left, the whole bordered with a\rdeep edging of red. Thefigures are extremely well executed, and the\rcolouring to the fleshtints remarkable. The flag was presented to the\rRock by Miss Stevenson tobe used as a table draping during divine\rservice.\r \rSeveral white butterfliesand moths innumerable were seen passing here\rthis month. It seems theseinsects have their migratory periods as\rwell as birds, and atstations favourable for their observation they\rappeared, to quote from awriter in a recent number of “Chambers’s,”\r“as a dense snowstormdriven by a light breeze, and this not for one\rday only, but for many insuccession. Whereas birds come and go with\rclockwork regularity, theimmigration of butterflies is uncertain,\rand of all those whichsurvive the perils of the deep no single one\rreturns.”\r \r \r \r \r                           _SEPTEMBER 1902._\r \r \rA good deal of heavyweather has been experienced on the Rock this\rmonth, and the stabilityof our new lantern subjected to a fair strain,\rthough probably nothing towhat it will have to encounter during the\rcourse of the winter. Thelantern--composed of gun metal astragals,\rnarrowed to the utmostlimit compatible with strength, in order to\rintercept as little lightas possible--may be looked upon as a huge\rhollow cylinder of glass,which in itself seems but a feeble barrier to\rthe onslaughts of thestorm. But the three tiers of triangular panes\rare of heavy plate glass,and the apparently slim like astragals are\rbraced together in themost effective manner to ensure the greatest\rdegree of strength, andneed cause no uneasiness to the stranger\rviewing the outlook duringthe progress of a gale. It is awful to think\rthat out in that darkvoid, amid the warring elements, fellow beings\rmay be battling for theirlives in close proximity to where we sit in\rcomfort and security,totally ignorant of their condition, and utterly\rhelpless to render themthe slightest assistance. Probably a case in\rpoint occurred during thegale of the 3rd. On the 9th, about noon, we\rwere somewhat surprised tosee the gunboat _Seamew_ approaching the\rRock with a hoist offlags, indicating that they wished to communicate\rwith us. Bringing up closeto the Rock, they signalled, “Have you seen\ra vessel in distress?” towhich we answered “No”; and then remembering\rwe had seen a torpedo boatpass the day previous, and fearing another\rcase of “buckling” hadoccurred, we asked “Was it a torpedo boat?” in\rreply to which theycommunicated the intelligence, “No; it is a sailing\rcraft from Anstruther lastWednesday, and seven hands.” On our replying\r“We have not seen her,”the signal “Thank you” was hoisted, and the\rgunboat steamed out to theeastward on her sorrowful quest. Passing a\rtorpedo boat at gunpractice, she was seen to signal her also, with the\rdifference that the flagsthen used had no existence in our code. Later\rin the evening she wasagain seen making for Dundee.\r \rWe have had several takesof fish of late, though there seems to be\ra scarcity of “fry”compared with last year, the absence of which\rprobably accounts for theterns failing to call upon us with their\ryoung for a few weeks’feasting prior to commencing their migratory\rjourney southwards.Gannets may be seen at present striking at fish\rwithin a few feet of ourdoorway, while a flock of young gulls hover\rexpectantly, with feeblepeeping cries anticipating the feast in store\rfor them when the dinnerscraps make their appearance. Further off a\rfew eider ducks--who onlyarrived on the 25th, somewhat later than last\ryear--evidently eye theproceedings of these juvenile degenerates with\rdisdain, preferring torefrain from such pampered luxuries and dine\ron the products of thechase alone. The eiders present are as yet all\radult males, the femalespresumably still occupied with family cares\rteaching the young ideahow to shoot, or rather fish, if plucking\rmussels, catching crabs,etc., can be called so, for such is their\rdiet, and does not includefish. Strange that the foremost arrivals\ramong migratory birds areall males. Why this is so is not agreed upon\rby observers, somesupposing that the females are detained by maternal\rduties; others, again,affirm that they migrate _en masse_, and that\rthe more vigorous malessoon outstrip and ungallantly leave the gentler\rsex to bring up the rear.On the 6th we had our first intimation of\rthe autumnal migratoryflight in the arrival of a flock of wheatears,\raccompanied by a solitarywren. On the 27th several greenfinches,\rlarks, and starlings weremaking insane efforts to follow the line\rof _most_ resistance,resulting in our new lantern receiving its\rfirst baptism of blood, asthe glass next morning testified. Several\rporpoises are to be seenpuffing and blowing a mile off, and on the\r28th a school of “finner”whales were seen heading north.\r \rI see by the _ArbroathGuide_ that one of our old fog bells has been\rpresented by ourCommissioners to the Arbroath Museum, a fit resting\rplace after its longsojourn on the Rock. Should the date upon it\rhappen by any chance tobecome erased, what possible controversies it\rmay yet become the subjectof amongst posterity as to its connection\rwith that mythicalpersonage “Ralph the Rover.” I myself can testify\rto its having conformed inone respect at least with that of the poem,\rfor on lowering it fromits position on the balcony for shipment the\rtide had overflowed theRock about a couple of feet, causing the bell\rto settle with an audiblegurgle, or as one of the seamen (Fraser)\rappropriately quoted, “Thebell sank down with a gurgling sound.”\r \r \r \r \r                            _OCTOBER 1902._\r \r \rWe have had occasionalvisits of feathered migrants during the month,\rbut it is a matter ofremark that each year sees a decrease in the\rnumber of arrivals here.Probably the increased number of lights on our\rcoast accounts for thisdiminution, some proving more attractive than\rours. A few years ago itwas quite on the cards at this season of the\ryear--thanks to themigratory instinct--to have an additional course\rat dinner, to whichfieldfares, blackbirds, and redwings were the\rvoluntary contributors,and even at times the gamey woodcock “graced\rthe groaning board”--forour “board,” being double-leaved and somewhat\rsenile, does occasionallygroan, and this without reference to any\rsuperincumbent strain.Amongst the more noteworthy of our captures\rhere, at various times,the following may be mentioned:--A peregrine\rfalcon, large horned owl,small brown owl, kestrels, sparrow hawks,\rcrows, cormorants,corn-crakes, and a turtle dove. Birds generally\rarrive here in a faggedcondition, and are easily captured. As an\rinstance, a kestrel landedon our balcony railing during fog, and,\rdespite the explosions ofour fog-signal twenty feet overhead, tucked\rhis head under his wingand fell sound asleep. Another arrival of note\rwas a common blue pigeon,which, after a few hours’ stay, surprised\rus by depositing an egg inour doorway. Disturbed on our appearance,\rit reluctantly desertedits treasure, but not without many backward\rglances before spreadingits wings shorewards.\r \rPodley-fishing has beenfairly successful during the month, and\rseveral codlings have beentaken from the pools at low water. Whilst\rphotographing lately,another of our number was busy endeavouring to\rextract a breakfast fromPort Hamilton. Hooking a fair sized codling,\rthe camera was turned onthe scene, and fish _à la photo_ figured in\rour bill of fare nextmorning. A few years ago a photo was taken of a\rpaidle cock and hen, bothof which were taken from their nests for this\rpurpose, and provedamenable sitters; the cock appearing in the photo\rquite conscious of hisimportance, though the hen appeared somewhat\rbored, having been snappedin the middle of a huge “gape,” which some\rof my previous sittersmight interpret as a yawn. Both were returned\rto their nests none theworse of their unique experience, and possibly\ryet relate their feelingsbefore the camera to the admiring wonder of\rfishy audiences, tillpuffed with the idea of their own importance they\rnow probably suffer from adisease (peculiar to some higher vertebrates\rwith as slender areputation) resulting in what is colloquially known\ras “swelled head.”\r \rWouldn’t the fishermen ofArbroath fancy their lines had fallen in\rpleasant places should thefish they pursue at such hazard come sailing\rvoluntarily into theharbour, and even without the usual ceremony of\rdropping them a line,appear on the surface, mutely asking to be lifted\rout? Such, however, wasour experience lately. Shortly before daybreak\rone quiet morning ourattention was attracted by the movements of a few\rgulls, evidentlyinterested in some object in the water at the edge of\rthe reef. As daylightadvanced it was seen to be a large fish wobbling\rerratically upon thesurface. On extinguishing the light and descending\rto the rocks, which theadvancing tide had not yet covered, the fish\rwas seen to have enteredthe Johnny Gray boat track, and was propelling\ritself, keel upwards, inour direction. A fish in this unusual position\rindicates an abnormaldistension of the swimming bladder, which, by\rover-increasing itsbuoyancy, entirely upsets its centre of gravity,\rand forces it topsy-turvyto the surface. A steam trawler, which had\rbeen working close to theRock for several days previous, was probably\rresponsible for ourfriend’s “blown” condition. Stepping gingerly over\rbeds of white whelks as wewade bare foot to welcome our visitor,\rwe mentally contrast ourinferiority with more juvenile days--a time\rwhen even road metal couldbe safely negotiated. The screaming gulls\rresent our interferencewith their expected feast, no doubt slanging us\runmercifully as we landour capture, an arm-long lythe, safely on the\rgrating. Their clamouring,however, is soon stilled, as each retires\rwith as big a share of theoffal as his strength and agility can\rcommand.\r \rThe long-tailed ducks arenow only wanting to complete the list of our\rwinter boarders, and theiradvent may be looked for early next month.\rThe eiders have nowattained their numerical strength for the winter,\rand are busily engagedpicking up a living, not only for themselves,\rbut also for theparasitical gulls which hover in close attendance,\rshepherding them withunwearied diligence. The peculiar cackling of\rthe eiders--not unlikethat of wild geese--becomes somewhat disturbing\ras their operations areoccasionally carried on underneath our bedroom\rwindow. Gannets are nowrarely seen here, but at their breeding haunts\ron the Bass Rock--which wehad the opportunity of visiting while on\rour way here lastrelief--they are still in evidence, though by the\rend of the month they willhave commenced their journey southwards.\rA new light is beingcompleted on the Bass Rock, and on the first of\rDecember, yet anotherfactor in our dwindling list of visitors will be\rin operation--ostensibly alighthouse--but to our feathered friends,\ralas! a veritableslaughter-house.\r \r \r \r \r                            _NOVEMBER 1902._\r \r \rExceedingly stormyweather, with a prevalence of sou’-easterly winds\rand heavy seas, has beenour portion here this month, restricting our\rmovements out of doors,till with circling round our promenade on the\rbalcony one almost doubtsthe possibility of ever again being able\rto hold a straight coursewhen opportunity offers. Workmen have been\rengaged this month fittingup a service of copper piping from the\rgrating at the base of thetower to the cisterns in the oil store on\rthe third flat, wherebythe operation of storing oil will in future\rbe rendered much easier.The oil will now be landed in forty-gallon\rcasks, instead of thesmall six-gallon ankers as formerly, emptied into\ra sifting tank on thegrating, and by means of a rotary pump forced\rupwards to the oilcisterns--a vast improvement on the old system, when\reach anker had to behoisted indoors, and then shouldered upstairs to\rthe cisterns.\r \rA pleasing incident of themonth was the arrival of a handsome present\rfor each of the keepers,consisting of a silver mounted briar pipe,\ra pound of golden bartobacco, and a liberal supply of first class\rreading matter. Allkeepers throughout the service--over 200--were\rsimilarly supplied, sothat the gift will be seen to be a pretty\rextensive one, and thedonor, James Coats, junr., Paisley, has without\rdoubt earned the gratitudeof the service by this generous act of\rkindness.\r \rAbout the beginning of themonth we had a few feathered visitors,\rchiefly blackbirds,fieldfares, and starlings. On the morning of\rthe 5th several struckheavily on the lantern, but were swept away\rby the strong sou’-eastwind then blowing. The gannets have now all\rdisappeared, none havingbeen seen since the 27th. The eiders continue\rin close attendance andhave had their numbers augmented by the\rarrival of the longtailson the 9th, a week earlier than last year,\rthus completing our listof regular boarders for the winter. At 6 p.m.\ron the 13th we wereprivileged with the unusual spectacle of a lunar\rrainbow. The bow--a faintwhite arc against the dark background--was\rdistinctly visible in thenor’-west, though, of course, void of the\rvivid colouringinseparable from its solar namesake.\r \rWhile taking a turn roundthe balcony on the evening of the 15th,\rour attention wasattracted to what appeared to be a peculiar shaped\rmass of foam resting onthe rocks immediately beneath us. On careful\robservation, however, theobject was seen to move slightly in the\rfaint moonlight, and bythe aid of our telescope the outline of a seal\rcould be dimly seen. Onthe change of the watch at 6 p.m. an attacking\rparty, including theworkmen then on the Rock, was organised, and a\rplan of campaign drawn up.Descending the outside ladder, which was\rfortunately in deepshadow, we were able to gain a footing on the Rock\runperceived. Hissuspicions had, however, evidently been aroused,\ras he was seen to lift hishead sniffing uneasily in our direction.\rBracing ourselves withinthe margin of the shadow cast by the tower, we\rcharged down upon him atthe double, expecting to see him beat a hasty\rretreat to the water; but,to our surprise, he made no effort whatever\rin that direction, butseemed to consider himself quite a match for\rus, and that there was nopresent necessity for retreating. Snarling\rand snapping viciously aswe surrounded him, he appeared at a great\rdisadvantage compared withhis agile movements when in his element, his\rhind flippers being now ofpractically little use to him, his lumbering\rmovements being effectedby the aid of the fore flippers alone. His\rfurious efforts to sampleportions of our anatomy were easily avoided,\rand by laying hold of hishind flippers, as one would trundle a barrow,\rhe was immediately placed_hors-de-combat_. An unfortunate squid or\rcuttlefish, which had beenleft stranded by the receding tide, when\rpushed within his reachwas seized and energetically shaken with all\rthe vim of an accomplishedratter. The wooden shaft of a boat-hook was\rsimilarly treated, andstill bears evidence of his utter ignorance of\rthe dental profession. Arope being procured, a clove hitch was slipped\rover one of hishind-flippers, the other end made fast to an eye-bolt\ron the Rock. Thus secured,he was left to his novel reflections for the\rnight.\r \r[Illustration]\r \rAs the tide covered theRock he could be seen in the clear moonlight\rploughing along the creamysurface, stretching his tether in every\rdirection in futile effortsto escape. At daylight next morning\rhe was found shelteringunder a projecting ledge of rock. What a\rclean, well-groomed fellowhe looked, with his sleek, glossy coat\rglistening in thesunshine, his squat, plump body adapting itself to\rthe inequalities of thesurface on which it rested. His coat, by the\rway, as much fur as thatof a horse--grey above, mottled with dark\rspots, while the undersurface is of a creamy yellow. His beautiful\rteeth gleaming whiteagainst the scarlet interior of his mouth, as he\rsnapped fruitlessly oneither side, suggested the maximum of robust\ranimal health. As amemento of his visit the camera was brought on the\rscene, and anotheraddition made to our list of illustrious visitors.\r \rLiberating him proved tobe more difficult than his capture, for when\rcut adrift he persisted infacing us instead of making for the water,\rtowards which weendeavoured to drive him. After some manœuvring,\rhowever, he was driven tothe edge of the gulley, but even with his\rbody half submerged hemaintained a defensive attitude, not seeming to\rrealise that he was atliberty to depart. An incoming wave, however,\rmoved him to a sense ofhis position, and with a defiant snort he\rslipped under water.Omitting, in his hurry, to take proper bearings,\rhe took the wrongdirection, and, finding himself in a _cul-de-sac_,\rmade his appearance againon the surface, and with a hurried glance at\rhis position again sank,this time making a bee-line for the outlet,\rbeing clearly seen, as hepassed under water close to where we stood,\rand was last seenbuffeting his way through the foaming breakers,\revidently none the worsefor his compulsory detention on the Rock.\r \r \r \r \r                            _DECEMBER 1902._\r \r \rThe broken stones andother debris, consequent upon the late\ralterations here, whichhad collected in various holes in the Rock and\rmaintained their positionup till now, have nearly all been cleared out\rby the severe gales ofthis month, and a couple of heavy iron poles,\rerected lately to mark theboat tracks or entrances to the landings,\rand which were sunk twofeet in the solid rock and heavily cemented,\rhave been shaken loose intheir sockets by the pounding seas which have\rbeen besieging us of late.The rocks appear bleak and bare, and utterly\rvoid of vegetation. Thewhite whelks have collected their scattered\rforces, and gone intowinter quarters. Secure in sheltering nooks,\rthey lie huddled togetherin close packed squadrons. Numerous small\rwhite banded whelks adhereto the base of the tower with a tenacity\rthat seems surprisingconsidering the swirling seas they are subjected\rto. This species, however,never seem to dream of hibernating. The\reiders and longtails, withan unswerving attention to business, pursue\rtheir calling amid thehurly-burly of broken, tumbling seas--evidently\rlittle concerned whetherthe weather be fair or foul--and in the glassy\rhollows alternatingbetween the breakers they can be distinctly seen\rscurrying over the rocksurface like so many fish. Gannets this month\rare conspicuous by theirabsence, and only a few parasitic gulls divide\rtheir attention betweenthe kitchen refuse and the hard won earnings of\rthe eiders.\r \rOn several occasionsduring the month our fog signal was brought into\raction through theoccurrence of heavy snowfalls. A silent, feathery\rfall on shore no doubt hascharms peculiarly its own, but at sea\rconstitutes a very seriousdanger to the anxious mariner as he steams\rat reduced speed throughthe fleecy curtain, shrieking his every two\rminute warning, hisvessel’s head scarcely visible from the bridge.\rIn snowstorms such as wehave had of late our lantern soon becomes\rplastered up with snow onthe weather side, necessitating constant\rremoval to prevent it fromcompletely blinding our light in that\rdirection. This is anoperation often accomplished with difficulty,\respecially when carriedout in the teeth of a gale--an experience\rsomewhat akin to lying outon a yardarm under similar conditions, only\rone doesn’t have the liftand ’scend of the vessel to contend with;\ryet his grip must beequally as sure, or, as the old salts phrase\rit, “Every finger afish-hook,” on such occasions. Mounting by an\routside ladder to thegrated gallery which encircles the base of the\rlantern, one is exposed tothe full force of the blast, and a firm\rgrip must be taken toavoid being blown away. Below, the seas in wild\rtumult break against thebuilding with a deafening roar, sending a\rperceptible tremor throughthe entire structure with each impact. Only\rby energetically haulingon the hand-rail can the slightest progress\rbe made in the desireddirection, the wind’s eye being the objective\rpoint, where possibly onarrival one may find himself pinned flat to\rthe lantern, like anentomological specimen, by the force of the wind.\rThe snow removed, thereturn journey is effected by simply allowing\roneself to be blowngradually back.\r \rWhile relieving the BassRock on our way ashore last relief, a good\ropportunity was affordedof witnessing the mode of effecting a landing\runder adversecircumstances. On arrival there, it was considered\rdangerous to attempt alanding at either of the two landing places,\rowing to the heavy seathen running. The landings--a flight of concrete\rsteps from the water edgeto the rocks above--are situated on either\rside of a slightpromontory immediately beneath the lighthouse; and as\rdeep water obtains to therock face, it will be obvious that similar\rconditions must frequentlyprevail at either landing. The boat being\rloaded with the necessarystores, and the relieving keeper on board,\ran approach was made towithin suitable distance of the Rock. A kedge\ranchor was then thrownoverboard, and the boat slacked down till\rwithin working distance.The keepers meanwhile had been busy erecting\ran iron pole or derrick onthe rocks above the position now occupied\rby the boat, and which,being slightly inclined seawards, a tackle\rfrom its extremity wasdrawn by means of a guy-line to the boat, and\rthe stores hoisted ashoreby the keepers in charge of the tackle-fall\rabove. Seated in a loop ofthe rope, the relieving keeper was then\rhoisted, and hisshore-going neighbour similarly lowered. As an extra\rprecaution, a second boatwas sent from the ship to stand by the\rworking boat in case of accident.Fortunately, however, their services\rwere not required.\r \rOur final relief here forthe year was effected with some difficulty\ron the 29th. Owing to thedoubtful aspect of the landing, only one\rboat was sent ashoreinstead of two as usual. The fortnightly supply\rof coal and water beingomitted on this occasion does not, however,\rinconvenience us, as athree months’ reserve stock of necessaries is\ralways maintained duringthe winter months.\r \r \r \r \r                        _JANUARY-FEBRUARY1903._\r \r \rBright, sunny weathercharacterised the opening day of the year, the\rsea assuming a suspiciousplacidity quite summer-like in appearance\rbut for the keen nip inthe air perceptible out of doors. This state\rof affairs, however,proved but ephemeral, and for the remainder of\rthe month we haveexperienced most boisterous weather. Strong westerly\rwinds occasionallyattained the force of a gale, accompanied with\rdriving seas, which roaredand sang a lullaby scarcely compatible\rwith the shore-dwellers’sense of security, but which, strange to\rsay, has a more somnolenteffect upon us than a breathless stillness,\rthough an occasionalthumper of a sea, more forceful than its fellows,\rdemonstrates the stabilityof our domicile by imparting a gentle\rtremor to the entirestructure, awakening in the sleeper a glimmer of\rconsciousness and a hazyimpression of a traction-engine lumbering\rsomewhere in the vicinity.\r \rOur entrancedoorway--thirty feet from the Rock--faces south-west, and\ris guarded by a heavydouble leaved door, which opens outwards, and\rheld open against thebuilding by means of heavy brass thumb-snecks.\rAn inner or vestibule doorof solid brass is placed six feet further\rinwards--the walls here,by the way, being seven feet thick, tapering\rto one foot immediatelybeneath the balcony, sixty feet higher up.\rThis door is alsodouble-leaved, with the upper panels of heavy plate\rglass, frequently obscuredby the strong westerly wind whipping the\rtops of the seas as theyrise in front, and carrying them souse into\rthe doorway. Standing hereduring the prevalence of a gale, the outlook\ris being constantlydarkened by a curtain of hissing foam drawn across\rthe doorway, as each seabreaks against the base of the tower, flinging\rthe spray high overhead.Fifteen miles in front of us lies the Isle of\rMay, with its castle-likelighthouse crowning its summit, while on a\rlower level stands awhitewashed relic--remnant of a time, not so long\rago, when the Islandboasted a double light, and electricity had not\ras yet usurped sole sway.Emerging from the right of the May appears\rthe bluff outline of theBass Rock, while away in the far distance\rNorth Berwick Law cleavesthe sky-line. Away to St Abb’s Head, on the\rleft, the Haddington coaststretches hazy and indistinct, while the\rgreen, grassy slopes ofFife, with the spires of St Andrews faintly\rvisible, fill in the rightof the picture. Laying hold of the man-ropes\rsuspended in the doorway,and turning to the right, the Forfarshire\rcoast is seen extendingfrom the Tay in a long unbroken line, with the\rsnow-clad Grampianstowering majestically in the background. Right\rin front of us are thesmoking stalks of Arbroath. Two conspicuous\rwhite dots in theforeground mark the pierheads, in front of which\ran impatient “flaxer”cruises in glorious uncertainty of ever being\rpermitted to fulfil hercharter and deposit her Riga-run freight on the\rright side of the bar.This is the panorama from the viewpoint of our\rdoorway on a clear day,but, as seen of late through sheets of flying\rfoam, it reminds one of acinematograph display, in which the films are\rfar from perfect.\r \rOn the first Sunday of theyear hundreds of gulls were seen resting\ron the surface of the sea,half a mile nor’-west from here, evidently\rby their movementsenjoying a feast of “fry,” and in all probability\rproclaiming the presenceof herring shoals. During the gale of 10th\rJanuary over a dozengannets were seen swooping and diving, presumably\rat herring. Only withdifficulty could we maintain our position on\rthe balcony, owing to theforce of the wind, yet these birds circled\rand dived amid the turmoilof wind and water with a graceful ease and\rprecision that seemedtruly wonderful considering the force of wind\rthey occasionally beat upagainst, or, as they turned broadside on,\rwere wafted without theleast exertion in the opposite direction.\rThe first week of Februarysaw hundreds of these birds back to their\rbreeding haunts on theBass Rock. From the deck of the “Relief” steamer\rlying within a few hundredyards their movements are clearly seen. Each\rprojecting ledge of theprecipitous cliffs is tenanted by some members\rof the cackling crowd,their heads see-sawing from side to side. The\rbirds are evidentlyengaged in brisk conversation, a monopoly of which\ris certainly not toleratedamongst them, judging by the vigorous\refforts of each to beheard above his neighbour. Probably the new\rlighthouse is beingdiscussed in the light of an innovation on their\rancestral rights ofpossession, and later, as its beams fall athwart\rtheir nursery, traditionmay recall man’s former intrusion on their\rsolitary keep many hundredyears ago. No doubt their ups and downs\rsince last meeting on_terra firma_ are fully discussed, for it is a\rcurious fact that thesebirds are rarely, if ever, known to rest on\rshore except when engagedin domestic duties. Occasionally a depraved\rspecimen may be seenfloating helplessly on the water, a victim of his\rown gluttony, having dinednot wisely but too well.\r \rFebruary has been arepetition of its predecessor, cold and blowy,\rwith excessive rainfalls.In a shallow depression on the higher rock\rsurface our attention hasbeen attracted to a solitary plant, a\rspecimen, I understand, of“_Himanthalia lorea_.” A cylindrical stem\r(an inch in length)supports a thick, fleshy disc, about an inch in\rdiameter. From the centreof this disc three separate branches rise\rwith their terminals,blunted at first, but which were gradually seen\rto bifurcate. This is_our_ “flower in the crannied wall,” and is in\rits own way equally assuggestive.\r \rThe eiders areoccasionally seen varying their diet with a vegetable\rcourse. Seizing the tip ofa tangle blade two or three inches from the\rsurface, they spin roundit like a top, till the portion held in their\rbill is twisted off andgreedily swallowed. No need for them to evade\rthe gulls while engaged inthis repast. It is most amusing to witness\rthe discomfiture of thegulls as they hurry from a distance expecting\rto share in somethingedible, only to find the duck negotiating six\rinches of seaweed. Thatthe white whelk itself is not immune from\renemies was recentlybrought before our notice, one being picked up\rwith a long black wormdangling from its mouth. On withdrawing the\rworm--somewhat resemblinga boot lace--portions of the deceased tenant\rfollowed. Doubtless everyorganism has its own particular parasite.\r \r    “Big fleas have little fleas upon theirbacks to bite ’em,\r    And these again have lesser fleas and so_ad infinitum_.”\r \r \r \r \r                             _MARCH 1903._\r \r \rTraditionally correct, theadvent of this month was decidedly leonine,\rand its exit as certainlylamb-like; but between these periods, though\ra few really beautifuldays could be credited to the latter symbol\rof peacefulness, the lionwas largely in the ascendant. Borne on the\roff-shore wind comes theodour of heather--not the fragrant perfume\rone usually associateswith this sweet-smelling plant, but the smoky\rincense consequent onmoor-burning--and at night the higher levels of\rthe coast line exhibitlights which are certainly not recognised in the\rMariners’ SailingDirections.\r \rOver a score of steamtrawlers have been busy in our neighbourhood\rall the month. Sunday orSaturday is all the same to them; they are\rat it night and day, andthe weather must be bad indeed to detain\rthem in port. Often theyare seen passing here burying themselves to\rthe foremast in the season their way to the fishing grounds, perhaps\rtwenty miles outside ofus. The Rock seems to be a recognised stage\rin their journey; for,whenever abreast of it, over goes their log,\rand a compass course islaid for the distant banks. Here, far outside\rthe three-mile limit, thepresence of the _Brenda_ or the _Minna_[1]\rcauses no alarm; and,providing their numbers are correctly exposed,\rreceive no interferencefrom these coasting policemen. A few summers\rago, one of these sametrawlers, while on her way out from Dundee one\rSunday, surprised us bydriving right up on the reef in broad daylight,\ra hundred yards from thetower. Fortunately, the sea was like glass at\rthe time, otherwise theconsequences must have been disastrous. The\rtide being on the ebb,their attempts to back off were unsuccessful;\rand there they remainedhard and fast from one o’clock till six in the\revening, when a passingtrawler succeeded in towing them off, evidently\rnone the worse of theirbrief acquaintance with the Bell Rock. During\rtheir detention, the crewpaid us a visit in their boat, recalling\rto our mind a story inwhich a clumsily handled brig, in coming to\ran anchorage in a crowdedharbour, ran aboard of a vessel already\ranchored. Visiting thisvessel a few days later, to apologise for the\roccurrence, the offenderwas thus announced by the steward: “Captain\rS----has come on board,Sir.” “Oh, indeed,” sarcastically remarked the\raggrieved mariner. “Has hebrought his brig with him?”\r \rThe rocks are this yearmore plentifully strewn with mussel-spawn and\racorn barnacles thanusual; and already the whelks have sallied from\rtheir winter’s sleep, benton their destruction. Hundreds of hermit\rcrabs have also made theirappearance, notably first in the deeper\rpools, but graduallytaking up their quarters in the shallows. Towards\rthe end of the month, afew small spats of paidlefish spawn were seen\rdeposited in convenientcrevices of the rocks. This is unusually early\rfor “nesting” operations,and engenders hopes of an early fishing, as\rthe ova is generally thefirst inducement for the wandering cod to\rcome within reach of our rods.Numerous clusters of the wheat-like ova\rof the white whelk arealso seen; but, unlike that of the paidlefish\r(lumpsucker)--which may bedetached from its gelatinous fastenings in\ra solid mass--each eggadheres separately by its own footstalk. Though\rthe adult “paidles” areonly to be seen here during the period of\rincubation--the term seemsquite applicable, seeing that the guardian\r“cock” is always in closeattendance, with his nose thrust into the\rcentre of the mass of ova,at which point there is always a depression,\rand frequently a holeright through it--juveniles are occasionally met\rwith at all seasons; and,on the first anniversary of their birthday,\rare seen to have attainedthe length of two inches.\r \rNumbers of peculiarlooking slugs are met with at present, somewhat\rresembling a section of asmall orange with the skin attached. On their\rupper surface, near to oneend, a minute orifice is seen, through which\ra small rosette likearrangement is protruded when at rest, but which\ris instantly withdrawnwhen the animal is disturbed. This is the only\rvisible sign of life inthis otherwise inert object, and is probably\rits means of obtaining aliving. Its under or ambulatory surface is\rsimilar to that of alimpet, without its tenacity, but with a somewhat\rsimilar rate ofprogression. Another small slug noticed this month--no\rlarger than one’s fingernail and recalling the general appearance of\rthe “fretful porcupine,”with “quills” arranged along its back, and\rdisplaying beautifulshades of brilliant blue and crimson.\r \r_Saturday, 14th._--Abeautiful warm sunny day, the sea like glass,\rdappled here and therewith great greasy-like patches peculiar to\rstill weather. Flocks ofeiders, longtails, and gulls appear to be\rhaving a day off, andfloat listlessly hither and thither, seeming only\rintent on makingthemselves aggressively audible in the stillness, the\rlongtails piping a shrilltreble to the sonorous bass of the eiders,\rwhile the gulls contributea fairly good imitation of a laughing\rchorus. Later, the gullsare seen to bestir themselves, as myriads of\rsmall circles break theglassy surface in their vicinity, betraying\rthe presence of “fry,”their legitimate food. Pecking from side to\rside as they floatsilently through the shoal, they evidently enjoy\rthe feast thus providedfor them. The sight of the gulls thus engaged\rapparently reminds theducks of their negligence in this respect, and\rpaddling full speed ahead,they are soon busy diving in the shallower\rwater of the reef. Thelongtails push their way right up to the base\rof the tower, round whichthey are seen circling, plucking at the\rgreen vegetation adheringto the stonework, and cackling loudly as\rthey breathe for a fewseconds on the surface, all unconscious of our\rpresence on the balconyabove them. A small piece of coal dropped while\rthey are still under watercauses them to shoot away like startled\rminnows, and only whenthey have put some distance between them and the\rsource of alarm do theymake their appearance on the surface, evidently\rmuch flustered by themysterious noise. Though a couple of fathoms\rdeep, their alarm wasapparent at the same moment the coal struck the\rsurface, proving that thesound and not the appearance of the falling\rbody was the disturbingcause. The end of the month still sees them\rin close attendance, butany day now may witness their exodus. But\rfew spring migrants havecome our way this month, principally a few\rblackbirds, thrushes, andstarlings.\r \r \r     [1] Fishery Board cruisers.\r \r \r \r \r                             _APRIL 1903._\r \r \rWarm, sunny weather in theearlier part of the month raised our hopes\rof a change of diet, and,coupled with the early appearance of the\rpaidlefish spawn, ourexpectations of an early fishing ran high. On the\r8th, the capture of threesmall cods in “Johnny Gray” track increased\rour hopes, and again onthe 9th, eight were taken, but since then\rwe’ve had no other. Cold,blowy weather, with heavy seas, has rendered\rall attempts in thisdirection futile; however, the attraction--as\revidenced by the stomachsof those captured--still increases, and\rnumbers of bloated paidle“hens,” with their lower jaws protruding like\ra prize bull-dog, are seencruising sluggishly among the tangles in\rquest of a suitablenesting place. The nests this season are unusually\rsmall; sometimes theycontain as much ova as would fill a quart pot.\rEach ovum is a sixteenthof an inch in diameter, and were all permitted\rto come tomaturity--instead of becoming food for other fishes as most\rdo--would soon fill thesea of themselves. “All nature is at one with\rrapine and war,” andnecessarily so, otherwise we would soon be crowded\rout of existence.\r \rOur winter residents, theeiders and longtails, have gradually\rdisappeared. On the 4th, arepresentative pair of each alone remained,\rbut these have now thoughtbetter of it and gone the way of their more\rsensible comrades. A fewgulls, herring, and kittiwakes hover about,\rand guillemots and gannetsare now common.\r \rThe gannets, I am informedby the keepers on the Bass Rock, commenced\rlaying there on the 11th.The solitary egg these birds deposit is\rheavily coated with lime,which, when scrubbed off, exposes a pale blue\rsurface. This coating isprobably the origin of the fallacy that these\rbirds ensure the safety oftheir eggs by cementing them to the bare\rrock. On the contrary,each nest is composed of quite a barrow-load\rof material of the mostmiscellaneous description. One of these nests\rnoted on the Bass thisseason was seen to have the end of a soft-soap\rbarrel for a foundation,armfuls of withered grass, dried tangles, bits\rof rope, string, cottonwaste, and other flotsam and jetsam picked up\rabout the Rock. Amongstthe lining of the nest, pheasant and partridge\rfeathers were seen, whichwere certainly not garnered on the Bass.\rThe harvesting of thewithered grass was accomplished between dark\rand daylight, and,therefore, unnoticed by the keepers, but the area\rof their operations, asseen next day, suggested the presence of a\rlawn mower. Thousands ofthese birds are slaughtered annually by the\rSt Kildians as an articleof diet, and the wonder is, considering the\rsolitary egg deposited andthat three years elapse before the adult\rstage is reached, thatthey continue so numerous.\r \rDr Wallace, in his“Natural Selection,” speaking of birds in general,\rtells us that, ifpermitted to live, in the ordinary course of\rproduction “in fifteenyears each pair of birds would have increased to\rmore than two thousandmillions. Whereas we have no reason to believe\rthat the number of thebirds of any country increases at all in fifteen\ror in one hundred andfifty years. On the average, all above one become\rfood for hawks and kites,wild cats or weasels, or perish of cold and\rhunger as winter comeson.”\r \rMyriads of white whelksare now scattered over the Rock surface, and\ralready patches of musselsand acorn barnacles have been cleared by\rtheir voracity. Their ova,which is to be met with in almost every\rnook and cranny, is leftto take care of itself. A patch of this ova\ris situated in a positionwhich a paidle-hen subsequently fancied for\ra nursery, and, scorningall rights of possession, plastered her ova\rindiscriminately over thatof the whelks, with the result that they are\rnow under the special careof the guardian “cock.”\r \rA stranded cuttlefish wasan object of much interest one evening\rthis month. What aqueer-looking object it appeared, with its eight\rlong tentacles squirmingin all directions, its body a slobbery mass\rof animated mucilage.Although only a foot in diameter it required\rsome force to detach itfrom the rock, as each of the tentacles\ris furnished with rows ofsuckers on its under side. By extending\rthe tentacles in front,the animal was able to move along the Rock\rsurface, not in a jerkyfashion, as might be expected, but with a\rcontinuous gliding motion,clearly showing that each sucker acted\rindependently of itsneighbour. If taken hold of, one or other of the\rtentacles is immediatelytwisted round the hand with a tenacity that\rseems surprisingconsidering the size of the animal, and one can then\rrealise to some extent thestories occasionally heard of its giant\rrelatives of the tropics.Irritated, it appears to have the properties\rof the chameleon, flushingthrough all the gradations of colour in\rquick succession, andlatterly discharging a jet of fluid of inky\rblackness. This resource,however, was utterly useless in the present\rcircumstances, but, onplacing the animal in a shallow pool of water,\rits use was at onceapparent, for on being touched it immediately\rrendered itself invisibleby the inky fluid discharged. Frequent\rirritation, however,exhausted its stock of ink, and latterly only\rclear water was expelled.This expulsion, when effected on the Rock,\rwas accompanied by anaudible murmur. The narrow slits of eyes closely\rresemble those of adog-fish, and the head, with the anterior tentacle\relevated in the air,grotesquely reminds one of an elephant in the act\rof trumpeting.\r \r \r \r \r                              _MAY 1903._\r \r \rDuring the first few hoursof this month our lantern was the centre\rof a twittering throng offeathered migrants. Wheatears, rockpipits,\rstarlings, wrens, androbins fluttered erratically through the rays or\rclamoured in theirinnocence against the glass, apparently desiring a\rcloser acquaintance withthe source of light. Puffs of feathers floated\raway on the easterlybreeze as some unfortunate, less discreet than\rhis fellows, crashedagainst the invisible barrier. The coming dawn,\rhowever, reveals to thesurvivors the absurdity of their position,\rand ere the light isextinguished they have resumed their journey\rshorewards. Frequent fogsoccurred in the earlier part of the month,\rand during the prevalenceof a long spell a long-eared owl was captured\ron the balcony and heldprisoner for a week, during which time various\rsamples of ourcommissariat were offered for his acceptance without\ravail. A luckless sparrow,the only one by the way I have seen here,\rwas then captured andplaced at his disposal. This proved more in\rhis line of business, foron the morning after the rump and tail\rfeathers alone were left.Next day the indigestible portions, feathers,\retc., were cast up in theform of a compact ball. Later a thrush was\rsimilarly offered, butafter a couple of days in each other’s company\rremained untouched. It wasamusing to see the spirited attitude assumed\rby the thrush when in thepresence of his natural foe. Screaming\raggressively at theslightest movement of the owl, he would lunge\rfuriously in hisdirection, his bill all the while snapping audibly.\rThe fog having clearedsomewhat, both were then set at liberty.\r \rAnother very rare visitorseen here this month was a sheldrake, which\rpassed close overheadflying south. This is the first I have seen\rhere, but in Orkney thesebirds are very numerous and are there known\ras the burrow duck, orsly-goose. Sly they certainly are, as evidenced\rby a pair which nestedregularly within a couple of hundred yards of\rthe lighthouse at which Iwas then stationed. A covered drain was\rthe site annually chosen,the nest being placed several yards from\rthe mouth, which openedout on a spacious grassy hollow. The bright\rbrown and white plumage,with vermilion bill and feet, render these\rbirds most conspicuousobjects in an ordinary landscape; but squatting\ron a shingly beach, wheretheir colours harmonise better with their\rsurroundings, theirpresence is less easily detected. Frequently I\rhave watched theirmovements with a telescope from the lantern, and\rthough no one was stirringwithin seeing distance of them, the greatest\rcaution was alwaysexercised in approaching the nest. Lighting a\rhundred yards from thenest, a pretence of feeding diligently was made,\rthough their heads couldbe seen frequently lifting in the direction\rfrom which intrusion wasto be expected. Gradually circling nearer the\rnest, passing andrepassing it with apparent indifference, till within\ra few feet of it theywould then suddenly vanish. The exact moment of\rtheir entrance I was neverable to note, as they appeared to assume\ran invisibility during theremaining few feet of their journey that\rwas really astonishing,but which is less a matter of surprise when\rone has witnessed thesquatting in concealment of a hen pheasant on\rsparse grassy ground.Burrow duck is a name applied to these birds\rfrom their habit ofnesting in disused rabbit burrows. I have counted\ras many as forty youngones following a single pair, while others may\rhave only three or fourjuveniles in their train. It is said they do\rnot scruple to steal theyoung ones from each other. If alarmed while\rfeeding among the decayingseaware on the beach, some of the parents\rwill fly to meet theintruder and endeavour to divert his attention in\ranother direction, whilethe others fly seawards, followed by their\rcallow broods flappingtheir little wings, while their feet tip-tip the\rsurface--a veritablewalking on the waters.\r \rJust as the rocks werebeing overflowed the other day, we had a\rvisit of another birdwhich is but rarely seen here, namely, the\royster-catcher. Theplumage beautiful black and white, the feet and\rbill a brilliant red; thelatter, which is flattened vertically,\rsuggestive of a stick ofsealing wax. Though fairly well acquainted\rwith this species, I neverhad the good fortune till now to see them\rin the _rôle_ of limpetpickers, by which name they are known in some\rlocalities. From thebalcony, with the aid of the telescope, his\rmovements were broughtwithin a few feet of us. Wading an inch or so\rdeep, where the limpetswere probably opening to the influence of the\rincoming tide, he appearedto make a judicious selection; then, with a\rsingle sidelong blow ofhis chisel-like bill, he turned the no doubt\rastonished mollusc upsidedown. Seizing it in his bill, he carried\rit to a still dry portionof the Rock, and in a twinkling he had the\rlimpet out of its shell,and journeying up his long bill to its doom.\rThe tip of the uppermandible appeared to do the scooping out, while\rthe lower merely acted asa resistance outside the shell, the operation\rbeing performed morequickly than even the adroit oyster-man turns out\rhis wares on thehalf-shell. Though not web-footed nor in the habit of\rdiving, I remember seeingone of these birds, which had been winged\rwith a gun-shot, diverepeatedly in order to escape further injury.\r \rOn the afternoon of the16th, two days earlier than last year, a loud\rchorus of discordantvoices floating to our bedroom windows announced\rthe presence of a largeflock of terns--their first arrival here\rsince wintering in thesunny south. Screaming and diving, they appear\rtireless in the pursuit oftheir prey, which, with the aid of the\rtelescope, is seen toconsist of inch-long “fry.” How trim and neat\rthey appear as theycluster on the rocks as the tide recedes, pruning\rtheir feathers andchattering vociferously; the head enshrouded in a\rblack, glossy skull-cap,the back and wings a bluish grey, the under\rparts of unsullied white;the long sharp-pointed scarlet bill tipped\rwith black in harmony withthe legs, and small webbed feet. This\ractive little bird is alsocalled the Sea Swallow, an _alias_ assumed\rfrom its long narrow wingsand forked tail.\r \rThe sea has been literallyalive with large poddlies this month.\rMorning and evening theycan be seen “breaking” on the surface in\rpursuit of “fry,”splashing loudly in their efforts. Though somewhat\raverse to our lure, wegenerally manage to secure a breakfast. On\rquiet, still days, goodsized cod are seen prowling over the rocks;\rand, though lines were setat low water, they were seen at high water\rto pass the temptationwith indifference. Fishermen aver that all fish\rhave times when the mosttempting delicacy fails to attract their\rattention; and possiblythis is the case with those which have been\rlately under ourobservation. Hermit crabs at present are seen to be\rcarrying spawn; and onewhich was removed from its shell was seen to\rhave the spawn so faradvanced that, when placed in a shallow pool,\rthey released theirattachment with the parent, and began life as\rfree swimmers. A smallfish of the blenny species, when taken from\rthe crevice in which thetide had left it, was quite dark coloured,\rbut when placed in a poolwas seen to adapt itself to the colouring\rof the bottom on which itrested, assuming a mottled grey scarcely\rdistinguishable from thepool bottom.\r \rPainters have been busyfor the latter half of this month repainting\rthe outside of thebuilding. Favoured with suitable weather, a\rfortnight sufficed for theoperation of donning the triennial coat,\rwhich will explain theapparent proximity with which it has been lately\rviewed from Arbroath.\r \r \r \r \r                           _JUNE-JULY 1903._\r \r \rA close inspection of theflowing tide as it swirls around our gratings\rreveals the presence ofmyriads of minute globular jellyfishes--the\r_cydippe pileus_--said tobe the favourite food of the arctic whale,\rthough one would scarcelyexpect these bulky cetaceans to thrive or\reven subsist on suchwatery diet. Ranging in size from a pin head to\ra walnut, what a gap eachmouthful must make in their numbers. The\rpoddlies themselves arenot averse to this form of food, as they are\roccasionally seen todisgorge them when landed in our doorway. The\rcommon jellyfishprogresses through the water with a pulsating movement\rof the entire disc, suchmovement being termed “pulmonigrade,” and\rsomewhat resembles theaction of an umbrella being partially opened\rand closed. The mode ofprogression in the case of the _cydippe_ is,\rhowever, different, and istermed “ciliograde,” as the propulsion is\reffected by means of eightvertical bands of cilia or minute plates\roverlapping each other.Each plate having an independent action of\rits own, the animal can propelitself in any desired direction, or,\rby resting them againstits spherical body, sink to the bottom. In\rsunshine these animals intheir evolutions emit the most beautiful\rcombinations of colour onecould imagine, but “you seize the flower,\rits bloom isshed”--scooped up in the hollow of the hand their beauty\rvanishes, and only a smallspat of inert transparent jelly remains.\rHere at present in theRock pools one may witness a peculiar phase in\rthe evolution of thejellyfish. Along with many beautiful varieties of\rmarine vegetation,miniature forests of fir trees garnish the bottom\rof each shallow pool.These lilliputian firs, with their branches no\rthicker than a hair, arebut plants in semblance, for here is the\ropening chapter in thelife history of the medusae. Under the lens\reach fragile shoot is seento consist of multitudes of small discs\rpiled upon each other likeso many saucers, each of which will, in\rdue course, detach itselffrom its neighbour and enter on its new\rexistence as fullyequipped as the exaggerated specimens frequently\rseen stranded on ourbeaches. Lurking amongst the vegetation in the\rpools are numerous tinyspider-crabs, roaming about in search of food.\rOnly by their movementscan they be located, as each bears about with\rit quite a luxuriantgrowth of vegetation, with which I understand all\rcrustaceans would becomeinvested did they not--ludicrous as it may\rseem--regularly attend totheir toilet. The “spider,” however, unable\rto procure a living byforce of arms like his bigger brother, has\rrecourse to the subterfugeof posing as an innocent patch of marine\rvegetation, and by suchconcealment is enabled to capture food which\rwould be otherwiseunattainable. The females at present are seen to be\rcarrying spawn. When changingtheir position in the pool it is somewhat\rsurprising to see aportion of the plants, which one has been admiring,\rsuddenly become endowedwith the powers of locomotion, detach itself\rfrom the mass, and,ambling leisurely round the pool, come to rest on\rthe fringe of some otherpatch with which it completely harmonises.\r \rDuring the whole of June,at daybreak and again in the evening, the\rsea around us appearedliterally alive with large-sized poddlies.\rTheir continual flip-flopon the surface in pursuit of “fry” could be\rdistinctly heard from thebalcony. Though frequently within reach of\rour attempts from thedoorway, they failed to appreciate our invitation\rto any extent, and onlywith much perseverance did we occasionally\rmanage to breakfast attheir expense. A few cod have been taken from\rthe pools at low water.The deepest of these pools is about a couple\rof fathoms at low water,and has the reputation of being a sort of\rconvalescent home, as fishare occasionally taken there which are in\ranything but the pink ofcondition. Fishing there lately, I hooked\ra cod two feet long, andwas somewhat surprised to see the feeble\rresistance it made. Onlanding it, however, it was seen to be a most\rphthisical-lookingspecimen and in the last stages of emaciation, the\rbones almost protrudingthrough the skin. Needless to state, his life\rwas spared, and thepatient returned to his element. I have frequently\rseen emaciated specimensof the cod family, but as they were full\rgrown, fishermenattributed this to old age, but this was certainly not\rthe case with our catch,it being but half grown.\r \rI often wonder if any onehas noticed the following peculiarity. When\rfish show an unusualtenacity of life, that is, after being gutted and\rcleaned, exhibit strongmuscular action for some time after, that this\rphenomenon invariablyprecedes a change of some kind in the weather,\rusually more wind orheavier sea. This at least is my experience from\rseveral years’observations.\r \rThe remaining patches ofwhite whelk ova now appear flaccid and empty.\rBrushing the hand over theapparently empty capsules, a granular\rdeposit adheres to theskin, which on close examination is seen to\rbe minute whelks. Evenwith the aid of the lens the sulci or furrow,\rthrough which boringoperations are conducted, is not yet apparent, but\rwhich later is common tothis species. The rocks at present are thickly\rsewn with these juveniles,and myriads of adults are busy clearing\rthe rocks of barnacles andimmature mussels. As late as 28th July a\rsolitary paidle-cock wasseen guarding its nest; this is unusually\rlate, as they aregenerally finished nursing by the end of June.\r \rThe middle of July broughtus our first young tern, and towards the\rclose of the month severalwere in attendance. A large school of\rbottle-nose whales crossedthe reef on the last Sunday of July, their\rpuffing and blowing beingquite audible as they headed north, probably\rafter herring.\r \rPleasure steamers fromDundee have been frequently round the Rock\rduring June and July, someof the trippers evidently enjoying the sail,\rothers emphatically not.One of the passengers, as the steamer got to\rwindward of us, favouredus with a cornet solo, which we gratefully\racknowledged with a dip ofour flag. On several evenings an hour’s\rfishing was given thepassengers, but their catches could scarcely\rbe expected to have anyappreciable influence on the market. Broken\rweather, excessive rain,with occasional thunderstorms, describes the\rweather we have beenhaving, the seasonable days of sunshine and warmth\rbeing few and far between.\r \r \r \r \r                             _AUGUST 1903._\r \r \rA month of variableweather, much rain and heavy seas occasionally\rcompelling the boatsengaged in the herring fishing to run for it.\rDearly bought indeed istheir silvery freight as they thresh their way\rhomewards followed by astiff sou’-easter, their oilskins glistening\rwith repeated drenchings,and twelve miles’ ploughing and a doubtful\rbar yet to be negotiatedere safety is reached. How different! no\rrunning for home with us;here we remain secure and comfortable amid\rthe hurly-burly, and trustto the stability of the grand old building\rfor our safety. Right welldoes it merit our confidence. After a\rcentury’s buffetings withthe elements, not a single sign of weakening\rin the never ceasingconflict is evident. Surely a creditable testimony\rto the honesty of thelabour employed in its erection.\r \rThat herring areoccasionally in our vicinity is evidenced by the\rindustrious diving of thegannets, accompanied by large flocks of gulls\rand terns, and also by thepresence of whales snorting and puffing\rclose to the Rock. At lowwater the reef is covered with gulls and\rterns resting from theirlabours of the tide. Scorning such relaxment,\rthe gannets, wheeling anddiving, maintain their ceaseless chase,\restablishing their kinshipwith that bird of the Ancient Mariner,\rthe tireless albatross. Askua or robber-gull has billeted himself\ramongst the gulls andterns, and is frequently seen harrying them\rof their legitimate prey.It is surprising that the terns at least,\rwith their needle-pointedbills and belligerent propensities, suffer\rthemselves to be sodespoiled, and make no attempt to combine and drive\roff this pirate on thefruits of their industry. On the contrary,\rafter a fruitless twistingand doubling in mid-air, in which they are\rinvariably worsted, theyseem to accept these periodic attacks of the\rskua as a matter ofcourse.\r \rAmateur fishers have beenbut seldom in evidence here this summer; even\rthe lobsters have enjoyeda season of comparative rest. Possibly the\runcertain state of theweather prevented their usual visits. Towards\rthe close of the month atrio of amateurs cast anchor--or rather what\rdoes duty as such--withinhail of our kitchen window, a favourite spot\rof theirs. Lines were nosooner down than a brisk business began in\rcod, varied by anoccasional poddley which has little or no market\rvalue, but which to ushere is always acceptable, and forms the\rprincipal part of ourcatches. Several good catches of these have been\rtaken here during themonth. What appears to be whitings two inches in\rlength is seen to be theirfood at present. The terns also are seen\rto be on similar diet, andthough engaged in conveying a mouthful to\rtheir young ones, it in noway impedes their full flow of language, nor\rmuffles in the slightestdegree their strident throat notes.\r \rDuring the unusually lowtides occurring this month an opportunity was\rafforded of examining amost peculiar form of animal life of which I\rhave nowhere seen anyaccount. Attached to the rocks amongst groups of\rcorallines this curiousobject[2] has all the semblance of a bird’s\rclaw. Imagine the leg of abird amputated at the knee, firmly fastened\rto the rock by the cutend, and imbued with life, and you have a fair\ridea of this animal. Abouthalf an inch in length, the “leg” is seen\rto be composed ofsegments, and terminates in three toes, furnished\rwith sharp, curved claws,which keep up a constant clutching--at what\ris not apparent; but theaction strongly reminds one of a similar\reffect produced byjuveniles who have become the proud possessor of\ra hen’s foot, and for apiece of slate pencil--the usual juvenile\rcurrency--demonstrate toadmiring companions the utility of the\rextensor muscles.\r \rLast month we had theunique experience of being serenaded by the\rDundee trippers with acornet solo, but the last Saturday of this\rmonth fairly eclipsed thisperformance. As we were about to sit down\rto tea we were somewhatstartled to hear the regular beat of a drum\rand the unmistakeablemusic of the bagpipes. A hasty survey from the\rkitchen window sent usflying to the balcony, there to witness the\rnovel sight of a ship,manned by boys--a training brig evidently, bound\rfor Dundee. Bearing downupon us from the eastward, she approached\rclose to the Tower, thetide being about full. Flag courtesies being\rexchanged, crowds ofjuvenile faces were seen lining the rail, while\rmidships pipers discoursedsome lively music, including the “Cock o’\rthe North.” The wind beinglight, the vessel made but little way, and\ras she slowly crossed thereef the youngsters lustily cheered us, which\rwe returned as best wecould. Breaking into song, the whole ship’s\rcompany favoured us with“Poor Cock Robin,” the youthful voices having\ra most pleasing effect inthe stillness of a really beautiful summer’s\revening. Applauding ourloudest, cheers were again exchanged as she\rslowly drifted beyond ourhearing, the whole scene strongly reminiscent\rof “H.M.S. Pinafore.”\r \r \r     [2] Whale-louse.\r \r \r \r \r                       _SEPTEMBER-OCTOBER1903._\r \r \rThe man that pours thewater out has certainly been paying attention\rto his business, and inconjunction with the puffy bellower of storms\rfavoured us with weather anythingbut peaceful. Unlike the farmers,\rwe have little cause ofcomplaint. No sodden fields or ruined crops\rappal the eye, for evenafter a “regular snorter” things here remain\rpretty much as they were.True, the aspect changes as the season\radvances. The whitewashedappearance of the rock surface in summer,\rdue to the presence of theacorn barnacle, has now vanished--thanks to\rthe voracity of the whitewhelk--and the rocks appear in their natural\rcolour, a reddish-brown.The “sere and yellow” is well represented\rin the once luxuriantcrops of heavy tangles, but lately swaying on\rthe surface with afreshness and beauty peculiarly their own, now\rstorm-tossed, frayed andabraded, denuded of their palm-like fronds,\rthey appear but a vestigeof their former selves. The turbulent state\rof the weather interferesseriously with our fishing, keeping the\rpoddlies at a respectfuldistance from our door; indeed, any approach\rin our direction atpresent would certainly denote suicidal mania on\rtheir part. At a safedistance outside the breakers, they are to be\rseen playing on thesurface in the early morning and evening, so that\rour expectations are stillhigh should the weather but abate.\r \rThe eider ducks, which onthe 20th September were represented by a\rsolitary individual--thefirst arrival--now number over a hundred. The\rlongtails are stillawanting to complete our list, but their advent\rmay be looked for earlynext month. On suitable nights for the past\rtwo months we have alwayshad some feathered visitors “becking and\rbooing” to us through thelantern. On 4th October an extremely rare\rvisitor--here atleast--made its appearance, namely, the ring-ousel,\rthe first I have seen.
