Insize, shape, and general colouring, this\rmigrant might easily bemistaken for a hen blackbird, but for the\rconspicuous white crescentacross the throat, in this instance somewhat\rfaint, but well defined,owing possibly to the bird being in immature\rplumage. On the morning ofthe 24th October over two dozen tiny\rgold-crest wrens werecircling round our lantern, jostling and tumbling\rover each other in franticefforts to keep in line with the white\rflash, the red flashevidently having no attraction for them. A skylark\rand robin were also of thecompany, as well as several redwings. The\rrobin always seems to havea truer sense of his position than any other\rof our visitors. While theothers clamour futilely against the glass he\rmaintains an aloofness andself-possession truly remarkable. His eyes\rseem to be everywhere, andonly with difficulty and the exercise of a\rlittle strategy is hiscapture effected. Of course, our captures are\rbut temporary, and merelyfor the sake of a few minutes’ examination.\r \rWe had rather adisappointing experience with the Channel Fleet while\rcruising in these waterslast month (September). Passing north in the\rdark, we were quiteunaware of their presence, the _Sutlej_ alone being\rseen later steaming northat 6 p.m. on the 21st, nearer to Arbroath\rthan to us. On returningsouth a string of brilliant lights passing\rthree miles outside of usat two o’clock in the morning was all we saw\rof the procession.\r \rOn 29th October a flock ofthirteen field-fares passed at 9 a.m.,\rflying towards Arbroath.This is the first arrival here of these birds,\rand earlier than usual.\r \rOn examining a lark whichhad been killed on the lantern the other\rnight, a small land shellwas found adhering to the feathers on the\runder part of the body.Arguing from this instance, the assumption\rthat they also are imbuedwith the migratory instinct and adopt this\rmode of travelling wouldprobably be considered far-fetched. That\rthere is much undreamt ofin our philosophy is as pregnant as when\ruttered, and possibly theconnection between mollusc and bird was due\rto circumstances otherthan purely accidental.\r \r \r \r \r                            _NOVEMBER 1903._\r \r \rSunday, 1st.--A flat calm.A pleasant change, indeed, after our recent\rexperience, and one whichhas fortunately continued for the greater\rpart of the month. Fish,which had maintained a safe distance during\rthe turmoil of last month,now ventured within catching distance, and\rseveral good takes werehad. After the middle of the month heavy seas\ragain drove them out ofreach into deep water. Those that were caught\rwere seen to be gorgedwith soil half an inch in length, resembling\ra piece of white threadwith a black dot on either side at one end\rrepresenting the eyes.Amongst the first that were taken the small\rjellyfish--_cydippepileus_--seemed to have been their principal diet,\rbut latterly the soilappeared to be preferred to the medusae. Outside\rthe breakers they arestill occasionally seen playing on the surface\rin the evenings. “Playing”is scarcely correct, as their play is, in\rreality, strict attentionto business, and their appearance on the\rsurface merely denotestheir having overleaped themselves in pursuit\rof their legitimate prey.Our flock of eider ducks, much larger than\rit has been for severalyears back, now numbers 120. Amongst the\rsmothering breakers theyseem to be in their glory, and are busily\rengaged in clearing offthe immature mussels that have escaped the\rvoracity of the whitewhelks. On the 2nd, the first two longtails were\rseen, exactly a weekearlier than last year, but their numbers are\rbeing but tardilyreinforced, as they only totalled six at the end of\rthe month. Though the mainbody of the solan geese or gannets left\rtheir breeding haunts onthe Bass Rock on the 5th of the month for the\rfishing grounds--in theMediterranean it is said--occasional stragglers\rare still seen in ourvicinity.\r \rOn the night of the 8th wehad a few migrants on the lantern, ten\rblackbirds--three only ofwhich were males--and three fieldfares.\rSeveral of them appearedmuch fatigued, and after a few preliminary\rhops round the lantern,settled down on the lee side to have a nap.\rA fresh breeze blowing atthe time, those still on the move were\rfrequently hustled by thewind against the sleepers, who, thus\rrudely awakened,vigorously resented what they no doubt considered a\rdeliberate attempt toassault, with the result that all hands were at\rtimes engaged in a battleroyal; the hen “blackies” only engaging with\rthose of their own sex,while the cocks and fieldfares tackled all\rcomers indiscriminately.It was rather amusing to witness the finish\rbetween a pair thusengaged. Edging round the narrow pathway in their\rstruggle, they graduallycame under the influence of the wind sweeping\rround the lantern, whensuddenly one of them would be wheeled off its\rfeet away into thedarkness, its opponent peering after it in evident\rastonishment, and probablycongratulating itself on its prowess. The\rhaze, responsible fortheir appearance here, clearing after midnight,\rbefore 3 a.m. they had allresumed their journey shoreward. On the\r20th, a pair of grey crowspassed, going east, and on the 22nd a heron\rwas seen travelling in thesame direction. Again, on the night of\rthe 27th, three henblackbirds and a starling had the lantern all to\rthemselves.\r \rThe white whelks have nowgone into winter quarters, and only a few\rare to be seen lingeringamong patches of immature mussels. The\rblack edible whelk, orperiwinkle, whose vegetarian habits demand a\rmore inshore life, is hereconspicuous by its absence. Occasionally,\rduring the summer months,a very close search reveals a few solitary\rspecimens. Two differentvarieties of slugs have been much in evidence\ramong the rocks here oflate. One of them (_Doris coccinea_),\rresembling in shape andcolour a section of an orange, I have already\rdescribed; the othersomewhat resembles the common snail. Furnished\rwith anterior horns andfleshy spines, ranged along the back, it curls\ritself up when out ofwater like a hedgehog. Earlier in the season they\rwere mostly of a beautifulbluish colour, now they appear quite red.\rWithout any visible meansof defence, one can fancy these shell-less\rmolluscs furnishing adelectable tit-bit for a hungry cod.\r \rTurning over some loosestones in the shallow pools numbers of young\rpaidle-fish are seenadhering to the under sides by means of their\rbreast suckers, and whentaken in the hand readily adhere to the\rfingers. I lately saw anillustration in which the paidle “hen” was\rdepicted as leading abrood of about two dozen juveniles after the\rmanner of the domesticfowl. This is stretching the simile with a\rvengeance, and not inaccordance with facts. The “hen,” on depositing\rthe ova, takes no furtherinterest in it, and the “cock” alone guards\rthe nest till the youngare hatched out, when he also disappears,\rneither of them being seentill the following season. Considering that\reach nest probablycontains millions of embryos, one can imagine the\rmaternal anxiety in“airing” such a brood.\r \rCooped indoors so long,one is glad to take advantage of the quiet\rweather and the absence ofthe tide to enjoy a spin along the gratings,\reven though at night andin darkness. At first the darkness seems\rto preclude allpossibility of holding a straight course along the\rnarrow path, but as theeyes get accustomed to it the twenty steps\rand a round turn can beaccomplished with wonderful precision. Should\rthe round turn be omitted,however, you will probably be reminded of\rit by coming a cropper onthe Bell Rock, which, though historical,\ris not at all sympathetic.A similar omission at the other end meets\rwith more sympathy, ifsuch sentiment can be said to enter Neptune’s\rembrace. The flash fromthe lantern overhead sheds no light below,\rthough some fugitive raysescaping between the flashes illuminate the\routlying perches orboat-guides. Any attention to these wandering\rrays occasions a haltingtendency in one’s steps and a disposition to\rlurch laterally, demandingour undivided attention. The night is clear\rand dark and the variouslights along the coast, which on moonlight\rnights are partiallyeclipsed, now show to the best advantage.\rFifteen miles to thesou’-west the powerful electric light of the\rIsle of May flings itsquadruple flash with startling brilliancy,\ra faint bar of lighttravelling athwart the base of our tower with\reach flash similar to whatwould be produced by a lighted carriage\rpassing at a few yardsdistance. This light is said to be of three\rmillion candle-power andis of the arc type, using carbons one and\ra-half inch in diameter.To a stranger entering the light-room while\rthe light is in action asomewhat disagreeable sound is heard. This\ris occasioned by thetremendous current bridging the arc between the\rcarbons, and for all theworld resembles the sound made by a circular\rsaw passing throughexceedingly knotty timber. The Bass Rock emerges\rfrom the right shoulder ofthe “May,” and prevents us seeing the light\rlately erected on itssouth side. A little to the right of the “May,”\rthe eye encounters thefixed white light of the North Carr Lightship,\rthree miles off Fife Ness,and distant from us nine miles. This light\rconsists of six smallargand lamps, set in silvered reflectors and\renclosed in a lanternencircling the mast half-way up. Colza oil was\rthe illuminant used untilrecently in the North Carr Lightship, as\rit was formerly in all theNorthern lighthouses, where it had ousted\rthe more expensive sperm,but which in turn has been superseded by\rparaffin. The lamps arehung on gimbals to obviate as much as possible\rthe pitching and rollingof the vessel. With due allowance for the\rexaggeration that a pennypiece placed on the deck shows “heads” or\r“tails” at the vessel’sown sweet will, one can understand that the\rmotion in bad weather mustbe considerable. Table guards, though\rretaining the dishes onthe table, do not in the slightest restrain\rthe liberty of theircontents, which find lodgment as they list. On\rsuch occasions the menresort to the expedient of squatting on the\rdeck of their quarterswith their backs against the bulkhead and their\routstretched feet firmlyopposed to those of their opposite neighbour,\rand only thus, plate inhand, are they enabled to discuss their soup\rwith any degree ofcertainty.\r \rFurther to the right, inline with the town of Crail--landlocked from\rus--a dull red glare inthe sky marks the position of Edinburgh,\rdistant forty miles as thecrow flies. Following the loom of the\rFife coast, the twinklinglights of St Andrews next meet the eye,\rwhile further up the Firththe two fixed lights of Tayport greet\rtheir doubles ofBuddonness on the opposite side. Midway between the\rlights of Tayport andBuddon a single flash every half minute marks\rthe position of theAbertay Lightship. Unlike the other lights here\rmentioned, the three lastnamed are under the control of the Dundee\rCorporation. Journeyingnorthwards till almost at right angles to our\rstarting point, the nextvisible are the lights of Arbroath, twelve\rmiles distant. Viewedthrough the telescope how dreary and desolate\rthey appear, without theusual accompanying signs of life, a feeble\rcluster in the vicinity ofthe harbour dwindling away to the Victoria\rPark in a solitary line.Further north the occulting light of Montrose\rNess catches the eye withits thirty seconds of light followed by\rthirty seconds’ darkness.Northwards still, twenty-five miles from us,\rthe light of Tod Head,near Bervie, limits our view in that direction.\rOnly in exceptionallyclear weather is it visible from here, and then\ronly from the elevation ofour balcony. The characteristics of this\rlight are six whiteflashes in quick succession during fifteen seconds,\rfollowed by fifteenseconds’ darkness. Returning to our starting point,\rthe Isle of May, andjourneying till thirty miles due south from here,\rour view is again limitedby St Abb’s Head, showing a white flash every\rten seconds. About midwaybetween the latter light and the “May” the\rlight of Barns Ness, nearDunbar, is, like St Abb’s and Tod Head, only\roccasionally seen, itscharacteristic being a triple white flash every\rthirty seconds. Thepresence of these lights makes our coasts as safely\rnavigable by night as byday, and the demand is still for more--a\rfact which drew from afacetious old “salt” the remark that “sailors\rnowadays want a hand-railalong the coast.”\r \r \r \r \r                            _DECEMBER 1903._\r \r \rA month of dull, dark,unsettled weather, with scarcely any sunshine to\rspeak of, and admitting ofbut little heliographic communication with\rthe “shore,” a conditionof things, by the way, preventing the “shore\rstation” proclaiming toanxious eyes the interesting advent of another\raddition to the census.Quite a depressing effect is experienced\rat such prolonged absenceof the land, and the reappearance of the\rGrampians, though swathedin winter vestments, would be a welcome\rsight. Our fish supplyceased early in the month, and its renewal need\rnot be expected before themonth of May. Gulls are numerous at present,\rand evidently on shortrations considering their vigilant attention\rto the kitchen slops. Ouronly feathered visitor for the month was a\rbelated bullfinch, whoreached us only to die. The eiders and longtails\rcontinue in evidence, andhave now the company of four cormorants.\r \rStar-fish are alwaysplentiful here, though of course more numerous\rin summer. All are of thefive-rayed variety, including the “brittle”\rstar-fish, which, unlikeits fellows, discards its rays on the\rslightest irritation, andpossesses a body no larger than a shirt\rbutton, in ludicrouscontrast with the squirming rays two inches in\rlength. In startlingcontrast with the latter was a specimen found in\ra shallow pool early inthe month, and which was quite new to us here.\rSix inches in diameter,the stranger appeared all body, with very short\rrays, of which there weretwelve. Unlike the usual five-pointed star\rshape, it might be betterdescribed as a deeply serrated disc, the\rupper surface being richlycoloured with concentric rings of crimson.\rAnother object of note atpresent is seen scattered about the rocks,\rresembling small coils ofribbon, apparently the egg-cases of some\rfish. These are white incolour, and somewhat resemble the outline of\rthe human ear. Theenveloping membrane, of rubber-like consistency, is\rquite transparent, and isseen to contain a frothy fluid. The inner\redge of each coil isfurnished with an adhesive margin, by means of\rwhich it is firmly fixedto the rock surface.\r \rIt is interesting to notethe different modes adopted by fish to ensure\rthe propagation of theirspecies. Some, apparently careless of results,\rconsign the spawn to themercy of the waves, while others conceal\rit from predatoryneighbours in the soft, sandy bottom. The skate\rfamily, adopting adifferent procedure with their egg cases--those\rpurse-like receptaclesoften seen cast up on our beaches--moor them\rsecurely to the vegetationon the sea bottom by the long elastic\rtendrils--prolongations ofthe four corners of the case. Parental\rinterest is, perhaps,better evinced in the case of the “paidle-fish”\rstanding guard over hisnest with unwearied vigilance, exhibiting all\rthe care of a brooding henfor his future offspring. Again, in the\rcase of the dog-fish--theplague of fishermen--how different. Here the\ryoung are brought forth,after the fashion of mammals, fully developed.\rA common sight in fishingboats where these pests are brought on\rboard, is to see thefinger-long juveniles swimming briskly about in\rthe bilge-water with theyolk-sac still attached. In some parts it is\rcustomary to split and drythese fish for winter consumption, though\rthe flavour of roasted“dogs” would scarcely recommend itself to\ranyone unaccustomed to itsuse, nor its relationship to fish even be\rsuspected. The liver atone time supplied the natives of the Hebrides\rwith lamp oil, and wasalso considered a panacea for all bovine\railments, the method ofadministering the dose being to keep the head\rof the cow elevated whilethe mouth was forced open, and the entire\rliver, as removed from thefish, slipped gently down the throat; no\r“sugar-coated pills” aboutthat!\r \rSpring tides occurring atthe “full” and “change” of the moon, and our\rgratings consequentlybeing then uncovered for a much longer period\reach tide, the “reliefs”are so arranged as to fall on or about these\rdates. Consequently,during the winter months, when the reliefs are\rmade after dark, there isalways the chance of every alternate relief\rbeing favoured with fullmoonlight. On the night of the 18th our final\rrelief for the year waseffected in comparatively quiet weather. At\rrelief times, providingthe weather is quiet, the landing gratings\rbegin to uncover when theebb has run four hours. Whenever a footing\ris possible the keepersdescend with the signal-lamps, and by their\rcolour--red, green, orwhite--indicate to the relieving steamer the\rlanding they consider itsafest to attempt. Two boats are immediately\rdispatched from thesteamer in charge of the first and second officers,\rand, guided by thesteamer’s searchlight, cautiously approach the\rlanding signalled. Givenquiet weather, the narrow passages leading to\rthe different landings areeasily negotiated, though to a stranger,\reven in quiet weather, theattempt would be extremely hazardous. Should\rthere be any surf on theRock, the boats take up a position as near\rthe entrance as is prudentwith safety, and there wait the opportunity\rof a lull. This generallyoccurring at the termination of three bigger\rwaves than usual, theofficer gives the word, and the first boat shoots\rforward into the boilingtrack. Talk about “shooting the rapids,” why,\rit isn’t a circumstance toit. Swinging through “Johnny Gray” track\ron a dirty night inmid-winter is quite “rapid” enough to satisfy the\rmost morbid desire forexcitement. At times disaster lies beneath the\rvery oars, but thenecessary impetus has already been given to the\rboat, and she clears itwith a rush, to be met the next moment with a\rdrenching sea on the portbow, which threatens to slew her upon the\ropposite ledge, despitethe strenuous resistance of the starboard\roars, the tips of whichgrate on the shelving ledge as they urge her\rthrough the narrow channelinto safety, the entire effort affording a\rsplendid demonstration ofthe necessity for doing the right thing at\rthe right moment. Theseamen understand exactly what is expected of\rthem, and respond withalacrity to the officers’ orders. Despite the\rdanger attending suchwork, that no serious accident has ever been\rrecorded reflects muchcredit on all concerned, from the captain, who,\ras a boy, began his careeron board the vessel which he now commands,\rdownwards. Particularly isthe second officer--a veteran of forty\ryears’ experience in thiswork--to be congratulated on the possession\rof a “clean sheet” aftersuch protracted service in what is frequently\ran extremely hazardouscalling.\r \r \r \r \r                            _JANUARY 1904._\r \r \rThe weather continues dulland dark, but comparatively quiet--a matter\rof much importance to usat relief times. We have no aversion to a\rrousing gale betweenreliefs; then one can afford to appreciate the\rgrandeur of the warringelements; but as the appointed time draws near,\rand no sign of abatementis evident, all hands become a trifle uneasy,\respecially the man whoseturn it is for shore duty. It is rather\rtantalising to see therelief steamer cruising doubtfully round the\rRock, then finally takeher departure, unable to effect a landing, all\ron account of “that nastyswell,” which possibly a week ago we were\reulogising as “sublime!”It is a matter of remark here how quickly the\rboisterous nor’-east seasare subdued by the westerly wind. At times\rthe morning presents ascene anything but peaceful, the whole reef\renveloped by shouting,tumbling seas, which bang our domicile till the\rcrockery rattles, andblind by their spray our kitchen windows, seventy\rfeet from the Rock--yet,let the wind but freshen from the westward\rand the conflictimmediately becomes visible. The seas, now driving\rin the teeth of the wind,have their curling crests whipped cleanly\roff and carried leewardlike clouds of steam. Perceptibly their force\rdiminishes as they “liftand ’scend” in the struggle for supremacy,\rtill by evening tide acomparatively easy relief may be effected. Home\rnews and the doings of theouter world are then at our disposal, as\rwell as a welcomeconsignment of fresh provisions. Considering his\ralmost seven weeks’confinement on the Rock, the shore-going keeper may\rbe pardoned a feeling ofrelief and elation as he steps on board the\rrelieving steamer--afeeling, by the way, not at all to be confounded\rwith that of the returnjourney. As an instance how dissimilar\rthe same object may appearfrom different view-points, our lonely\rhabitation never seems toassume such a pleasing aspect as when seen\rvanishing astern. Verily,it is we who appreciate the truth of the\rIrishman’s illogicalremark that “the best thing about going away from\rhome is getting backagain.”\r \rA round of the differentfishing pools was made this month at low\rwater, resulting in thecapture of a most unhealthy-looking specimen\rof a poddley in the“Hospital” (Neill’s Pool). Long, lank, and lean,\ra post-mortem revealed theliver attenuated to a mere thread. It is\rmost remarkable why thesesickly fish should favour this pool alone.\rAbout twenty feet indiameter and twelve feet deep, with the bottom\rthickly strewn withrounded boulders, there is always a shallow wash\rinto it at the loweststate of the tide. Possibly its greater depth\roffers a safer refuge forthese convalescents than the other pools.\rWhatever the reason, thefact remains that in this pool alone these\rspecimens are found; notonly poddlies, but lythe and cod as well.\rWith the flying fish ofthe tropics we are more or less familiar, and\rof tree-climbing fish andoverland travellers we have the testimony\rof travellers that suchperverse specimens do exist. The _ceratodus_\rof Queensland, forinstance, which, with its peculiar respiratory\rarrangement and ambulatoryfins is enabled to transport itself over\rswampy ground in migratingfrom pool to pool, a feat suggestive of\rthe Yankee’sshallow-draught steamer, to which an ordinary meadow was\reasily navigable,providing there had been a heavy dewfall. The cause\rof these reflections wasthe discovery of a small fish, some four\rinches in length, on thecleaning path encircling our lantern, over\ra hundred feet from itsusual habitat. Of the “cobbler” variety, the\rexpanded pectoral finsmight, with a little imagination, be imbued with\rthe powers of flight, butmore than likely our visitor owed its exalted\rposition to some predatorygull, which, unable to bolt its victim or\rescape from covetousneighbours, had dropped it where found.\r \rA solitary lapwing was ouronly feathered visitor for the mouth.\rApropos of these days of“retaliation,” there is an old Scottish Act\rof Parliament of the timeof Edward the First relating to this bird,\rin which all its eggs areordered to be broken when found, “in order\rthat Peesweeps may not gosouth, and become a delicious repast to our\runnatural enemies theEnglish!”\r \rA quiet night on the 31stseemed to augur favourably for our relief,\rwhich was due thefollowing evening; by that time, however, the\rprospect was completelychanged by a strong sou’-east wind, and\rconsequently heavy sea,which rendered landing extremely doubtful. The\rfollowing morning the_Pharos_ made her appearance, and attempted a\rlanding at daybreak. Thetwo boats despatched from the steamer for this\rpurpose, on approachingthe Rock, found the passage unsafe to attempt,\rand returned to thesteamer. Weighing anchor, the _Pharos_ proceeded to\rthe relief of the NorthCarr Lightship, where, owing to the tempestuous\rstate of the weather, shebroke the hawser by which she moors to the\rlightship three timesduring the operation. Landing the relief men\rfrom the lightship andBass Rock--which had been relieved the previous\rday--at North Berwick, andsheltering overnight at the Isle of May,\rshe returned to us onWednesday morning and succeeded in effecting the\rrelief.\r \r \r \r \r                            _FEBRUARY 1904._\r \r \rCormorants have been morein evidence here this month than usual. At\rpresent a flock ofthirteen is to be seen diving in the deep water\rsurrounding the reef.Scorning the crustaceans, molluscs, and other\rground game of the eidersand longtails, these birds subsist entirely\rupon fish, in pursuit ofwhich they are extremely dexterous. The long\rsharp-pointed bill isexcellently adapted for securing their prey,\rthe extremity of the uppermandible curving over the lower in a sharp\rhook, the efficiency ofwhich I once saw forcibly demonstrated. One of\rthese birds, while flyinghigh overhead, was winged by a gunshot, and\ron striking the grounddisgorged a recently swallowed poddley, some\rten inches long. A boy ofthe party, having the temerity to thrust his\rfoot towards the bird, hadthe upper leather of his boot pierced and\rthe foot slightly woundedby the sharp hook-like process of the upper\rmandible. During anexceedingly rigorous winter in Orkney--in ’94, if\rI rememberaright--hundreds of these birds perished from hunger. In\ra roofless hut, a fewyards from high-water mark, I counted fourteen\rdying and dead. Rats werebusy devouring the dead, while the living\rstumbled weakly over thehalf-eaten bodies of their comrades. In\rthe most unlikely placesthey were to be met with, coming right up\rto our doors as if beggingfor shelter. One of them surprised me by\rwaddling into theworkshop, passing over my boots as if unconscious\rof my presence, andsettling underneath the bench to die. Any food we\rcould offer them wasalways rejected. One evening my attention was\rdrawn to our poultry,which, instead of being on their roost, stood\rhuddled about theentrance. Thinking the entrance had been accidentally\rblocked from within, Ientered by the doorway to investigate. Judge\rmy astonishment at finding“Mister _Phalacrocorax Carbo_”--such is\rthe cormorant’s scientifictitle--standing Horatius-like holding\rthe diminutive passageagainst all comers. Wisps of feathers, with\rshreds of skin adhering tothem, lay strewn in front of him, while his\reffective “hook” gleamedgory from the carnage. Needless to state, his\rejectment was summarilyeffected. When in pursuit of prey their method\rof diving is conspicuouslydifferent from other birds of the diving\rfraternity, and they maybe identified at a long distance by this\rpeculiarity alone. Bracingthemselves together, they spring forward as\rif surmounting someimaginary obstacle on the surface, the entire body\rassuming the form of anarc, reminding one of a fractious pony in the\ract of “bucking.” Theducks, on the other hand, with wings half open,\rmerely topple over andunder, turning on their own axis, so to speak.\rHaving secured a fish, itis brought to the surface, where, after some\rpreliminary adjustments tofacilitate transit, it disappears head\rfirst, the long neckdenoting its course by “swelling wisibly.” This\ris the bird which theChinese train to fish for them. A ring is placed\ron the bird’s neck, whichprevents it appropriating its earnings for\rits own use. Whenever aswollen neck appears the owner is hauled on\rboard the “sampan,” andthe “swelling” reduced by a rough and ready\rform of massage.Occasionally the constricting ring is removed, and the\rbird permitted to enjoyits catch as a stimulant to further exertions.\rHistory records the use ofthis bird for similar purposes in our own\rcountry in the oldentimes, a leather strap being used instead of the\rring. Last year, fishermenin the south of England petitioned for power\rto destroy these birds atall seasons on the plea of the destruction\rcaused by them amongstfish in the estuaries. The cormorant measures\rthree feet in length, andbelongs to the pelican family, of which we\rhave but two other Britishrepresentatives--the shag, a smaller edition\rof the cormorant by eightinches, and the gannet or solan goose.\r \rOn several occasionsduring the month a seal was observed sporting\ramongst the breakers. Theother evening he was seen within a few yards\rof the tower, busydevouring a huge cod. Mastication was entirely\rdispensed with; tiltinghis snout in the air, each ragged mouthful\rdisappeared at a singlegulp. The fish was allowed to sink after every\rmouthful; and two or threeminutes would be spent under water before\rbringing it to the surfacefor another attack. In a remarkably short\rtime the head and backbonealone were left.\r \rOur feathered visitors forthe month were represented by a couple of\rskylarks, three songthrushes, a pair of carrion crows, and a solitary\rstarling. Eiders andlongtails still continue in attendance, and\rgannets are now plentiful.The latter arrived at their breeding haunt\ron the Bass Rock fromtheir southern sojourn on the 9th of last month.\r \rThe month has been wet,cold, and stormy, exceptionally heavy seas\rprevailing in the earlierhalf. The closing day of the month was\rbeautifully clear andsunny, but cold and frosty, our heliograph\rintimating on that date asimilar state of weather on shore.\r \r \r \r \r                             _MARCH 1904._\r \r \rOf the mighty steeds ofillustrious riders, from the Bucephalus of\rAlexander down to thefamous chargers of our present-day Generals, much\rhas been written and evensung. Favourites of fortune, their lives\rwere mostly cast inpleasant places; and after a brilliant career,\rmore or less useful,permitted to end their days in secluded luxury--a\rprivilege, by the way, notalways extended to their riders. The subject\rof these remarks is in noway connected with the glorious achievement\rof arms, nor is itrecorded that he ever scented the battle even from\rafar; yet, thoughcompelled to wear, so to speak, the hodden grey of\requine society, his claimto distinction may none the less be justified.\r \rIn July 1810, a somewhatqueer procession might have been seen\rwending its way throughEdinburgh towards the Port of Leith. Upon a\rcart, drawn by a powerfulhorse, decorated with bows and streamers\rof various colours, anddriven by James Craw, the famous Bell Rock\rcarter, similarlybedecked, lay the last principal stone of the Bell\rRock Lighthouse. From thecentre of the stone rose a flagstaff,\rcarrying the nationalflag, while seamen and stonecutters--a strange\rcombination--gailybedecked with variegated ribbons--the latter donning\rbrand new aprons for theoccasion--marched in joyful procession. When\rabreast of the TrinityHouse of Leith, they were joined by the Officer\rof that Corporation,resplendent in full uniform, and bearing his staff\rof office; and on arrivingat the harbour, where the _Smeaton_--engaged\rin transporting materialto the Bell Rock--lay, the entire shipping\rhoisted their colours insalute, thus indicating the amount of public\rinterest evinced in theprogress of the Lighthouse.\r \rAn item of interest, atthis time, was a visit by Mrs Dickson, a\rdaughter of Smeaton ofEddystone fame--whose principles were largely\rtaken advantage of in theconstruction of the Bell Rock Lighthouse--to\rinspect the vessel, namedin honour of her distinguished father. “In\rstepping on board,” writesMr Stevenson in his ‘Bell Rock Lighthouse,’\r“Mrs Dickson seemed quiteovercome by so many concurrent circumstances\rtending in a peculiarmanner to revive and enliven the memory of\rher departed father; and,on leaving the vessel, she would not be\rrestrained from presentingthe crew with a piece of money.”\r \rThough the site of theworkyard in connection with the building\rwas situated in Arbroath,from its contiguity to the Rock, it was\rfound necessary, owing tothe liability of the stones procured from\rMylnefield Quarry, nearDundee, to injury from frost--from which cause\rmany valuable stones hadalready been lost--to procure stones for\rthe cornice of thebuilding and parapet wall of the lightroom which\rwould admit of beingwrought with safety during the winter months. The\rdesired qualities ofdurability and immunity from injury by frost were\rultimately found in thefamous Liver-rock of the Craigleith Quarry. At\rGreenside, Edinburgh, avacant piece of ground was procured; and here\rthe cornice and parapetwall were hewn and built in position for the\rfitting of the hugecast-iron lantern.\r \rThe horse in question had,with his driver, been employed in the\rworkyard at Arbroath, andwas computed to have drawn the materials\rof the lighthouse,extending to upwards of two thousand tons in its\rfinished state, three orfour times--in removing the blocks of stone\rfrom the ship to theworkyard, again to the platform upon which each\rcourse was temporarilybuilt, from the workyard to where they were\rshipped for the Rock,besides occasional movements to and from the\rhands of the stonecutters.Deciding that “Bassey” and his driver\rshould have the honour ofparticipating in the closing scene of the\rundertaking, they wereaccordingly transported by sea to Leith.\r \rIn the course of theirpassage in the _Smeaton_, the vessel narrowly\rescaped shipwreck. Underorders to call at the Rock for lumber, they\rhad apparently lost theirbearings through fog; for, suddenly startled\rby the sound of thesmith’s hammer and anvil, they had just time to put\rthe ship about and escaperunning full tilt on the north-west portion\rof the Rock, which, fromthis incident, still bears the name of “James\rCraw’s Horse.”\r \rOn the completion ofoperations at the Rock, the horse “Bassey,”\rfailing somewhat from age,was pensioned off by the Commissioners,\rand allowed to roam atliberty on the island of Inchkeith till\rhis death in 1813. “Thefame of this animal’s labours,” writes Mr\rStevenson, “together withhis strength and excellent proportions as a\rdraught-horse, havingattracted the attention of Dr John Barclay, that\reminent anatomist procuredthe bones and set them up in his museum.\rThis valuable collection,it is understood, is to be bequeathed to the\rCollege of Surgeons ofEdinburgh; so that the bones of the Bell Rock\rhorse” (to use thedoctor’s own language) “will be seen and admired\ras a useful skeleton and asource of instruction when those of his\remployers lie mingled withthe dust.”\r \r       *      *       *       *      *\r \rWith the exception of afew days, the weather this month has been\rextremely favourable;indeed, for the greater part, summer-like--a\rpleasant change from whatwe have experienced of late. The peculiar\rwhite rubber-like folds ofribbon which have been adhering to the Rock\rsurface for the past twomonths, and which we erroneously supposed to\rbe the ova of some fish,turn out to be the spawn of the slugs I have\ralready described, andwith which the Rock has been freely invested of\rlate--proof of whichseveral have been seen in the act of extrusion.\rThese shell-less molluscshave been much in evidence this season; and\rrepresentatives of threedistinct families are to be met with, namely,\rthe Onchidoridæ,Tritoniidæ, and Eolididæ. Cannibals, they attack\rtheir own species withoutcompunction, and devour each other’s spawn.\rDarwin computed that some“ribbons” contained as many as six hundred\rthousand eggs. The acornbarnacles which have escaped the voracity of\rthe white whelks have insome places attained a height of two inches.\rOn examination, eachshelly casement is seen charged with spawn, which,\rlater on, will beliberated as free swimmers, totally unlike the parent\rform, to enjoy a briefperiod of unrestricted freedom before settling\rdown on the Rock surface,or, for that matter, any immersed object that\rcomes handy, andultimately assuming the adult form. The young swimmer,\rfeeling itself graduallybecoming invested with a shelly covering,\rcasts about for a suitablesite to pass the remainder of its existence.\rSelecting the Rocksurface, it attaches itself by its head, the antennæ\rbecome cemented to thesurface, the eyes remain in a rudimentary\rform, the shelly plateswhich latterly form the door of its domicile\rappear, a few more pairsof legs are developed, and by a series of\rfrequent moultings (likeother crustaceans) arrives at the perfect\rstate. The bunches of“fingers” which we see this animal protrude and\rwithdraw when under waterare in reality its feet, of which there are\rtwelve pairs, the rhythmicexpansion and contraction of which induce\ra current in the waterattracting to its mouth the minute objects\rupon which it feeds, thusgiving rise to the saying that this animal\rstands on its head andliterally kicks its food into its mouth. In all\rother crustacea the sexesare distinct, the barnacles alone having the\rpeculiarity of beingbi-sexual, or having both sexes united in the same\rindividual. The generaltendency throughout nature--the evolution from\ra lower to a higher order,from the simple to the complex--appears in\rthe case of the barnacleto be reversed. Gifted in the initial stage\rof its existence with allthe functions of a free-swimming animal, and\rpossessing organs whichultimately become rudimentary, the final phase\rin which all power ofvolition is lost, certainly does not appear one\rof progression.\r \rHermit crabs are atpresent abundant, and also demonstrate their\rwonderful fecundity.Starfishes--principally the five-rayed\rvariety--are now numerous,and garnish each shallow pool. Sea-urchins,\rthough never plentifulhere, are occasionally met with, some having\rbeen found recently nolarger than a pea. On the 20th the advent of\rthe paidle-fish wasannounced by a small patch of ova underneath a\rprojecting ledge of rock,and, on the same date, by a reconnoitring\r“cock.” The young of lastsummer are met with adhering to stones in\rthe shallow pools; and,contrary to our expectations, though only two\rinches long, were found tocontain spawn. The spring migratory movement\rhas sent but few birds ourway this year. A few thrushes, blackbirds,\rlarks, starlings, and acouple of pied wagtails composed our list. By\rthe middle of the month,the longtailed ducks had gone north to nest,\rand but four pairs ofeiders now remain.\r \r \r \r \r                             _APRIL 1904._\r \r \rA perusal of Stevenson’s“Bell Rock Lighthouse” reveals many\rinteresting episodes ofthat period in connection with the undertaking.\rThe following facts arefrom this source, and may be of sufficient\rgeneral interest towarrant repeating. The facts mentioned have\rreference to anotherprovidential escape from serious disaster recorded\rduring the earlier stagesof the operations. The workmen at this period\rhad their quarters onboard the lightship, anchored a mile from the\rRock, as the beacon-house,on which they were latterly housed on the\rRock, had not yet beenerected. As was customary, whenever the tide\radmitted of a footing onthe Rock, all hands were landed, and the\rboats retained in one ofthe creeks till the rising tide suspended\roperations. On thisparticular occasion, besides the usual two boats\rfrom the lightship, theywere reinforced by an additional boat from the\r_Smeaton_, which hadarrived from Arbroath with a fresh consignment of\rworkmen. The windfreshening in the course of the work, the seamen of\rthe _Smeaton_, fearing fortheir vessel’s moorings, left the Rock in\rtheir own boat with theintention of taking some extra precautions,\rand returning. Scarcelyhad they boarded her, however, when, to Mr\rStevenson’s consternation,she was seen to break adrift and drive\rhelplessly away before thewind. The danger of the situation at once\rflashed through his mind.Thirty-two men--three boat-loads--on a rock\rwhich would shortly befathoms under water, with only two boats at\rtheir disposal! What wasto be done? The workmen, engrossed in their\rlabours, had failed tonotice the departure of the boat, and were as\ryet ignorant of theirdangerous position. The _Smeaton_, now far to\rleeward, was seen to havemade sail, and making every effort to beat\rup to the Rock, but withthe wind still freshening and the flood tide\rdead against her, it wasutterly hopeless to expect any assistance\rin that direction. Savethe deserted lightship no other sail was in\rsight. Taking thelanding-master cautiously aside, to avoid alarming\rthe men, he explainedtheir dangerous situation. After consultation, it\rwas decided thateverything of weight should be abandoned, the men to\rstrip their upperclothing, the two boats to be manned to their utmost\rcapacity, and theremainder of the men to support themselves in the\rwater by clinging to thegunwales. By this means they hoped to drift\rdown on the _Smeaton_, aperilous journey under such circumstances,\reven in quiet weather, butin the now disturbed state of the sea, a\rforlorn hope. The workingsbeing now awash with the flowing tide--the\rusual signal for ceasingwork--the workmen were in the act of retiring\rto the boats to don theirshoes and stockings when they noticed the\rabsence of the boat, andrealised their danger. On attempting to\raddress them with hisproposal, Mr Stevenson found his mouth so parched\rthat he was totally unableto articulate a single word. Stooping to\rmoisten his lips with seawater, he was suddenly startled by the\rgladsome shout of “A boat!A boat!” and looking around, there, sure\renough, a large boat wasseen through the haze making straight for the\rRock. This opportunearrival proved to be James Spink, the Bell Rock\rpilot, employed incarrying letters between Arbroath and the Rock. For\rhis services on thisoccasion it is gratifying to learn that in after\ryears Spink was in receiptof a pension from the Board, and permitted\rto wear the uniform andbadge of the Lighthouse Service.\r \rPaidle-fish are now fairlynumerous, their nests, with attendant\rcocks, being met with onevery hand. While observing one of these\rnests the other day, atlow water, I had an interesting experience of\rthe necessity for thesurveillance exercised by the cock. Stretched\ralong the rock, my faceclose to the surface of the pool, I had\ran excellent view of thenest and its guardian, two feet below.\rSpeculating as to thereason for so close attendance on the ova--his\rnose being thrust into anorifice in the mass, his mouth opening and\rshutting energetically,evidently forcing a stream of water through\rthe opening--I carelesslydropped a few whelks on his back. This mild\rform of bombardment didnot in the slightest disconcert him; for,\rthough they struck androlled off on either side, he appeared to\rtake no notice of them.Suddenly, a white whelk (not one of those I\rhad dropped) made itsappearance on the outer margin of the ova, and\rsettled down with theapparent intention of dining. This impertinence,\rhowever, was not to betolerated; for, with a swirling rush that\rplainly betokened anger,the red-coated sentry seized the offender\rin his teeth--and herefollows the surprising part of it. Instead of\rdropping the whelk to thebottom there and then, as I expected, he\rmounted rapidly throughthe intervening two feet of water, and when\rnear the surface, to myastonishment, spat the whelk almost into my\rface! That his intentionwas retaliatory I do not presume to say, but\rthe action certainlyappeared an intelligent attempt to “return fire.”\rSince then, I haverepeatedly seen them remove predatory starfishes and\rwhelks in a somewhatsimilar manner.\r \rThe wheat-like ova of thewhite whelks is also largely in evidence this\rmonth, though somewhatlater than last year. Exposed at every fall of\rthe tide, it appears torequire no attention, each capsule, pendant or\rupright, firmly adheringto the Rock surface by means of its flattened\rfoot-stalk. The whelksthemselves appear in every conceivable corner\rwhere food is to be found.\r \rA shallow pit cut into theRock, measuring two feet by one, and\rone foot deep--originallythe socket of the central support of the\rbeacon-house in which theworkmen were lodged during the construction\rof the lighthouse--servesas a receptacle for anything of interest we\rmay pick up during ourrambles round the rocks. Fitted with a grated\riron cover, it was at onetime used for the purpose of soaking salt\rjunk; but, as every marineorganism appeared to consider this a\rspecial provision fortheir needs, it was ultimately abandoned. At\rpresent arepulsive-looking “poach” or “cobbler,” some ten inches long,\rshares this prison with acouple of large star-fishes, an unusually\rlarge hermit crab, and aderelict mass of “paidle” spawn. The spawn\rdaily decreases in inverseratio to the “poach’s” liveliness. Apart\rfrom this, however, thespawn shows signs of deterioration, a proof\rthat the attention of thecock is necessary for its well-being.\r \rOn the 17th, the remainingfour pairs of eiders took their departure,\rand only a few gulls nowremain.\r \rOwing to my transferenceto another station, it now becomes necessary\rfor me to conclude theserandom jottings. To the patient reader who has\rcared to follow me throughthese notes I bid farewell. Written without\rany pretensions toliterary skill or scientific accuracy, they have\rnevertheless, in my case,served to enliven many a weary hour in an\risolated calling, andhave--may I hope?--proved not altogether void of\rinterest to the reader.\r \r \r \r \r                                THE END.\r \r \r \r \r            _Edinburgh: George Waterston &Sons, Printers._\r \r \r \r \rTranscriber’s Note:\r \rWords may have multiplespelling variations or inconsistent hyphenation\rin the text.
